# PROJECT

--- SENTENCE 24 ---
The American Samoa Coral Reef Inventory (ASCRI) is a comprehensive survey of coastal and nearshore marine resources intended to assist the American Samoa Government (ASG) and Federal agencies in the management and prudent use of these resources.

--- SENTENCE 25 ---
This project is intended to supplement the territory's Coastal Zone Management Study (CZM), particularly with respect to proposed guidelines for coastal ecosystems management and identification of areas where proposed activities would have a high potential for damaging coastal ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 26 ---
Further, the ASCRI documents should prove a valuable support for technical studies necessary for the development of baseline inventories of ecosystems supporting rare and endangered species,.

--- SENTENCE 27 ---
development and management of coastal zone resources, and establishment of marine areas worthy of preservation.

--- SENTENCE 28 ---
Planning and resource management agencies will benefit from the study results and compilations during evaluation of impacts from shoreside development.

--- SENTENCE 29 ---
Finally, the documents should prove useful to anyone interested in seeking literature citations and/or conducting field studies specific areas of the American Samoa coastal zone.

--- SENTENCE 30 ---
Basic emphasis of the project is on the coral reefs surrounding the islands of American Samoa, but considerable information on shoreline and coastal areas, as well as deeper waters seaward of threefs, is included.

--- SENTENCE 31 ---
Coral reefs constitute one of American Samoa most valuable resources and are subjected to a wide variety of uses and functions, some of which may be conflicting.

--- SENTENCE 32 ---
The ASCRI project is a first comprehensive attempt at both defining the extent of recorded knowledge about the coral reef resources of American Samoa and organizing the information into a handy reference document.

--- SENTENCE 33 ---
Specific objectives of the ASCRI project include: (1) an inventory and (2) mapping of nearshore areas around American Samoa; (3) a compilation of past and present scientific information of use to resource planners and managers; (4) a description of important, dominant, and unique characteristics of the areas; and (5) recommendations for further studies in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 34 ---
These objectives are met in the two ASCRI documents: Part A -- a narrative encompassing purpose, objectives, methods, results, discussions, conclusions, and recommendations; and Part B -- an atlas of maps (scale 1:6200) encompassing most of the coastlines of the islands of Tutuila, Anu'u, Ta'u, Ofu, and Olosega.

# FIELD SURVEY

--- SENTENCE 37 ---
The American Samoa Coral Reef Inventory (ASCRI) encompasses a review and synthesis of previous surveys in marine areas of the Samoan Islands and presents the results of supplemental surveys of many reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 38 ---
These supplemental surveys were undertaken by a team of specialists in coral reef ecology.

--- SENTENCE 39 ---
The basic tasks of the field team were to obtain a general appraisal of reef areas and their biotic communities and to provide ground-truth feedback information for the mapping program.

--- SENTENCE 40 ---
Time constraints limited this portion of the ASCRI project to 20 field days; thus only selected priority sites of either special use, interest, or representativeness could be covered.

--- SENTENCE 41 ---
The number of days spent by the ASCRI team for specific coastal segments is shown in Figure 2.

--- SENTENCE 42 ---
Co-ordination of the field team efforts with the goals of the overall program was mediated through working maps drawn on the same scale, and resembling generally the atlas maps.

--- SENTENCE 43 ---
A set of aerial photographs was provided as well.

--- SENTENCE 44 ---
Instructions to the field team were provided with a set of the working maps and data-recording sheets printed on water-proof paper.

--- SENTENCE 45 ---
After each day's survey, team members transcribed their field notes into presentable data summaries.

--- SENTENCE 46 ---
With respect to biotic components, the field team made general observations of fishes, corals, algae, and conspicuous macroinverte-brates.

--- SENTENCE 47 ---
Information on species observed was recorded semi-quantitatively using a rating scale of 1 to 4, where:

- 1 = dominant species; abundant.
- 2 = common, but not dominant.
- 3 = occasional (several sightings in the area).
- 4 = rare (one or at most a few sightings in the area).

--- SENTENCE 48 ---
Fringing reefs occur along much of the southern coast of Tutuila and in embayments on the northern coast, around portions of Aunu'u, and around much of the coasts of the islands of the Manu'a Reef flat zonation, while somewhat variable from site to site, does show five basic biotope's from shore.

--- SENTENCE 49 ---
These are the shoreline, inner reef flat, middle reef flat, outer reef flat, and reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 50 ---
Wherever possible, the field team attempted to characterize each of these reef zones in the survey of each area.

--- SENTENCE 51 ---
Fish counts were generally made just before and ahead of the examination of other reef components.

--- SENTENCE 52 ---
Upon reaching the seaward part of the tract, the team would proceed laterally and then return to shore making notation of changes or similarities over a second part of the reef Much of the north shore of Tutuila was surveyed by boat (~7 inflatable Avon raft with an outboard engine) in the absence 🔳 access to the shore by road.

--- SENTENCE 53 ---
A survey of Nafanua Bank and the perimeter of Aunu'u Island also was made using the Avon boat.

--- SENTENCE 54 ---
Coastal areas were further documented by photographs of shorelines

!

--- SENTENCE 55 ---
NUMBER OF DAYS SPENT ALONG COASTAL SEGMENTS OF AMERICAN SAMOA BY THE FIELD SURVEY TEAM.

--- SENTENCE 56 ---
and associated exposed reef areas, and compliment interpretation of aerial photographs.

--- SENTENCE 57 ---
Estimates of percent cover of live coral and algae were made at most sites.

--- SENTENCE 58 ---
The field team also noted utilization of the reef areas during the survey period and what elements were being utilized.

--- SENTENCE 59 ---
Information on observed shoreline and offshore uses (actual or potential), water conditions, depth, bottom type, and other factors deemed relevant to the project was noted.

--- SENTENCE 60 ---
In order to maximize information about Samoan reef fish assemblages in the limited time alloted for the ASCRI surveys three methods of observing and enumerating fish populations were utilized.

--- SENTENCE 61 ---
Around the islands of Ta'u, Ofu, and Olosega data were collected by visually censusing the fishes associated with particular study sites.

--- SENTENCE 62 ---
A 330-foot (100 m) length of line was laid on the bottom and all fishes within 3 feet (1 m) on either side of the line and 6 feet (2 m) above it were identified, counted, and their size estimated.

--- SENTENCE 63 ---
Around Tutuila and Aunu'u Islands a modified Jones and Thompson species enumeration over time method was employed.

--- SENTENCE 64 ---
(1978)technique entails the acquisition of a cumulative list of species over short intervals of time.

--- SENTENCE 65 ---
In one version of the method, the diver records the names of all fishes observed in the first five minute interval of an essentially free-ranging survey.

--- SENTENCE 66 ---
During the next five minute interval he records additional species not previously observed . . .

--- SENTENCE 67 ---
and so on for a total of 30 minutes (6 survey The method assumes that the most abundant species will be encountered in the earlier survey intervals.

--- SENTENCE 68 ---
A third method wa used in some areas, particularly where fish surveys had been conducted by earlier workers or where observation time was limited.

--- SENTENCE 69 ---
The relative abundance of fish species was subjectively rated on the 1 to 4 scale described above.

--- SENTENCE 70 ---
Surveys conducted by Dr. Wass in the Manu'a Islands were of a similar type, although a three point scale was used (to quote from a letter by Dr. Wass to the ASCRI project):

A "+" indicates the species was dominant (taking both individual numbers and biomass into consideration); a "-" indicates the species occurred occasionally to abundantly and made up a significant proportion of the fish biomass in the area; and a "-" indicates that one to few individuals were observed (though in the case of some carangids, scarids and labrids a single individual can account for a significant proportion of the biomass in the area).

--- SENTENCE 71 ---
# PRODUCTION OF THE ATLAS

--- SENTENCE 72 ---
The purpose of the Atlas portion of ASCRI is to provide reference maps of the coastline and offshore areas on a sufficiently detailed scale to be of use to both planners and managers of coastal zone resources as well as field parties contributing to a continued inventory of these resources.

--- SENTENCE 73 ---
The maps include major classes of shorelines, offshore features (such as ava), boundaries of major bottom types, locations of surveys conducted in the marine environment, and symbolic representations of common uses where these uses occur.

--- SENTENCE 74 ---
The sectional map sheets are drawn at a scale of 1:7200 (one inch equals 600 feet).

--- SENTENCE 75 ---
This scale permits sufficient detail to be portrayed without requiring an unwieldy number of maps.

--- SENTENCE 76 ---
A total of 30 maps encompasses nearly the entire coastline of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 77 ---
An additional map covers Aunu'u, and 10 maps portray portions of the coastal areas of Ofu, Olosega, and Ta'u (The Manu'a group).

--- SENTENCE 78 ---
The maps are based on interpretation of selected contact prints of aerial photographs taken in 1971 by Aero Services Corporation (of California) under contract to the Government of American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 79 ---
Ninty-four photographs at scales of either 1 inch = 642 feet (1:7700) or 1 inch = 1200 feet (1:14400) were provided by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.

--- SENTENCE 80 ---
# Terrestrial Areas / Shoreline

Inclusion of a significant proportion of the land is deemed desirable from the standpoints of shoreline use considerations and as an aid to accurate orientation.

--- SENTENCE 81 ---
The included land area represents a tradeoff between satisfying these goals and extending far enough offshore to encompass the fringing reef margin or water depths of 130 feet (40 m) off coasts lacking shallow reefs.

--- SENTENCE 82 ---
In most cases, map sheets are oriented with the long axis running more or less parallel with the coast (see Figure 3).

--- SENTENCE 83 ---
Details of terrestrial features were provided by a 50% reduction of topographic maps drawn at a scale of 1 inch = 200 feet (1:2400) by Aero Services Corporation.

--- SENTENCE 84 ---
These reductions also served to establish control on the Atlas maps.

--- SENTENCE 85 ---
The topographic maps were produced by Aero Services Corp. using stereographic methods from photographs dated May-July 1971.

--- SENTENCE 86 ---
Certain features of the land were added or redrawn on the ASCRI maps based on interpretation of the aerial photographs, although in general, roads, elevations, and shoreline features are presented without modification from the reduced topographic sheets.

--- SENTENCE 87 ---
The major interpretive feature of the land appearing on the maps is in the zone between the shoreline and the vegetation line (or road).

--- SENTENCE 88 ---
This zone is stippled to illustrate one of three types of coastlines: beach, low rocky coast, or high rocky coast.

--- SENTENCE 89 ---
The shoreline (essentially the water line at the scale of the atlas

--- SENTENCE 92 ---
#### Offshore Features

A dashed line is used to designate the boundary between conspicuous bottom types seaward from the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 93 ---
The basis for differentiating various bottom types is discussed below.

--- SENTENCE 94 ---
No reasonable number of aerial photographs can reveal complete boundaries for all offshore areas out to a depth of 130 feet (40 m).

--- SENTENCE 95 ---
Even with excellent color photographs, bottom types at depths of 30 feet or greater are in most cases difficult to interpret and boundaries uncertain.

--- SENTENCE 96 ---
Only large sand bodies can be seen with ease (see Campbell, et al., 1970).

--- SENTENCE 97 ---
At lesser depths, some boundaries are obscured by breaking waves, clouds or cloud shadows, complex gradations between more or less distinct bottom types, turbid water, or lack of penetration due to sun angle.

--- SENTENCE 98 ---
Further, the complex mosaic of bottom materials which are particularly characteristic of reefand coral bottom areas are not amenable to mapping as individual substratum types on a scale of 1:7200.

--- SENTENCE 99 ---
A particular problem is the designation of the seaward boundary of a sloping reef face, as the bottom type (limestone - rcl) extends to depths below the limits of visibility in the photographs.

--- SENTENCE 100 ---
Thus any attempt to draw a seaward limit produces a line of no consistent meaning because the maximum depth of image reflection varies depending upon a number of factors from photograph to photograph and even from one part of a photograph to another part.

--- SENTENCE 101 ---
Another feature apparent in aerial photographs of offshore areas is of interpretive value: the line of wave break.

--- SENTENCE 102 ---
Although it is realized that this line can vary position depending upon the tide, sea state, wind, and bottom topography, the general vicinity of the wave break appearing in the base aerial photographs imparts some useful information about bottom topography and the location of the reef margin (if present).

--- SENTENCE 103 ---
Because breaking waves sometimes render the water surface too reflective for bottom details (such as the reef margin) to show in photographs, breaking waves constitute the only useful information available concerning some specific locations.

--- SENTENCE 104 ---
The wave break is indicated on the atlas maps by dotted, arcuate lines (convex in the direction of wave propagation) wherever the waves break along a reasonably well-defined line.

--- SENTENCE 105 ---
Every attempt has been made to complete boundaries between bottom types within the scope of each map.

--- SENTENCE 106 ---
However, an incomplete image, or coverage, or a feature extending into deeper water as a fading and then disappearing image, frequently can only be represented as a dashed line terminating at some point short of the map margin.

--- SENTENCE 107 ---
The atlas user must appreciate that the outlines represent interpretations from a limited set of photographs and, in many cases because of depth or poor water clarity, even major bottom features will be only partially represented.

--- SENTENCE 108 ---
Unlike terrestrial features, underwater terrain will always be incompletely represented.

--- SENTENCE 109 ---
Substratum (bottom) types are indicated by codes such as "rcl", or "sc".

--- SENTENCE 110 ---
These codes represent standard bottom types through the Atlas and definitions are given in Table

--- SENTENCE 111 ---
I (as well as the Atlas).

--- SENTENCE 112 ---
Note that this system is not related to the habitat classification given on pages 20-23.

--- SENTENCE 113 ---
The bottom type could be converted to habitat codes, although each system designed for a different use.

--- SENTENCE 114 ---
The bottom type (map) codes simplified in order to express categories readily diffentiated the available aerial photographs.

--- SENTENCE 115 ---
The habitat codes are design primarily for use in the field.

--- SENTENCE 116 ---
TABLE I - SUBSTRATUM CODES USED IN PART B (ASCRI ATLAS)

#### MARINE BOTTOM TYPES

# HARD (VOLCANIC)

--- SENTENCE 117 ---
BOTTOM TYPES

- rb Massive rock bottom (possibly veneered by limestone)
- rbb Close-set talus (boulders of massive size) often directly off a high rocky coast.
- rbc Cobbles and small boulders, usually off a revetment or stream mouth.
- rbs Massive rock bottom (possibly veneered by limestone) with sand pockets, the latter less than 50% of the area.

--- SENTENCE 118 ---
- rs Large sand pockets and/or sand veneer over hard bottom; sand areas more than 50% of total area.

#### REEF COMPLEX BOTTOM TYPES

- co Areas of live coral exceeding 50% bottom cover.
- rc Predominantly limestone fragments of mixed sizes (gravel, rubble, boulder) with minor amounts of sand.
- rcl Consolidated limestone platform (possibly with minor amounts of mixed fragments).
- rcs Predominantly sand or loose limestone fragments (rubble, boulder, small outcrop) with major amounts of sand.

--- SENTENCE 119 ---
#### SOFT BOTTOM TYPES

- sc Large sand deposits and channels at depths less than 30 feet (10 m).
- sd Large sand deposits and channels at depths of 30 feet (10 m) or greater.

# ORGANIZATION OF THE TEXT

Part A of the American Samoa Coral Reef Inventory is, an extensive description of the coast, shoreline, and basically, offshore areas of the Islands of American Samoa, with emphasis on the resources represented by coral reefs and reef habitats.

--- SENTENCE 121 ---
The primary purpose is to provide an inventory, in a standard and easily read format, of these resources and the varied aspects of Samoan life, coastal topography, water quality, and the like which have a bearing on present-day as well as future utilization of these re-Ideally, an inventory of reef areas should somehow encompass all that is present; realistically, an inventory of this kind, at best, can list only all that is known.

--- SENTENCE 122 ---
To this end, three sources of information are reported: 1) printed material from studies and surveys conducted in American Samoa, 2) recent surveys by the ASCRI field team, and 3) results of a village by village reef utilization survey conducted by the Development Planning Office of the American Samoa Government.

--- SENTENCE 123 ---
The text description proceeds around each of the islands of Tutuila, Aunu'u, Ofu, Olosega, and Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 124 ---
The text is divided into major sections arranged in the following order:

- 1.

--- SENTENCE 125 ---
Pago Pago Harbor (Tutuila)
- 2.

--- SENTENCE 126 ---
Southeast Coast (Tutuila)
- 3. Northeast Coast (Tutuila)
- 4. Northwest Coast (Tutuila)
- 5.

--- SENTENCE 127 ---
Southwest Coast (Tutuila)
- 6. South/Central Coast (Tutuila)
- 7. Taema and Nafanua Banks
- 8.

--- SENTENCE 128 ---
Ta'u

Each of these major sections begins with a general discussion which usually includes a brief description of the coast and basic infrastructure (as related to coastal zone access).

--- SENTENCE 129 ---
Although the text and headings refer to map numbers of the ASCRI Atlas (always as "MAP"), the material in the text is organized instead in a sequence of coastal segments beginning in MAP I covering inner Pago Pago Harbor and running counter clockwise around the coastline of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 130 ---
The Taema Bank, Nafanua Bank, Aunu'u Island, Ofu Island, Olosega Island, and Ta'u Island are each treated in a similar manner.

--- SENTENCE 131 ---
Generally, a coastal segment encompasses a village (or part of a village).

--- SENTENCE 132 ---
Most extend from one prominent point of land to another.

--- SENTENCE 133 ---
The length of coast in a coastal segment is small where much site-specific information is available or villages occur close together, and great where little information is available and/or villages are few.

--- SENTENCE 134 ---
All of Aunu'u Island is treated as a single coastal segment.

--- SENTENCE 135 ---
Within each coastal segment, information is presented under the topic headings of Physiography (geography and geology), Flora and Fauna (results of biological surveys), Water Conditions (water quality and oceanographic considerations), Historical/Archaeological Sites, and Use Considerations.

--- SENTENCE 136 ---
The text of Part A is purposely brief on individual subjects to allow a maximum range of information to be presented - users interested in greater detail on any particular point are encouraged to seek original sources (see References Cited).

--- SENTENCE 137 ---
Reference sources are credited throughout the text by numbers appearing in parentheses and listed in the References Cited at the end of Part A. One of the tasks of the ASCRI Project was to compile a listing of studies conducted in marine and coastal areas around American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 138 ---
Some of this source material consists of unpublished material and so-called "grey" literature - reports printed and distributed in limited numbers.

--- SENTENCE 139 ---
On the other hand, certain valuable literature of a general nature (that is, published studies which do not contain site-specific information) may not be cited in Part A.

Each coastal segment description has been written using a standard format which dictates generally where in the text specific facts and kinds of information appear.

--- SENTENCE 140 ---
It should be appreciated, however, that the descriptions are intended to be site specific and therefore gaps in the generally available knowledge about locations along and off the coastlines of each island may appear as obvious omissions.

--- SENTENCE 141 ---
No concerted effort has been made in the descriptions to extend knowledge about one area to general statements about some larger section of the coast.

--- SENTENCE 142 ---
The descriptive text is presented as a page of text accompanied on the facing page by a running index.

--- SENTENCE 143 ---
The format and rationale of this system are described below.

--- SENTENCE 144 ---
Note the change in style of type and page numbering from page 45 on.

--- SENTENCE 145 ---
# Page Headings

Both the left-hand and right-hand pages of the text have headings which serve as a quick index based on the geographical location of the information contained on each page.

--- SENTENCE 146 ---
On the left-hand page, the heading gives the island (e.g., TUTUILA), the district (e.g., EASTERN DISTRICT), and the county (e.g., MAUPUTASI CO.).

--- SENTENCE 147 ---
The heading on the right-hand page gives the appropriate geographical area of the coast and either a MAP NUMBER or a GENERAL designation.

--- SENTENCE 148 ---
Under GENERAL headings will appear information of a general nature pertaining to all of the indicated geographical area.

--- SENTENCE 149 ---
The MAP NUMBER designation refers to a specific map in the Atlas (ASCRI - Part B).

--- SENTENCE 150 ---
Right-hand Page (Text)

Information is arranged in the text by geographical location.

--- SENTENCE 151 ---
Thus, the results of a study on corals based on five separate survey

sites would be summarized in five different places in the text.

--- SENTENCE 152 ---
The geographical basis for this arrangement of information is the coastal segment.

--- SENTENCE 153 ---
Each coastal segment is given as a centered heading on the right-hand page directly below a solid line appearing on both the left- and right-hand pages.

--- SENTENCE 154 ---
Subheadings on each text page refer to specific locales and coastal features (villages, shorelines, offohore islets, beaches, reef flats, etc.) addressed by the paragraph(s) which follow.

--- SENTENCE 155 ---
# Left-hand Page (Index)

The left-hand pages of the report contain a running (illustrated) index matched to the text on the right-hand page.

--- SENTENCE 156 ---
The running index is intended to enable the reader to locate quickly a coastal area or specific coastal zone feature of interest without reading large portions of text.

--- SENTENCE 157 ---
Subheadings on the left-hand page indicate the locale of the text description and usually give the name of the village within the coastal segment.

--- SENTENCE 158 ---
A MAP NUMBER is centered on each page, and refers to maps contained in the ASCRI Atlas.

--- SENTENCE 159 ---
Within each coastal segment, information is presented by topic under one of the following titles: PHYSIOGRAPHY, FLORA AND FAUNA, WATER CONDITIONS, HISTORICAL/ARCHAEOLOGICAL, or USE CONSIDERATIONS.

--- SENTENCE 160 ---
The running index also includes key-words and areas of special concern to the Coastal Zone Program, the latter identified as to the appropriate paragraph in the American Samoa Coastal Zone Management Program document (ASG, Dev.

--- SENTENCE 161 ---
The key-words and areas of special CZM concern are preceded by a "(" and "(\*" respectively.

--- SENTENCE 162 ---
Special areas are those coastal sites and features which have been designated for special management (e.g., registered as National Natural Landmarks), are candidates for National Natural Landmark status, are under consideration as marine preserves or underwater parks, are natural area reserves or wildlife sanctuaries, are

--- SENTENCE 163 ---
areas identified has having high value for recreation (MKGK/ Yamamoto, Inc, 1980) or scenic interest, or constitute environments of exceptional marine productivity or diversity.

--- SENTENCE 164 ---
Two sites (Pago Pago Harbor and Pala Lagoon) are designated by the American Samoa CZM program as "Special Areas"; all other sites so indicated in the index are considered to have potential only.

--- SENTENCE 165 ---
A symbol (coral, fish, or starfish) is placed opposite the portion of the text which describes a biological resource representing reef life of exceptional quality or interest.

--- SENTENCE 166 ---
In general, locations identified by either a coral or fish symbol are distinguished by high species abundance and/or diversity.

--- SENTENCE 167 ---
On most pages a topographic map excerpt is included to assist in locating prominent features and establish a geographic relationship to the text.

--- SENTENCE 168 ---
These maps are from the U.S. Geological Survey topographic series of 1963, printed at a scale of 1:24000 (1 inch = 2000 feet).

--- SENTENCE 169 ---
The maps are oriented with north toward the top of the page.

--- SENTENCE 170 ---
These maps are not considered figures and are not numbered.

# GENERAL DISCUSSION

--- SENTENCE 217 ---
In a broad sense the coastal zone is that part of the land influencing and influenced by the sea, and that part of the sea influencing and influenced by the land.

--- SENTENCE 218 ---
For practical purposes, in the Samoan Islands the coastal zone encompasses most or all of the land and the shallow reef areas, offshore banks, and marine areas to a considerable depth off the several islands of the group.

--- SENTENCE 219 ---
This definition is not a legal one, but generally describes the extent of the area of concern in coastal zone management.

--- SENTENCE 220 ---
The islands are the peaks of great, yet mostly submerged, volcanoes, and an event or phenomenon of any magnitude on the land or the sea will not likely terminate in its effects at the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 221 ---
The General Discussion section presents background information arranged under each of the topic categories indexed in the text.

#### **PHYSIOGRAPHY**

The following discussion and classification scheme is taken from the Hawaii Coral Reef Inventory (AECOS, 1979).

--- SENTENCE 222 ---
The discussion has been modified and extended to serve the situation of Samoan reef physiography.

--- SENTENCE 223 ---
The classification scheme, on the other hand, was originally developed for central Pacific reefs and requires no modification.

--- SENTENCE 224 ---
Included under the category PHYSIOGRAPHY are descriptions of the physical features of the coast, nearshore, and offshore areas in or off the particular coastal segment.

--- SENTENCE 225 ---
Generally, descriptions are sub-divided into shoreline and fringing reef descriptions, with additional subdivisions possible (for example: reef flat and reef front).

--- SENTENCE 226 ---
Most descriptions in the Physiography category are followed (within the coastal segment) by a matching biological description under the Flora and Fauna category.

--- SENTENCE 227 ---
Along the interface between sea and land, coastal processes have added to (prograded) and carved away (aggraded) the volcanic masses of the Samoan Islands to create a wide variety of features which today comprise the varied shoreline and nearshore environments of the Islands.

--- SENTENCE 228 ---
Volcanism, the production (or more precisely, the movement to the earth's surface) of magmatic materials continues to play a role in the coastal geology of the islands.

--- SENTENCE 229 ---
Eruptions have occurred in historic times on Savai'i and Upolu (Western Samoa)

--- SENTENCE 230 ---
(Krear and Wood, 1959); and an undersea eruption that occurred about 1866 between Olosega and Ta'u is described by Friedlander (1910).

--- SENTENCE 231 ---
The material deposited by volcanic activity is eroded and reworked by wind and waves — ultimately, the net result is a down slope or offshore movement and loss of this material from coastal systems.

--- SENTENCE 232 ---
The tropical waters which bathe the Samoan Archipelago support the growth of biogenic reefs - shallow water structures produced by living organisms.

--- SENTENCE 233 ---
The major organisms involved in this growth are corals (Cnidarians) and calcareous (or coralline) algae, whose skeletons of calcium carbonate (limestone) contribute to both the welded framework as well as the loose accumulation of coarse and fine sediments filling voids.

--- SENTENCE 234 ---
Although erosive processes ultimately also move limestone downslope, this loss from the coastal system can be regenerated by continued skeletal growth.

--- SENTENCE 235 ---
Therefore, the net process can be one of equilibrium or even active accumulation and extension of a reef.

--- SENTENCE 236 ---
The process is a slow one, and its fragility becomes apparent with the realization that growth is directly a function of the health of the biological community comprising the relatively thin veneer of a living reef.

--- SENTENCE 237 ---
These processes are illustrated in general terms in Figure 5.

--- SENTENCE 238 ---
The detailed specifics of each of the inputs and losses of material occurring at any given point along the coastline will vary, and the range of variability is expressed in the variety of coastal forms encountered: beaches, dunes, benches, cliffs, reefs, banks, channels, etc.

--- SENTENCE 239 ---
Increasing interest and awareness of the natural environment eventually leads to the development of classification schemes.

--- SENTENCE 240 ---
Classification provides both a means of storing and accessing information, and a logical approach to pattern recognition.

--- SENTENCE 241 ---
The occurrence of patterns, or the repetition in space and/or time of conditions and events, permits application of manmade concepts and plans.

!

--- SENTENCE 242 ---
GENERALIZED GEOLOGICAL PROCESSES DIAGRAM FOR THE SAMOAN COASTAL ZONE.

--- SENTENCE 243 ---
Nearshore marine environments have been classified numerous times, with the usual approach emphasizing easily recognized physical attributes (e.g., degree of exposure to wave energies, substratum types).

--- SENTENCE 244 ---
An ideal approach, certainly from the standpoint of current ecological theory, should emphasize biological community structure and function, but the community concept too often becomes nothing more than a statistical artifact when stringently applied in nature.

--- SENTENCE 245 ---
Further, a community approach to classification requires levels of effort and expertise seldom acheivable except in intensive studies of rather localized areas.

--- SENTENCE 246 ---
Nonetheless, the sub-division of any area into biotopes and facies (for example, see Environmental Consultants, 1977) represents an approach along these lines.

--- SENTENCE 247 ---
Certainly some success has been achieved in classifying littoral (intertidal) assemblages, in part because of their high degree of universiality (that is, comparable organisms are arranged in similar zones around the world), but primarily because of the strong relationship between physical factors and biological distribution which characterizes shoreline environments.

--- SENTENCE 248 ---
A community approach to classification of sublittoral marine environments has met with far less success because community structure is a function of more subtle physical and biological relationships.

--- SENTENCE 249 ---
The most practical approach is to utilize physical attributes, and, conceptually at least, arrive at a community approach as subcategories once the latter become evident through closer scrutiny of physical habitats.

--- SENTENCE 250 ---
Three co-ordinate and interlocking factors are important in the distribution of shore and reef invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 251 ---
These are (a) the degree of wave shock, (b) the type of bottom, and (c) the tidal exposure.

--- SENTENCE 252 ---
These characteristics are recognized as a basis of at least one classification scheme developed for Hawaiian waters (Hawaii Coastal Zone Management Program, 1976) and can be utilized equally effectively in Samoan waters.

--- SENTENCE 253 ---
A provisional classification of coastal water ecosystems developed by Maragos (Maragos, et al., 1975; see also HCZMP, 1975) was intended to point out the variety of marine habitats extant in Hawai'i.

--- SENTENCE 254 ---
Maragos stresses that the narrow tidal range and high wave action characteristic of Hawaiian near-shore environments render classification schemes developed for higher latitude, continental coasts (e.g., the west coast of the U.S.) inappropriate (cf.

--- SENTENCE 255 ---
The strong modifying influence of coral reefs on shoreline environments further reduces the applicability of such schemes.

--- SENTENCE 256 ---
The primary effect of the presence of a reef structure is to nullify, or at least seriously modify, the concepts of open and protected outer coasts as put forth by Ricketts and Calvin (1962).

--- SENTENCE 257 ---
The importance of wave energy regime in the determination of organism distribution remains unchanged.

--- SENTENCE 258 ---
Rather, the presence and form of the reef itself determines the nature of the wave regime at and near the shore, and therefore, reef form must be a primary category in any classification applicable to tropical coastal zones (see Morton and Challis, 1969).

--- SENTENCE 259 ---
The classification scheme presented here attempts to encompass all the reef biotopes extant in the Samoan Islands.

--- SENTENCE 260 ---
The scheme is

hierarchical, beginning with more general levels of categorization (coastal macro scale) and progressing to smaller scale, substratum considerations.

--- SENTENCE 261 ---
The proposed scheme recognizes that the coastal province includes three zones (after Maragos, et al., 1975): (a) an inland zone, (b) a shore zone, and (c) an offshore zone.

--- SENTENCE 262 ---
However, the actual boundaries of these divisions in the tripartite approach used here are defined more broadly and thus allow inclusion of all environments in the broadly defined coastal zone to be encompassed:

- (a) Terrestrial Realm (terrestrial environments; designated by the letter "T");
- (b) Transition Environments (shoreline transitions from terrestrial to aquatic realms; designated by the letter "S");
- (c) Aquatic Realm (marine, brackish, and fresh water environments; designated by the letter "A").

--- SENTENCE 263 ---
Each of these "zones" or realms is treated individually, commensurate with the special needs and problems encountered in these very different environments.

--- SENTENCE 264 ---
Only the marine portion of the Aquatic Realm is treated herein.

--- SENTENCE 265 ---
Readers interested in the classification schemes developed for the shoreline and inland areas may consult the introduction (Part A) to the Hawai'i Coral Reef Inventory (AECOS, 1979).

--- SENTENCE 266 ---
The classification scheme is expressible as an alphanumeric code.

--- SENTENCE 267 ---
Any code is not a necessity of classification, merely a convenience.

--- SENTENCE 268 ---
The alphanumeric is more amenable to tabular presentations and computer handling of data than is a written description.

--- SENTENCE 269 ---
Further, at certain levels of discussion, the alphanumeric is less ambiguous than brief or common-name descriptions, because the boundary conditions are defined.

--- SENTENCE 270 ---
Nonetheless, the real world environment is characterized by not only variety, but gradients and subtle transitions which defy precise ordering into categories obstensibly representing the variety.

--- SENTENCE 271 ---
In the present undertaking, this reality is encountered not only in attempting to classify coastal habitats, but in translating aerial photographs (close approximation of the real world filtered by the limitations of lens resolution and film sensitivity) into maps (ordered representations of real world variety).

--- SENTENCE 272 ---
In both processes (map production and habitat classification), decisions are required which in effect ignore transitions at some acceptable level of resolution.

--- SENTENCE 273 ---
# Reef Habitats Classification System

The classification of aquatic environments is expressed as a 5-digit alphanumeric with the letter "A" as the first digit followed by four numbers representing orders of classification from general exposure to substratum type.

--- SENTENCE 274 ---
Assignment of these orders can be accomplished with the "key" given in Table II.

--- SENTENCE 275 ---
Note that the key is not strictly dichotomous: it represents a "web" which leads the user

through the assignment of numbers, in order, to each digit position.

--- SENTENCE 276 ---
The orders or digit positions represent progressively finer scale descriptions of physiography, the 5-digit alphanumeric describing a habitat type based ultimately on substratum (bottom) type.

--- SENTENCE 277 ---
Partial codes can be used to express larger scale features.

--- SENTENCE 278 ---
For example, the code Al2 represents fringing reefs on open (non embayed) coasts.

--- SENTENCE 279 ---
The first subdivision (lst order - 2nd digit) differentiates fresh, brackish, and marine waters.

--- SENTENCE 280 ---
Additional subdivisions of fresh and brackish waters could be accommodated, although this is presently beyond the scope of the ASCRI project.

--- SENTENCE 281 ---
Note, however, that the designation "brackish waters" in this case refers only to inland, polyhaline water bodies.

--- SENTENCE 282 ---
Essentially marine bodies of water subject to occasional marked depressions in salinity are classified as marine.

--- SENTENCE 283 ---

The following numbered paragraphs provide definitions and more detailed explanations to clarify choices required at specific points in the above key to the classification of aquatic environments.

--- SENTENCE 310 ---
§ 1 - Embayments - Not all bays in American Samoa are sufficiently enclosed to represent conditions substantially different from those encountered along the open coast.

--- SENTENCE 311 ---
Coastal features geographically defined as bays range from relatively open forms typified by Faga'itua Bay, to moderately protected waters such as Vatia Bay Afono Bay, to relatively enclosed bodies of water such as Pago Pago Harbor and Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 312 ---
In Hawai'i, the Technical Committee on Water Quality Standards (State of Hawaii, Dept. of Health, 1978) with the problem of distinguishing certain geographical (actually bights in many cases) from true embayments or relatively restricted coastal indentations by defining the latter on the basis the residence time of the water.

--- SENTENCE 313 ---
The committee determined, from examination of existing water quality measurements, that a residence time of several days was necessary if point and non-point sources of nutrients and terrigenous sediments were to have a substantial lasting impact on the biota in an embayment.

--- SENTENCE 314 ---
The residence time can crudely approximated by using the ratio of a bay's total volume to the cross-sectional area of its entrance.

--- SENTENCE 315 ---
A threshold in water quality parameters appears to occur when this ratio equals or exceeds 700.

--- SENTENCE 316 ---
Although the ratios for presumed "embayments"

--- SENTENCE 319 ---
A few bays with restricting coral reefs (for example, Afono and Masefau) are possibly true embayments.

--- SENTENCE 320 ---
The classification system attempts to differentiate the relatively protected waters of embayments from the relatively unprotected waters of an open coast.

--- SENTENCE 321 ---
Thus, couplet 2 includes several other criteria (barrier reef, breakwater) which give rise to protected waters along the coast.

--- SENTENCE 322 ---
Note that, excepting the quiet waters of a lagoon protected by a barrier reef, coastal habitats associated with reef features are treated in couplet 2 as open-coast habitats (unless, of course, the reef occurs within an embayment).

--- SENTENCE 323 ---
- §2 Wave Surge

--- SENTENCE 324 ---
The classification scheme treats habitats on the front slope of any reef type as representing the same conditions of exposure to wave surge as habitats along a coast lacking a reef.

--- SENTENCE 325 ---
Although reefs represent special biogenic features with a generally unique offshore topography, the organisms inhabiting high surge zones in front of the reef margin are confered no protection from surge by the presence of the reef.

--- SENTENCE 326 ---
Most distinctions which could be made are essentially differences in substratum type.
- §3 Reef Forms

--- SENTENCE 327 ---
The terminology applied to gross geomorphology of biogenic reefs (reef form) is expansive (see Stoddart, 1978).

--- SENTENCE 328 ---
A wide variety of reef types have been described and inter-related in morphogenic schemes, the most basic of which is that of Darwin (1842).

--- SENTENCE 329 ---
Darwin's idea, which, despite a long period of controversy, remains widely accepted today, relates how fringing reefs become barrier reefs, and barrier reefs become atolls with the gradual submergence of an island mass.

--- SENTENCE 330 ---
Examples of fringing reefs are most common around the volcanic (high) islands of American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 331 ---
Patch reefs are less common (examples occur in Pago Pago Harbor; i.e., Whale Rock, Amaula Rock).

--- SENTENCE 332 ---
Both Swains and Rose Islands are examples of atoll reefs, although Swains is not typical in form.

--- SENTENCE 333 ---
Barrier reefs are not present, although the Nafanua and Taema Banks appear to be an ancient drowned barrier reef (Mayor, 1920).

--- SENTENCE 334 ---
The fringing reefs of American Samoa are well developed and typical of similar structures extant throughout the central and southern Pacific Ocean.

--- SENTENCE 335 ---
A profile of a fringing reef is illustrated in Figure 6A and demonstrates basic reef structure: a broad, more or less level or low relief platform (the reef flat); an outer reef margin or reef crest; and an abruptly descending reef front or seaward reef slope.

--- SENTENCE 336 ---
The form shown is characteristic of Pago Pago Harbor reefs which have a particularly steep reef front.

--- SENTENCE 337 ---
Along more exposed coasts the reef front is not nearly so steep.

--- SENTENCE 338 ---
Note the gentle net upward slope from the base of the beach deposit near the shoreline to the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 339 ---
The profiles off Ogegasa (Tutuila, north coast) and Leone (Tutuila, southwest coast) (Figure 6B) show less well

--- SENTENCE 342 ---
In particular, the reef margin is "submerged" -- that is, the margin has not grown up to sea level and, therefore, does not provide the same degree of protection to the reef flat and shore.

--- SENTENCE 343 ---
In the classification scheme, the "reef flat" habitat is coded differently if associated with a submerged as opposed to a sea level reef.

--- SENTENCE 344 ---
The importance of this distinction lies primarily in the nature of the surge associated with the two types of fringing reefs.

--- SENTENCE 345 ---
On a true fringing reef, wave energies are largely dissipated on the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 346 ---
Over submerged reefs, waves progress much of the way into shore, and the surge zone is correspondingly broader.

--- SENTENCE 347 ---
§4 - Reef Flat Zonation - The differentiation of zones on reef flats has long been a subject of interest to coral reef ecologists.

--- SENTENCE 348 ---
The complexity of the biological and physical processes involved in establishing reef structure produce patterns which sometimes are distinctly arranged in bands from the outer reef slope to the shore, and sometimes appear as patches not distinctly zoned.

--- SENTENCE 349 ---
The purpose of the 3rd order term in the case of reef flats is to broadly distinguish zones on a reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 350 ---
These "zones" are not always easily differentiated in the field where the substrata and biota grade imperceptably from one type into another.

--- SENTENCE 351 ---
The user should, therefore, not become overly concerned with the precise part of the reef (i.e., outer, middle, or inner reef zone in the classification scheme) represented where zonation is indistinct.

--- SENTENCE 352 ---
In many cases, particularly where a reef is narrow, all three zones may not be The distinction is based not on position, but on the represented.

--- SENTENCE 353 ---
predominance of certain physiographic conditions.

--- SENTENCE 354 ---
The outer reef zone includes the reef margin and is the zone of maximum wave surge in shallow water.

--- SENTENCE 355 ---
On well developed, sea level reefs, much of this zone may be exposed at extremely low tides (Randall, et al., 1978).

--- SENTENCE 356 ---
The bottom is dominated by consolidated limestone and coralline algae are prominent inhabitants (Dahl, 1971).

--- SENTENCE 357 ---
Coral cover may or may not be extensive, although for any given section across a reef in Hawai'i, the highest coral cover shoreward of the margin is usually in the outer reef flat zone.

--- SENTENCE 358 ---
The middle reef zone occurs shoreward of the outer reef flat and is characterized by a mixture of substrata, with consolidated reef-rock and coarse sediments (rubble, boulders) predominating.

--- SENTENCE 359 ---
Sand is present in depressions and is coarse-grained.

--- SENTENCE 360 ---
This zone is further characterized by an abundance of fleshy algae on many Hawaiian reefs.

--- SENTENCE 361 ---
Water circulation is generally good, except perhaps at extreme low tides, when patches of reef-rock may uncover.

--- SENTENCE 362 ---
The inner reef flat occurs near shore (on fringing reefs) and is characterized by an accumulation of sediments, particularly medium to fine grained sand.

--- SENTENCE 363 ---
This zone is typically, although not necessarily, one of sluggish water movement, even at high tide on particularly broad reefs.

--- SENTENCE 364 ---
On narrow reefs, a distinct inner reef flat may not be present.

--- SENTENCE 365 ---
The inner reef flat may harbor a sparse growth of fleshy algae or may be rich in species adapted to low turbulence.

--- SENTENCE 366 ---
Corals are usually present in only low abundance --

!

--- SENTENCE 367 ---

scattered heads of <u>Cyphastrea</u> sp., <u>Pocillopora</u> <u>damicornis</u>, and/or <u>Porites</u> <u>lutea</u> may be present.

--- SENTENCE 368 ---
On some reefs with a shallow outer reef zone, the inner reef zone (or a portion of it) may be a shallow channel running parallel to shore.

--- SENTENCE 369 ---
This channel, sometimes called a "boat channel" serves to drain away water brought onto the reef flat by waves breaking over the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 370 ---
Usually a boat channel connects to a break in the reef or a seaward running channel (ava), through which strong rip currents develop whenever large waves break over the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 371 ---
§5 - Lagoons, Channels, Borrow Pits, Reef Holes - The designator applies to large holes or dredged channels and borrow pits behind a reef margin, and small lagoon-like features on fringing reefs.

--- SENTENCE 372 ---
These depressions can occur anywhere on a reef flat, but are characterized by the protection from wave surge provided by a surrounding reef structure.

--- SENTENCE 373 ---
Ordinarily, the "boat channel" referred to above is too shallow (1 meter deep or less) to be coded here.

--- SENTENCE 374 ---
Any channel of considerable length and depth over two meters, cut from outside the reef into shore will change from A.Ol.

--- SENTENCE 375 ---
to A..4. at a point where wave surge ceases to be a regular occurence.

--- SENTENCE 376 ---
Determination of this transition generally must be made in the field based on bottom type and biota.

--- SENTENCE 377 ---
These environments are nearly always characterized by an accumulation of fine sediments, including a preponderance of silt in many cases.

--- SENTENCE 378 ---
Note that true lagoons, such as are associated with barrier and atoll reefs, are coded in the 1st order (A2...).

#### FLORA AND FAUNA

Even very small units of area are inhabited by more kinds of organisms than it would be possible to list.

--- SENTENCE 379 ---
Most surveys which develop species lists concentrate on conspicuous forms which dominate by virtue of size and numbers — in marine areas, the demersal fishes, corals, fleshy algae, and certain conspicuous macroinvertebrates (particularly the larger echinoderms) are usually noted.

--- SENTENCE 380 ---
Small and/or cryptic forms frequently are not.

--- SENTENCE 381 ---
This same emphasis is applied in the ASCRI text.

--- SENTENCE 382 ---
Included under the category FLORA AND FAUNA are descriptions of prominent organisms inhabiting maritime, estuarine, and marine areas covered by the particular coastal segment.

--- SENTENCE 383 ---
Terrestrial (coastal zone) and land aquatic areas are treated first, then shoreline areas, followed by nearshore and reef flat environments, and finally offshore and deep water environments.

--- SENTENCE 384 ---
Unusual, rare, or endangered species are often mentioned in addition to the most common, conspicuous, or economically valuable organisms reported in surveys conducted at each site.

--- SENTENCE 385 ---
The extent of a particular description is dependent, of course, on the availability of information.

--- SENTENCE 386 ---
The ASCRI project supplemented published and unpublished survey data with field surveys conducted in October 1979 (see pages 2-4).

--- SENTENCE 387 ---
In general, biological descriptions are given in a present tense in keeping with the tone of the Part A text as a whole.

--- SENTENCE 388 ---
This practice deviates from the usual scientific style of refering to the data of others in third person, past tense.

--- SENTENCE 389 ---
The effect is an implication that the biological information is complete, current, and In fact, the information presented is merely the best available for all or some portion of the area defined by the subheading.

--- SENTENCE 390 ---
The short-comings of all survey data must be realized by the reader and assumed to apply, even though unstated, to the descriptions of flora and fauna given in the text.

--- SENTENCE 391 ---
For the algae in particular, and many other groups generally, species dominance -indeed, the presence of many forms - changes regularly or seasonally.

--- SENTENCE 392 ---
No attempt could be made in the brief descriptions presented to consistently compensate for this fact.

--- SENTENCE 393 ---
Moreover, for most locations the necessary up-to-date surveys simply have not been conducted and the possibility of changes must be assumed by the reader.

--- SENTENCE 394 ---
Where one or more studies have been conducted in a given area, emphasis is placed on the most recent, which will be given in present tense.

--- SENTENCE 395 ---
The results of older studies are given in past tense where there is reason to believe that the descriptions no longer apply.

--- SENTENCE 396 ---
Scientific nomenclature is utilized in the FLORA AND FAUNA sections along with non-specific common names (e.g., "the surgeon-fish,...").

--- SENTENCE 397 ---
Scientific names are underlined (italicized in tables).

--- SENTENCE 398 ---
Most non-marine organisms are presented with both a specific common name, samoan name, and scientific name; for example, "reef heron (matu'u; Egretta sacra sacra)..."

--- SENTENCE 399 ---
Scientific names have been carefully checked for proper spelling and validity.

--- SENTENCE 400 ---
Species names synonymized since appearing in older source documents are presented in ASCRI in accordance with currently accepted practices.

--- SENTENCE 401 ---
Common names (both samoan and english) are used in the USE CONSIDERATIONS sections.

--- SENTENCE 402 ---

The reef-building or hermatypic corals are animals limited in their distribution to warm seas where they are a major contributor

(along with coralline algae) to the structure of reefs.

--- SENTENCE 404 ---
A diverse coral community provides a wide variety of habitats that supports a rich assemblage of other invertebrates and fishes.

--- SENTENCE 405 ---
Areas of exceptionally diverse coral assemblages or coral cover exceeding 50% of the bottom are flagged in the text index (left hand page) with the coral head symbol (shown on the left).

# Palolo Worms (Phylum Annelida)

Most reef areas in American Samoa are popular places for the gathering of "palolo" worms (<u>Eunice viridis</u>) which swarm over wave-washed areas 7 days after the full moon (3rd quarter), usually between October and November of each year (Wass, pers.

--- SENTENCE 408 ---
Considerable excitement accompanies the annual harvest of palolo

--- SENTENCE 436 ---
Palolo are caught with scoops and baskets, and fine mesh nets.

--- SENTENCE 437 ---
This much-prized food is eaten raw or cooked and is preserved for eating over the long period when palolo are not available (Smetzer, 1959).

--- SENTENCE 439 ---
Alamea (Phylum Echinodermata)

!

--- SENTENCE 440 ---
The alamea (crown-of-thorns starfish; Acanth-aster planci) has attracted considerable attention in the central Pacific in recent years because of large population build-ups in reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 441 ---
The alamea is a usual inhabitant of reef front areas where it occurs in small numbers and feeds on coral tissue.

--- SENTENCE 442 ---
Feeding usually occurs at night and often results in the death

of the coral head.

--- SENTENCE 443 ---
When the starfish appears in an area in large numbers the consequences can range from considerable to near total destruction of the coral bottom assemblage.

--- SENTENCE 444 ---
A number of studies have been directed at following the progress of the recent "outbreak" of alamea (beginning in mid-1977) around Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 445 ---
Results of these studies reflecting either large numbers of starfish or significant damage to the coral assemblage are flagged in the text index (left-hand page) by the alamea symbol shown here.

# USE CONSIDERATIONS

Under the heading USE CONSIDERATIONS are presented the activities engaged in and facilities provided for, residents of and visitors to, the coastal areas of American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 515 ---
follows presence, abundance, and quality of the utilization resources available in any given place, and the best identifiers of particular resources are the users themselves.

--- SENTENCE 516 ---
The ranking of popularity of subsistence fishing methods and descriptions of common catches are summarized from the village by village Fishing and Farming survey conducted by the Development Planning (Government of American Samoa, Development Planning Office, 1980) and supplemented by interviews with village chiefs and councils.

--- SENTENCE 517 ---
No attempt has been made in the text to plan or otherwise suggest partitioning of resources among user categories (plans already developed in government documents are noted).

--- SENTENCE 518 ---
The relative degree to which certain activities take place and the quality of the resources being utilized are discussed, although frequently only in general terms.

--- SENTENCE 519 ---
Many uses are described without crediting sources.

--- SENTENCE 520 ---
In such cases the information derives from observations and/or the expertise of consultants to the ASCRI project.

#### Reef Uses

Fringing reefs, such as those occurring off the coast of much of American Samoa, are among the most important of coastal zone resources.

--- SENTENCE 521 ---
Although American Samoans no longer depend upon their traditional nearshore fishery as a primary source of food, subsistence fishing remains the predominant use of reefs in Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 522 ---
Despite increasing use of reefs (primarily by non-Samoans) for sport diving, surfing, shell collecting, and other recreational activities, subsistence fishing must be considered the highest priority use based on the number of participants.

--- SENTENCE 523 ---
However, it can be argued that such fishing is as much for sport as for subsistence

purposes.

--- SENTENCE 524 ---
The majority of subsistence fishing activity in American Samoa is undertaken by villagers on reefs adjacent to their villages.

--- SENTENCE 525 ---
Samoans traditionally maintain that reef areas adjacent to their villages are village property, although some villages are stricter in regulating use by outsiders than others.

--- SENTENCE 526 ---
The need to obtain local village approval for access to the shoreline and reef in populated areas is common courtesy expected of outsiders and, to a certain degree, inhibits inappropriate uses, overuse, or uses incompatible with subsistence fishing needs of the village.

--- SENTENCE 527 ---
Isolated areas usually lack roado or means of easy access, and this also serves to discourage overuse.

--- SENTENCE 528 ---
In general, destructive practices such as the use of poison or explosive charges (both illegal under Samoan law) are uncommon.

--- SENTENCE 529 ---
A probable case of reef poisoning in Avatele Passage in 1973 appeared to be associated with a fish-trap constructed by non-Samoans (Lamberts, 1974).

--- SENTENCE 530 ---
A large percentage of the population of American Samoa lives along the perimeter of inner Pago Pago Harbor (MAPs 1 and 2) where much of the reef flat has been filled to gain level land or dredged for harbor facilities.

--- SENTENCE 531 ---
The degradation of reef flat envaronments fronting heavily populated areas in the inner harbor severely restricts the fishing methods and catches there.

--- SENTENCE 532 ---
Although pelagic and migratory fishes are still caught with line or net along the inner margins of the harbor, the diverse catches of reef fishes and invertebrates typically occurring elsewhere in the islands are no longer possible in Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 533 ---
Many of the people of this "urban" population simply do not fish, or do so mainly for sport (Hill, 1978).

--- SENTENCE 534 ---
Major alterations of reef flats (e.g., harbor development, dredging to obtain fill for roads or land reclamation) should be carefully evaluated in areas of intact reefs fronting villages which retain a tradition of subsistence fishing.

--- SENTENCE 535 ---
In the past, indiscriminate dredging has destroyed or reduced the diversity of fishery resources.

--- SENTENCE 536 ---
Except in inner Pago Pago Harbor, where continued dredging and filling appears consistent with expansion of harbor facilities and economic growth, large scale disturbances of reef environments in other areas is incompatible with village fishing activity.

--- SENTENCE 537 ---
Small-scale disturbances of reef environments through destruction of coral beds is also detrimental to subsistence fishing.

--- SENTENCE 538 ---
Coral bottoms contribute to shelter and habitat for fish life, particularly juvenile and small fishes of importance in maintaining populations of larger, edible fishes.

--- SENTENCE 539 ---
Thus, intentional damage to living coral heads caused by collecting as curios (either by or for tourists) or unintentional damage resulting from boat anchors, are incompatible with subsistence fishing and other reef uses dependent on diverse and abundant marine life.

--- SENTENCE 540 ---
Non-consumptive recreational uses, such as sport-diving and surfing, undertaken primarily by non-Samoan residents and visitors to Samoa, do not generally conflict with subsistence fishing.

--- SENTENCE 541 ---
Sport

diving is generally concentrated on the reef front, and surfing occurs mainly near or off the reef margin at high tide when fishing is least likely to occur at the margin.

--- SENTENCE 542 ---
Beaches are focal points for water sports seldom undertaken by Samoans and which may be incompatible with traditional fishing activity in areas of Tutuila outside of the population centers around Pago Pago Harbor and on the outer islands, which retain a more traditional lifestyle.

--- SENTENCE 543 ---
Problems result not only from competition for space, but also from beach use by tourists and non-natives on Sundays, a practice discouraged by Samoans for religious reasons.

--- SENTENCE 544 ---
Tourist-oriented water sports (such as sailing) should be concentrated in Pago Pago Harbor and in areas not closely associated with specific villages.

--- SENTENCE 545 ---
An area with exceptional potential for sport-diving and underwater photography is a nearshore lagoon off the Ofu airport (northwest from Papaloloa Point).

--- SENTENCE 546 ---
Other areas with high potential for ocean recreation (activities other than subsistence fishing) have been indicated in marginal notes in the running index of the text (left-hand page).

--- SENTENCE 547 ---
Water quality problems are a cause of reef degradation heavily populated areas of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 548 ---
Waste disposal in Pago Pago Harbor has contributed to the destruction of the fringing reef community, although the reef remains structurally intact.

--- SENTENCE 549 ---
Road construction projects (particularly the "Top Mile" road between Aua and Afono, and a road along the ridge to the TV transmitter on Mt. Alava) have accelerated soil erosion.

--- SENTENCE 550 ---
Sediments carried by the streams have severely damaged the reef flats fronting Aua and Fagasa villages (M & E Pacific, 1978).

--- SENTENCE 551 ---
Both sedimentation from poor land management practices and nutrient enrichment from sewage disposal inevitably interfere with reef uses dependent upon a diverse assemblage of marine life.

--- SENTENCE 552 ---
In at least one case, public health is directly endangered by waste disposal.

--- SENTENCE 553 ---
Cesspool seepage into Pala Lagoon raises bacterial concentrations above levels considered safe for consumption of clams collected from the lagoon (Helfrich, et.

--- SENTENCE 554 ---
The need for marine preserves in American Samoa is probably limited to a few areas considered especially pristine or unspoiled and not actively fished.

--- SENTENCE 555 ---
Two such areas, Fagatele Bay and Larsen Bay, are presently under consideration for marine preserve status (Wass, pers.

--- SENTENCE 556 ---
It is important to note that preservation from human disturbance does not guarantee the safe-guarding of reef The rich coral beds in both bays were devastated in the recent plaque of alamea (crown-of-thorns starfish; Acanthaster planci) which destroyed living corals in many areas around Tutuilla, Aunu'u, and on the offshore banks.

--- SENTENCE 557 ---
Apparently, infestations of alamea are periodic phenomena affecting Samoan reefs.

--- SENTENCE 558 ---
At present, several unspoiled examples of rich coral growth have been identified: in Sita Bay and Fagafue Bay on the northwestern coast of Tutuila and at Ofu (off the airport).

--- SENTENCE 559 ---
The Tutuila examples are genrally isolated from most users and therefore protected without The Ofu example is easily official designation as preserves.

--- SENTENCE 560 ---
accessible and an excellent candidate for designation as a preserve.

--- SENTENCE 561 ---
An area of exceptional coral growth and a remarkably diverse fish assemblage is around the margins of the old borrow areas adjacent to the reef runway at Pago Pago International Airport.

--- SENTENCE 562 ---
This reef area

is an excellent candidate for marine preserve status, although the area is presently protected from overuse due to the controlled access across the airport property.

--- SENTENCE 563 ---
Generally rough seas limit approach to this area from seaward.

#### MISCELLANEOUS

Place names generally follow U.S.G.S. topographic maps with, however, additions and corrections provided by Otto Thomsen of the Development Planning Office, American Samoa Government.

--- SENTENCE 564 ---
Spelling of place names is based on pronunciation with inclusion of the glottal stop.

--- SENTENCE 565 ---
Measurements given in the text are presented in the English System with Metric System equivalents provided in parentheses.

--- SENTENCE 566 ---
Note, however, that the two values given are not direct conversions (i.e., one foot equal to 0.3048 meters).

--- SENTENCE 567 ---
Instead, an equivalent level of precision is given.

--- SENTENCE 568 ---
Thus, where an original observation appears to be an estimate (for example, "500 feet"), a metric estimate is provided ("150 meters", not 152.4 meters).

# AMERICAN SAMOA

--- SENTENCE 628 ---
The Territory of American Samoa comprises the six eastern islands of the Samoa Archipelago and one other island (Swains Atoll) geographically belonging to the Tokelau Island Group.

--- SENTENCE 629 ---
American Samoa is located in the tropics (14°S latitude, 170°W longitude) of the Central Pacific Ocean 2,300 nautical miles (4,420 km) southwest of Hawai'i, 1,500 miles (2,400 km) north of Aukland, New Zealand, 1,200 miles (2,000 km) northwest of Tahiti, and 80 miles (130 km) southeast of Western Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 630 ---
The five volcanic islands are aligned along the crest of a discontinuous submarine ridge which extends over 300 miles (480 km) and trends roughly northwest by southeast.

--- SENTENCE 631 ---
These are the major inhabited islands of American Samoa and include Tutuila, Aunu'u (a island located one mile (1.6 km) off the southeast coast of Tutuila), Ofu, Olosega, and Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 632 ---
The latter three islands are collectively referred to as the Manu'a Group and lie about 66 miles (106 km) east of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 633 ---
Rose Island (Nu'uomanu), located about 100 miles (161 km) east of Tutuila, is an uninhabited coral atoll less than 1 square mile (2.6 sq km) in land area.

--- SENTENCE 634 ---
Island is a National Wildlife Refuge.

--- SENTENCE 635 ---
Swains Island, about 225 miles (360 km) north of Tutuila, is a coral atoll privately owned by the descendants of a New England whaling captain.

# TUTUILA ISLAND

Tutuila is a narrow island covering about 54 square miles (140 sq.km).

--- SENTENCE 638 ---
The island had a complex origin in the eruptions of five overlapping centers of volcanic activity which merged roughly in a west to east line.

--- SENTENCE 639 ---
Maximum length of Tutuila is just over 20 miles (32 km).

--- SENTENCE 640 ---
The width varies from 1 to 2 miles (1.5 to 3.5 km) across the eastern half of the island and from 1 to 6 miles (1.5 to 10.0 km) across the western half.

--- SENTENCE 641 ---
The rugged terrain is characterized by steep mountainous slopes and narrow valleys and coastal plains.

--- SENTENCE 642 ---
The highest elevation is 2,100 feet (640 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 643 ---
The drowned river valley of Pago Pago nearly cuts the island in two near its center (28;54;65).

--- SENTENCE 644 ---
The island is surrounded by deep ocean with depths over 9900 feet (3000 m) between it and the Manu'a Islands to the east (55).

--- SENTENCE 645 ---
Tutuila was considerably broader in the geological past.

--- SENTENCE 646 ---
Following the cessation of early stage volcanic activity, deep valleys were eroded by streams and a highly irregular coastline shaped by wave attack.

--- SENTENCE 647 ---
After a long quiescent period, renewed eruptions built an extensive plain of tuffs and basalts on the southwestern side of the Tutuila between Nu'uuli and Leone over a submerged reef.

--- SENTENCE 648 ---
A small, contemporaneous eruption off the southeastern end of Tutuila formed the tuff cone today Aunu'u Island.

--- SENTENCE 649 ---
Subsequent erosion of Tutuila produced the present rugged terrain and deeply embayed coastline.

--- SENTENCE 650 ---
Collapse of the summit of Pago volcano formed a caldera.

--- SENTENCE 651 ---
The Pago River created a wide, deep canyon along the north wall of the caldera.

--- SENTENCE 652 ---
Pioa cone at Aua diverted the river to the south of the caldera.

--- SENTENCE 653 ---
Rapid submergence by rising sea level created Pago Pago Bay and other bays by drowning the river valley mouths.

--- SENTENCE 654 ---
Drainage is by deeply-incised stream valleys radiating from the summit of each volcanic cone (28;54;65).

--- SENTENCE 655 ---
Around the volcanic mass of the Island sedimentary deposits formed at the base of steep slopes (talus), on valley floors (alluvium), and on narrow coastal plains and beaches (calcareous sand and rubble).

--- SENTENCE 656 ---
The bays of Tutuila tend to be formed in regions of weak rocks flanked by more resistant lavas.

--- SENTENCE 657 ---
Precipitous cliffs rise to several hundred feet above the shoreline around much of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 658 ---
Many of the promontories and offshore seastacks are dense lavas which filled cinder cone craters.

--- SENTENCE 659 ---
Wave erosion has long since worn away the softer cinder beds once surrounding the sea stacks.

--- SENTENCE 660 ---
Wave-cut benches a few feet above present sea level are conspicuous at the base of basalt cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 661 ---
Sea caves positioned above present-day sea level are common around the Island (28;54;59).

## REEFS

Fringing reefs are nearly continuous off the south and east shores of Tutuila, but are developed only in embayments along the north shore where high cliffs plunge into the ocean.

--- SENTENCE 662 ---
The absence of a more or less continuous fringing reef around Tutuila is

--- SENTENCE 663 ---
A fringing reef hugs the coastline in places where submarine slopes are not too steep.

--- SENTENCE 664 ---
Fringing reefs have not developed off many basalt promontories where the bottom drops away steeply.

--- SENTENCE 665 ---
Also, a fringing reef has not formed off the geologically recent plain between Fagatele Bay (MAP 25) and the International Airport, where lava cliffs terminate in deep water (MAP 27)(59).

--- SENTENCE 666 ---
The Taema and Nafanua Banks south of Tutuila represent a former barrier reef now submerged some 60 feet (18 m) or more.

--- SENTENCE 667 ---
Depth in the former lagoon behind the banks is up to 330 feet (100 m)(15;54;59).

--- SENTENCE 668 ---
Soundings clearly indicate that a reef which extended over a mile (1.6 km) offshore of Tutuila is now submerged a few hundred feet deep (54;59).

--- SENTENCE 669 ---
The modern fringing reefs vary in width generally between 300 and 990 feet (90 to 300 m).

--- SENTENCE 670 ---
The widest reef flat occurs off Nu'uuli (MAP 29) where the margin occurs some 3000 feet (900 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 671 ---
In places, particularly off stream mouths, the fringing reef may be cut by a channel known as an ava.

--- SENTENCE 672 ---
Algal ridges reaching up to low tide depth are well-developed at the margins of reefs along the south coast.

--- SENTENCE 673 ---
Algal ridges are rather poorly developed on north shore reefs, which tend to be narrow and confined to the flanks and heads of small bays.

--- SENTENCE 674 ---
The seaward reef margin sometimes projects as an overhanging shelf, below which is a precipitous reef slope (59).

--- SENTENCE 675 ---
On wave-exposed coasts the reef front is moderately to steeply sloped with extensive spur-and-groove formations.

--- SENTENCE 676 ---
In Pago Pago Harbor the reef front is sheer (26).

#### TSUNAMIS AND HURRICANES

--- SENTENCE 677 ---
Although Samoa has experienced 17 tsunamis over a 43\ year period (1917-1960), only Pago Pago (MAP 1) has reported any sizeable runup.

--- SENTENCE 678 ---
The 1960 tsunami produced a runup of 4.5 feet (1.4 m) at the harbor entrance and 10.7 feet (3.3 m) at the head of the harbor (29;66).

--- SENTENCE 679 ---
Tsunamis which do little or no damage elsewhere in American Samoa may generate high runup in the inner harbor due to the funneling effect of the harbor's configuration (64).

--- SENTENCE 680 ---
American Samoa lies in the path of hurricanes approaching primarily from the north but occasionally from the east, southwest, or west.

--- SENTENCE 681 ---
The most severe hurricane to affect American Samoa in recent decades passed through the islands in January 1966 (22;69).

# PAGO PAGO BASIN

#### PAGO PAGO HARBOR

Pago Pago Harbor, which nearly bisects the Island of Tutuila, is a deep natural embayment.

--- SENTENCE 683 ---
It is presumed to have been formed by erosion of a wide and deep canyon through weak tuff deposits along the north wall of the Pago caldera during a period when sea level was much lower than at present.

--- SENTENCE 684 ---
The ancestral stream that cut the valley was diverted south of the caldera by the formation of the bulky Pioa cone (MAP 2).

--- SENTENCE 685 ---
This cone also caused the Aua tributary to cut a deep amphitheater-like valley in the caldera wall on the northwestern side of the cone.

--- SENTENCE 686 ---
Thus, Pago Pago Harbor is a drowned valley which owes its unusual size to its large drainage area, weak rocks in its floor, and high caldera walls on its north side (54).

--- SENTENCE 687 ---
Rapid subsidence resulted in flooding of the ancient valley, forming one of the deepest and most sheltered natural harbors in the Pacific (64).

--- SENTENCE 688 ---
The embayment is about 3 miles (4.8 km) long and encompasa water surface area of approximately two square miles (5.2 square km).

--- SENTENCE 689 ---
From its southward opening entrance, the harbor about 1.5 miles (2.4 km), where it makes a sharp inward turn to the west and extends an additional 1.5 miles (2.4 km) to Pago Park at its head (6;58).

--- SENTENCE 690 ---
The innermost reaches of the Harbor are within 3500 feet (1060 m) of the northern coast of Tutuila at Agapie Cove (MAP 15), although a steep ridge rising to an elevation of over 1000 feet (300 m) separates the two coasts.

--- SENTENCE 691 ---
Depths reach 250 feet (75 m) at the harbor mouth, decreasing to 120 feet (35 m) three-quarters of the way into the harbor (37;58;64;65).

--- SENTENCE 692 ---
Average depth is approximately 200 feet (60 m)(13).

--- SENTENCE 693 ---
The entrance to the harbor is approximately 2800 feet (850 m) wide between Faga'alu reef and Breakers Point.

--- SENTENCE 694 ---
The channel narrows to 1600 feet (487 m) at Whale Rock where the navigation channel is restricted to the eastern side of the harbor (65).

--- SENTENCE 695 ---
# STREAMS

Upland drainage throughout Tutuila, especially in the areas above Pago Pago Harbor, is provided by deeply incised valleys radiating from the summit of volcanic cones and characterized by steep stream gradients (64).

--- SENTENCE 696 ---
Several streams with a combined drainage area of approximately 5 square miles (8 sq. km) enter Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 697 ---
Although flows are continuous, volumes are highly variable.

--- SENTENCE 698 ---
Faga'alu, Vaipito, and Lalolamauta Streams drain the largest watersheds.

--- SENTENCE 699 ---
Vaipito Stream, draining the largest watershed tributary to Pago Pago Harbor and having the largest volume of flow, enters the harbor at its head near Pago Pago Village (MAP 1).

--- SENTENCE 700 ---
Much of this stream's length has been modified by concrete and riprap walls.

--- SENTENCE 701 ---
Lalolamauta Stream discharges into the middle harbor at Aua (MAP 2).

--- SENTENCE 702 ---
The stream bed grades to gravel, sand, and silt near the mouth.

--- SENTENCE 703 ---
The stream's lower reach has been subject to realign-

--- SENTENCE 706 ---
Faga'alu Stream empties into outer Pago Pago Harbor at Faga'alu Bay (MAP 3).

--- SENTENCE 707 ---
Numerous other streams flow intermittently into the harbor around most of its perimeter.

--- SENTENCE 708 ---
The land adjoining the lower reaches of Faga'alu and Vaipito Streams is densely settled.

--- SENTENCE 709 ---
The lower reach of Vaipito Stream flows through a landfill at the head of Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 710 ---
This stream is choked at several points with accumulated trash (71).

--- SENTENCE 711 ---
The water quality of several other streams which discharge into Pago Pago Harbor is influenced by urban and agricultural activities in their drainage areas.

--- SENTENCE 712 ---
These streams show a definite increase in nutrients above levels in pristine streams.

--- SENTENCE 713 ---
Streams draining urban and agricultural areas have high turbidity after heavy rainfall and occasionally have low or fluctuating levels of dissolved oxygen which are detrimental to most forms of stream life and may occasionally cause fish kills.

--- SENTENCE 714 ---
Urban-influenced streams frequently have concentrations of fecal coliforms far in excess of water quality standards (40).

--- SENTENCE 715 ---
# COASTLINE

The entire perimeter of Pago Pago Harbor is accessible by a two-lane, paved road which provides vehicular access to all the villages along the southern coast of Tutuila (23).

--- SENTENCE 716 ---
The coastal area around the perimeter of Pago Pago Harbor is the major population, commercial, and industrial center of American Samoa (64).

--- SENTENCE 717 ---
Utulei on the western shore (MAP 2), with the principal hotel , facilities on Tutuila, is a center for tourism.

--- SENTENCE 718 ---
activities, including marine repair facilities and tuna canneries (located in the village of Anua), are situated along the north shore of the inner harbor (MAP 1).

--- SENTENCE 719 ---
Commercial and government activities are centered along the western and southern shorelines.

--- SENTENCE 720 ---
Residential areas are almost continuous around the harbor perimeter.

--- SENTENCE 721 ---
The only hospital facility is located at Faga'alu 3)(37;63).

--- SENTENCE 722 ---
Pago Pago Park occupies a filled area off the stream mouth at the head of the bay (MAP 1)(56).

--- SENTENCE 723 ---
Access to the shoreline is generally unrestricted, except in the vicinity of the dry dock facility and tuna canneries along the north shore of the inner harbor where public access is limited (63).

--- SENTENCE 724 ---
A second paved road extends over the backbone of Tutuila from Pago Pago Village to the village of Fagasa on the north shore (MAP 16)(64).

--- SENTENCE 725 ---
"Top Mile Road", which connects Aua Village to the villages of Afono (MAP 12) and Vatia (MAP 13) on the north shore, is presently under improvement (39).

--- SENTENCE 726 ---
The original shoreline of Pago Pago Harbor has been modified considerably as a result of various land reclamation projects undertaken since 1900 by the U.S. Navy and Government of American Samoa (37).

--- SENTENCE 727 ---
The most dramatic changes have occurred in the inner
