--- SENTENCE 728 ---
Much of the margin of inner Pago Pago Harbor is occupied by harbor facilities.

--- SENTENCE 729 ---
Undeveloped sections of the inner and middle harbor are stabilized with rudimentary seawalls and revetments.

--- SENTENCE 730 ---
Typically, a narrow beach of rubble, small boulders, and silty sand fronts a steep backshore scarp or bank rising 6 feet (2 m) to the coast road (49;ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 731 ---
Sediment deposits at the shoreline are coarser-grained along the southern shore than along the northern shore.

--- SENTENCE 732 ---
This pattern suggests that the prevailing longshore currents move in a counterclockwise direction (56;58).

Mangrove forests once abundant around the perimeter of Pago Pago Harbor have been destroyed and the swamps filled for village use.

Minor patches remain near Aua Village (15;71).

--- SENTENCE 736 ---
# INNER HARBOR SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 737 ---
The deep water accessible from the landfill shore of inner Pago Pago Harbor is conducive to shore fishing.

--- SENTENCE 738 ---
An active seasonal fishery for atule (big-eye scad) occurs at piers in the harbor.

--- SENTENCE 739 ---
Juvenile big-eye scad are the most common fish hooked in the harbor (26).

--- SENTENCE 740 ---
Pole fishing and throw-netting are common along the shoreline of the inner harbor.

--- SENTENCE 741 ---
Jacks and anae (adult mullet) are commonly caught (65).

--- SENTENCE 742 ---
Baitfish are commonly collected close to shore.

--- SENTENCE 743 ---
Water-contact activities along the north shore of inner Pago Pago Harbor are discouraged by the degraded environment (58).

--- SENTENCE 744 ---
# FRINGING REEFS

Fringing reefs border most of Pago Pago Harbor (40).

--- SENTENCE 745 ---
Even the innermost harbor was once fringed by a narrow reef except off the mouth of Vaipito Stream (46).

--- SENTENCE 746 ---
Width of the reefs in the Harbor varies considerably, but is usually around 1000 feet (300 m)(40).

--- SENTENCE 747 ---
The widest sections (up to 1,500 feet or 460 m) occur along the perimeter of the outer Harbor (13), where more or less continuous reefs are cut only by narrow channels (avas) opposite stream mouths (6).

--- SENTENCE 748 ---
Exploratory drilling on the reef flats offshore of Utulei and Aua in 1931 revealed that they are composed almost entirely of bedded calcareous sand and silt, except at the surface, where there is a veneer of cemented coral, coralline algae, and calcareous sand.

--- SENTENCE 749 ---
Basalt rock was encountered at depths of 156 and 121 feet (48 and 37 m) respectively below the reef surface approximately 500 feet (150 m) offshore of Aua and Utulei (6;47).

--- SENTENCE 750 ---
The seaward face of the fringing reefs descends steeply into deep water (40).

--- SENTENCE 751 ---
Talus slopes extending below a depth of 60 feet (18 m) gradually merge with the relatively flat, mud bottom of the harbor (47).

--- SENTENCE 752 ---
( CORAL GROWTH STUDIES

GENERAL

FLORA AND FAUNA

At one time some 6 miles (10 km) of reef flat fringed the perimeter of Pago Pago Harbor between Niuloa Point and Breakers Point (11).

--- SENTENCE 753 ---
However, these reefs have undergone a long history of man-made alteration (6).

--- SENTENCE 754 ---
They have been filled to provide land for urban use and dredged for construction and landfill material.

--- SENTENCE 755 ---
It is estimated that about 23% of the original reef flat area had been filled by 1973 (40).

--- SENTENCE 756 ---
Filling by the U.S. Navy extended the shoreline to the reef margin in many areas of the inner bay (6).

--- SENTENCE 757 ---
Major alterations occurred during World War II, when the military dredged several inshore areas for landfill.

--- SENTENCE 758 ---
Additional dredging occurred after 1960 (11).

--- SENTENCE 759 ---
Loss of fringing reef area is most significant in the inner harbor, where up to 95% of the original reefs have been converted to dry land altering the original shoreline configuration (37).

--- SENTENCE 760 ---
Tidal mudflats off the mouth of Vaipito Stream were filled to create Pago Pago Park at the head of the Harbor (65).

--- SENTENCE 761 ---
Coral growth studies conducted at three locations in Pago Pago Harbor indicate that growth and survival of transplanted corals in the inner harbor (at Fagatogo) is substantially lower than at outer harbor sites (at Utulei and Faga'alu)(43).

#### HARBOR BOTTOM

--- SENTENCE 762 ---
The relatively flat bottom of Pago Pago Harbor is mud-covered.

--- SENTENCE 763 ---
The inner harbor bottom is considerably influenced by stream discharges of fine terrigenous sediment (58).

--- SENTENCE 764 ---
Early investigations of the bottom sediment indicate that brown volcanic mud comprises 67% of sample weight at the head of the harbor but only 6% of the sample weight at the harbor mouth (47).

--- SENTENCE 765 ---
Anoxic black muds particularly notable near the tuna canneries and Pago Pago Park.

--- SENTENCE 766 ---
The thickness of anoxic black silt near the canneries varies from one to 5 feet (0.3 to 1.5 m).

--- SENTENCE 767 ---
Black anaerobic sediment averages 23 inches (60 cm) deep in the inlet between the Star-Kist cannery and the dry dock facility.

--- SENTENCE 768 ---
Across the harbor, gray sediment averages 7 inches (16 cm) deep off Fagatogo.

--- SENTENCE 769 ---
In general, surface layer is underlain by a mixture of dense grey mud, silty sand, gravel, rock, and broken coral fragments extending at least 50 to 60 feet (15 to 18 m) below the harbor bottom (37).

#### HARBOR WATERS

The plankton (microscopic plants and animals in harbor waters) exhibits a gradient of decreasing concentration from the inner to outer harbor.

--- SENTENCE 770 ---
The eastern side of the harbor has the highest concentrations of most kinds of plankton although fish eggs and larvae are more abundant on the western side of the harbor, especially off the Government Dock and Atu'u (37).

--- SENTENCE 771 ---
In general, phytoplankton populations in the outer harbor are low and dominated by diatoms, whereas standing crops increase significantly and are dominated by dinoflagellates in the inner harbor (58).

--- SENTENCE 772 ---
The most common baitfishes in Pago Pago Harbor are mackerel (Rastrelliger kanapurta) and sardines (Sardinella melanura and Herklotssichthys punctatus)(25).

--- SENTENCE 773 ---
The green turtle (Chelonia

#### INNER PAGO PAGO HARBOR

The inner portion of Pago Pago Harbor is the most stressed area of the harbor because of long residence time, limited mixing, and inputs of freshwater, nutrients, and sediments (56).

--- SENTENCE 776 ---
The long, narrow configuration of the harbor and low tidal amplitude (maximum 4.2 feet or 1.3 m) contribute to sluggish circulation and slow flushing at the head of the harbor (11;40).

--- SENTENCE 777 ---
Exchange of water in deeper layers in the harbor with the open ocean may require weeks.

--- SENTENCE 778 ---
Extensive filling of reef flats bordering the harbor has reduced the water surface area, decreasing tidal exchange and increasing residence time of the harbor waters (40).

--- SENTENCE 779 ---
The waters of the outer harbor, with higher rates of water exchange, are of better quality than those of the inner harbor (39;57) which suffer from varying degrees of stress from land drainage and industrial and domestic sewage discharges (20).

--- SENTENCE 780 ---
Water quality has significantly declined in the inner harbor since 1950 (57).

--- SENTENCE 781 ---
Studies prior to the completion of the Pago sewage collection and treatment system and before construction of wastewater treatment facilities at the tuna canneries indicate that the most seriously degraded portion of the inner harbor is along the north shore between Pago Pago Park and Trading Point, an area contaminated by tuna cannery wastes, tuna boat bilge water, cesspool seepage, and stream runoff (28;50).

--- SENTENCE 782 ---
and subtidal surfaces are covered by silt, green algae, and scums of oil and grease.

--- SENTENCE 783 ---
The usual intertidal organisms are generally absent or in poor condition.

--- SENTENCE 784 ---
Assorted refuse including chunks of concrete, old machinery, tires, bottles, cans, rags, and other solid waste litter the shoreline at Anua and Atu'u (50).

--- SENTENCE 785 ---
in the vicinity of the tuna canneries are sometimes discolored and turbid (28).

--- SENTENCE 786 ---
Wind-blown trash, oil, and other floating debris normally accumulate against the north shore from Pago Pago Park to Atu'u.

--- SENTENCE 787 ---
Refuse such as cans, bottles, rubbish, etc. is conspicuous alongshore between Atu'u and Aua, less so between Aua and Tafananani (5).

--- SENTENCE 788 ---
The worst conditions are found in an area of extremely poor circulation near Pago Pago Park in the northwest corner of the inner harbor.

--- SENTENCE 789 ---
The ebbing tide removes a layer of oil and floating rubbish, exposing a lifeless bottom of black mud.

--- SENTENCE 790 ---
Total and fecal coliform counts in access of 100,000 MPN/100 ml have been recorded in shallow waters off Pago Pago Park, as well as along the north shore from Satala to Atu'u (50).

--- SENTENCE 791 ---
Dissolved oxygen levels are depressed in surface waters off Pago Pago Park and the tuna canneries.

--- SENTENCE 792 ---
Water quality generally improves markedly proceeding seaward from Pago Pago Park.

--- SENTENCE 793 ---
Toward the ocean from the point where the harbor bends southward, water quality is affected locally by domestic sewage outfalls near Ututafa Point and Aua

Seriously degraded reefs of the inner harbor have apparently been subjected to environmental stress for many years and showed relatively little change through the first half of the 1970's (53).

--- SENTENCE 794 ---
The inner harbor continues to exhibit signs of biological degradation, including a marked decrease in coral coverage and diversity, a decrease in fish diversity, periods of dissolved oxygen (DO) concentrations, accumulation sediment and floating refuse, elevated nutrient levels, and The source of floating waste includes grease plankton blooms.

--- SENTENCE 795 ---

--- SENTENCE 796 ---
Because of the prevailing wind directions, floating material accumulates along the Pago Pago Park shoreline and in on the west shore of the outer harbor (56).

--- SENTENCE 797 ---
The most serious water quality problems in the inner harbor still occur near the tuna canneries, which have discharged partially-treated wastewater since 1974 (64).

--- SENTENCE 798 ---
Surface waters in the inner harbor frequently dark and turbid, and a plume of discolored water can often be observed in the vicinity of the canneries (11).

--- SENTENCE 799 ---
Surface slicks have been noted in the cannery area, but their exact source is uncertain (39).

--- SENTENCE 800 ---
A sewage collection, treatment and disposal system serving harbor's western perimeter from Faga'alu to Pago Pago has been in operation since 1968 and was extended from Pago Pago to Atu'u in the 1970's (5;13;50).

--- SENTENCE 801 ---
This collection system contributes wastewater to the Utulei treatment plant.

--- SENTENCE 802 ---
After treatment, sewage is discharged beyond the reef into the outer harbor through an outfall off Ututafa Point (5;50).

--- SENTENCE 803 ---

--- SENTENCE 805 ---

--- SENTENCE 806 ---
The Utulei sewage treatment plant and collection system reportedly is not performing well (5) and poorly-treated effluent is being discharged into Pago Pago Harbor (39).

--- SENTENCE 807 ---
Pago Pago Harbor is characterized by stratification of water masses of differing quality and independent water movement, with an upper layer primarily influenced by the wind and a the lower layer driven by the tide.

--- SENTENCE 808 ---
The more turbid surface layer (down to a depth of 10 to 30 feet or 3 to 10 m) is distinctly different from the clearer lower layer, which has a consistently low turbidity at least halfway into the inner harbor (40).

--- SENTENCE 810 ---
An early report describes a flood in 1920 which was accompanied by sediment discharge into Pago Pago Harbor, apparently causing widespread damage to coral colonies.

--- SENTENCE 811 ---
Even at this early date, some of the damage was attributed to improper land management and excessive soil erosion

--- SENTENCE 812 ---
A road (Top mile road) built over the mountain pass between Aua and Afono Village (MAP 12) has caused heavy siltation in Pago Pago Harbor (7).

--- SENTENCE 813 ---
Construction of the first section has exposed bare soil to torrential rains.

--- SENTENCE 814 ---
Large quantities of eroded soil have been carried into Pago Pago Harbor by Suaia and Lalolamauta Streams.

--- SENTENCE 815 ---
Much of this sediment has been deposited on the reef fronting Aua Village (39).

--- SENTENCE 816 ---
Dredging activities have been continuous for several years in the inner harbor with attendant high levels of turbidity and siltation (11).

--- SENTENCE 817 ---
Siltation seriously degraded the inner portions of the especially near Pago Pago Park (5).

--- SENTENCE 818 ---
High levels of turbidity and siltation have resulted in the death of corals in the inner harbor (1).

--- SENTENCE 819 ---
A decline in the growth and survival of corals noted in a 1978 revisit of coral growth study sites monitored in 1971-1972 is attributed to sedimentation, sewage discharge, and general pollution of the inner harbor (65).

--- SENTENCE 820 ---
Elevated nutrient levels are found in the upper water layer of Pago Pago Harbor, particularly in the inner harbor (11;40).

--- SENTENCE 821 ---
Nutrient concentrations are higher in surface waters and in the inner harbor than in waters at greater depth or the outer (56).

--- SENTENCE 822 ---

--- SENTENCE 825 ---
With a ready supply of nutrients, excessive phytoplankton growth in inner and even in outer Pago Pago Harbor indicate that there are occasions (during early morning hours) when dissolved oxygen is reduced to levels too low to support fish life.

--- SENTENCE 826 ---
Although phytoplankton growth is confined largely to the upper layer of water in the inner harbor (40), progressively higher densities of phytoplankton are found moving into the head of the harbor from Goat Island Point.

--- SENTENCE 827 ---
There is a 1,000 to 2,000-fold increase in chlorophyll-a concentrations from the harbor entrance to Pago Pago Park (56).

--- SENTENCE 828 ---

--- SENTENCE 834 ---
VI.B.1 (21) counts are generally higher along the shoreline and at stream mouths than in the middle harbor, are higher at the surface than in deeper water, and increase during periods of high rainfall (50).

--- SENTENCE 835 ---
Open water samples, even in the inner harbor, have relatively low coliform bacteria concentrations (39).

--- SENTENCE 836 ---
Fecal coliform levels in urban-influenced streams and near their mouths in Pago Pago Harbor are far in excess of bacteriological standards (40).

--- SENTENCE 837 ---
Although both total and fecal coliforms are in high concentrations near stream mouths and in areas of wastewater discharges, they are almost absent from the center of the harbor and in deep water because of a rapid rate of disappearance in seawater (56).

--- SENTENCE 838 ---
Occasional small oil spills cause fuel slicks near the fuel dock area during transfer operations despite the use of containment booms (11;39;44).

--- SENTENCE 839 ---
Boating activities, including bilge wastes and deck washings from tuna fishing boats, discharges from freighters, and sanitary wastes from the numerous yachts that anchor in Pago Pago Harbor, contribute to localized pollution problems in the Harbor and in Faga'alu Bay (64).

--- SENTENCE 840 ---
Underwater visibility gradually decreases approaching the inner harbor along the north shore.

--- SENTENCE 841 ---
Off Lepua, horizontal visibility is about 33 feet (10 m).

--- SENTENCE 842 ---
At the reef margin off Aua, in the path of incoming ocean water from the outer harbor, visibility underwater is about 100 feet (30 m) horizontally and about 30 feet (10 m) vertically (11).

--- SENTENCE 843 ---
Water clarity, as measured by Secchi disc, ranges from 2 to 9 feet (0.6 to 2.7 m) in the inner harbor, compared with outer harbor readings of 25 to 50 feet (8 to 15 m) (13).

--- SENTENCE 844 ---
# DEEP DRAFT HARBOR

Pago Pago Harbor is considered one of the best deep draft harbors in the Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 845 ---
The natural embayment has never required dredging.

--- SENTENCE 846 ---
The right angle bend in the harbor provides the inner basin with excellent protection from open ocean waves and swell.

--- SENTENCE 847 ---
Inter-island transportation is provided between Pago Pago Harbor, Aunu'u and the Manu'a Islands by small boats (64).

--- SENTENCE 848 ---
The main docks for both fishing vessels and government vessels are located at Fagatogo (41).

--- SENTENCE 849 ---
Two tuna canneries are situated at Anua on the northern shoreline of Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 850 ---
Both are equipped with unloading docks.

--- SENTENCE 851 ---
Cans are supplied by a can plant located between the two canneries.

--- SENTENCE 852 ---
Vessel repair and dry dock facilities are provided by the Government of American Samoa Marine Railway Department located west of the Star-Kist cannery (37).

--- SENTENCE 853 ---
Pago Pago Harbor is the home port of a large ocean-going fleet of commercial fishing ships which supply the tuna canneries (11).

--- SENTENCE 854 ---
Although bait fishery resources are not abundant, there is enough to support one or two small skipjack tuna vessels (65).

--- SENTENCE 855 ---
In addition to large cargo vessels, cruise ships, and inter-island vessels, Pago Pago Harbor is visited by numerous smaller boats and yachts, most of which are undertaking trans-Pacific voyages (64).

--- SENTENCE 856 ---
The principal anchorage for large yachts is the Malaloa fishing pier, where boats may tie up or anchor off.

--- SENTENCE 857 ---

--- SENTENCE 858 ---
A boat launch ramp is present in the inner harbor (41).

--- SENTENCE 859 ---
From September until March, yachts congregate in the harbor until after the hurricane season has passed.

--- SENTENCE 860 ---
Typically there are over thirty yachts anchored in the inner harbor, with eight to ten more anchored in Faga'alu Bay in outer Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 861 ---
Vaipito Valley funnels strong winds into the inner harbor, causing yachts to drag their anchors on the soft mud bottom.

--- SENTENCE 862 ---
For this reason Faga'alu Bay is considered a more favorable yacht anchorage.

--- SENTENCE 863 ---
However, mooring space in Faga'alu Bay is limited, and the access channel through the fringing reef is shallow and unmarked (64).

--- SENTENCE 864 ---
Utulei is the center of sailing activity for residents.

--- SENTENCE 865 ---
A yacht club at Utulei offers land storage of small sailboats and these are launched from the beach park and the nearby hotel beach.

--- SENTENCE 866 ---
Fautasi (longboat) races are held in Pago Pago Harbor (41).

--- SENTENCE 867 ---
Except for atule fishing, the majority of subsistence fishing activity in the harbor occurs where shorelines have not been extended onto the fringing reef by filling.

--- SENTENCE 868 ---
The effect of landfilling upon subsistence fishing is indicated by the greatly reduced fishing activity adjacent to the inner bay village areas of Atu'u, Satala, Pago Pago, Autapini, and Malaloa.

--- SENTENCE 869 ---
However, \*fishing is more intensive on reefs of the outer harbor than elsewhere around Tutuila (26).

--- SENTENCE 870 ---
Although mangrove crabs (pa'alemago; Scylla serrata) have been caught in the inner harbor by the National Marine Fisheries Service, crabbing is not a conspicuous activity (65).

--- SENTENCE 871 ---
The turbid waters of inner Pago Pago Harbor are unsuitable for sport diving (64).

# INNERMOST PAGO PAGO HARBOR

# SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 874 ---
The shoreline north of the stream mouth at Pago Pago Park consists of alluvium with basalt cobbles sloping gently up to a 2-to 4-foot (0.6 to 1.2 m) scarp.

--- SENTENCE 875 ---
In places, basalt boulders have been added at the base of the scarp for shoreline protection.

--- SENTENCE 876 ---
Between Pago Pago Park and the marine railway at Satala is steep embankment up to 6 feet (2 m) high at the shore.

--- SENTENCE 877 ---
Basalt boulders lie along the base of this scarp.

--- SENTENCE 878 ---
Erosion is apparent along the eastern end (49).

--- SENTENCE 879 ---
Southeast of the stream mouth at Pago Pago Park the landfill is protected by seawalls and revetments.

--- SENTENCE 880 ---
A gently sloping foreshore of alluvium -- up to 50 feet (15 m) wide at low tide -- extends from the base of the protective structures.

--- SENTENCE 881 ---
The shoreline between the park and Malaloa is a gently sloping beach of basalt cobbles, limestone rubble, and alluvium.

--- SENTENCE 882 ---
The shore west of the yacht basin at Malaloa is protected by a four-foot (1.2 m) high, rock seawall fronted by a cobble foreshore exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 883 ---
A short reach near the yacht basin is unprotected.

--- SENTENCE 884 ---
A 20-foot (6 m) wide beach of basalt cobble and limestone rubble extends along the shore between the yacht basin and the Marine Fisheries pier at Fagatogo.

--- SENTENCE 885 ---
The backshore is an eroding, 3-foot (1 m) high scarp (49).

--- SENTENCE 886 ---
In the main dock area east of the Malaloa fishing pier, a revetment slopes from sea level up to 5 feet.

--- SENTENCE 887 ---
A grouted revetment west of the inter-island and main dock facilities is collapsing in places from erosion (49).

## SHORELINE

The usual intertidal invertebrates are scarce or absent altogether along the north shore of Pago Pago Harbor from Pago Pago Park to Atu'u (MAP 2)(50).

--- SENTENCE 888 ---
# INNER HARBOR REEF

The 1.2 mile (2 km) length of reef fronting the innermost harbor between the canneries (at Anua) and the main docks (at Fagatogo) has been devoid of living coral for many years (11).

--- SENTENCE 889 ---
Early investigations of inner harbor reefs concluded that live corals were destroyed as a result of extensive alteration of natural conditions since 1900 (6).

--- SENTENCE 890 ---
Reef areas located farther into the harbor than Trading Point or Nu'ututai Point are seriously degraded, with very few live coral heads (58).

--- SENTENCE 891 ---
The black anoxic silt bottom near the canneries is nearly devoid of invertebrate life.

--- SENTENCE 892 ---
Few fishes are present.

--- SENTENCE 893 ---
Only six species of fish are recorded, the most abundant of which is a jack (Caranx sp.)(20).

--- SENTENCE 894 ---
One source states that fishes are abundant in the inner harbor but diversity is low (58).

# FRINGING REEF FRONT OFF MALALOA WHARF

The reef front northeast of Malaloa Wharf harbors an abundance of fishes.

--- SENTENCE 896 ---
The assemblage of at least 46 species is dominated by the rabbitfish, <u>Siganus argenteus</u>.

--- SENTENCE 897 ---
Although far less abundant, the snapper, <u>Lutjanus kasmira</u>, is common (76).

--- SENTENCE 898 ---
The perimeter of inner Pago Pago Harbor is frequented in the daytime by fishermen seeking anae (adult mullet) and fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota (small jack), pelupelu (sardine), and, seasonally, i'asina (juvenile goatfish) and atule (big-eye scad) with throw and hand nets (20).

--- SENTENCE 899 ---
The largest proportion of fishing effort is with bamboo poles.

--- SENTENCE 900 ---
Rod and reel fishing and throw-netting receive somewhat less effort and little effort is expended on other fishing methods (76).

#### MALALOA FISHING PIER

A concrete fishing pier at Malaloa serves small commercial vessels.

--- SENTENCE 901 ---
Shoreside facilities in this area include a dry storage area and ramp for small boats (69).

--- SENTENCE 902 ---
# HARBOR (NORTH) COAST BETWEEN SATALA AND TRADING POINT

## SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 903 ---
The shoreline fronting the marine railway is protected by a rock revetment, 2- to 3-feet (up to 1 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 904 ---
A scarp is eroded above the rocks.

--- SENTENCE 905 ---
The canneries are constructed on landfill, which is presently being extended toward the marine railway (49).

--- SENTENCE 906 ---
The waters fronting the village areas of Satala, Anua, and Atu'u along the northern margin of inner Pago Pago Harbor are fished in the daytime by rod and reel and/or handline.

--- SENTENCE 907 ---
Malauli (large jack), lupota (small jack), and palagi (yellowfin surgeonfish) are caught in the waters fronting the marine railway and tuna canneries.

--- SENTENCE 908 ---
Atule (big-eye scad) and ga or kavakava (little tuna) are taken here seasonally (20).

# FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 914 ---
The reef fringing the south shore of inner Pago Pago Harbor between the wharf area and Rainmaker Hotel was partially dredged in 1969.

--- SENTENCE 915 ---
The bottom is mostly a sand slope with scattered outcrops of reef rock extending 165 feet (50 m) offshore into deep water (11).

--- SENTENCE 916 ---
The reef extends around Nu'ututai Point (49).

## FRINGING REEF

A few coral colonies (<u>Porites</u> aff.

--- SENTENCE 917 ---
<u>lobata</u> and several other species) have established themselves on outcroppings of limestone in the dredged area between the main docks and the Rainmaker Hotel on Goat Island Point (11).

--- SENTENCE 918 ---
Although fishes are not particularly abundant in the dredged area, the shallow-water fauna off Fagatogo includes at least 28 species of fishes.

--- SENTENCE 919 ---
The damselfish, <u>Glyphidodontops biocellatus</u>, is most abundant, followed by the jack, <u>Selar crumenophthalmus</u> (20).

The reef front harbors an abundance of fish.

The American Samoa Government, Office of Marine Resources maintains a narrow boat ramp and moorings for scientific vessels at Fagatogo.

--- SENTENCE 923 ---
Fish-aggregating buoys are deployed from this facility (41).

--- SENTENCE 924 ---
The wharf area between Fagatogo and Utulei (MAP 2) is frequented by fishermen using bamboo pole, rod and reel, and handline.

--- SENTENCE 925 ---
Rod and reel fishing and handlining yields day and night catches of malauli (large jack), gatala (honeycomb grouper), lupota (small jack), taiva (one-spot snapper), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and, in season, atule (big-eye scad).

--- SENTENCE 927 ---
Night catches include malau (squirrelfish) and, in season, pa'umalo (filefish).

--- SENTENCE 928 ---

--- SENTENCE 929 ---
Day catches include fuafua (juvenile mullet), and night catches include mataeleele, taiva, matapula (bigeye snapper), and, seasonally, atule (20).

--- SENTENCE 930 ---
Other fishing methods receive little effort (76).

# FRINGING REEF

Coral cover is generally impoverished along a two-mile (3.2 km) length of reef centering off Lepua.

--- SENTENCE 946 ---
Pocillopora brevicornis is the most prominent of sparse coral growth inshore west of Lepua and is associated with <u>Porites lutea</u>, <u>Pavona frondifera</u>, <u>Leptastrea purpurea</u>, and <u>Montipora</u> sp.

--- SENTENCE 947 ---
No <u>Acropora</u> or branched Porites are evident west of Lepua.

--- SENTENCE 948 ---
A similar distribution of corals but in even lower abundances is found off Leloaloa (11).

--- SENTENCE 949 ---

--- SENTENCE 950 ---

Encrusting coralline algae cover much of the reef rock and rubble surfaces.

--- SENTENCE 955 ---
Patches of Amphiroa sp. are common.

--- SENTENCE 956 ---
A few sand patches are embedded with chaetopterid worm tubes and small colonies (ASCRI-2B6).

--- SENTENCE 957 ---
Live stony corals are not evident at the reef margin, but considerable soft coral occurs along the edge (ASCRI-2B7).

--- SENTENCE 958 ---
Occasional large heads of <u>Porites</u> aff.

--- SENTENCE 959 ---
<u>lutea</u> are visible seaward of the reef edge.

--- SENTENCE 960 ---
In the areas adjacent to the tuna canneries, no recently dead or live coral is present, except inshore at a depth of 10 inches (25 cm), where <u>Leptastrea</u> purpurea and small heads of Porites lutea are seen (11).

--- SENTENCE 961 ---
Fishes are not abundant nor is the fauna diverse on the reef flat fronting Leloaloa Village because of the lack of bottom cover and the heavy sedimentation.

--- SENTENCE 962 ---
At least 19 species are present in low numbers.

--- SENTENCE 963 ---
Juveniles are most conspicuous, but feeding scars on corals indicate adult surgeonfish and parrotfish are present in the area.

--- SENTENCE 966 ---
At least 56 species of fish inhabit the reef flat off Lepua Point.

--- SENTENCE 967 ---
Glyphidodontops leucopomus is most common, followed in abundance by <u>Stegastes albofaciatus</u>.

--- SENTENCE 968 ---
The fish fauna is highly diverse but fishes are only moderately abundant on the reef front between Lepua Village and Leasi Point.

--- SENTENCE 969 ---
<u>Pomacentrus melanopterus</u> is most abundant of at least 92 species.

--- SENTENCE 970 ---
<u>Ctenochaetus striatus</u> is second most abundant (76).

#### INNER HARBOR OFF LELOALOA

Underwater visibility is poor (about 15 feet or 5 m) on the inner reef flat off Leloaloa Village.

--- SENTENCE 972 ---
Areas of turbid water are evident offshore (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 973 ---
(See: PAGO PAGO/GENERAL/WATER CONDITIONS/INNER HARBOR)

#### SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 974 ---
The shoreline from Atu'u to Lepua villages is generally accessible.

--- SENTENCE 975 ---
Care is required in crossing the steep road embankment fronting Leloaloa to reach the reef flat (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 976 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF LELOALOA AND LEPUA

The reef flat in front of the village of Leloaloa and off Lepua is frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 977 ---
Fishing also occurs in deeper waters beyond the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 978 ---
Throw-netting (kili) is the most active fishery, followed in popularity by spearing and rod and reel The largest proportion of fishing effort at Leloaloa Village is given to reef gleaning, followed by day spearing according to one source.

--- SENTENCE 979 ---
Bamboo poles are used as much as rod and reel in pole fishing.

--- SENTENCE 980 ---
Other fisheries are less active (76).

--- SENTENCE 981 ---
Throw-netting is primarily a daytime activity which results in catches of anae (adult mullet), fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota (small jack), pelupelu (sardine), and, seasonally, i'asina (juvenile goatfish) and atule (big-eye scad).

--- SENTENCE 982 ---
Spearing brings in day and night catches of alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), lupota, anae, fe'e (octopus), and eel.

--- SENTENCE 983 ---
catches include malauli (large jack) and laea (large parrotfish).

--- SENTENCE 984 ---
Night catches include manini (convict tang), fuafua, and papata (slipper lobster) (20).

--- SENTENCE 985 ---
Throw-netting occurs off the man-made groin at Leloaloa.

--- SENTENCE 986 ---
O'io (bonefish), are caught by gill netting on the inner reef fronting Lepua.

--- SENTENCE 987 ---
Faisua (giant clam) were reportedly once abundant on Leloaloa reef.

--- SENTENCE 988 ---
The reef fronting Lepua is said to be one of the better shell collecting areas in American Samoa (ASCRI).

#### COVE AND SHORELINE

A deep cove at Utulei represents the drowned portion of a branch stream valley opening into the much larger valley constituting Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 994 ---
A former drainage course provides a channel (ava) through the reef (6).

--- SENTENCE 995 ---
The shoreline fronting The Rainmaker Hotel is protected by boulder revetments, with the exception of a 200-foot (60 m) length of man-made beach along the southern portion of the hotel grounds (49).

--- SENTENCE 996 ---
A short public swimming beach at Utulei is bounded at its northern end by a revetment and at its southern end by an eroding seawall.

--- SENTENCE 997 ---
The calcareous sand beach is 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) wide at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 998 ---
The beach slopes gently to a channel of silty-sand dredged parallel to shore in the inner reef flat (49;ASCRI-2B1).

--- SENTENCE 999 ---
A 20-foot (6 m) wide beach of calcareous sand and rubble slopes to a backshore elevation of 4-5 feet at the southeastern end of Utulei.

--- SENTENCE 1000 ---
Near Ututafa Point, the shoreline is characterized by a scarp eroded from the high water line to the road elevation of 8 to 12 feet (3 to 4 m).

--- SENTENCE 1001 ---
Fronting this scarp is a 10- to 20-foot wide basalt boulder beach.

--- SENTENCE 1002 ---
The scarp is protected along most of its length by boulders or riprap.

--- SENTENCE 1003 ---
An exception is a section of recent fill at Ututafa Point where bare earth is exposed.

--- SENTENCE 1004 ---
A rock seawall extends from sea level up to the 7-foot elevation in the reach between Ututafa Point and Tulutulu Point (49).

--- SENTENCE 1005 ---
The fringing reef is 300 feet (90 m) wide off The Rainmaker Hotel beach and 450 feet (140 m) wide off Ututafa Point (49).

--- SENTENCE 1006 ---
The inner reef offshore of the Rainmaker beach has been dredged to provide a sandy area for swimming (34).

--- SENTENCE 1007 ---
Revetments along the shore merge with shallow areas of rubble and boulders (ASCRI-2B3).

--- SENTENCE 1008 ---
The bottom off the beach at Utulei is silty-sand rubble and boulders offshore (ASCRI-2B1).

--- SENTENCE 1009 ---

--- SENTENCE 1010 ---
The margin of the reef southeast of The Rainmaker Hotel appears to be eroding, with sedimentation more evident than in 1971-72 (44).

--- SENTENCE 1011 ---
The shallow reef margin is elevated and irregular.

--- SENTENCE 1012 ---
A portion of the reef margin off the Hotel has been dredged to provide a sand-bottom access passage 1 to 3 feet (0.3 to 1.0 m) deep across the reef (ASCRI-2B3).

--- SENTENCE 1013 ---
The sharply-defined reef margin is characterized by rocky overhangs dropping abruptly down the reef slope to the harbor bottom (34).

--- SENTENCE 1017 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF THE RAINMAKER HOTEL)

--- SENTENCE 1018 ---
Corals are sparse on the inner reef and dredged swimming area, and coral cover totals 5% or less on the outer reef flat and reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 1019 ---
Some Acropora humilis, Porites lutea, and encrusting Montipora sp. are present.

--- SENTENCE 1020 ---
Soft corals are conspicuous at the reef margin, increasing in abundance southward along the margin toward Utulei (34).

--- SENTENCE 1021 ---
Concentrations of small starfish (Linckia laevigata), have been reported on the reef flat offshore of the Hotel (3).

--- SENTENCE 1022 ---
Shallow areas of rubble and boulders on either side of The Rainmaker Hotel Beach shelter numerous juvenile fishes (mostly butterflyfish, surgeonfish, and rabbitfish)(ASCRI-2B3).

--- SENTENCE 1023 ---
Colonies of a sea anemone (matamalu; <u>Rhodactis</u> sp.), as well as other anemones and anemone fish, are conspicuous on the reef front off The Rainmaker Hotel at depths between 10 and 25 feet (3 to 8 m).

--- SENTENCE 1024 ---
Coral cover ranges from 20% to 40%.

--- SENTENCE 1025 ---
Both stony and soft corals colonize the reef front at depths of 25 to 90 feet (8 to 28 m).

--- SENTENCE 1026 ---
Major stony corals occuring here include <u>Pachyseris speciosa</u>, <u>Echinophyllia aspera</u>, <u>Porites</u> (<u>Synaraea</u>) <u>horizontalata</u>, and <u>Diploastrea heliopora</u>.

--- SENTENCE 1027 ---
A number of butterflyfishes are conspicuous along the upper reef slopes, their abundance declining with depth (ASCRI-2B4).

--- SENTENCE 1028 ---
Fishes are not abundant on the reef flat off Goat Island Point.

--- SENTENCE 1029 ---
Glyphidodontops leucopomus dominates an assemblage of at least 55 species.

--- SENTENCE 1030 ---
The fish fauna is much more diverse, although fishes are not more abundant, on the reef front off Goat Island Point.

--- SENTENCE 1031 ---
Most common are Glyphidodontops cyanea, Pomacentrus melanopterus, and Meiacanthus ditrema (76).

--- SENTENCE 1032 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF UTULEI BEACH)

--- SENTENCE 1033 ---
The green alga, <u>Halimeda</u> cf.

--- SENTENCE 1034 ---
<u>discoidea</u>, is conspicuous on the sandy, inner reef flat off Utulei Beach.

--- SENTENCE 1035 ---
The sea urchin, <u>Mespilia globulus</u>, is quite common on the rubble and boulder bottom farther seaward.

--- SENTENCE 1036 ---
<u>Ralfsia sp.</u> and a turf of brown algae are abundant on many rocks.

--- SENTENCE 1037 ---
Soft corals are common at the reef margin (ASCRI-2B1).

--- SENTENCE 1038 ---
The outer reef flat is encrusted by pink <u>Porolithon</u> algae and corals (<u>Acropora</u> and <u>Pocillopora</u>) are present.

--- SENTENCE 1039 ---
Corals are relatively diverse at the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 1040 ---
Damselfishes, butterflyfishes, wrasses, filefishes, mullet, and surgeonfishes are common (44).

--- SENTENCE 1041 ---
<u>lutea</u> is a dominant coral on the upper portion of the reef slope off Utulei Beach.

--- SENTENCE 1042 ---
At depths between 4 and 40 feet (1 to 12 m), the silted slopes are populated by soft corals, upright sponges, and a reddish cyanophyte (blue-green alga).

--- SENTENCE 1043 ---
A sea urchin (<u>Diadema</u> sp.) inhabits crevices in the limestone (ASCRI-2B2).

# FRINGING REEF (NEAR UTUTAFA POINT)

--- SENTENCE 1047 ---
High densities of soft corals and sea cucumbers (Polyplectana sp. and Holothuria sp.) occur on the reef off the southeastern end of Utulei Village and Ututafa Point (5;34).

--- SENTENCE 1048 ---
A few coral heads (Porites andrewsi and Pocillopora sp.) inhabit the reef flat here.

--- SENTENCE 1049 ---
Near the reef margin are large plates of dead Acropora humilis.

--- SENTENCE 1050 ---
Montipora sp. is abundant along the reef margin and several large banks of Diploastrea heliopora are present (34).

--- SENTENCE 1051 ---
When surveyed in 1973, this reef harbored numerous alcyonarians, large heads of Porites, some large heads of Favites rotumana, and smaller numbers of Acropora (11).

--- SENTENCE 1052 ---
A 1978 revisit of a survey site on Utulei reef revealed a decline in coral abundance since an earlier survey (1971/72) when middle to outer reef areas were dominated by branching Porites sp. and Acropora sp.

--- SENTENCE 1053 ---
These corals have declined significantly: A. formosa is now nearly absent, whereas Porites andrewsi, although greatly reduced in abundance from the early 1970's, remains the most common coral.

--- SENTENCE 1054 ---
Several Fungia spp., abundant in 1971/72, are now absent.

--- SENTENCE 1055 ---
Diploastrea and other brain corals remain common.

--- SENTENCE 1056 ---
Fish abundance and diversity are reduced compared to 1971/72 (44).

--- SENTENCE 1057 ---
A diverse fish fauna of at least 68 species inhabits the reef flat off southeastern Utulei.

--- SENTENCE 1058 ---
Ctenochaetus striatus and Stegastes albofasciatus are the most abundant fishes.

--- SENTENCE 1059 ---
Scarus sp., Stegastes nigricans, and Halichoeres hoeveni are common.

--- SENTENCE 1060 ---
The reef front shelters a highly diverse assemblage of fish numbering at least 93 species.

--- SENTENCE 1061 ---
However fishes are less abundant than on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1062 ---
Ctenochaetus striatus and Amblyglyphidodon leucogaster are most common, followed in abundance by Pomacentrus melanopterus and P. vaiuli (76).

--- SENTENCE 1063 ---
#### MIDDLE HARBOR - WEST SIDE

Nearshore waters off Utulei Beach and Hotel beach are well protected from waves (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1064 ---
Like other coves indenting the margin of Pago Pago Harbor, Utulei is well protected from open ocean swell.

--- SENTENCE 1065 ---
However, high surf can cause rip currents which flow seaward through the ava (6).

--- SENTENCE 1066 ---
Offshore waters southeast of Utulei toward Tulutulu (Blunts) Point can be rough (34).

--- SENTENCE 1067 ---
Outer reef flat areas from Tulutulu Point to the harbor mouth are exposed to high surf (6).

--- SENTENCE 1068 ---
Dredging off Utulei has damaged the reef and resulted in a large basin with inadequate circulation, contributing to siltation and murky water in the area particularly accessible to tourists (7).

--- SENTENCE 1069 ---
Oil slicks emanating from the Standard Oil dock at Nu'ututai Point are also a deterrent to swimming and snorkeling (44).

--- SENTENCE 1070 ---
Off the southeastern end of Utulei near Ututafa Point, underwater visibility is 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m), improving to 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) on the outer reef (10).

--- SENTENCE 1071 ---
Waters are turbid and considerable trash litters the bottom (11).

--- SENTENCE 1072 ---
Visibility is generally poorer now than in 1971-1972 (44).

# UTULEI BEACH PARK AND HOTEL BEACH

A man-made beach reserved for use of notel guests is located at The Rainmaker Hotel.

--- SENTENCE 1080 ---
The private hotel beach and a public beach park nearby provide sandy areas for swimming and sunbathing (64).

--- SENTENCE 1081 ---
Utulei is one of the few public beaches suitable for swimming, so it is heavily used (49).

--- SENTENCE 1082 ---
Rafts are anchored inshore for swimmers.

--- SENTENCE 1083 ---
Utulei is the only officially-designated beach park in American Samoa (41).

--- SENTENCE 1084 ---
A shallow passage dredged through the reef off the hotel is suitable for swimming and provides swimmers with access to the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 1085 ---
Elsewhere, the elevated and irregular reef margin can be reached only by walking over the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1086 ---
The reef fronting the northern end of Utulei Beach Park also has been dredged and provides a good swimming area (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1087 ---
The reef off Utulei is one of the most popular areas sport diving by non-Samoans (76).

--- SENTENCE 1088 ---
The waters around Goat Island Point (offshore of The Rainmaker Hotel) are used by tourists for snorkeling and underwater exploration (39).

--- SENTENCE 1089 ---
Some spearfishing occurs around Goat Island Point, with surgeonfishes comprising the majority of the catch (13).

--- SENTENCE 1090 ---
SCUBA divers gain access to the reef front from Utulei Beach Park and hotel beach, but diving is frequently limited by turbid conditions and poor visibility during wet weather (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1091 ---
Reef areas off the hotel and Utulei Beach Park are under consideration by the Office of Marine Resources as a tourist-oriented underwater observation park (39;41;44).

--- SENTENCE 1092 ---
Small waves off The Rainmaker Hotel are surfed by novices during high tide (51).

--- SENTENCE 1093 ---
Sailing occurs off the hotel beach and small craft anchor off Utulei Beach Park.

--- SENTENCE 1094 ---
The private Pago Pago Yacht Club behind the southwestern end of Utulei Beach Park is the center of resident sailing activity in American Samoa (41).

--- SENTENCE 1095 ---
The reef fronting Utulei Village is considered a "critical reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1096 ---
The reef flat southeast of Utulei Beach around Tulutulu Point (Blunts Point) is the most frequently fished area.

--- SENTENCE 1097 ---
Diving with home-made spears (mata), seine netting (upega), and drive-netting (lau) are rated as the most popular activities by one source (20), whereas bamboo rod fishing, day gleaning, and spearing receive nearly equal fishing effort according to another source Rod and reel fishing and throw-netting are slightly less popular (20;76).

--- SENTENCE 1098 ---
Seine netting, night spearing and gleaning are practiced less (76).

--- SENTENCE 1099 ---
Day spearing results in catches of alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), and fe'e (octopus).

--- SENTENCE 1100 ---
Night spearing generally brings in anae (adult mullet), crab, ula (spiny lobster), and lupota (small jack).

--- SENTENCE 1103 ---
# HARBOR (EAST) COAST BETWEEN LEASI POINT AND AVA POINT

# SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 1104 ---
Fronting Aua Village is a revetment of small basalt boulders which rises 2 to 8 feet (0.6 to 2.5 m) above the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 1105 ---
The exposed bank at the top of the revetment is eroding.

--- SENTENCE 1106 ---
Near Leasi Point are remnants of a former sand beach (26;49).

--- SENTENCE 1107 ---
High tide completely covers sand in front of the revetment (26).

#### **AUA ESTUARY**

Waters from Lalolamauta, Suaia, and Matagimalie Streams, flow into Pago Pago Harbor through Aua Estuary.

--- SENTENCE 1108 ---
The estuary is 3 feet (1 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 1109 ---
Its water is usually murky and large silt loads are carried into the harbor by storm runoff (5).

--- SENTENCE 1110 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

A small cove indents the shoreline off Aua Village.

--- SENTENCE 1111 ---
fringing reef varies in width from 500 to 800 feet (150 to 245 m)(49).

--- SENTENCE 1112 ---
A well-defined channel (ava) cuts through the fringing reef off the mouth of Lalolamauta Stream.

--- SENTENCE 1113 ---
Here, the reef flat narrows to about 300 feet (90 m) (13).

--- SENTENCE 1114 ---
Northwest of Lalolamauta Stream mouth, most of the inner reef area is covered by extensive flats which are relatively free of silt.

--- SENTENCE 1115 ---
limestone outcrops are interspersed (ASCRI-2B8).

--- SENTENCE 1116 ---
In general, the inner and mid-reef areas off Aua consist of sand and/or rubble Some limestone and basalt rocks are exposed on the extensive sand flats, which are a mixture of calcareous and terrigenous sediment up to 2.6 feet (0.8 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 1117 ---
Limestone rubble flats on the middle reef are a mixture of rubble, calcareous sand, and occasional limestone blocks at depths of 1 to 5 feet (0.3 to 1.4 m)(6).

--- SENTENCE 1118 ---
South of Lalolamauta Stream mouth, the base of the road revetment rests on an inner reef flat of silty-sand (predominantly of volcanic origin) interspersed with volcanic cobble and small boulders (ASCRI-2S2).

--- SENTENCE 1119 ---
The inner sand flats southeast of the stream mouth, are covered by a layer of mud 3 to 6 inches (7.6 to 15.2 cm) deep over dark fine sand.

--- SENTENCE 1120 ---
Depth at high tide is 3 to 4 feet (1.0 to 1.2 m)(ASCRI-2B9).

--- SENTENCE 1121 ---
The middle to outer reef is about 4 feet (1.2 m) deep, with a bottom of consolidated limestone and considerable silty-sand (ASCRI-2B10).

--- SENTENCE 1122 ---
The outer reef flat off Aua is a low relief platform of consolidated limestone at depths of 0.5 to 2.5 feet (0.2 m to 0.8 m) (26).

--- SENTENCE 1123 ---
A rubble and limestone pavement is cemented by encrusting coralline algae (ASCRI-2B11).

--- SENTENCE 1124 ---
Northwest of Lalolamauta Stream mouth, most of the inner reef area is covered by extensive sand flats which are relatively

# FRINGING REEF FRONT

--- SENTENCE 1128 ---
The front of the reef off Aua decends steeply from the margin to depths of 80 to 90 feet (24 to 27 m).

--- SENTENCE 1129 ---
The slope varies from 30 to 90 degrees.

--- SENTENCE 1130 ---
The upper face of the reef in places overhangs the slope by as much as 5 feet (2 m)(13).

--- SENTENCE 1131 ---
A narrow shelf at depths of 3 to 16 feet (1 to 5 m) occurs in places along the reef front (26).

--- SENTENCE 1132 ---
The reef margin is broken by several avas, sheer-sided channels from 3 to 16 feet (1 to 5 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 1133 ---
Avas are the primary areas of outflow for water pushed onto the reef by waves breaking on the margin and for fresh water disharged onto the reef by streams.

--- SENTENCE 1134 ---
Bottom relief is about 5 to 6 feet (1.5 to 2.0 m) on the upper slope (to -10 feet or -3 m) of the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 1135 ---
Seaward, to a depth of 20 feet (6 m), occur massive broken limestone outcrops and mounds of dead Porites deeply undercut with caves and tunnels.

--- SENTENCE 1136 ---
Vertical relief is considerable, with mounds rising to within 2 feet (0.6 m) of the surface (ASCRI-285).

--- SENTENCE 1137 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

The inner reef northwest of Lalolamatua Stream mouth, is populated by numerous sea cucumbers (<u>Stichopus chloronotus</u>).

--- SENTENCE 1138 ---
The cowrie, <u>Cypraea annulus</u>, is common.

--- SENTENCE 1139 ---
Coralline algae encrust hard surfaces.

--- SENTENCE 1140 ---
Soft corals are present in relatively low abundance (ASCRI-2B8).

--- SENTENCE 1141 ---
Corals are sparse in inshore areas of the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1142 ---
Southeast of the stream mouth, a silt-covered green alga (<u>Halimeda</u> sp.) is present on submerged boulders (ASCRI-2B9;26).

--- SENTENCE 1143 ---

--- SENTENCE 1145 ---

--- SENTENCE 1146 ---

--- SENTENCE 1147 ---

The reef flat off Aua is well protected from Turbid waters and heavy sedimentation characterize the reef flat fronting Aua Village, with only slight improvement toward the reef margin (ASCRI).

sand flats occur off Aua Estuary which are frequently swept by silt-laden stream discharges.

--- SENTENCE 1178 ---
The reef flat between Leasi Point and Ava Point is considered "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1179 ---
The Aua reef is well protected from large surf, allowing line and net fishermen, divers, and fishermen using paopaos (canoes) to frequent the reef margin and front more often than they do in open bays and off the coast elsewhere on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 1180 ---
A dredged lagoon south of Ava Point is fished from shore by line.

--- SENTENCE 1181 ---

--- SENTENCE 1182 ---
productive areas The submerged reef sill lying between the fringing reef and offshore patch reefs is an area of heavy paopao activity, from which handlining takes place (26).

--- SENTENCE 1183 ---
A longboat house and a concrete launching ramp are situated at Leasi Point (49).

--- SENTENCE 1184 ---
Shells are collected, primarily by non-Samoans, on the Aua reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1185 ---
The entire reef flat southward from Leasi Point to Breakers Point, in front of the villages of Aua, Anasosopo, and Tafananai, is fished regularly.

--- SENTENCE 1186 ---
Fishing also occurs in deeper water off the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 1187 ---
Throw-netting (kili) and reef gleaning are the activities.

(mata), rod Day gleaning receives the greatest proportion of fishing effort at Aua Village.

# ON AMU'ULA ROCK

Corals are well developed along the northwest face of Amu'ula Rock, with an abundance of Millepora sp., Pavona sp., Fungia sp., and Acropora spp.

# HARBOR (EAST) COAST AVA POINT TO ANASOSOPO POINT

#### SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 1212 ---
Although "Ava Point" appears on most recent maps of Pago Pago Harbor, the older name for this area is Aua Point (200).

--- SENTENCE 1213 ---
A 10- to 20-foot (3 to 6 m) wide beach of basalt cobbles and limestone rubble is backed by basalt boulders dumped to protect the backshore from erosion.

--- SENTENCE 1214 ---
However, the boulders have slumped to the base of a bare scarp exposed to wave attack (49).

#### FRINGING REEF

Immediately north of Ava Point the nearshore region is composed of large limestone boulders (up to 6.5 feet or 2 m across) projecting above a sand bottom with moderate relief.

--- SENTENCE 1215 ---
Depth ranges from 0.5 to 3 feet (0.2 m to 1.0 m) (26).

--- SENTENCE 1216 ---
At Ava Point, the reef extends approximately 1,400 feet (425 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 1217 ---
The reef flat is widest south and west of the point, where wave action is strongest and no large streams enter the harbor.

--- SENTENCE 1218 ---
Reef flat depth varies from one to 4 feet (0.3 to 1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 1219 ---
Inshore areas are characterized by rubble (13;26;34) and small boulders (up to 3 feet or 1 m across) grading seaward into larger boulders and grooved solid limestone (13).

--- SENTENCE 1220 ---
The reef is nearly bissected by a sand channel 6 to 30 feet (2 to 9 m) wide which merges with a sand and rubble flat bordered by reef ledges south of Ava Point.

--- SENTENCE 1221 ---
Seaward of the large sand patch is considerable coral rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1222 ---
The outermost 165 to 195 feet (50 to 60 m) of the reef flat contains increasing numbers of boulders and old coral heads (13).

--- SENTENCE 1223 ---
About 600 feet (180 m) south of Ava Point, a nearshore borrow pit forms a lagoon inside the inner reef (11).

--- SENTENCE 1224 ---
This depression, with a maximum depth of 18 feet (5.5 m), was dredged to obtain roadbed fill material (13).

--- SENTENCE 1225 ---
The borrow pit apparently traps sand moving to the north (49).

--- SENTENCE 1226 ---
The sheer sides borrow pit drop to a bottom of calcareous sand and mud with scattered outcrops of reef rock (11).

--- SENTENCE 1227 ---
South of Ava Point the outer reef is exposed to considerable wave force.

--- SENTENCE 1228 ---
The reef is mostly a consolidated limestone platform 1 to 3 feet (0.3 to 1.0 m) deep (26).

--- SENTENCE 1320 ---
# FAGA'ALU STREAM

Faga'alu Valley is the product of erosion by spring-fed Faga'alu Stream, which drains one of the larger watersheds emptying into Pago Pago Harbor (54).

--- SENTENCE 1321 ---
The waters of Faga'alu Stream are diverted upstream to supply drinking water for the government water system.

--- SENTENCE 1322 ---
The lower reach of this stream has been greatly modified by channel realignment and bank protection structures (6).

--- SENTENCE 1323 ---
The northeastern margin of Faga'alu Bay consists of a steep bank between a 10-foot wide foreshore of basalt and limestone rubble and the coastal highway at the 12-foot elevation.

--- SENTENCE 1324 ---
bank is stabilized by basalt boulders extending halfway up the base.

--- SENTENCE 1325 ---
The shoreline fronting Matafao School is eroding fill lined with basalt boulders and other material.

--- SENTENCE 1326 ---
A 3-foot scarp is eroded above the boulders, which have slumped to the base of the West of the school is a 10- to 15-foot (3 to 5 m) wide foreshore of basalt and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1327 ---
A small public park protruding from the northern margin of Faga'alu Bay is protected by a rudimentary seawall, separated from the seawalls near Faga'alu Stream by a narrow strip of calcareous sand and debris.

--- SENTENCE 1328 ---
Southeast of the stream mouth, at the head of the bay, there is a narrow beach of silty-sand which slopes gently to sand bottom extending offshore.

--- SENTENCE 1329 ---
An extensive fill area presumably developed from material dredged from the reef occurs along the south shore of Faga'alu Bay and is used as a public park.

--- SENTENCE 1330 ---
Most of the park shoreline consists of limestone rubble, basalt boulders, and sand, with one section of rock seawall.

--- SENTENCE 1331 ---
A 2- to 3-foot scarp is eroded in the backshore along the unprotected reach (48;49).

--- SENTENCE 1332 ---
High water extends to the base of a rocky seawall about 6 feet (2 m) high bordering the coastal highway east of the park (49).

#### FRINGING REEF

Faga'alu Bay is a deep cove which receives freshwater flow from one of the larger streams on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 1333 ---
A large channel bisects the bay, approaching shore off the mouth of Faga'alu Stream (6).

--- SENTENCE 1334 ---
Mud flats southeast of the stream mouth have been reclaimed for a park (65).

--- SENTENCE 1335 ---
The reef fringing Faga'alu Bay varies in width from 150 feet at the bay head to 1,400 feet along the flanks (49).

--- SENTENCE 1336 ---
The inner reef flat off the southeastern perimeter of Faga'alu Bay averages 1.3 feet (0.4 m) deep at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 1337 ---
The bottom is composed primarily of volcanic and limestone boulders, with a few as large as 2 feet (0.6 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 1338 ---
A small amount of sand occurs in pockets on the inner reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1339 ---

Between 330 and 410 feet (100 to 125 m) offshore the depth varies from 1.5 to 3 feet (0.5 to 0.8 m).

Northwest of the park, a sand beach merges with mud flats submerged at high tide.

The mud flats extend 165 feet (50 m) seaward to a large channel (ava) which crosses the center of the bay and approaches shore.

#### FRINGING REEF FLAT

Burrow holes, most formed by fiddler crabs (<u>Uca marionis</u>), are evident over the mud flat which extends from the beach to a large channel crossing the center of Faga'alu Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1355 ---
The upper, silt-covered surfaces of rock outcrops along the channel margin are largely devoid of corals and other invertebrates, but support a sparse growth of algae.

--- SENTENCE 1356 ---
Very few fishes inhabit the shallow mud flat.

--- SENTENCE 1357 ---
Only two species (<u>Arothron immaculatus</u> and <u>Therapon jarbua</u>) are recorded.

--- SENTENCE 1358 ---
Dominant fishes at the rock outcrops along the channel margin are the damselfish, <u>Pomacentrus pavo</u>, and the snapper, <u>Lutjanus fulvus</u>.

--- SENTENCE 1359 ---
The lionfish (<u>Pterois volitans</u>), is also present here (48).

--- SENTENCE 1360 ---
Small colonies of the corals Porities lutea, Psammocora contigua, and Pocillopora damicornis total about 1% bottom cover on the inner reef flat off the southeastern end of Faga'alu Village.

--- SENTENCE 1361 ---
Encrusting coralline algae are apparent throughout the inner reef area.

--- SENTENCE 1362 ---
Fishes are not common.

--- SENTENCE 1363 ---
Coral cover, mostly as small colonies, increases to 30% between 80 and 250 feet (25 to m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 1364 ---
Dominant species are <u>Psammocora contigua</u>, Pocillopora sp., encrusting Porites, branching P. andrewsi, and <u>Pavona</u> spp.

--- SENTENCE 1365 ---
Considerable dead coral is also evident.

--- SENTENCE 1366 ---
Rocks are encrusted with coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 1367 ---
A sea star (Linckia laevigata), synaptid sea cucumber (Polyplectana sp), and a sea urchin (Echinometra mathaei) are conspicuous invertebrates occurring in Beyond 250 feet (75 m) from shore, staghorn coral <u>(Acropora formosa)</u> occurs along with clumps of soft coral (<u>Sclerophytum</u>).

--- SENTENCE 1368 ---
Between 330 and 410 feet (100 and 125 m) from shore, conspicuous invertebrates include a sea urchin (<u>Diadema</u> sp.), sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus and Holothuria argus), and a brittle star (Ophiarthrum elegans, under rocks).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

Infestation of the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) along the reef front off Faga'alu was reported in early 1973 (45) although, in general, infestations in outer Pago Pago Harbor involved smaller numbers of starfish than infestations elsewhere around Tutuila (73).

--- SENTENCE 1382 ---
Current abundance or extent of damage to corals is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1383 ---
Older residents remember an episode of reef infestation by the crown-of-thorns starfish at Faga'alu approximately 50 years ago (34).

--- SENTENCE 1384 ---
The reef front shelters an abundant and diverse fish fauna of at least 97 species.

--- SENTENCE 1385 ---
<u>Pomacentrus coelestis, Ctenochaetus striatus</u>, and <u>Scarus psitticus</u> are most abundant.

--- SENTENCE 1386 ---
<u>Plectroglyphidodon lacrymatus</u> is common (76).

--- SENTENCE 1387 ---
An abundant and diverse fish fauna occurs around the patch reefs directly east of Faga'alu Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1388 ---
<u>Ctenochaetus striatus</u> dominates an assemblage of at least 36 species.

--- SENTENCE 1389 ---
<u>Acanthurus nigrofuscus</u> and <u>Stegastes fasciolatus</u> are also abundant (76).

--- SENTENCE 1393 ---
The water over the reef flat fringing the southeastern margin of Faga'alu Bay is especially clear, with underwater visibility about 100 feet (30 m).

--- SENTENCE 1396 ---
# FAGA'ALU PARK

Faga'alu Park was developed on an extensive fill area over mud flats near the head of Faga'alu Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1397 ---
There is no adequate beach here, and little if any swimming takes place off the park.

--- SENTENCE 1398 ---
A concrete pad at the shore is used for launching boats (41).

--- SENTENCE 1399 ---
The inner bay and northern side of the reef are well protected from waves (6), but longshore currents can be strong (48).

--- SENTENCE 1400 ---
The southern side of the reef is exposed to waves (6).

--- SENTENCE 1401 ---
Good surfing waves develop during the months between November and April.

--- SENTENCE 1402 ---
The best surfing conditions result when southeast swell and an incoming tide combine with northwest winds or calm wind conditions.

--- SENTENCE 1403 ---
The shallow reef is a potential hazard (51).

--- SENTENCE 1404 ---
BAY AND REEF

The reef fronting Faga'alu Village is considered a "critiuse reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1405 ---
According to one source, the reef flat is the most frequently fished area (20).

--- SENTENCE 1406 ---
However, another informant reports that most fishing is off the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 1407 ---
Some fishermen catch young jacks by casting feather lures from shore near the head of the bay (48).

--- SENTENCE 1408 ---
Reef gleaning is a preferred activity (20), with more fishing effort during the day than at night (76).

--- SENTENCE 1409 ---
Seine netting (upega) follows in popularity, according to one source (20), but rod and reel fishing is next most popular, followed by day spearing and bamboo pole fishing, according to another source (76).

--- SENTENCE 1410 ---
Throw-netting and spearing are ranked as less popular fishing methods by one source (20).

--- SENTENCE 1411 ---
Less fishing effort is applied to spearing and rod and reel fishing than reef gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 1412 ---
Bamboo pole fishing follows spearing and rod and reel fishing in level of activity.

--- SENTENCE 1413 ---
Throw-netting and seine netting activities are light (76).

--- SENTENCE 1414 ---
Fe'e (octopus), tuitui and sava'e (sea urchins), and eel are the usual daytime catches from gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 1415 ---
Night gleaning yields alili (sea snail).

--- SENTENCE 1416 ---
Rod and reel fishing, usually practiced in the daytime, brings in malauli (large jack), lupota (small jack), and gatala (honeycomb grouper).

--- SENTENCE 1417 ---
Throw-netting is a daytime activity resulting in catches of fuafua mullet), manini (convict tang), alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), and, seasonally, i'asina (juvenile goatfish), and lo (rabbitfish).

--- SENTENCE 1418 ---
Rod and reel fishing is the most popular activity on the reef northeast of Faga'alu Village (20).

FLORA AND FAUNA

Usually a number of sailing yachts wait out the hurricane season at anchor in the channel in Faga'alu Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1420 ---
The area also is used as an anchorage by small craft (41;48).

--- SENTENCE 1421 ---
Some sport diving by non-Samoans occurs off Faga'alu Village (76).

--- SENTENCE 1422 ---
HARBOR (EAST) COAST BETWEEN TAFAGAMANU POINT AND BREAKERS POINT SHORELINE

South of Tafagamanu Point is a narrow foreshore of basalt boulders, cobbles, limestone rubble, and scattered pockets of calcareous sand.

--- SENTENCE 1423 ---
Segments of beachrock are exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 1424 ---
A scarp stabilized with basalt rocks rises from the beach to the road at an elevation of 10 feet (3 m).

--- SENTENCE 1425 ---
The southern end of the reach (at Tafananai) is eroding (49;ASCRI-3S1).

--- SENTENCE 1426 ---
A 200 foot (60 m) length of shoreline at the base of the embankment is beachrock, embedded with volcanic rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1427 ---
This exposure varies in width from 6 to 20 feet (2 to 6 m) and dips gently seaward.

--- SENTENCE 1428 ---
West of Tafananai, along the headland toward Namumea'avaga Point, the shoreline is calcareous sand and gravel and volcanic talus (gravel and boulders)(ASCRI-3S1).

--- SENTENCE 1429 ---
# FRINGING REEF

A broad fringing reef extends along the coast south of Aua (MAP 2) to Breakers Point (13).

--- SENTENCE 1430 ---
Off Tafananai, the reef flat is 600 feet wide (49).

--- SENTENCE 1431 ---
The inner reef flat fronting Tafananai varies in depth from one to 3 feet (0.3 to 1.0 m).

--- SENTENCE 1432 ---
Rubble, sand, and gravel cover most of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 1433 ---
Basalt boulders occur inshore along the base of the headland which forms Breakers Point (ASCRI-3B1).

--- SENTENCE 1434 ---
Limestone rubble predominates at a depth of 2 feet (0.6 m) on the mid-reef.

--- SENTENCE 1435 ---
Low (one foot or 0.3 m high) outcrops of limestone also occur (ASCRI-3B2).

--- SENTENCE 1436 ---
The outer reef is composed of consolidated limestone at a depth of one foot (0.3 m) and is extensively exposed at low tide (ASCRI-3B3).

--- SENTENCE 1437 ---
A channel (ava) crosses the reef at an angle, narrowing toward shore off Tafagamanu Point.

--- SENTENCE 1438 ---
The margins of the channel are uneven.

--- SENTENCE 1439 ---
Depth varies from one to 8 feet (0.3 to 2.4 m).

--- SENTENCE 1440 ---
The bottom is mostly consolidated limestone, but rubble and gravel pockets are evident (ASCRI-3B4).

--- SENTENCE 1441 ---
# FRINGING REFE

Coral cover is less than 5% on the reef flat fronting Tafananai where 11 species representing seven genera are recorded.

--- SENTENCE 1442 ---
Virtually all corals occur in the deeper areas along the margins of a channel (ava) which tapers toward shore off the sanitary landfill.

--- SENTENCE 1443 ---
An unusual feature here is a large stand of Acropora cf.

--- SENTENCE 1444 ---
Elsewhere, the reef is almost devoid of corals (ASCRI-3B1; B2; B3; B4).

--- SENTENCE 1445 ---
A few crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) are present along channel margins where fresh feeding scars on Acropora demonstrate predation by this coral-eating species (ASCRI-3B4).

--- SENTENCE 1446 ---
Algae are conspicuous over all of the reef flat, although cover is low.

--- SENTENCE 1468 ---
# FRINGING REEF FRONT (OFF BREAKERS POINT)

--- SENTENCE 1469 ---
The reef front was reportedly infested by the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea;  $\underline{Acanthaster}$  planci) in early 1978 (45).

--- SENTENCE 1470 ---
However, the numbers of starfish were less in outer Pago Pago Harbor compared to other areas of infestation at that time (73).

--- SENTENCE 1471 ---
Current abundance of  $\underline{Acanthaster}$  and the extent of damage to corals is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1472 ---
A highly diverse fish fauna (of at least 103 species) inhabits the reef front off Breakers Point.

--- SENTENCE 1473 ---
Pomacentrus melano-pterus is most abundant, followed by Plectroglyphidodon dickii, Ctenochaetus striatus, and Plectroglyphidodon lacrymatus (76).

--- SENTENCE 1474 ---
# FRINGING REEF - OUTER HARBOR

Oceanic water sweeping over the reef flat north of Breakers Point at the entrance of Pago Pago Harbor provides clear waters.

--- SENTENCE 1475 ---
Underwater visibility is about 50 feet (15 m)(ASCRI).

# SHORELINE AND REEF

In several places at Tafananai the height of the road above the shore is only two or three feet (0.6 to 1.0 m), allowing easy access to the water.

--- SENTENCE 1478 ---
Beachrock exposures along a 200 foot (61 m) length of shore are coated with algae, making the surface slippery.

--- SENTENCE 1479 ---
Metal and glass refuse discarded along the shoreline are additional hazards (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1480 ---
Strong currents flow through the ava which crosses the reef.

--- SENTENCE 1481 ---
The reef flat fronting Tafananai is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1482 ---
Octopus (fe'e) and edible sea urchins are collected on the reef flat fronting Tafananai Village.

--- SENTENCE 1483 ---
Atule (big-eye scad) are caught in season with throw-nets and gill nets.

--- SENTENCE 1484 ---
Groupers are caught by pole and line at the reef edge.

--- SENTENCE 1485 ---
Ula (spiny lobster) are taken at night along the reef front (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1486 ---
# WHALE ROCK

A diverse fish fauna of moderate abundance inhabits the waters around Whale Rock between Tulutulu Point and Tafananai.

--- SENTENCE 1487 ---
Damselfishes dominate an assemblage of at least 102 species.

--- SENTENCE 1488 ---
Most common is <u>Pomacentrus melanopterus</u> followed in abundance by <u>Abudefduf sexfasciatus</u>, <u>Plectroglyphidodon dickii</u>, and <u>P. lacrymatus</u> (76).

--- SENTENCE 1491 ---
THE SOUTHEAST COAST OF TUTUILA

Highway transportation along the southeast coast of Tutuila uses the paved road which extends from Pago Pago Harbor to Tula Village (MAP 9)(64).

--- SENTENCE 1492 ---
An unpaved road continues beyond Tula around the northeastern tip of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 1493 ---
A secondary road of graded soil, covered in places with coral fill, extends from the village of Faga'itua (MAP 6) to Masefau on the north shore (MAP 11).

--- SENTENCE 1494 ---
This road is steep and curving and washes out frequently when there is a heavy rain.

--- SENTENCE 1495 ---
A similar road extends from the village of Amouli (MAP 7) on the south shore through a pass to Aoa (MAP 10) on the north shore.

--- SENTENCE 1496 ---
This route too is subject to washouts during heavy rains (23).

--- SENTENCE 1497 ---
Major improvements are planned for both the Aoa and Masefau Roads (39).

# COAST BETWEEN BREAKERS POINT AND FAGAITUA POINT

#### BREAKERS POINT

Breakers Point lies off the western end of a steep hill rising 170 feet (52 m) beside the entrance to Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 1501 ---
A lighthouse is positioned on top of the hill.

--- SENTENCE 1502 ---
Sea cliffs up to 100 feet (30 m) in height occur along the coast east of Breakers Point (26;41).

--- SENTENCE 1503 ---
#### SHORELINE

Lauli'ifou Village is fronted by a narrow beach of calcareous sand, which decreases in width from 60 feet (18 m) at its western end to about 10 feet (3 m) at its eastern end.

--- SENTENCE 1504 ---
The beach is backed by a scarp, the base of which is stabilized by scattered boulders.

--- SENTENCE 1505 ---
Beachrock is exposed in places along shore.

--- SENTENCE 1506 ---
East of the village is a narrow foreshore of basalt boulders and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1507 ---
Earth fill behind the rocks is eroding.

--- SENTENCE 1508 ---
At the western end of this section, a peninsula constructed of fill juts 60 feet (18 m) seaward of the old shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 1509 ---
A grouted rock seawall 6 feet high protects the shore (49).

--- SENTENCE 1510 ---
The beach is submerged at high tide (26).

--- SENTENCE 1511 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF FA'ATA'AGA POINT

--- SENTENCE 1512 ---
The inner reef flat east of Fa'ata'aga Point is a rugged platform of consolidated limestone broken by sand-bottom channels and depressions.

--- SENTENCE 1513 ---
The depth varies from 8 to 31 inches (20 to 80 cm)(26).

--- SENTENCE 1514 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT OFF LAULI'IFOU VILLAGE

Calcareous sand covers the inner reef platform off Lauli'ifou.

--- SENTENCE 1515 ---
Large amounts of reef rubble and boulders occur on the eastern portion of the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1516 ---
By filling sections of the inner reef fronting Lauli'ifou an Acropora thicket now occurs directly off an elevated rocky shore.

--- SENTENCE 1517 ---
Patches of sand and coral rubble are interspersed with live coral, which covers approximately 50% of the bottom (26).

--- SENTENCE 1518 ---
The middle and outer reef flat fronting Lauli'ifou Beach consists of a low relief platform of semi-consolidated to consolidated limestone, portions of which are exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 1519 ---
Depth of the mid-reef varies from -2.0 to +0.7 feet (-0.6 to +0.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 1520 ---
The outer reef shoals to depths of -3 to +8 inches (-20 to +20 cm) and is strewn with scattered limestone blocks up to 3 feet (1 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 1521 ---
The reef margin exhibits a distinct algal ridge.

--- SENTENCE 1522 ---
An ava (channel) with sheer to overhanging walls cuts through the reef off Lauli'ifou.

--- SENTENCE 1523 ---
The depth of the ava varies from 3 to 33 feet (1 to 10 m).

--- SENTENCE 1524 ---
The ava acts as the main discharge area for water thrown onto the reef flat by waves breaking on the outer edge of the reef (26).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

--- SENTENCE 1527 ---
The reef front slopes moderately to steeply off Lauli'ifou, reaching depths of about 165 feet (50 m) within 165 feet (50 m) seaward of the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 1528 ---
Depths are considerably greater toward Breakers Point.

--- SENTENCE 1529 ---
The slopes are characterized by a high relief, spur-and-groove system (26).

--- SENTENCE 1530 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT OFF FA'ATA'AGA POINT

Coralline algae cover much of the platform.

--- SENTENCE 1531 ---
Assorted corals, including Montipora elschneri, Pocillopora sp., and Acropora spp., total about 25% bottom cover on the inner reef flat (26).

--- SENTENCE 1532 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT OFF LAULI'IFOU VILLAGE

Acropora formosa and A. humilis are most common on the inner reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1533 ---
Intact acroporan skeletons covered with filamentous algae account for about 30% cover.

--- SENTENCE 1534 ---
The sea urchins, Echinometra mathaei and Diadema sp., occur in low densities (26).

--- SENTENCE 1535 ---
Coralline algae and considerable non-coralline algae cover the middle reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 1536 ---
A diverse coral assemblage includes Montipora elschneri, Psammocora contigua, Porites (Synaraea) undulata, Pocillopora spp., and Acropora spp.

--- SENTENCE 1537 ---
The outer reef is heavily encrusted by coralline algae, some non-coralline algae, and wave-resistant corals (26).

--- SENTENCE 1538 ---
Juvenile crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) were observed on the Lauli'ituai reef flat in August 1977.

--- SENTENCE 1539 ---
By December 1977, an estimated 70 to 90% of the coral on the reef flat between Breakers Point and Alega (MAP 5) had been destroyed by the starfish (45).

--- SENTENCE 1540 ---
A number of the crown-of-thorns starfish were observed in early 1978 on the fringing reef flats between the villages of Lauli'ifou and Aumi (45;74).

--- SENTENCE 1541 ---
Fishes are not particularly abundant on the reef flat off the eastern side of Lauli'ifou Village.

--- SENTENCE 1542 ---
At least 44 species are present however, of which <u>Ctenochaetus</u> sp. and <u>Scarus</u> sp. are most abundant.

--- SENTENCE 1543 ---
<u>Stegastes</u> <u>albofasciatus</u> is common (76).

--- SENTENCE 1544 ---
# FRINGING REEF FRONT

--- SENTENCE 1545 ---
Although crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was reported off Breakers Point in 1978 (45), none was observed on the forereef slopes in January and February 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 1546 ---
Acanthaster was generally rare on the forereef slopes between Breakers Point and Sinatau Point (MAP 6), except off Alega (MAP 5) and Sinatau Point (74).

--- SENTENCE 1547 ---
The starfish was sparse on the upper reef front at depths between 6 and 33 feet (2 and 10 m) off Lauli'ifou in August and September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 1548 ---
About 60% of the corals in this area were alive (75).

# FRINGING REEF

Lauli'ifou reef is exposed to severe wave and wind action and is known for the dangerous currents which flow through an ava (channel) which crosses the reef there (26).

--- SENTENCE 1553 ---
FRINGING REEF BETWEEN FA'ATA'AGA POINT AND SILIATALIGALU POINT

--- SENTENCE 1554 ---
The fringing reef east of Breakers Point to Siliataligalu Point (fronting the villages of Lauli'ifou, Lauli'ituai, and Aumi) is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1555 ---
The reef flat is the most frequently visited fishing area (20), with most activity occurring on the outer and middle portions of the reef (26).

--- SENTENCE 1556 ---
Reef gleaning, seine netting (upega), and diving with home-made spears (mata) are the most popular fishing methods with throw-netting and rod and reel fishing less common methods (20).

--- SENTENCE 1557 ---
A second source reports that most fishing effort is given to gleaning (day and night) and daytime spearing (76).

--- SENTENCE 1558 ---
A third source considers gleaning and diving the only fishing methods of any consequence at Lauli'ifou (26).

--- SENTENCE 1559 ---
Daytime gleaning yields mainly fe'e (octopus), eel, tuitui and sava'e (sea urchins) (20).

--- SENTENCE 1560 ---
Night gleaning on the reef flat accounts for a large proportion of the fishing effort at Lauli'ifou Village (76).

--- SENTENCE 1561 ---
Spearing occurs both day and night.

--- SENTENCE 1562 ---
Catches of alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), and laea (large parrotfishes) are made both day and night.

--- SENTENCE 1563 ---
Daytime catches include fe'e (octopus), eel, malauli (large lupota (small jack), and mutu.

--- SENTENCE 1564 ---
Nighttime diving yields manini (convict tang), anae (adult mullet), and ula (spiny lobster).

--- SENTENCE 1565 ---
Although less popular, throw-netting (kili) in the daytime brings catches of anae and fuafua (juvenile mullet), manini, pelupelu (sardine), alogo, pone, lupota, and, in season, atule (big-eye scad).

--- SENTENCE 1566 ---
Pole and line fishing is sometimes Gatala (honeycomb grouper), filoa (large emperor practiced.

--- SENTENCE 1567 ---
fish), lupota, and mataeleele (small emperor fish) are caught both day and night.

--- SENTENCE 1568 ---
Day catches also include savane (blue-lined snapper), lupo (juvenile jack), and ulaoa (bar-tailed goatfish).

--- SENTENCE 1569 ---
Night catches include matapula (bigeye snapper), malau (squirrelfish), malai (paddletail snapper), and, in season, atule (20).

--- SENTENCE 1570 ---
Good surfing is possible off Lauli'ifou during periods of south swell and a rising tide, especially when tradewinds are light (51).

# COAST BETWEEN PAGAITUA POINT AND LAFIGA POINT

# SHORELINE

Sections of shoreline between the villages of Lauli'ifou and Lauli'ituai have been extended by filling (ASCRI-4S1).

--- SENTENCE 1574 ---
A 25-foot (8 m) wide sand beach borders the western end of Lauli'ituai Village.

--- SENTENCE 1575 ---
Beachrock is exposed in places along the shore.

--- SENTENCE 1576 ---
A backshore scarp is partly protected with basalt rocks.

--- SENTENCE 1577 ---
Unprotected areas are eroding (49).

--- SENTENCE 1578 ---
Vaitele Stream flows through a culvert into the head of the small cove fronting Lauli'ituai (ASCRI-4S1).

--- SENTENCE 1579 ---
A small sand delta has built up at the mouth of the stream.

--- SENTENCE 1580 ---
The steep backshore slope is protected by a revetment, which is eroding in some areas (49).

--- SENTENCE 1581 ---
Lafiga Point, east of the village, is about 20 feet (6 m) high (ASCRI-4S1).

--- SENTENCE 1582 ---
# FRINGING REEF

A delta of small volcanic stones and sand is exposed at low tide on the reef flat fronting the mouth of Vaitele Stream.

--- SENTENCE 1583 ---
Large basalt boulders are exposed off Lafiga Point and in the vicinity of Fatutoaga Rock, a 30 foot (9 m) high seastack.

--- SENTENCE 1584 ---
A channel (ava) crosses the outer reef off Lauli'ituai (ASCRI-4B1).

--- SENTENCE 1585 ---
In early 1978 the reef flat off Lauli'ituai Village was densely populated by the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci).

--- SENTENCE 1586 ---
Although a few A. planci were observed on the reef face, most corals there were undamaged (45;73;74).

--- SENTENCE 1587 ---
However, Acanthaster was sparse on forereef slopes in May 1978, but considerable coral damage was apparent at depths between 65 and 85 feet (20 to 25 m)(74).

--- SENTENCE 1588 ---
# FRINGING REEF

(For fishing uses see: LAULI'IFOU / USE CONSIDERATIONS)

South or easterly swells generate surfable waves off Lauli'ituai.

--- SENTENCE 1589 ---
The best surfing conditions require a high or rising tide and calm or northwest wind conditions (51).
