# FRINGING REEF OFF ALEGA AND AVAIO VILLAGES

--- SENTENCE 1649 ---
The reef flat between Siliataligalu Point and Fa'alogologotala Rock (fronting the villages of Alega and Avaio) is a frequently-used fishing area.

--- SENTENCE 1650 ---
The most popular fishing methods are diving (mata), throw-netting (kili), and seine netting Less popular are pole, and rod and reel fishing, and occasional reef gleaning.

# FAGA'ITUA BAY

Faga'itua Bay, the second largest embayment on Tutuila, owes its unusual size to the drowning of the eroded caldera of Alofau volcano (54).

--- SENTENCE 1660 ---
The fringing reef is extensive, averaging 700 to 1,000 feet (210 to 305 m) in width.

--- SENTENCE 1661 ---
The reef is indented by three major channels (ava) aligned off stream mouths.

--- SENTENCE 1662 ---
The shoreline consists of pocket beaches separated by volcanic headlands (49).

# SHORELINE

Fa'asouga Point terminates in a cliff 15 feet (5 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 1665 ---
Between Faga'ili'ili Point and Fa'asouga Point is a small pocket beach of calcareous sand with scattered limestone and basalt rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1666 ---
The entire length of the 35-foot (11 m) wide beach is bordered by beachrock at the waterline.

--- SENTENCE 1667 ---
A 3-foot (1 m) high seawall protects the backshore (49;ASCRI-5S1).

--- SENTENCE 1668 ---
The western end of Auto Village is fronted by a beach of calcareous sand, limestone and basalt rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1669 ---
The eastern end of the village is fronted by a boulder beach.

--- SENTENCE 1670 ---
Foreshore width varies from 30 to 60 feet (9 to 18 m).

--- SENTENCE 1671 ---
The backshore is defined by a 3- to 5-foot (1 to 2 m) scarp, eroding at its western end but stabilized by boulders or vegetation at its eastern end (49;ASCRI-5S2).

--- SENTENCE 1672 ---
Huliolevai Stream discharges into the ocean at Auto Village through a 20 foot (6 m) wide culvert passing under the coast highway.

--- SENTENCE 1673 ---
During periods of low flow, the culvert outlet is nearly barred by sand (ASCRI-5S2).

--- SENTENCE 1674 ---
A narrow boulder beach in front of Afulei is backed by a 4-foot scarp, whose middle section is eroding (49).

--- SENTENCE 1675 ---
Talus occurs at the base of a cliff along the southwest face of Anape'ape'a Point.

--- SENTENCE 1676 ---
Beaches are absent and the rocky coast drops 3 to 10 feet (1 to 3 m) to the water (ASCRI-5S3).

#### FRINGING REEF OFF FA'ASOUGA POINT

--- SENTENCE 1677 ---
A fringing reef extends some 600 feet (180 m) offshore of Fa'asouga Point.

--- SENTENCE 1678 ---
A channel, 1 to 2.5 feet (0.3 to 0.8 m) deep, runs parallel to and just off the beach.

--- SENTENCE 1679 ---
Width of the sand and rubble bottom channel is about 200 feet (61 m).

--- SENTENCE 1680 ---
The bottom of the middle reef is predominantly rubble (ASCRI-5B1).

--- SENTENCE 1681 ---
The outer reef flat is composed of more consolidated rubble and limestone pavement at depths of 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) (ASCRI-5B2).

#### FRINGING REEF OFF AUTO VILLAGE

Lava boulders predominate in inshore areas adjoining the road revetment.

--- SENTENCE 1682 ---
Some calcareous sand occupies pockets off the revetment.

--- SENTENCE 1683 ---
A large sand channel (ava) cuts through the reef off Auto village (ASCRI-5B3).

--- SENTENCE 1684 ---
The reef flat extends 500 feet (150 m) from shore and is covered with sand from the mouth of Muliolevai Stream to the channel margin (49).

--- SENTENCE 1685 ---
Southwest of the ava there are rubble tracts and scattered occurences of consolidated limestone.

--- SENTENCE 1686 ---
Near the ava margin occur microatolls with sand and gravel accumulated around their bases.

--- SENTENCE 1687 ---
The inshore portion of the ava is a depression about 2 to 3 feet (0.6 to 1.0 m) below the level of the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1688 ---
The ava bottom is sand inshore and consolidated limestone offshore (ASCRI-5B3).

The fringing reef northeast of Muliolevai Stream mouth and the ava is about 300 feet (90 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 1691 ---
Extensive rubble flats extend offshore to a narrow zone of consolidated limestone near the reef margin (ASCRI-5B4).

--- SENTENCE 1692 ---
Inshore areas northeast the ava consist of rubble covered by sand and silty-sand.

--- SENTENCE 1693 ---
Northeast of the ava, between 75 to 150 feet (25 to 45 m) offshore, coral wheels (old Porites microatolls) up to 2 feet across high and 6 feet (0.6 by 2.0 m) are separated by areas of unconsolidated rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1694 ---
About 225 feet (70 m) northeast of the stream culvert is a submerged exposure of old beachrock embedded with volcanic rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1695 ---
This feature lies about 60 feet (20 m) offshore of the road embankment.

--- SENTENCE 1696 ---
A formation of beachrock about 20 feet (6 m) wide trends slightly seaward towards the ava (ASCRI-5B3).

--- SENTENCE 1697 ---
The reef widens off Anape'ape'a Point.

--- SENTENCE 1698 ---
# REEF FLAT OFF FA'ASOUGA POINT

Corals are abundant (50% cover) north of Fa'asouga Point along the sides of a channel on the inner reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1699 ---
Large banks of Acropora (A. exigua or A. formosa) and considerable Pavona sp. occur in depressions on the reef flat seaward of the channel.

--- SENTENCE 1700 ---
Dead coral heads account for about 10% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 1701 ---
At least 18 coral species representing 7 genera are present on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1702 ---
Two sea cucumbers, Holothuria hilla and Stichopus chloronotus, are common, the latter species increasing in abundance to seaward.

--- SENTENCE 1703 ---
The channel, extending seaward, harbors a few areas of staghorn Acropora thickets but overall coral cover is low.

--- SENTENCE 1704 ---
From about 200 feet (60 m) offshore, the reef shoals slightly to seaward and much less coral (about 5% cover) is present.

--- SENTENCE 1705 ---
Pavona and Porites are common genera.

--- SENTENCE 1706 ---
Algal cover is light on the low relief middle reef, and consists mostly of turf-forming species (ASCRI-5B1).

--- SENTENCE 1707 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF AUTO VILLAGE

Fronting the outlet of Muliolevai Stream and northeast of the ava, areas of sandy-rubble nearshore are carpeted by a green, algal turf.

--- SENTENCE 1708 ---
Closer to the ava, Padina sp. and a turf of mostly brown algae are present.

--- SENTENCE 1709 ---
Coral cover is about 10% and is mostly massive Porites lutea in the form of coral wheels occurring between 75 and 150 feet (25 to 45 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 1710 ---
Some Pavona sp. and Leptastrea purpurea are present also, but species of Acropora are absent.

--- SENTENCE 1711 ---
Dead coral heads account for 50% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 1712 ---
Reduced circulation apparently limits the development of corals in nearshore areas.

--- SENTENCE 1713 ---
An algal turf covers areas of unconsolidated rubble between coral wheels.

--- SENTENCE 1714 ---
Farther offshore, a turf of brown algae and some Dictyota sp. cover rubble (ASCRI-5B3).

--- SENTENCE 1715 ---
Fishes are moderately abundant on the inner reef fronting Auto Village.

--- SENTENCE 1716 ---
The assemblage includes at least 56 species.

--- SENTENCE 1717 ---
Dominant types are wrasses and damselfish.

--- SENTENCE 1718 ---
In areas of acroporan corals, one damselfish (<u>Dascyllus aruanus</u>), is dominant; elsewhere, another (<u>Glyphidodontops cyanea</u>), is dominant.

--- SENTENCE 1719 ---
<u>Thalassoma hardwickei</u> is the most common wrasse in all areas.

--- SENTENCE 1720 ---
Butterfly fishes (<u>Chaetodon trifasciatus</u> and <u>C. trifascialis</u>), are abundant

Dominant species also differ from inshore areas.

--- SENTENCE 1733 ---
In early 1978 the reef front in Faga'itua Bay between Auto Village and Asasama Point was reportedly infested by the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci)(54).

#### FRINGING REEF OFF AUTO

Underwater visibility is about 75 feet (25 m) on the reef northeast of Fa'asouga Point.

--- SENTENCE 1734 ---
Off the mouth of Muliolevai Stream, suspended matter keeps nearshore waters turbid and visibility is reduced compared to areas to the southwest.

--- SENTENCE 1735 ---
Water circulation shoreward of the ava is apparently restricted, resulting in noticeably warmer and more murky waters (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1736 ---
Strong surge makes the reef margin off Auto difficult to approach and may limit fishing use.

--- SENTENCE 1737 ---
A strong current flows through the ava (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1738 ---
A sand and rubble beach northeast of Fa'asouga Point is accessible down a moderately-sloping road embankment up to 6 feet (2 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 1739 ---
Shoreline access is more difficult fronting Afulei Village, where a drop 3 to 10 feet (1 to 3 m) across a rocky shore is necessary to reach the water (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1740 ---
# FRINGING REEF ALONG THE WESTERN PERIMETER OF FAGA'ITUA BAY

--- SENTENCE 1741 ---
The reef flat fronting the villages of Amaua and Utusia is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1742 ---
The reef fringing the western perimeter of Faga'itua Bay (fronting the villages of Auto, Amaua, and Utusia) is a frequently-used fishing ground, with throw-netting

--- SENTENCE 1743 ---

--- SENTENCE 1750 ---
Night catches include anae, crab, ula (spiny lobster), papata (slipper lobster), and ume (unicornfish).

--- SENTENCE 1751 ---
Rod and reel fishing yields day catches of malauli (large jack), lupota, and gatala (20).

# COAST BETWEEN ANAPE'APE'A POINT AND AMAUA VILLAGE

#### SHORELINE

Anape'ape'a

--- SENTENCE 1753 ---
Point is a cliffed headland south of the village of Amaua.

--- SENTENCE 1754 ---
At the base of the cliff, a lava rock platform about 3 to 5 feet (1.0 to 1.5 m) high projects seaward.

--- SENTENCE 1755 ---
A basalt boulder fan extends off the northeastern side of the headland (ASCRI-5S4).

--- SENTENCE 1756 ---
North of Anape'ape'a Point is a basalt boulder beach containing some limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1757 ---
The beach widens at its eastern end fronting the village of Amaua.

--- SENTENCE 1758 ---
The backshore is defined by a scarp rising to an elevation of 9 to 12 feet (3 to 4 m).

--- SENTENCE 1759 ---
Except in places protected by randomly-placed boulders, the base of the scarp is unstable and eroding (49).

--- SENTENCE 1760 ---
A storm drain under the road enters the ocean northwest of Anape'ape'a Point (ASCRI-5S4).

# CAVES NEAR ANAPE'APE'A

--- SENTENCE 1762 ---
Two caves are found along the coast between the villages of Auto and Amaua.

--- SENTENCE 1763 ---
One measures 40 feet (12 m) wide, 15 feet (4.6 m) high, and about 15 feet (4.6 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 1764 ---
The floor has a shallow sand layer.

--- SENTENCE 1765 ---
U.S. Marines built a series of concrete steps (about 5 feet or 1.5 m high) up to the cave entrance and a nearby low wall.

--- SENTENCE 1766 ---
A larger cave known as Anape'ape'a ("Bat Cave") is situated on the point of the same name southwest of Amaua Village.

--- SENTENCE 1767 ---
This cave measures about 40 feet (12 m) high and 40 feet (12 m) wide at the entrance.

--- SENTENCE 1768 ---
The floor drops about 15 feet below the mouth (30).

--- SENTENCE 1769 ---
The floor of this large cave is nearly 16 feet (5 m) at its entrance above high tide (12).

--- SENTENCE 1770 ---
The bottom directly offshore of Anape'ape'a Point consists of basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 1771 ---
North of the Point there is beachrock exposed

The black noddy (gogo; Anous tenuirostris minutus), a resident seabird uncommon in American Samoa, nests on Anape'ape'a Point.

Sheath-tailed bats (pe'ape'avai; Emballonura semicaudata) roost in caves at Anape'ape'a Point (15).

Basalt boulders immediately offshore of Anape'ape'a Point appear quite barren.

Algal cover is considerable on inshore areas of silted rubble extending into the nearshore channel from a small stream-mouth beach at Amaua.

--- SENTENCE 1790 ---
A brown alga (<u>Padina tenuis</u>) accounts for 50% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 1791 ---
The reef flat seaward of the nearshore channel is distinguished by coral cover in places approaching 75% of the bottom.

TOLISI POINT AND LEANAOSAUALI'I POINT

# SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 1806 ---
An outcrop of lava rock rises approximately 10 feet (3 m) above the inner reef off Tolisi Point.

--- SENTENCE 1807 ---
Another low outcrop is exposed farther offshore (ASCRI-537).

--- SENTENCE 1808 ---
The shoreline at Faga'itua is mostly a boulder revetment extending from near sea level up to the 7- or 8-foot elevation (26;49;ASCRI-6S1).

--- SENTENCE 1809 ---
The revetment is interrupted by a number of culverts and drainage pipes (26).

--- SENTENCE 1810 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF TOLISI POINT

--- SENTENCE 1811 ---
The fringing reef is up to 850 feet (260 m) wide off Tolisi Point (49).

--- SENTENCE 1812 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF TOLISI POINT

--- SENTENCE 1813 ---
The reef flat off Tolisi Point harbors a diverse and moderately abundant fish fauna.

--- SENTENCE 1814 ---
Stegastes nigricans is most abundant of at least 75 species.

--- SENTENCE 1815 ---
Ctenochaetus striatus and Chromis caerulea follow in abundance.

--- SENTENCE 1816 ---
Fishes are more abundant and the fauna more diverse on the reef front off Tolisi Point than on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1817 ---
At least 107 species are present.

--- SENTENCE 1818 ---
Most abundant is Pomacentrus melanopterus, followed by Plectroglyphidodon dickii, Ctenochaetus striatus, and Scarus sp. (76).

--- SENTENCE 1819 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF FAGA'ITUA VILLAGE

The shoreline and reef at the head of Faga'itua Bay lie in somewhat sheltered waters.

--- SENTENCE 1820 ---
Stream-deposited fans of basalt boulders and gravel accumulate at and slightly above sea level at the mouths of Siapapa and Vaialufai Streams (26).

--- SENTENCE 1821 ---
Vaialufai Stream is usually dry, discharging only after a heavy rainfall (ASCRI-6S1)

--- SENTENCE 1822 ---
A channel dredged through the reef off the mouth of Vaialufai Stream merges offshore with an ava.

--- SENTENCE 1823 ---
The steep-sided channel varies in depth from 2 to 3 feet (0.6 to 2.4 m).

--- SENTENCE 1824 ---
The bottom of the channel consists of basalt rocks and gravel, limestone rubble, roadside litter, and sediment (26).

--- SENTENCE 1825 ---
A shallow, sand-bottom lagoon, from 3 to 6 feet (1 to 2 m) deep, extends from shore off the western end of Faga'itua Village (26;34).

--- SENTENCE 1826 ---
West of Vaialufai Stream mouth inshore rubble areas merge with a platform of limestone and rubble extending across the middle reef.

--- SENTENCE 1827 ---
Depth generally varies from 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m), but portions of this platform shoal almost to mean sea level.

--- SENTENCE 1828 ---
Bottom relief decreases toward the middle and outer reef.

--- SENTENCE 1829 ---
Extensive Acropora thickets occur at mid-reef, where the depth varies from 0.9 to 3.0 feet (0.2 to 1.0 m).

--- SENTENCE 1830 ---
Patches of sand and

--- SENTENCE 1832 ---
Much of the outer reef is exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 1833 ---
Depth varies from -1.0 to +0.9 feet (-0.3 to +0.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 1834 ---
A partly consolidated pavement of limestone rubble grades offshore to a more consolidated surface.

--- SENTENCE 1835 ---
Large limestone blocks (up to 3 feet or 1 m high) are conspicuous on the outer reef flat (26).

--- SENTENCE 1836 ---
East of Vaialufai Stream mouth, sand flats extend offshore for about 165 feet (50 m) (26;34) and the depth varies from 1.3 to 2.0 feet (0.4 to 0.5 m) (26).

--- SENTENCE 1837 ---
The reef margin is characterized by an algal ridge exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 1838 ---
Depth varies from -8 to +16 inches (-0.2 to +0.4 m).

--- SENTENCE 1839 ---
The reef front off Faga'itua slopes moderately steeply, reaching a depth of about 65 feet (20 m) within 330 feet (100 m) of the margin.

--- SENTENCE 1840 ---
Reef slopes are characterized by a low-profile spur-and groove system.

--- SENTENCE 1841 ---
A large, well defined channel (ava) crosses the reef off the eastern side of Faga'itua Village (approximately aligned with the mouth of Vaialufai Stream) varying in depth between 6 and 33 feet (2 to 10 m).

--- SENTENCE 1842 ---
The ava walls are sheer to overhanging.

--- SENTENCE 1843 ---
The ava is the main discharge area for water flowing off the reef flat (26).

# FRINGING REEF

Large thickets of <u>Acropora formosa</u> 50 to 100 feet (15 to 30 m) across rise to near the surface in a lagoon off the western side of Faga'itua Village.

--- SENTENCE 1845 ---
This growth is apparently of recent development, as the lagoon was barren in 1974 (34) and only scattered patches of staghorn <u>Acropora</u> (totaling about 10% cover) were seen in 1978.

--- SENTENCE 1846 ---
A sea urchin (<u>Echinometra mathaei</u>) occurs in low densities (26).

--- SENTENCE 1847 ---
Juvenile Acanthaster (alamea), were observed on Faga'itua reef flat in August 1977 (45).

--- SENTENCE 1848 ---
Patches of dead corals on the reef flat in late 1978 attested to predation by the crown-of-thorns starfish, present in low abundance (34).

--- SENTENCE 1849 ---
An earlier (pre-Acanthaster infestation) study reports coral cover of 40% to 60% on the inner and middle reef flat areas west of Vaialufai Stream mouth.

--- SENTENCE 1850 ---
Porites lutea was most common inshore, whereas Psammocora contigua and Pavona decussata were most common on the middle reef platform (26).

--- SENTENCE 1851 ---
A later study reports no evidence of once-extensive beds of Psammocora (34), and Staghorn acroporans, Pavona frondifera, Pocillopora damicornis, Porites andrewsi, and P. (Synarea) undulata were significantly less abundant.

Coralline algae encrust partly consolidated and consolidated limestone on the outer reef, with some non-coralline algae present toward mid-reef.

--- SENTENCE 1857 ---
Scattered, wave-resistant corals, notably Acropora humilis and Pocillopora verrucosa (26;34), account for 5% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 1858 ---
A sea cucumber (Holothuria sp.), mollusc (Turbo sp.), and sea urchins (Diadema sp. and Echinothrix sp.), are present in low densities (26).

--- SENTENCE 1859 ---
Patchy growths of an alga (Halimeda sp.) occur on sand flats extending about 165 feet (50 m) from shore east of Vaialufai Stream outlet (26).

--- SENTENCE 1860 ---
Large heads of Pocillopora damicornis and scattered heads of Porites andrewsi occur on the inner reef flat off the eastern end of Faga'itua Village.

--- SENTENCE 1861 ---
On the middle reef flat, 492 feet (150 m) offshore, coral cover approaches 100% and is dominated by Porites sp., and Porites (S.) sp.

--- SENTENCE 1862 ---
The margins of the ava are covered with beds of Acropora (mostly A. formosa)(34).

--- SENTENCE 1863 ---
Wave-resistant corals, including <u>Acropora humilis</u>, <u>Pocillopora verrucosa</u>, and others inhabit the reef margin off Faga'itua (26).

--- SENTENCE 1864 ---
In early 1978 the reef front in Faga'itua Bay, between Auto Village and Asasama Point, was reported to be heavily infested by <u>Acanthaster</u> (45).

--- SENTENCE 1865 ---
# FRINGING REEF

Soil eroded from the Masefau Road above Faga'itua is carried by Tialu Stream into Faga'itua Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1866 ---
No damage to the reef has been observed, but turbid waters nearshore is a common occurrence after rainfall (34;39).

--- SENTENCE 1867 ---
In the past, dredging activities have caused siltation problems and high turbidity in Faga-'itua Bay (7).

--- SENTENCE 1868 ---
Underwater visibility is excellent on the reef off the western side of Faga'itua Village.

--- SENTENCE 1869 ---
Refuse covers the inshore bottom here (34).

#### SHORELINE AND FRINGING REEF

The shoreline fronting Faga'itua Village is accessible across a road embankment which drops several feet (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1870 ---
The reef fringing the villages of Faga'itua and Pagai at the head of Faga'itua Bay is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1871 ---
The reef flat is the most frequently fished area.

--- SENTENCE 1872 ---
According to one source, pole and line fishing is the most popular method.

--- SENTENCE 1873 ---
Spearing is second most popular.

--- SENTENCE 1874 ---
Some reef gleaning occurs off Faga'itua Village (20).

--- SENTENCE 1875 ---
Another source emphasizes the importance of gleaning and spearing on Faga'itua reef.

--- SENTENCE 1876 ---
Weir and gill-net fishing are reported to be significant methods of fishing along the outer margins of the ava, with "paopao" fishing in deeper waters off the reaf.

--- SENTENCE 1877 ---
The large ava and mid-reef Acropora thickets are focal points of spearing and "paopao" activity.

--- SENTENCE 1878 ---
Exposure of the reef margin to moderate surf discourages line fishing or throw-netting there, and consequently, most pole fishing takes place along the inner reaches of the ava during low tide.

--- SENTENCE 1879 ---
Throw-netting is not considered an important fishery at Faga'itua (26).

Gatala (honeycomb grouper), filoa (large emperor fish).

--- SENTENCE 1883 ---
mataeleele (small emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper) are caught both day and night by pole fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 1884 ---
Daytime catches include lupota (small jack) and lupo (juvenile jack).

--- SENTENCE 1885 ---
catches include malau (squirrelfish), malai (paddletail snapper), and matapula (bigeye snapper).

--- SENTENCE 1886 ---
Spearing results in day and night catches of alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), and laea (large parrotfish).

--- SENTENCE 1887 ---
Day spearing also yields faisua (giant clam), fe'e (octopus), eel, fuga (small parrotfish), and gatala.

--- SENTENCE 1888 ---
Night spearing yields anae (adult mullet), lobster), papata (slipper lobster), and ume crab, ula (spiny lobster), papata (slipper lobster), and ume (unicornfish) (20).

--- SENTENCE 1889 ---
The inner and middle portions of Faga'itua reef harbor especially large populations of tuitui (sea urchin) (26) and other invertebrates commonly sought by shell collectors and gleaners (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1890 ---
# COAST BETWEEN LEANAOSAUALI'I POINT AND ASASAMA POINT

# SHORELINE

Pagai Village is situated at the head of a small cove indenting the coast between Leanaosauali'i Point and Asasama Point (both volcanic headlands) (ASCRI-6S1).

--- SENTENCE 1891 ---
A pocket beach of calcareous sand and alluvium fronting Pagai is aboux 35 feet (11 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 1892 ---
The beach slopes gently up to a 3-foot (1 m) scarp and undercut trees indicative of shoreline erosion (49).

--- SENTENCE 1893 ---
Much of the coast is bordered by a low, man-made road embankment constructed of large basalt boulders (ASCRI-6S1).

--- SENTENCE 1894 ---
# FRINGING REEF

A broad channel (ava) indents the reef opposite Punaomaniua Stream mouth and approaches to within 300 feet (90 m) of shore (49).

--- SENTENCE 1895 ---
# SHORELINE AND FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 1896 ---
The shoreline fronting Pagai Village is not open to public access (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1897 ---
For fishing uses see: FAGA'ITUA / USE CONSIDERATIONS.

# ALOFAU MANGROVE SWAMP

A small mangrove forest is present in the vicinity of Alofau Village (15).

#### FRINGING REEF FLAT

Dredging of Alofau reef was discontinued in late 1970.

--- SENTENCE 1907 ---
A causeway which extended onto the reef was removed to improve water circulation (23).

--- SENTENCE 1908 ---
Remnants of the causeway, about 15 feet (5 m) across, are exposed during low tides (ASCRI-6B2).

--- SENTENCE 1909 ---
Silty-sand along shore grades into sand bottom (with gravel) at a depth of 1 or 2 feet (less than 1 m) on the inner reef off Alofau Beach (ASCRI-6B1).

--- SENTENCE 1910 ---
Borrow pits in the reef reach depths of 15 feet (5 m).

--- SENTENCE 1911 ---
Soft mud covers the bottoms of these dredged areas (ASCRI-6B2).

--- SENTENCE 1912 ---
The middle of the reef flat seaward of the dredged area is covered mostly by a fine white sand with some rubble.

--- SENTENCE 1913 ---
Depths are generally from 2 to 4 feet (0.6 to 1.2 m), but some dredged areas here are 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 m) deep (ASCRI-6B3).

--- SENTENCE 1914 ---
The outer reef flat shoals to a depth of about one foot (0.3 m) with a bottom composed almost entirely of rubble The reef margin is a partially developed algal (ASCRI-6B4).

--- SENTENCE 1915 ---
ridge which drops vertically from depths of 3 to 6 feet (1 to 2 m) to 15 to 20 feet (5 to 6 m) at the reef front (ASCRI-6B5).

--- SENTENCE 1916 ---
In places, broad fans of rubble and boulders begin at around feet (-6 m) and slope steeply beyond -60 feet (-13 m) (ASCRI-6B6).

--- SENTENCE 1917 ---
A deep channel cuts through the reef off the mouth of Fogalilimu Stream and approaches to within 600 feet (180 m) of shore (49).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

Depressions at the reef margan provide one or two-foot vertical relief (ASCRI-6B5).

--- SENTENCE 1918 ---
The generally steep-sloping reef front is undercut, with extensive accumulations of coral rubble and boulders occurring at the base.

--- SENTENCE 1919 ---
Typically, a broad rubble fan begins at a depth of 20 feet (6 m) and slopes steeply below 60 feet (18 m) (ASCRI-6B6).

--- SENTENCE 1920 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

Nide bands of a blackish-brown cyanophyte (blue-green alga) extend about 50 feet (15 m) offshore from Alofau Beach.

--- SENTENCE 1921 ---
A green alga (Halimeda cf. discoidea) is common on the inshore sand bottom (ASCRI-6B1).

--- SENTENCE 1922 ---
Lysiosquilla sp. are common.

--- SENTENCE 1923 ---
Scattered Acropora thickets, some 20 feet (6 m) across and 3 feet (1 m) high, inhabit dredged areas.

--- SENTENCE 1924 ---
These thickets are especially dense in a shallow area south of an old causeway.

--- SENTENCE 1926 ---
Coral cover is up to 30% and at least 31 species representing 16 genera are present on Alofau reef.

--- SENTENCE 1927 ---
Two species of algae (Actinotrichia sp. and Dictyota sp.) cover large areas of the bottom seaward of the borrow pits.

--- SENTENCE 1928 ---
The algae, Lyngbya sp., Polysiphonia sp., and Gelidiopsis intricata coat dead areas of branching staghorn corals.

--- SENTENCE 1929 ---
The sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, is common to abundant.

--- SENTENCE 1930 ---
Large holes and cone-snaped mounds of silty-sand on the bottom of dredged depressions provide evidence of annelid worms and other burrowing forms (ASCRI-6B3).

--- SENTENCE 1931 ---
Very little live coral (about 1% cover) grows on the shallow outer reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 1932 ---
Encrusting coralline algae and Ralfsia sp. are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 1933 ---
A green cyanophyte (Hormothamnion sp.) is common in patches along with the red alga, Actinotrichia sp.

--- SENTENCE 1934 ---
The sea cucumber, Holothuria hilla, is relatively common (ASCRI-6B4).

--- SENTENCE 1935 ---
Coral cover varies from place to place along the reef margin (0 to 10%) and is mostly wave-resistant species of Acropora.

--- SENTENCE 1936 ---
Dead coral heads are prominent and many appear to have been killed recently.

--- SENTENCE 1937 ---
The coralline alga, Porolithon sp., encrusts the algal ridge.

--- SENTENCE 1938 ---
A few small colonies of soft corals are present (ASCRI-6B5).

--- SENTENCE 1939 ---
Fishes are moderately abundant and the fauna diverse on the reef flat fronting the northwestern end of Alofau Village.

--- SENTENCE 1940 ---
Chromis atripectoralis, Stegastes nigricans, and Dascyllus aru-anus are most abundant (76).

--- SENTENCE 1941 ---
A highly diverse and abundant fish fauna characterizes the reef flat and dredged lagoon in front of Alofau Village.

--- SENTENCE 1942 ---
At least 85 species are present.

--- SENTENCE 1943 ---
families are butterflyfishes and damselfishes.

--- SENTENCE 1944 ---
The damselfish, Dascyllus aruanus, is most abundant and Glyphidodontops cyanea, G. glaucus, G. leucopomus, and Pomacentrus coelestis are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 1945 ---
Chaetodon trifasciatus is the most common butterflyfish, with schools of 10 to 20 individuals common around coral thickets in the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 1946 ---
<u>Chaetodon auriga</u>, <u>C. citrinellus</u>, reticulatus also are abundant throughout the area.

--- SENTENCE 1947 ---
Cardinalfish and pipefish are common among Acropora thickets.

--- SENTENCE 1948 ---
Conspicuous in the layoon as well as on the adjacent reef flat are species of adult mullet in schools numbering 20 to 50 individuals in the shallow waters.

--- SENTENCE 1949 ---
Prominent species include atherinids, the pipefish, Corythoichthys flavofasciatus, the mullets, Liza vagiensis and Velamugil seheli, the cardinalfishes, Apogon kallopterus, A. novemfasciatus, and Cheilodipterus macrodon.

--- SENTENCE 1950 ---
The goatfish, <u>Mulloidichthys vanicolensis</u>, is among the dominant species found over sandy areas of the lagoon, while <u>Parupeneus</u> <u>Chryseredros</u> is the most abundant goatfish elsewhere.

--- SENTENCE 1951 ---
Other abundant species include the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus nigrofuscus and A. triostegus, the wrasses, Halichoeres margaritaceus Thalassoma hardwickei, and several species of parrotfishes (ASCRI-6F1).

--- SENTENCE 1952 ---
The reef front off Alofau is nearly devoid of live coral, except for some Acropora humilis.

# FRINGING REEF OFF LIFALIFA POINT

--- SENTENCE 1963 ---
The inner reef flat fringing the northern face of Lifalifa Point is sand, with silty-sand accumulating in extensive patches of a sea grass (Halophilia sp.).

--- SENTENCE 1964 ---
Small gastropods are common foraging around the sea grass (ASCRI-6B7).

--- SENTENCE 1965 ---
# FRINGING REEF (EASTERN FAGA'ITUA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 1966 ---
Underwater visibility is about 20 feet (6 m) in nearshore areas fronting Alofau Village.

--- SENTENCE 1967 ---
Visibility improves to about 30 feet (9 m) seaward of the dredged section of reef and to 40 feet (12 m) at the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 1968 ---
Sixty feet (18 m) is the limit of visibility along the reef front (ASCRI).

#### SHORELINE

The shoreline fronting Alofau Village is easily accessible down a low road embankment.

--- SENTENCE 1969 ---
Beaches are narrow or absent, however.

--- SENTENCE 1970 ---
The rocky shoreline along the northeast side of Lifalifa Point is inaccessible because of the high cliff (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1971 ---
The reef fringing the eastern perimeter of Faga'itua Bay in front of Alofau Village is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 1972 ---
The reef flat is the most frequently visited area for fishing by throw-netting (kili) and pole and line.

# COAST BETWEEN UEA POINT AND SINATAU POINT

#### SHORELINE

Cape Fogausa rises in high sea cliffs at Uea Point and Sinatau Point (ASCRI-6S3).

--- SENTENCE 1982 ---
A long beach of calcareous sand and rubble lies between these two points (49).

--- SENTENCE 1983 ---
# OFF SINATAU POINT

A few crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) were reported on forereef slopes off Sinatau Point in early 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 1984 ---
# SHORELINE

An area of private home sites near the shore on Cape Fogausa is not open to public access (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1985 ---
# COAST BETWEEN SINATAU POINT AND FALASE EITOAFA POINT

# SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 1986 ---
The shoreline between Sinatau Point and Matalesolo Point consists of volcanic headlands and sea cliffs separating three small pocket beaches of limestone rubble at the heads of Nu'uoleniu and Nu'uolema'a Coves.

--- SENTENCE 1987 ---
A 40- to 50-foot (12 to 15 m) wide pocket beach between Matalesolo Point and Maugaopea Point consists of calcareous sand with beachrock exposed at intervals along the shoreline (49).

--- SENTENCE 1988 ---
A small spit (tombolo) of sand and rubble has formed behind a lava rock outcrop offshore, forming Maugaopea Point (49; ASCRI-7S1).

--- SENTENCE 1989 ---
The fringing reef is only 100 to 150 feet (30 to 45 m) wide (49).

--- SENTENCE 1990 ---
From the high vantage point afforded by the coastal highway, spur-and-groove formations can be seen on the outer margin of the reef (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 1991 ---
The blue-gray noddy (laia; <u>Procelsterna cerulea</u>), a seabird uncommon in American Samoa, roosts and nests near Matalesolo Point (15).

# SHORELINE

From Cape Fogausa eastward to near Foga'au, the backshore rises steeply to the highway, which rounds Sinatau Point and Cape Fogausa at the 100- to 200-foot elevation.

# COAST BETWEEN FALASE'EITOAFA POINT AND MATAUTUELE POINT

--- SENTENCE 1995 ---
The neck of land between Amouli Bay and Aoa Bay (MAP 10) on the north shore of Tutuila resulted from the narrowing of the saddle between Olomoana and Alofau volcanoes by the drowning of two large canyons.

--- SENTENCE 1996 ---
The canyons are especially large because each carried the drainage from the slopes of two volcanoes (54).

--- SENTENCE 1997 ---
A sand beach stretches between sea cliffs at Falase'eitoafa Point and Matautuele Point.

--- SENTENCE 1998 ---
At the western end of this reach (fronting Siufaga) there is a deteriorating lava rock seawall rising 2 to 7 feet (1 to 2 m) behind a foreshore up to 20 feet (6 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 1999 ---
The wall stabilizes a backshore scarp.

--- SENTENCE 2000 ---
The beach nearly 40 feet (12 m) wide east of Siufaga (49).

--- SENTENCE 2001 ---
Beachrock is exposed at low tide in the central and eastern sections of the beach fronting Siufaga and Amouli.

--- SENTENCE 2002 ---
At least two streams (and a storm drain culvert) enter the ocean at Amouli (ASCRI-7S2), where a 30- to 60-foot (9 to 18 m) wide beach of calcareous sand and rubble is backed by a backshore scarp 2 to 6 feet high.

--- SENTENCE 2003 ---
North and south of Televai Stream, where houses are built on fill, the scarp is stabilized by a low rock seawall.

--- SENTENCE 2004 ---
A narrow beach of basalt boulders with scattered limestone rubble lies just west of Matautuele Point (49; ASCRI-7S2).

--- SENTENCE 2005 ---
# FRINGING REEF (AMOULI BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2006 ---
The fringing reef averages 750 feet (230 m) in width off Amouli (49).

--- SENTENCE 2007 ---
The inner reef flat off the southwestern end of Amouli Village grades from mostly sand to increasing proportions of basalt rubble along shore toward Matautuele Point.

--- SENTENCE 2008 ---
Farther offshore, the relatively flat bottom is mostly rubble at depths of 3 to 4 feet (1 to 1.2 m)(ASCRI-7B1).

--- SENTENCE 2009 ---
The bottom shoals to 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) over extensive mid-reef rubble

--- SENTENCE 2010 ---
These tracts are exposed at low tide (ASCRI-7B2).

--- SENTENCE 2011 ---
An outer reef platform of consolidated limestone with rubble tracts extends to an elevated reef margin and a reef face with spur-and-groove development (ASCRI-7B3).

--- SENTENCE 2012 ---
A 50-foot (15 m) wide ava approximately aligned off the mouth of Televai Stream indents the seaward face of the reef and approaches within 350 feet (105 m) of shore (49;ASCRI-7B4).

--- SENTENCE 2013 ---
The channel bottom is littered with sand-scoured boulders and rubble, as well as junk (including a car body) (ASCRI-7B4).

--- SENTENCE 2014 ---
The outer reef flat northeast of the ava is a consolidated limestone pavement with scattered loose, flat boulders (ASCRI-7B5).

--- SENTENCE 2015 ---
Inner reef areas shoreward of the ava contain rubble and consolidated limestone mixed with silty-sand to a depth of 3 feet (1 m) (ASCRI-7B6).

--- SENTENCE 2016 ---
A sand deposit off the mouth of Televai Stream extends offshore to the deep channel (ava)(49).

--- SENTENCE 2017 ---
The reef flat inside Matautuele Point has a rubble bottom, consisting of a mixture of volcanic and limestone fragments (ASCRI-7B6).

#### FRINGING REEF

A turf of brown alga is common on sand-veneered rubble of the inner reef off the southwestern portion of Amouli Beach.

--- SENTENCE 2020 ---
Coral cover is low (10 to 15%) at depths of 3 to 4 feet (1.0 to 1.2 m) on a predominantly rubble bottom of the middle reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2021 ---
Pavona sp. and Porites sp. are most common.

--- SENTENCE 2022 ---
The alga, Amphiroa sp., is conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 2023 ---
The sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, is common (ASCRI-7B1).

--- SENTENCE 2024 ---
Extensive mid-reef rubble tracts (exposed at low tide) harbor a few corals (about 5% cover), including <u>Porites lutea</u>, <u>Pocillopora damicornis</u>, and <u>Pavona frondifera</u>.

--- SENTENCE 2025 ---
The sea cucumber, <u>Stichopus chloronotus</u>, is the only other conspicuous invertebrate.

--- SENTENCE 2026 ---
Encrusting coralline algae are abundant; <u>Ralfsia</u> sp. and brown epiphytic algae are common (ASCRI-7B2).

--- SENTENCE 2027 ---
Live corals total about 10% cover on the outer reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 2028 ---
Acropora aspera, other acroporans, and Porites lutea are notable.

--- SENTENCE 2029 ---
The sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, occurs in lesser abundance than in shoreward reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 2030 ---
The elevated reef margin is encrusted by a few corals (ASCRI-7B3).

--- SENTENCE 2031 ---
A spikey, red-branched coralline alga and a patchy, yellowish cyanophyte (blue-green alga) are conspicuous along the northeastern margin of the ava (ASCRI-7B4).

--- SENTENCE 2032 ---
Few corals inhabit the outer reef pavement northeast of the ava.

--- SENTENCE 2033 ---
Acropora aspera growth is patchy.

--- SENTENCE 2034 ---
The brown alga, Ralfsia sp., is present (ASCRI-7B5).

--- SENTENCE 2035 ---
Inshore areas of rubble, limestone, and silty-sand off the northeastern part of the beach have coral cover of 5 to 10%.

--- SENTENCE 2036 ---
Pavona frondifera and Porites andrewsi are most common.

--- SENTENCE 2037 ---
The coral assemblage includes at least 15 species in 11 genera.

--- SENTENCE 2038 ---
No corals are evident in nearshore rubble areas off northeastern Amouli Village.

--- SENTENCE 2039 ---
The green alga, Valonia cf.

--- SENTENCE 2040 ---
aegogropila, is common on rubble (ASCRI-7B6).

--- SENTENCE 2041 ---
Considerable numbers of the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) were evident on the upper reef front (at depths of 6 to 33 feet or 2 to 10 m) off Amouli Village and Taulaotoga Rock in August/September 1979, but 30 to 90% of the coral heads were still alive (75).

--- SENTENCE 2042 ---
A moderately diverse fish fauna occurs on the reef flat in front of Amouli Village.

--- SENTENCE 2043 ---
Abundant fish populations are dominated by juveniles.

--- SENTENCE 2044 ---
The area is a protected lagoon with extensive thickets of acroporan corals providing habitat for juvenile fishes.

--- SENTENCE 2045 ---
Dominant species include the butterflyfish, Chaetodon citrinellus, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus lineatus, A. nigrofuscus, and A. nigroris, the damselfishes, Chromis atripectoralis, Stegastes albofasciatus, and Plectroglyphidodon leucozoma, the wrasse, Thalassoma hardwickei, and juvenile parrotfish, Scarus spp.

--- SENTENCE 2046 ---
The surf perch, Kuhlia mugil, occurs in large schools near shore (ASCRI-7F1).

#### AMOULI BAY

Waters are clear on the middle and outer reef southwest of the ava off Amouli: visibility underwater is 100 feet (31 m).

--- SENTENCE 2049 ---
Northeast of the ava, the water is very turbid.

--- SENTENCE 2050 ---
Turbid water occurs inshore off a filled area which lies between two stream outlets.

--- SENTENCE 2051 ---
Trash collects on the beach and sand bottom just off this small point.

--- SENTENCE 2052 ---
Refuse (including an old car body) litters the bottom of the ava and is also conspicuous at the base of Matautuele Point (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2053 ---
# SHORELINE AND FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 2054 ---
The beach at Amouli is easily accessible down the embank-ment of the nearby coastal road.

--- SENTENCE 2055 ---
Some throw-netting takes place on the inner reef fronting a small promontory of filled land (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2056 ---
The reef fringing the coast between Falase'eitoafa Point and Taulaotoga Rock is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2057 ---
The most frequently fished area encompasses the reef flat extending from Matalesolo Point to Taulaotoga Rock.

--- SENTENCE 2058 ---
The most popular fishing method off Foga'au is pole and line fishing, followed by spearfishing (mata).

--- SENTENCE 2059 ---
In front of Amouli, pole and line fishing is the preferred method, and seine netting (upega) is second most popular.

--- SENTENCE 2060 ---
Spearing (mata), reef gleaning, and trapping (egu) are practiced in descending order of popularity.

--- SENTENCE 2061 ---
Pole fishing results in day and night catches of gatala (honeycomb grouper), filoa (large emperor fish), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper).

--- SENTENCE 2062 ---
Lupota (small jack) and lupo (juvenile jack) are also caught by day, and malau (squirrelfish), malai (paddletail snapper), and matapula (bigeye snapper) by night.

--- SENTENCE 2063 ---
Spearing results in day and night catches of alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), and laea (large parrotfish).

--- SENTENCE 2064 ---
Day spearing also yields faisua (giant clam), fe'e (octopus), eel, fuga (small parrotfish), and gatala.

--- SENTENCE 2065 ---
Night diving brings in catches of anae (adult mullet), crab, ula (spiny lobster), papata (slipper lobster), and ume (unicornfish) (20).

#### COAST BETWEEN MATAUTUELE POINT AND TAUGAMALAMA POINT

#### SHORELINE

A 55-foot (17 m) wide sand beach fronts

--- SENTENCE 2066 ---
Aganoa, a village of 3 houses.

--- SENTENCE 2067 ---
Beachrock is exposed in places along the shoreline (49).

--- SENTENCE 2068 ---
# TAULAOTOGA ROCK

Taulaotoga Rock is a seastack which is a potential roosting and nesting sites for the reef heron (matu'u; <u>Egretta</u> <u>sacra</u> <u>sacra</u>), a resident seabird uncommon in American Samoa (15).

# COAST BETWEEN TAUGAMALAMA POINT AND MA'ATULAUMEA POINT

--- SENTENCE 2071 ---
A coastal terrace of alluvium, talus, and calcareous sand and gravel extends inland 400 to 800 feet (120 to 245 m) at Auasi, terminating at cliffs along the base of Olomoana Mountain.

--- SENTENCE 2072 ---
Leafu Stream and Vaisa Stream (a small drainage channel) discharge into the ocean after heavy rainfall (67).

--- SENTENCE 2073 ---
# SHORELINE

Fronting Auasi Village is a beach of calcareous sand mixed with volcanic cobbles and boulders.

--- SENTENCE 2074 ---
The beach varies in width from 10 to 70 feet (3 to 21 m).

--- SENTENCE 2075 ---
Rubble and boulders are more prevalent on the eastern part of the beach where there are only scattered pockets of sand (14;37).

--- SENTENCE 2076 ---
The western section of the beach broadens to 75 feet (23 m) and includes considerable limestone rubble as well as calcareous sand (49).

--- SENTENCE 2077 ---
Scattered boulders and beachrock are exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2078 ---
Beachrock is exposed in an outcrop some 33 to 40 feet (10 to 12 m) long just west of Ma'atulaumea Point.

--- SENTENCE 2079 ---
A deposit of (basalt and limestone) boulders and sand lie behind the outcrop.

--- SENTENCE 2080 ---
A narrow band of large basalt boulders border each of the steep-faced headlands (Taugamalama Point and Ma'atulaumea Point) at either end of Auasi Beach (14).

--- SENTENCE 2081 ---
At high tide and during storm conditions, waves run up to the base of coconut trees at the vegetation line behind the northeastern section of beach.

--- SENTENCE 2082 ---
Undercut trees demonstrate beach erosion of some 300 to 500 feet (90 to 150 m) near Ma'atulaumea Point (67).

--- SENTENCE 2083 ---
The shoreline near Ma'atulaumea Point has been modified considerably by construction of a small boat harbor.

--- SENTENCE 2084 ---
A 500-foot (150 m) length of shoreline immediately west of Auasi Harbor is experiencing severe erosion, which has toppled coconut trees and threatens several fales and seawalls in the backshore area.

--- SENTENCE 2085 ---
A narrow foreshore of limestone rubble and basalt cobble terminates in a 6-foot (2 m) high scarp.

--- SENTENCE 2086 ---
Erosion may be linked to harbor construction, which has altered the angle of wave approach.

--- SENTENCE 2087 ---
A revetment has been constructed east of the harbor to stabilize the sector between the eastern wall of the harbor and Ma'atulaumea Point (49).

--- SENTENCE 2088 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

The reef fronting Auasi Village has a maximum width of 700 feet (215 m).

--- SENTENCE 2089 ---
Extensive portions of the reef flat are exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2090 ---
A large natural channel (ava) cuts through the reef about 500 feet (145 m) west of Ma'atulaumea Point.

--- SENTENCE 2091 ---
The reef narrows somewhat west of the ava.

--- SENTENCE 2092 ---
The channel provides an opening 200 feet (60 m) wide through the reef front, narrowing to 50 feet (15 m) near shore.

--- SENTENCE 2093 ---
Isolated limestone knolls are evident in places, but the bottom of the outer channel consists mostly of

SA'OLE CO.

AUASI

scoured limestone, with some sand, gravel, and rubble present in pockets.

--- SENTENCE 2094 ---
Where the channel shoals shoreward, large limestone boulders are conspicuous on the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 2095 ---
The inner channel bottom grades to silty-rubble and some basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 2096 ---
Microatolls (Porites sp.) 3 feet (1 m) across line the western side of the inner channel (14;67).

--- SENTENCE 2097 ---
The ava serves as the main discharge area for water thrown onto the reef by waves and exerts considerable influence on water circulation over the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2098 ---
A strong current flows from west to east over the southwestern section of the reef.

--- SENTENCE 2099 ---
The ava is the only navigational passage through the reef to the open sea.

--- SENTENCE 2100 ---
The U.S. Navy modified the channel in the 1950's by blasting and dredging to improve access for the longboats from Aunu'u Island (MAP A1).

--- SENTENCE 2101 ---
Other, smaller channels are said to have been cut in the inner reef in 1963 to provide a safer beaching area for the longboats (14;67).

--- SENTENCE 2102 ---
More recently the ava has been widened in conjunction with construction of a small boat harbor near Ma'atulaumea Point (ASCRI-8B1).

--- SENTENCE 2103 ---
Nearshore areas (within 100 feet or 30 m of shore) just west of Ma'atulaumea Point have a bottom of mostly basalt boulders, with an admixture of limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 2104 ---
Farther to the southwest, nearshore areas consist predominantly of limestone rubble which covers over half the reef flat between 100 and 295 feet (30 and 90 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2105 ---
Much of this rubble bottom is exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2106 ---
Limestone boulders are conspicuous in nearshore areas off the southwest end of Auasi Beach.

--- SENTENCE 2107 ---
Consolidated limestone is common on the inner reef flat near Taugamalama Point.

--- SENTENCE 2108 ---
A greater cover of consolidated limestone and lesser amounts of rubble characterize the middle reef from 295 to 395 feet (90 to 120 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2109 ---
Consolidated limestone increases seaward from 395 feet (120 m) to the reef margin, about 590 feet (180 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2110 ---
The outer reef is strewn with limestone boulders.

--- SENTENCE 2111 ---
The middle reef platform is usually submerged, except at lowest spring tides.

--- SENTENCE 2112 ---
The reef margin, characterized by surge channels and a well defined algal ridge, is exposed at low tide (14).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

The reef front immediately southwest of the ava off Auasi shows a very irregular algal ridge and a spur-and-groove system which becomes more regular to the southwest.

--- SENTENCE 2113 ---
Isolated limestone pinnacles and knolls project to within 2 feet (0.6 m) of the surface in places.

--- SENTENCE 2114 ---
Surge channels and buttresses are moderately well developed southwest of the ava, but not so closer to Taugamalama Point, were the reef front slopes gently seaward from a depth of 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) to 60 feet (18 m) before descending steeply to a bottom of sand and isolated limestone outcrops in deep water (14).

--- SENTENCE 2115 ---
The reef front between the ava and Taugamalama Point is characterized by a number of descending spurs or buttresses up to 15 feet (5 m) high (ASCRI-8B1).

--- SENTENCE 2116 ---
Grooves up to 20 feet (6 m) deep contain limestone boulders and

A reef spur or knoll east of the channel into Auasi Harbor is known locally as the "wavemaker" because the shoaling effect causes waves to break in the entrance channel (202).

# FRINGING REEF FLAT

Shallow pools among rocks off the northeastern part of Auasi Beach are inhabited by numerous hermit crabs (14).

--- SENTENCE 2121 ---
The northeastern margin of a well-formed ava near Ma'atu-laumea Point is densely covered by corals, including Acropora spp. and encrusting Montipora sp.

--- SENTENCE 2122 ---
The channel shoals shoreward and coral cover is reduced from that at the outer edge.

--- SENTENCE 2123 ---
Conspicuous stands of Millepora sp. are evident along the northeastern margin at depths of 3 to 6 feet (1 to 2 m).

--- SENTENCE 2124 ---
Coral cover is further reduced inshore at depths of 1 to 3 feet (up to 1 m), but heads of Psammocora contigua and Porites sp. are evident along the inner channel between 195 to 295 feet (60 to 90 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2125 ---
Corals disappear shoreward where the ava mergds with a reef flat of silty rubble and basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 2126 ---
However, Porites microatolls up to 3 feet (1 m) across line portions of the inner channel along its southwestern margin (14).

--- SENTENCE 2127 ---
Coral cover is generally less than 5% on the inner rdef (to 100 feet or 30 m offshore) fronting the northeastern portion of Auasi Beach, with very small heads of Porites lutea present just west of Ma'atulaumea Point.

--- SENTENCE 2128 ---
Only off the southwestern section of the beach is coral cover substantial in nearshore areas, were cover ranges from about 10% up to nearly 40% in one area of Psammocora a few feet offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2129 ---
Porites lutea microatolls are well developed near shore in depressions which remain submerged at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2130 ---
Other reef depressions (mainly on the inner reef, but also at mid-reef) harbor small beds of Acropora formosa and A. corymbosa, with coral cover reaching 20% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 2131 ---
Pavona divaricata is common in a few places.

--- SENTENCE 2132 ---
The brown alga, Dictyota friabilis, mats inshore areas with considerable cover in places (14).

--- SENTENCE 2133 ---
The extensive rubble areas extending from shore to mid-reef are covered by encrusting nullipore algae.

--- SENTENCE 2134 ---
Fleshy algal cover, especially  $\frac{\text{Halimeda}}{90}$  sp., averages 10% on rubble flats 100 to 295 feet (30 to  $\frac{90}{90}$  m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2135 ---
Coral cover is 1 to 3% (14).

--- SENTENCE 2136 ---
Corals are common on the middle and outer reef platform, but cover is quite variable.

--- SENTENCE 2137 ---
Coral cover of less than 5% occurs on the outer reef off the western portion of Auasi Beach, but coral cover of between 10 and 30% is common off the southwestern end of the beach near Taugamalama Point.

--- SENTENCE 2138 ---
Scattered Porites andrewsi heads are present on the northeastern reef, whereas Acropora spp.

--- SENTENCE 2139 ---
account for most of the coral cover on the southwestern reef.

--- SENTENCE 2140 ---
Most common in areas of vigorous water movement is A. humilis.

--- SENTENCE 2141 ---
Fleshy algae are conspicuous, with Halimeda sp. and Dictyosphaeria sp.

Corals are well-developed on the outer reef near the ava, 395 feet (120 m) or more offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2144 ---
Coral cover ranges from 25% to 40% here.

--- SENTENCE 2145 ---
Off Ma'atulaumea Point, Acropora corymbosa is well-developed in contrast to shoreward areas of the reef.

--- SENTENCE 2146 ---
Coral cover is about 10 to 20% off Ma'atulaumea Point, where the reef flat is a shallow limestone pavement.

--- SENTENCE 2147 ---
The sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, is abundant (14).

--- SENTENCE 2148 ---
A distinctive assemblage of wave-resistant corals, including Acropora humilis and Pocillopora brevicornis occupies the outermost reef flat and reef margin, from 490 to 590 feet (150 to 180 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2149 ---
The margin exhibits turfs of brown and green algae and some beds of the soft coral, Palythoa sp. (14).

--- SENTENCE 2150 ---
Fishes are not abundant on the reef flat off Auasi Village.

--- SENTENCE 2151 ---
However, diversity is relatively high, with at least 72 species represented (14;76).

--- SENTENCE 2152 ---
A high proportion of the fauna is juveniles (14).

--- SENTENCE 2153 ---
Juveniles of the surgeonfish, Ctenochaetus striatus, are common throughout the reef flat from shore to the margin.

--- SENTENCE 2154 ---
Also very common are adults (mainly) and juveniles of the damselfishes, <u>Glyphidodontops</u> <u>glaucus</u> and <u>G. leucopomus</u> (14), the latter more abundant on the outer reef (14;76).

--- SENTENCE 2155 ---
In areas of cover, adults (mainly) and juveniles of the damselfish, Stegastes albofasciatus, are relatively common.

--- SENTENCE 2156 ---
In areas of branching coral thickets inshore, S. albofasciatus is joined by adults of the surgeonfish.

--- SENTENCE 2157 ---
Schools of juvenile rabbitfish (<u>Siganus spinus</u>) numbering up to about 200 individuals, graze on algae along the southwestern shore.

--- SENTENCE 2158 ---
Along the northeastern shoreline, in an area of rock and silty-sand, juveniles of the goatfishes, <u>Parupeneus</u> <u>bifasciatus</u> and <u>P. trifasciatus</u>, dominant, although not abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2159 ---
The wrasses, <u>Halicho</u> dominant, although not abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2160 ---
The wrasses, <u>Halichoeres</u> trimaculatus, <u>H. margaritaceus</u>, and <u>Thalassoma hardwickei</u>, are well distributed over the reef flat but are not as common as species mentioned above.

--- SENTENCE 2161 ---
Areas of coarse sand and rubble harbor juveniles of the surgeonfish, Acanthurus triostegus.

# FRINGING REEF FRONT

Prior to infestation by the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci), the reef slopes off Auasi were characterized by well-developed coral growth (14).

--- SENTENCE 2167 ---
The reef front at depths of 10 to 30 feet (3 to 9 m) was rich with corals, totaling over 60% bottom cover between the ava and Taugamalama Point.

--- SENTENCE 2168 ---
Acroporans dominated, particularly A. humilis and A. hyacinthus.

--- SENTENCE 2169 ---
Other species were also evident, including three or four other Acropora spp., Montipora spp., Pocillopora brevicornis, P. eydouxi, and several faviids.

--- SENTENCE 2172 ---
Coral cover was reduced southwest of the ava where the reef slope steepens from a depth of 60 feet (18 m) to a deep sand bottom.

--- SENTENCE 2173 ---
At depths of 165 to 195 feet (50 to 60 m), cover totaled about 30%.

--- SENTENCE 2174 ---
The burrowing sea urchin, Echinostrephus sp., is notable on the reef front, as are soft coral colonies (14).

--- SENTENCE 2175 ---
The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was not evident on forereef slopes off Auasi in early and mid-1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 2176 ---
Acanthaster was numerous on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off Auasi in August and September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 2177 ---

--- SENTENCE 2181 ---

--- SENTENCE 2183 ---
Other common species include adults of the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus triostegus, A. lineatus, A. glaucopareius, A. nigrofuscus, Zebrasoma scopas; the butterflyfish, Chaetodon reticulatus; the wrasse, Halichoeres centriquadrus; the goatfishes, Parupeneus bifasciatus and P. trifasciatus; the damselfishes, Chromis iomelas, Stegastes fasciolatus, Plectroglyphidodon johnstonianus, and P. vaiuli; and the parrotfishes, Scarus sordidus and S. oviceps (14).

#### LEAFU STREAM

Leafu Stream, draining an urban and agricultural area, frequently shows concentrations of fecal coliforms far in excess of water quality standards (40).

--- SENTENCE 2184 ---
Storm runoff through Leafu and Vaisa streams discharges large sediment loads to the ocean (67).

--- SENTENCE 2185 ---
# **NEARSHORE WATERS**

Water circulation on the inner reef fronting the northeastern end of Auasi Beach is more sluggish than elsewhere on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2186 ---
Depressed salinity along this section of the shoreline during relatively dry weather is from freshwater seepage.

--- SENTENCE 2187 ---
The inner portion of the ava cutting through Auasi reef is characterized by warm and turbid water.

--- SENTENCE 2188 ---
Visibility underwater increases with distance away from the ava (14).

--- SENTENCE 2189 ---
Construction of Auasi Harbor has altered the approach of waves and longshore currents (49).

--- SENTENCE 2190 ---
The sand beach at Auasi Village is easily accessible from the coastal road and is a good swimming beach.

--- SENTENCE 2191 ---
Small boats can be launched across the beach adjacent to the boat harbor (41).

# AUASI SMALL BOAT HARBOR

A small boat harbor has been constructed at Auasi near Ma'atulaumea Point.

--- SENTENCE 2194 ---
A dredged basin serves as a loading area for barges carrying stone for construction of a boat harbor at Aunu'u Island (MAP A1) southeast of Auasi (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2195 ---
Auasi Harbor provides docking for shallow-draft vessels (except during hurricane weather) and mooring for small fishing boats.

--- SENTENCE 2196 ---
Auasi is the traditional landing place for persons traveling between Tutuila and the small island of Aunu'u.

--- SENTENCE 2197 ---
The boat trip is hazardous during inclement weather -- especially on windy days.

--- SENTENCE 2198 ---
During the past 15 years, approximately 20 drownings have occurred as a result of overturned boats (67).

--- SENTENCE 2199 ---
The reef fringing the coast from Taugamalama Point to Matuli Point is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2200 ---
The reef flat is most frequently fished, with rod and reel the favored method.

--- SENTENCE 2201 ---
Second most popular is throw-netting (kili).

--- SENTENCE 2202 ---
Pole fishing is primarily daytime activity, bringing catches of malauli (large jack), lupota (small jack), gatala (honeycomb grouper), and afulu (large goatfish).

--- SENTENCE 2203 ---
Throw-netting yields catches of manini (convict tang), alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), (adult mullet), fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota, and, seasonally, atule (big-eye scad), lo (rabbitfish), and i'asina (juvenile goatfish) (20).

--- SENTENCE 2204 ---
At Auasi, pole fishing is practiced from ava margins, as well as from shore.

--- SENTENCE 2205 ---
Spearing occurs over the middle and outer reef platform but appears to be heaviest off the reef face and outer margins of the ava.

--- SENTENCE 2206 ---
Catches include gatala, alogo, tifitifi (moorish idol), as well as papata (slipper lobster).

--- SENTENCE 2207 ---
Torch fishing for fishes, octopus, and lobsters is relatively frequent, especially on the outer margin.

--- SENTENCE 2208 ---
The number of popular, edible fishes (14).

--- SENTENCE 2209 ---

# SHORELINE

# COAST BETWEEN MATULI POINT AND MALIUGA POINT

#### ALAO MARSH

Behind the village of Alao there is a 4 acre (1.6 hectare) coastal marsh.

--- SENTENCE 2225 ---
Little of the former natural vegetation remains (as with most other coastal marshes) because of extensive cultivation of taro (77).

--- SENTENCE 2226 ---
A wide beach of calcareous sand fronts the entire length of Alao Village (ASCRI-8S3) from near Matuli Point to Maliuga Point, a distance of 4,000 feet (1.2 km).

--- SENTENCE 2227 ---
Maliuga Point is a sandy spit terminating in a cluster of rocks which separates the long beaches fronting the villages of Alao and Tula.

--- SENTENCE 2228 ---
Limestone rubble is extensive in places, as are outcrops of beachrock at the waterline.

--- SENTENCE 2229 ---
A 6-foot scarp eroded in the backshore just north of Maliuga Point is stabilized by a revetment of randomly-dumped boulders.

--- SENTENCE 2230 ---
A small rubble seawall stabilizes a 1- to 4-foot high backshore scarp eroded along a section of beach fronting Alao (49).

--- SENTENCE 2231 ---
Although easily accessible from the coastal road, the beach is exposed to trade winds which normally blow onshore producing rough waters and strong currents across the reef.

#### MALIUGA POINT

--- SENTENCE 2232 ---
The rare Australian gray duck (toloa; Anas superciliosus pelewensis), has been sighted on occasion along the southeastern coast of Tutuila in the vicinity of Maliuga Point (15).

--- SENTENCE 2235 ---
About 75% of the corals were alive (75).

# FRINGING REEF OFF TULA VILLAGE

The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was not evident on forereef slopes off Tula Village in early and mid-1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 2254 ---
Acanthaster was sparse on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off Tula in August/September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 2255 ---
About 70% of the coral heads were alive (75).

--- SENTENCE 2256 ---
The reef front south of Tula Village harbors a highly diverse fish fauna.

--- SENTENCE 2257 ---
The assemblage includes at least 102 species but most are only moderately abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2258 ---
Most abundant is the damselfish, Pomacentrus melanopterus.

--- SENTENCE 2259 ---
Plectroglyphidodon dickii, Chromis xanthura, and Ctenochaetus striatus are common (76).

--- SENTENCE 2260 ---
The reef fringing the coast from Matuli Point to Fagasa Point (fronting the villages of Alao and Tula) is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2261 ---
The reef flat is the focus of fishing use.

--- SENTENCE 2262 ---
Rod and reel is the preferred fishing method.

--- SENTENCE 2263 ---
Throw-netting is the second favored method, followed by spearing (mata) and seine net-

ting (upega).

--- SENTENCE 2264 ---
Pole fishing is practiced primarily in the daytime and yields malauli (large jack), lupota (small jack), gatala (honeycomb grouper), and afulu (adult goatfish).

--- SENTENCE 2265 ---
Throw-netting is also a daytime activity, resulting in catches of manini (convict tang), alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), anae (adult mullet), fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota, and, seasonally, atule (big-eye scad), lo (rabbitfish), and i'asina (juvenile goatfish).

--- SENTENCE 2266 ---
Alogo, pone, and laea (large parrotfish) are caught day and night by spearing.

--- SENTENCE 2268 ---
Night catches include anae, crab, ula (spiny lobster), papata (slipper lobster), and ume (unicornfish).

Waves breaking off the reef between Matuli Point and Tula Village have potential for board surfing during the months of November to March.

--- SENTENCE 2273 ---
THE NORTHEAST COAST OF TUTUILA

The northeastern coastline of Tutuila is characterized by headlands forming high, rugged cliffs and deeply embayed stream valleys.

--- SENTENCE 2274 ---
Upland drainage is provided by deeply-incised stream valleys radiating from the summit of the volcanic cones (64).

--- SENTENCE 2275 ---
A secondary road (MAP 9) extends from Tula Village on the east coast across Cape Matatula to the north coast of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2276 ---
A spur road terminates at an active quarry facing offshore seastacks of Nu'utele Rock and Nu'uiti Rock.

--- SENTENCE 2277 ---
The quarry is the source of rocks used in construction of Aunu'u small boat harbor (MAP A1).

--- SENTENCE 2278 ---
A coastal trail extends westward from the quarry to Onenoa Village.

--- SENTENCE 2279 ---
The secondary road runs westward above the quarry site and terminates at Onenoa Village.

--- SENTENCE 2280 ---
This road, passable only during dry weather, affords a scenic view of the ocean and the seastacks between Cape Matatula and Papaloa Point (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2281 ---
A short secondary road of graded soil, covered in places with coral fill, extends from the village of Amouli (MAP 7) on the south shore through a pass to Aoa Village (MAP 10) on the north shore at Aoa Bay (23).

--- SENTENCE 2282 ---
Another road connects from the village of Faga'itua (MAP 6) on the south shore to Masefau (MAP 11) on the north shore, with a spur extending to the villages of Masausi and Sa'ilele (MAP 10).

--- SENTENCE 2283 ---
This road is extremely steep winding and washes out during periods of heavy rains (23).

--- SENTENCE 2284 ---
these roads are subject to erosion during rainstorms and impassable during wet weather except by four-wheel drive vehicles Major improvements are planned for Aoa Road (39), and the Masefau Road has been widened.

--- SENTENCE 2285 ---
Presently under construction is a new road to connect the north shore villages of Aoa and Masausi (64).

--- SENTENCE 2286 ---
Access to Afono Village (MAP 12) from Aua Village (MAP 2) on Pago Pago Harbor is afforded by a steep road currently under improvement (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2287 ---
Scenic views are afforded along the crest of the Afono road (41).

--- SENTENCE 2288 ---
Several villages on the north shore are not served by roads of any kind and are reached either by boat or by hiking over trails across the mountains running the length of Tutuila (23).

--- SENTENCE 2289 ---
Improvements to the Masefau and Aoa roads, as well as completion of the "top mile" road's lower section near Afono Village are planned (39).

--- SENTENCE 2290 ---
Two village sites, at the head of Amalau Bay and on the cliff-top trail between Onenoa and Aoa Villages, have been abandoned (30).

Papaloa Point is frequently used for fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2294 ---
Rod and reel fishing is the preferred activity, followed in popularity by diving with homemade spears (mata), and pole and line fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2295 ---
Alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), laea (large parrotfish), and eel are taken by spear day and night.

--- SENTENCE 2296 ---
Fe'e (octopus), faisua (giant sea clam), fuga (small parrotfish), and ume (unicornfish) are caught by day, whereas papata (slipper lobster), ula (spiny lobster), and crab are taken at night.

--- SENTENCE 2297 ---
Pole fishing yields day and night catches of gatala (honeycomb grouper), mataeleele (small emperor fish), filoa (large emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper).

--- SENTENCE 2298 ---
In addition, lupota (small jack), and sumu (triggerfish) are caught by day, and malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), and malai (paddletail snapper) at night (20).

# COAST BETWEEN FATUMAGA ROCKS AND SOLO POINT (ONENOA BAY)

#

--- SENTENCE 2313 ---
A crescent beach fronting Onenoa Village is bounded by volcanic boulders lying at the base of headlands.

--- SENTENCE 2314 ---
The 40-foot (12 m) wide foreshore consists mostly of calcareous sand and some volcanic sediment.

--- SENTENCE 2315 ---
A band of basalt boulders and cobbles separates the foreshore from the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2316 ---
A boulder seawall protects houses adjacent to Vaisa Stream.

--- SENTENCE 2317 ---
Fatumaga Rock is a seastack about 15 feet (5 m) in elevation lying a short distance off the headland to the east of the village (49;ASCRI-9S2).

--- SENTENCE 2318 ---
Onenoa Village consists of about 15 houses, several situated immediately behind the beach (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2319 ---
The fringing reef is 350 feet (105 m) wide off Onenoa (49).

--- SENTENCE 2320 ---
Volcanic boulders are exposed at low tide on the inner reef flanking the eastern side of Onenoa Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2321 ---
The bottom consists mostly of rubble with some silty-sand (ASCRI-9B1).

--- SENTENCE 2322 ---
An ava (channel) crosses the outer reef off Onenoa Village.

--- SENTENCE 2323 ---
Channel margins are consolidated limestone with deep undercuts.

--- SENTENCE 2324 ---
Consolidated limestone boulders on the channel bottom 15 to 20 feet (5 to 6 m) deep are silt-covered (ASCRI-9B2).

--- SENTENCE 2325 ---
Generally, the outer reef is shallower than inshore areas.

--- SENTENCE 2326 ---
However, depressions reaching 4 feet (1.2 m) are conspicuous, especially near the ava (ASCRI-9B3).

--- SENTENCE 2327 ---
Southwest of the ava, the inner reef is a platform of consolidated coral rubble, solid limestone, and loose rubble.

--- SENTENCE 2328 ---
Depth at high tide is not over 3 feet (1 m) (ASCRI-9B4).

#### FRINGING REEF

Pockets of silty-sand on the inner reef flanking the eastern side of Onenoa Bay harbor numerous sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus).

--- SENTENCE 2329 ---
Small barnacles are present on lava rocks exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2330 ---
The only conspicuous fleshy alga is an unidentified cyanophyte (blue-green)(ASCRI-9B1).

--- SENTENCE 2331 ---
The coralline alga, <u>Porolithon</u> sp., encrusts limestone boulders on the bottom of the ava.

--- SENTENCE 2332 ---
Coral heads in this area are mostly dead, possibly a result of predation by the crown-of thorns starfish (alamea; <u>Acanthaster planci</u>) although none is evident.

--- SENTENCE 2333 ---
A few large colonies of <u>Millepora</u> sp. are present, together with soft coral colonies (ASCRI-9B2).

--- SENTENCE 2334 ---
Corals are not well developed on the outer reef west of the ava, where cover approaches 10%.

--- SENTENCE 2335 ---
Algae also are poorly represented except for an abundance of encrusting coralline species.

--- SENTENCE 2336 ---
Sea urchins (Echinometra mathaei) are present (ASCRI-9B3).

# CAPE MATATULA

Cape Matatula, the northeastern tip of the Island of Tutuila, terminates in a point of dense lava rock which has been etched by wave erosion from the softer cinder bed materials that once surrounded it.

--- SENTENCE 2338 ---
This promontory is the largest of several dense lava plugs, crater fills, and remnants of associated cinder cones surrounding Olomoana Peak (54).

--- SENTENCE 2339 ---
# OFF CAPE MATATULA

Corals on the bottom at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off Cape Matatula were alive in August/September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 2340 ---
The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; <u>Acanthaster planci</u>) was uncommon (75).

--- SENTENCE 2341 ---
# COAST BETWEEN CAPE MATATULA AND PAPALOA POINT

#### SHORELINE

Much of the shoreline between Cape Matatula and Papaloa Point consists of volcanic boulders (talus).

East of Papaloa Point there is a 3,000-foot (900 m) long beach of basalt boulders, limestone rubble, and scattered sand patches.

--- SENTENCE 2343 ---
An exposed outcrop of beachrock is present.

Beach width is nearly 30 feet (9 m) (49;ASCRI-9S1).

Coral cover is sparse (about 1%) on the inner reef platform southwest of the ava.

--- SENTENCE 2356 ---

--- SENTENCE 2357 ---
At least 25 coral species representing 17 genera are present on the reef fronting Onenoa Village.

--- SENTENCE 2358 ---
Ralfsia sp., Actinotrichia sp., Halimeda sp. and encrusting corallines are the most conspicuous algae (ASCRI-984).

--- SENTENCE 2359 ---
The reef flat in front of Onenoa Village shelters a diverse and moderately abundant fish fauna.

--- SENTENCE 2360 ---
At least 54 species recorded.

--- SENTENCE 2361 ---
Large schools (1,500 to 2,000 individuals) of the surf perch, Kuhlia mugil, are seen occasionally in shallow water off the beach where a boulder habitat is otherwise impoverished.

--- SENTENCE 2362 ---
Atherinids are present in large numbers but are not conspicuous because of their small size.

--- SENTENCE 2363 ---

--- SENTENCE 2364 ---

--- SENTENCE 2365 ---
Abundance of all species increases along the margins of an ava, but parrotfishes and surgeonfishes are especially abundant there.

--- SENTENCE 2366 ---

ing the fish assemblage are atherinids, surf perch (Kuhlia butterflyfishes mugil), goatfish (Parupeneus chryserydros), (Chaetodon auriga and C. citrinellus), surgeonfishes (Acanthurus lineatus, A. nigrofuscus and A. triostegus), damselfishes (Glyphidodontops cyanea, G. leucopomus and Plectroglyphidodon leucozona), wrasses (Halichoeres hoeveni, Stethojulis bandanensis and Thalassoma hardwickei), and parrotfishes of several species (Scarus spp.) (ASCRI-9F1).

--- SENTENCE 2368 ---
A chief of Onenoa Village reports that alamea (Acanthaster planci) was never abundant in his lifetime until an outbreak in 1978, but he recalls from the talk of his elders that alamea was abundant many decades before (3).

--- SENTENCE 2369 ---
The largest aggregation of Acanthaster of the present infestation was first seen in May 1978, moving into Aoa and Onenoa Bays.

--- SENTENCE 2370 ---
Over half the total Acanthaster removed and buried on Tutuila during a bounty program from January 23 to October 25 1978, are reported to have been collected from the reefs near Onenoa Village.

--- SENTENCE 2371 ---
Only a few Millepora, alcyonarians and zoanthids were left untouched by the very abundant Acanthaster off Onenoa (3).

--- SENTENCE 2372 ---
In June 1978, a fairly large population of Acanthaster was located on forereef slopes between Nu'utele Rocks and Motusaga Point (MAP 10).

--- SENTENCE 2373 ---
Acanthaster was noted as conspicuous between Ogefao and Solo Point, although about 90% of the corals on the outer part of the reef flat were alive and relatively few starfish were observed there (74).

--- SENTENCE 2375 ---
East of the ava, water circulation is sluggish and visibility is reduced over the inner reef flat (ASCRI).

# FRINGING REEF

The reef flat fringing the coast from Onenoa Village to Solo Point is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by Villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2378 ---
The entire reef flat between Papaloa Point and Solo Point, is fished regularly.

--- SENTENCE 2379 ---
Diving with homemade spears (mata) is the favored method of fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2380 ---
Pole and line fishing is second most popular, followed by reef gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 2381 ---
Spearing and pole fishing provide catches of fish species similar to those taken east of Papaloa Point.

--- SENTENCE 2382 ---
Day gleaning off Onenoa yields fe'e (octopus), eel, and matapisu (limpets; Cellana sp.).

--- SENTENCE 2383 ---
Night gleaning yields alili and sisi (sea snails)(20).

--- SENTENCE 2384 ---
# COAST BETWEEN SOLO POINT AND MOTUSAGA POINT (AOA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2385 ---
The neck of land between Aoa and Amouli (MAP 5) represents the saddle between Olomoana and Alofau volcanoes narrowed by the drowning of two large canyons.

--- SENTENCE 2386 ---
The canyons are especially large because each carried drainage from the slopes of two volcanoes (54).

--- SENTENCE 2387 ---
Aoa Bay is backed by a narrow coastal plain bounded on three sides by steep mountain ridges (49).

#### TAPUA STREAM

Near its outlet to Aoa Bay, Tapua Stream forms a small estuary.

--- SENTENCE 2388 ---
The stream mouth shifts position along the sand shoreline (48).

# SHORELINE

The eastern perimeter of Aoa Bay consists of a basalt boulder wall between the low and high tide lines.

--- SENTENCE 2389 ---
The 3- to 5-foot (1 to 2 m) high wall is fronted by a gently-sloping foreshore of fine sand and basalt rubble.

--- SENTENCE 2390 ---
A small delta at the mouth of Laolu Stream consists primarily of basalt cobbles and small boulders.

--- SENTENCE 2391 ---
At the head of Aoa Bay is a crescent beach of sand with scattered basalt and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 2392 ---
The 30- to 50-foot (9 to 15 m) wide beach between Laoulu and Tapua Streams is broken by an outcrop of basalt (49).

--- SENTENCE 2393 ---
A school situated at the southwestern end of Aoa Village is protected by a seawall 710 feet (216 m) long (70).

--- SENTENCE 2394 ---
The western perimeter of Aoa Bay consists of a 30-foot wide sand beach fronted by a wide, shallow reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2395 ---
South of Motusaga Point there is a section of shoreline protected by a rock seawall extending from the reef flat to the 4-foot elevation (49).

--- SENTENCE 2396 ---
The reef fronting Aoa Village extends 800 to 1200 feet (245 to 365 m) offshore (62).

--- SENTENCE 2397 ---
Extensive sand flats occupy the inner reef at the head of Aoa Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2398 ---
A sand flat extending 80 feet (25 m) offshore is exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2399 ---
Minus tides expose a sand flat extending nearly 260 feet (80 m) offshore of the seawall

--- SENTENCE 2412 ---
The inner reef flat south of Motusaga Point consists of basalt cobbles, limestone rubble, and sand, and is exposed at low tide (49).

--- SENTENCE 2413 ---
# **AOA MANGROVE FOREST**

A 4 acre (1.6 hectare) mangrove forest behind the village of Aoa extends along several branches of the stream flowing into Aoa Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2414 ---
This forest consists largely of a mature stand of oriental mangroves (Bruguiera gymnorhiza), with some red mangroves (Rhizophora mangle) present lower down the shore (48;77).

--- SENTENCE 2415 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

Nearshore parts of the sand flat in Aoa Bay generally lack conspicuous biota, except for burrows of ghost crabs (Ocypoda sp.) near the seawall.

--- SENTENCE 2416 ---
Anemonies are numerous on the sand flat from 65 to 245 feet (20 to 75 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2417 ---
The seagrass, Halophila sp., is the dominant bottom form in the zone of muddy-sand.

--- SENTENCE 2418 ---
In some areas the seagrass is heavily covered by epiphytic algae.

--- SENTENCE 2419 ---
A sparse cover of algae, mostly Padina sp., occurs on rocks between 165 and 245 feet (50 and 75 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2420 ---
Rocks beyond 80 feet (25 m) are covered with Jania sp., Dictyota sp., and Halimeda sp.

--- SENTENCE 2421 ---
Numerous cowries (Cypraea annulus) occur in crevices in the larger rocks (48).

--- SENTENCE 2422 ---
Few fishes inhabit the inner reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2423 ---
The only species observed out to 330 feet (100 m) from shore are small schools of juvenile mullet (Chelon vaigiensis), goatfish (Mulloidichthys flavolineatus), and occasional small jacks (Caranx melampygus) (48).

--- SENTENCE 2424 ---
Coral is absent from the reef flat inside 330 feet (100  $\,$  m) of shore.

--- SENTENCE 2425 ---
In the area of large coral wheels, live tissue (Porites

--- SENTENCE 2427 ---
Elsewhere on the flat, coral-covered boulders are closely spaced and cover up to half the bottom with coral cover about 15%.

--- SENTENCE 2428 ---
Pavona frondifera is most common.

--- SENTENCE 2429 ---

A sparse algal cover on dead coral heads includes Jania sp. and Halimeda sp. Limestone rubble from 655 to 900 feet (200 to 275 m) offshore is partially-consolidated by encrusting coralline algae (mostly Porolithon sp.).
