--- SENTENCE 2435 ---
Coral heads on the sand and rubble flats provide shelter for small fishes.

--- SENTENCE 2436 ---
Most abundant are the damselfishes, Plectrogly-phidodon leucozona, Stegastes albofasciatus, Dascyllus aruanus, Chromis caerulea, Abudefduf coelestinus, the wrasses, Halichoeres trimaculatus and Thalassoma hardwickei, the surgeonfish, Acanthurus nigrofuscus, the butterflyfishes, Chaetodon citrinellus, C. vagabundus, and Heniochus chrysostomus, the grouper Epine-phelus merra, the snapper, Lutjanus fulvus, the rabbitfish, Siganus rostratus, the sharpnose puffer, Canthigaster solandri, the cardinalfish, Cheilodipterus quinquelineatus, and the moorish idol, Zanclus cornutus.

--- SENTENCE 2437 ---
On sand and rubble areas between coral heads are occasional gobies (Cryptocentrops maculosus and Cryptocentrus koumansi) sharing burrows with the snapping shrimp, Alpheus djiboutensis (48).

--- SENTENCE 2438 ---
The largest aggregation of <u>Acanthaster planci</u> in the recent infestation of Tutuila reefs was first seen in May 1978 in Aoa and Onenoa Bays.

--- SENTENCE 2439 ---
Over 25% of the <u>Acanthaster</u> reputed to have been removed and buried on Tutuila during a bounty program from January to October 1978, were reportedly collected on the reef fronting Aoa (3).

--- SENTENCE 2440 ---
A relatively large population of <u>A. planci</u> was located on forereef slopes between Nu'utele Rocks (MAP 9) and Motusaga Point in June 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 2441 ---
Only about 15% of corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) are alive.

--- SENTENCE 2442 ---
<u>Acanthaster</u> is sparse (75).

--- SENTENCE 2443 ---
# AOA BAY

Substantial quantities of sediment have been deposited at the mouth of Tapua Stream and entered Aoa Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2444 ---
However, there is no evidence of sedimentation or damage on the reef from erosion of the Aoa and Masefau roads (39).

--- SENTENCE 2445 ---
Currents flow seaward through the ava which cuts across Aoa reef.

--- SENTENCE 2446 ---
Underwater visibility is rather poor (about 6 feet or 2 m) over the reef flat (48).

# AOA VILLAGE - AOA BAY

The unimproved road to Aoa Village from Amouli Village on the southern shore (MAP 7) terminates at Tapua Stream (48).

--- SENTENCE 2449 ---
Fa'alefu is reached from Aoa by crossing a suspension bridge.

--- SENTENCE 2450 ---
A school is located on the western bank of Tapua Stream (62).

--- SENTENCE 2451 ---
Access to coastal areas west of Aoa is by foot trail (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2452 ---
A footpath parallels the eastern side of Aoa Bay, connecting several small tourist fales with the main village (41;49).

--- SENTENCE 2453 ---
The reef fringing Aoa Bay is considered a "critical reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2454 ---
reef flat is the most frequently fished area (20).

--- SENTENCE 2455 ---
Residents of Aoa Village report light fishing effort on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2456 ---
small amount of hook and line fishing is practiced, mostly by children.

--- SENTENCE 2457 ---
Occasionally, gleaners seek octopus, or search spiny lobster at night using torches along the outer edge of the reef (48).

--- SENTENCE 2458 ---
Throw-netting is the favored technique, followed by pole and line fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2459 ---
Spearing (mata) and reef gleaning are less popular activities.

--- SENTENCE 2460 ---
Manini (convict tang), alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), anae (adult mullet), fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota (small jack) are taken during the day by throw net.

--- SENTENCE 2461 ---
Atule (big-eye scad), lo (rabbitfish), and i'asina (juvenile goatfish) are also caught by this method in Spearing results in day and night catches of alogo, pone, laea (large parrotfish), and eel.

--- SENTENCE 2462 ---
In addition, fe'e (octopus), faisua (giant sea clam), fuga (small parrotfish), and ume (unicornfish) are speared by day, and papata (slipper lobster).

--- SENTENCE 2463 ---
ula (spiny lobster), and crab are speared at night.

--- SENTENCE 2464 ---
Day gleaners collect fe'e, eel, and matapisu (limpet).

--- SENTENCE 2465 ---
Night gleaners take alili and sisi, (sea snails) (20).

--- SENTENCE 2466 ---
No seine netting is reported.

--- SENTENCE 2467 ---
An incident of poisoning fish (probably using poison from local plants) was witnessed on the inner reef flat (48).

--- SENTENCE 2468 ---
# COAST BETWEEN MOTUSAGA POINT AND FOLAU POINT

#### SHORELINE

A pocket beach lies between Motusaga Point and Leanamanu Point.

--- SENTENCE 2469 ---
The foreshore is 50 to 60 feet (15 to 13 m) wide and consists mostly of calcareous sand (49).

--- SENTENCE 2470 ---
The beach off Sa'ilele is bounded by sea stacks which act as natural groins stabilizing the beach.

--- SENTENCE 2471 ---
The 60-foot wide foreshore is composed of calcareous sand with considerable limestone rubble, especially at the foreshore crest.

--- SENTENCE 2472 ---
A 5-foot scarp is cut in the foreshore crest at the eastern end of the beach.

--- SENTENCE 2473 ---
Aonoi Stream, a small intermittent stream, discharges through the center of the beach and has formed a small delta of basalt cobbles on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2474 ---
The western end of the beach grades to a foreshore of limestone and basalt rubble, with beachrock exposed at intervals along the shore (49).

#### TOLIGAI COVE

# MALO POINT AND FOLAU POINT

--- SENTENCE 2481 ---
The blue-gray noddy (laia; <u>Procelsterna cerulea</u>), an uncommon resident seabird, roosts and nests on both Malo Point and Folau Point (15).

# FRINGING REEF

Abundance of the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanth-aster planci) observed on the forereef slopes from Motusaga Point to Puputagi Point (MAP 11) in June 1978, steadily declined to just a few individuals (74).

--- SENTENCE 2482 ---
# BURIAL GROUND

A high chief burial ground is located along the coast near Sa'ilele Village (41).

--- SENTENCE 2483 ---
# SHORELINE

Access to Sa'ilele Beach is by courtesy of the village.

--- SENTENCE 2484 ---
Swimming conditions are excellent (41).

--- SENTENCE 2485 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF SA'ILELE VILLAGE

--- SENTENCE 2486 ---
The reef fringing the coast between Motusaga Point and Leanaopou Point is regularly fished (20).

--- SENTENCE 2487 ---
The reef flat between Motusaga Point and Malo Point is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2488 ---
Spearing (mata) is most common.

--- SENTENCE 2489 ---
Pole and line fishing is second in popularity, followed by reef gleaning and handlining at night from canoes.

--- SENTENCE 2490 ---
Fishes taken by spear, pole and line, and gleaning are similar to the catch from Aoa reef.

--- SENTENCE 2491 ---
Handlining at night from canoes results in catches of malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), mataeleele (small emperor fish), savane (blue-lined snapper), and filoa (large emperor fish)(20).

# FRINGING REEF

# OFF FOLAU POINT

Only about 20% of corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) were alive in August/September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 2504 ---
The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was relatively common at that time (75).

--- SENTENCE 2505 ---
# BAY AT MASAUSI

Masausi is protected from waves except those approaching from the north.

--- SENTENCE 2506 ---
Nearshore waters are turbid (49).

--- SENTENCE 2507 ---
The reef fringing an unnamed bay in front of Masausi Village is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2508 ---
The reef flat is most frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 2509 ---
Diving with homemade spears (mata) is the most common practice.

--- SENTENCE 2510 ---
Pole and line fishing ranks second, followed by reef gleaning and handlining at night from canoes.

--- SENTENCE 2511 ---
Catches by all methods are similar to those from Aoa and Sa'ilele reefs (20).

# COAST BETWEEN TIAPE'A POINT AND NU'USETOGA ISLET (MASEFAU BAY)

# TALALOA STREAM AND MASEFAU BAY

Perennial Talaloa Stream discharges into Masefau Bay near the village of Masefau.

--- SENTENCE 2513 ---
A catchment basin at a spring provides drinking water to the village (71).

--- SENTENCE 2514 ---
The stream drains a large saddle area between the Pago and Taputapu volcanoes.

--- SENTENCE 2515 ---
The large Masefau Bay and tributary valley arose due to the concentration of drainages between two lines of cones on the northeast rift zone of the Pago Volcano (54).

--- SENTENCE 2516 ---
# SHORELINE (SOUTHERN PERIMETER OF MASEFAU BAY)

Most of the shoreline around Masefau Bay has an erosion problem.

--- SENTENCE 2517 ---
Rudimentary seawalls and boulder revetments line the shore.

--- SENTENCE 2518 ---
Seawall sections are deteriorating and a wave-cut scarp approaches the road in ardas of the southeastern bay where the backshore is low (49).

--- SENTENCE 2519 ---
The shoreline along the southern perimeter of Masefau Bay has been eroding since the late 1960's when sand

# FRINGING REEF FLAT (SOUTHERN MASEFAU BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2524 ---
The fringing reef at the head of Masefau Bay has between 500 and 850 feet (150 to 260 m)(49).

--- SENTENCE 2525 ---
A rubble fan composed of mixed volcanic and limestone fragments stands somewhat higher than the surrounding inner reef flat off a small stream culvert along the southern shore of Masefau Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2526 ---
Surrounding areas composed mostly of sand (with rubble admixture) are exposed at low tide for distances of up to 75 feet (23 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2527 ---
Depths to 1.5 feet (0.4 m) occur between shore and 200 feet (60 offshore (ASCRI-11B1).

--- SENTENCE 2528 ---
The middle reef zone extends from 200 to 500 feet (60 to 150 m) offshore, with depths between 1 and 2 feet (0.3 and 0.6 m).

--- SENTENCE 2529 ---
Limestone boulders increase on the outer portion of the mid-reef, which is a limestone flat of dead <u>Pavona</u> elevated slightly above inner reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 2530 ---
The "Pavona" flat may be exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 2531 ---
Scars are evident in 1971 aerial photographs on the inner and mid-reef off the eastern end Masefau Village where sand was dredged in the late 1960's (ASCRI-11B2).

--- SENTENCE 2532 ---
From 500 to 800 feet (150 to 245 m) offshore the outer reef flat at depths of 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m).

--- SENTENCE 2533 ---
Rubble and sand are the predominant bottom types.

--- SENTENCE 2534 ---
Near the reef margin are large slabs of limestone and limestone boulders, some elevated above water (ASCRI-11B3).

--- SENTENCE 2535 ---
About 850 feet (260 m) from shore there is a consolidated limestone margin marked by a poorly developed algal ridge at a depth of 6 to 12 inches (15 to 35 cm) (ASCRI-11B4).

--- SENTENCE 2536 ---
A remnant of raised reef projecting above the fringing reef in Masefau Bay is considered evidence of a former higher stand of sea (54).

--- SENTENCE 2537 ---
# REEF FRONT (SOUTHERN MASEFAU BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2538 ---
The reef front is a steep slope of consolidated limestone.

--- SENTENCE 2539 ---
Spur-and-groove formations, although irregular and poorly developed inside the bay, are well-formed along the reef front in outer Masefau Bay (ASCRI-11B5).

#### TALALOA STREAM AND MANGROVE SWAMP

Talaloa Stream is considered to have exceptional natural value because of its largely pristine condition (71).

--- SENTENCE 2540 ---
Behind the village of Masefau is a mangrove forest covering an area of approximately 15 acres (6 ha).

--- SENTENCE 2541 ---
The vegetation is a mature forest of oriental mangroves (<u>Bruguiera gymnorhiza</u>) growing along the lower reach of Talaloa Stream (77).

# OFFSHORE BETWEEN TIAPE'A POINT AND MASEFAU

No crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) were evident on forereef slopes between Tiape'a Point and Masefau in June 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 2544 ---
# REEF FLAT (SOUTHERN MASEFAU BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2545 ---
Some areas of the inner reef flat along the southern perimeter of Masefau Bay have considerable cover of brown alga (Padina sp.) and lesser amounts of seagrass (Halophila sp.).

--- SENTENCE 2546 ---
Live coral covers less than 5% of the inner reef flat (ASCRI-11B1).

--- SENTENCE 2547 ---
Porites lutea and Pavona fondifera were reported most common on the inner reef in 1978 (10).

--- SENTENCE 2548 ---
Coral cover is around 10% on the middle reef flat, where Pavona (3 species) is most common, followed by Porites (3 species).

--- SENTENCE 2549 ---
Algae account for about 20 to 30% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 2550 ---
Some areas exhibit considerable Padina tenuis, and Padina sp., whereas other areas lack Padina and Actinotrichia sp., Halimeda discoidea, and a brownish cyanophyte (blue-green) are most common.

--- SENTENCE 2551 ---
The sea urchin, Echinometra mathaei, abundant, as is the sea cucumber, <u>Holothuria hilla</u>.

--- SENTENCE 2552 ---
<u>Stichopus</u> choloronotus is common.

--- SENTENCE 2553 ---
Patches of a whitish-green sponge occur a few areas (ASCRI-11B2).

--- SENTENCE 2554 ---
Abundant recruitment of small sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus) has been noted on the reef flat at Masefau Bay (3).

--- SENTENCE 2555 ---
Few corals inhabit the rubble tracts on the outer reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2556 ---
Fleshy algae cover up to 60% of the constantly submerged rubble areas, with <u>Padina</u> sp.

--- SENTENCE 2557 ---
Large limestone slabs near the reef margin are encrusted by coralline algae (ASCRI-11B3).

--- SENTENCE 2558 ---
The reef margin has less than 5% bottom cover by live corals.

--- SENTENCE 2559 ---
Staghorn <u>Acropora</u> and <u>Pocillopora</u> are most common.

--- SENTENCE 2560 ---
The sea urchin, <u>Diadema</u> sp., is found in holes in low abundance.

--- SENTENCE 2561 ---
Encrusting coralline algae are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2562 ---
The green alga, <u>Dictyosphaeria versluysii</u>, is common (ASCRI-11B4).

--- SENTENCE 2563 ---
In general, the reef flat affords little cover for fishes and abundance is low.

--- SENTENCE 2564 ---
At least 18 species are present, with damselfishes, wrasses, and gobies most common.

--- SENTENCE 2565 ---
Other species undoubtedly cross the reef flat at times.

--- SENTENCE 2566 ---
Dominant species are the surf perch, Kuhlia marginatus, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus nigrofuscus and A. triostegus, the damselfishes, Abudefduf septemfasciatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea, and G. leucopomus, and the wrasse, Thalassoma hardwickei.

--- SENTENCE 2567 ---
Three species of gobies are noted but not identified (ASCRI-11F1).

--- SENTENCE 2568 ---
A <u>Pavona</u> zone, distinct from adjacent reef flat areas, supports an abundant fish assemblage, consisting of at least 29 species.

--- SENTENCE 2569 ---
All species recorded from adjacent reef areas, except <u>Kuhlia marginatus</u>, also occur in the <u>Pavona</u> zone.

--- SENTENCE 2570 ---
Damselfishes and wrasses are the dominant families, but juvenile parrotfishes, goatfishes, mullets, and butterflyfishes are common.

--- SENTENCE 2571 ---
Among the most abundant species are the butterflyfish, <u>Chaetodon citrinellus</u>, the surgeonfishes, <u>Acanthurus nigrofuscus</u> and <u>A. triostegus</u>, the damselfishes, <u>Stegastes albofasciatus</u>, <u>Glyphidodontops cyanea</u>

--- SENTENCE 2574 ---
# REEF FRONT (SOUTHERN MASEFAU BAY)

Live coral covers up to 75% of the upper surfaces and sides of buttresses on the reef front, where large heads of <u>Platygyra</u> and <u>Leptoria</u> are present.

--- SENTENCE 2575 ---
Considerable tabular <u>Acropora hyacinthus</u> inhabits reef slopes, with some dead heads in grooves and along the edges of buttresses.

--- SENTENCE 2576 ---
<u>Acanthaster plancial</u> are present, and recent feeding scars are evident.

--- SENTENCE 2577 ---
Staghorn corals are well developed in grooves, where <u>Acropora intermedia</u> is dominant (ASCRI-11B5).

--- SENTENCE 2578 ---
In late 1978, prior to extensive damage by crown-of-thorns starfish, the reef margin and upper reef front exhibited luxuriant banks of Acropora formosa, considerable A. hyacinthus, and large heads of Montipora sp. and Leptoria phrygia (34).

--- SENTENCE 2579 ---
In 1978, Acanthaster moved into Masefau Bay and fed on the coral there but did not devastate the coral bottom.

--- SENTENCE 2580 ---
As in other infested areas, the starfish first attacked tabular Acropora (3).

--- SENTENCE 2581 ---
However, by August and September 1979, only 15% of corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off the eastern portion of the reef in Masefau Bay were alive.

--- SENTENCE 2582 ---
Acanthaster was relatively common (75).

--- SENTENCE 2583 ---
The reef front shelters an abundance of fishes including at least 79 species.

--- SENTENCE 2584 ---
Among the dominant species are atherinids, the goatfish, Mulloidichthys flavolineatus, and the butterflyfishes, Chaetodon auriga, C. citrinellus, and C. reticulatus.

--- SENTENCE 2585 ---
Damselfish are also abundant, with Chromis acares, C. caerulea, Glyphidodontops cyanea, and G. leucopomus especially numerous.

--- SENTENCE 2586 ---
The surgeonfish, Acanthurus lucatus, is common.

--- SENTENCE 2587 ---
Halichoeres margaritaceus and Thalassoma hardwickei are the most conspicuous wrasses.

--- SENTENCE 2588 ---
Parrotfishes of at least four species are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2589 ---
Adults are most abundant on the deeper reef slope, and juveniles more common along the reef margin (ASCRI-11F3).

#### MASEFAU BAY

Murky water flows through the ava which approaches the head of Masefau Bay off the mouth of Talaloa Stream (34).

--- SENTENCE 2590 ---
Inshore waters north of Talaloa Stream are turbid near shore.

--- SENTENCE 2591 ---
The sand flats fronting the northern end of Masefau Village are silted.

--- SENTENCE 2592 ---
Reef flat waters away from the influence of Talaloa Stream are clear and visibility underwater may be as much as 50 feet (15 m) on the inner reef.

--- SENTENCE 2593 ---
Underwater visibility is excellent (about 100 feet or 30 m) over the reef along the northern perimeter of the Bay (ASCRI)

--- SENTENCE 2594 ---
The shoreline along the northern portion of Masefau Village is eroding, with the consequent loss of a sand beach.

A short section of crescent-shaped beach which remains slopes gently

# FRINGING REEF IN NORTHERN MASEFAU BAY

A layer of dark, silty-sand covers the inner reef flat off central and northern parts of Masefau Village (ASCRI-11B6).

--- SENTENCE 2603 ---
Sand flats northeast of the village, fronting a cliff, extend to 100 feet (30 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 2604 ---
Common constituents of the sand are tests of a foram (Marginopora vertebralis), fragments of a calcareous alga (Halimeda discoidea), and bivalve shells.

--- SENTENCE 2605 ---
comprises up to 50% of the bottom from 100 to 200 feet (30 to 60 m) offshore, with scattered boulders occuring in this region.

--- SENTENCE 2606 ---
Overall, the inner reef consists of almost equal proportions of sand/gravel and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 2607 ---
Shallow sand and rubble flats continue along the base of the sea cliff as far northeast as the strait inside Nu'usetoga Islet (ASCRI-11B11).

--- SENTENCE 2608 ---
The middle reef, from 200 to 300 feet (60 to 90 m) offshore, is about 2 feet (0.6 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 2609 ---
About half the bottom is limestone rubble, with the remainder a low relief platform of consolidated limestone (ASCRI-11B7).

--- SENTENCE 2610 ---
The outer reef flat, 300 to 400 feet (90 to 120 m) offshore, consists of irregularly-consolidated limestone, with some areas of sand/gravel or rubble (ASCRI-11B8).

--- SENTENCE 2611 ---
The consolidated reef margin is about 20 feet (6 m) wide and exhibits a poorly-developed algal ridge (ASCRI-11B9).

--- SENTENCE 2612 ---
Two shallow channels (ava) indent the outer reef (49).

--- SENTENCE 2613 ---
The generally steep reef front is characterized by rubble-bottomed grooves between undercut limestone buttresses (ASCRI-11B10).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

Crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) are active on the reef front in northwestern Masefau Bay, where large patches of dead coral are conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 2641 ---
Groups of starfish and isolated individuals occur at the base of limestone outcrops.

--- SENTENCE 2642 ---
Tabular Acropora hyacinthus has been virtually eliminated by starfish, which are now preying on staghorn Acropora, although the coral assemblage is not entirely devastated (ASCRI-11B10;3).

--- SENTENCE 2643 ---
About 60% of corals on the upper reef front flanking the northern bay were still alive in August and September 1979 and Acanthaster was evident (75).

--- SENTENCE 2644 ---
Live coral cover of 50% was observed in October 1979, with considerable Montipora sp. and large areas of Porites (S.) undulata noted.

--- SENTENCE 2645 ---
Overall, at least 44 coral species in 22 genera are represented on the reef flat and reef front throughout Masefau Bay (ASCRI-11B1; B2; B3; B4; B5).

--- SENTENCE 2646 ---
Algal cover by non-coralline species is considerable (30 to 40%) on the reef front, especially between branches of <u>Porites</u> and <u>Porites</u> (S.) <u>undulata</u>.

--- SENTENCE 2647 ---
Patches of two soft corals (a brown, long fingered species and a mauve, short fingered species) increase near the ava at depths from 6 to more than 30 feet (2 to 9 m) (ASCRI-11B10).

--- SENTENCE 2648 ---
The reef margin is found relatively close to shore along the northern perimeter of Masefau Bay, causing inshore and deep water fish assemblages to occur in close proximity.

--- SENTENCE 2649 ---
High coral cover and large boulders on the reef margin and front provide habitat for cryptic fishes.

--- SENTENCE 2650 ---
The fish fauna is both abundant and diverse.

--- SENTENCE 2651 ---
At least 82 species are recorded, most of which are members of the butterflyfish, wrasse, or damselfish families.

--- SENTENCE 2652 ---
Dominant species include atherinids, the butterflyfish, Chaetodon reticulatus, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus nigrofuscus, A. ni-

# MASEFAU BAY

Masefau Bay is accessible by an unpaved road across the mountain from Faga'itua Village (MAP 7) on the south coast of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2656 ---
Although steep in places, the road has been improved and is passable by car except in very wet weather.

--- SENTENCE 2657 ---
This road offers picturesque views of both the north and south coasts of Tutuila (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2658 ---
The shoreline of Masefau Bay is easily accessible from a gently-sloping backshore.

--- SENTENCE 2659 ---
Shallow sand between exposed boulders along the base of the cliff northeast of Masefau Village can be traversed by foot at high tide.

--- SENTENCE 2660 ---
Shallow nearshore areas of sand and rubble extend northeast as far as Asaga Strait between Tutuila and Nu'usetoga Islet (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2661 ---
A private boat launching ramp is located at Masefau (41).

--- SENTENCE 2662 ---
The reef in Masefau Bay is regularly fished.

--- SENTENCE 2663 ---
Fishermen frequent deep water areas in the center of the Bay as well as the shallow reef flat (20).

--- SENTENCE 2664 ---
The Masefau reef flat (including Asaga Strait) is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2665 ---
The most common activity is pole and line fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2666 ---
Spearing (mata) ranks second and throw netting (kili) ranks third in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 2667 ---
Seine netting (upega) and handlining at night from canoes follow in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 2668 ---
(honeycomb grouper), mataeleele (small emperor fish), filoa (large emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper) are caught day and night by pole fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2669 ---
In addition, lupota (small jack) and sumu (triggerfish) are taken by day and malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), and malai (paddletail snapper) are caught at night.

--- SENTENCE 2670 ---
Spearing results in day and night catches of alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), laea (large parrotfish), and eel.

--- SENTENCE 2671 ---
Fe'e (octopus), faisua (giant sea fuga (small parrotfish), and ume (unicornfish) are additional day catch, and papata (slipper lobster), ula (spiny lobster), and crab are additional night catch by this method.

--- SENTENCE 2672 ---
Throw-netting is a daytime activity yielding manini (convict tang), alogo, pone, anae (adult mullet), fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota, and, seasonally, atule (big-eye scad), lo (rabbitfish), and i'asina (juvenile goatfish).

--- SENTENCE 2673 ---
The usual catch from night handlining is malau, matapula, malai, mataeleele, savane, and filoa (20).

# NU'USETOGA ISLET AND ASAGA STRAIT

# NU'USETOGA ISLET

The rare "ifilele" tree (Lutsia bijuga) is common on Nu'usetoga Islet, a seastack north of Masefau Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2678 ---
Nearly all the trees have regenerated from stumps after being cut down years ago.

--- SENTENCE 2679 ---
Ifilele trees are highly prized for their wood, which is still used in Western Samoa to make "kava" bowls.

--- SENTENCE 2680 ---
The existence of the tree has been threatened by cutting for its wood value, and Nu'usetoga Islet has been recommended as a natural area preserve in order to protect the ifilele tree (15).

--- SENTENCE 2681 ---
Nu'usetoga Islet is a possible roosting and nesting site for the reef heron (matu'u; Egretta sacra sacra), a resident seabird uncommon in American Samoa (15).

--- SENTENCE 2682 ---
#### FRINGING REEF

Basalt boulders lie at the base of the seacliff along the southern side of Nu'usetoga Islet.

--- SENTENCE 2683 ---
The bottom offshore is an uneven surface of consolidated limestone with rubble-bottomed depressions.

--- SENTENCE 2684 ---
Depth varies from 2 to 10 feet (1 to 3 m).

--- SENTENCE 2685 ---
The reef flat between Nu'usetoga Islet the Tutuila shoreline is about 240 feet (75 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 2686 ---
The reef terminates in an abrupt drop to a depth of about 60 feet (18 m) off the southeast face of Nu'usetoga (ASCRI-11B12).

--- SENTENCE 2687 ---
The reef face at depths of 15 to 20 feet (5 to 6 m) is characterized by limestone buttresses, some rising to within 5 feet (2 m) of the surface.

--- SENTENCE 2688 ---
Dead coral heads predominate on the spurs or buttresses.

--- SENTENCE 2689 ---
The bottom of grooves contain rubble, boulders, and some silted areas (ASCRI-11B13).

--- SENTENCE 2690 ---
## ASAGA STRAIT

A reef flat lies between Nu'usetoga Islet and the shoreline of Tutuila across Asaga Strait.

--- SENTENCE 2691 ---
The reef front at depths of 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) is formed into a series of spurs and grooves.

--- SENTENCE 2692 ---
Spurs 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) wide rise to within 4 feet (1.2 m) of the surface between long, narrow (6 feet or 2 m across) grooves (ASCRI-11B14).

--- SENTENCE 2693 ---
#### FRINGING REEF

Coral is abundant on the narrow reef extending off the southeastern side of Nu'usetoga Rock.

--- SENTENCE 2694 ---
Coral cover of 60% is common and in some areas is as high as 80 to 100% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 2695 ---
Acropora hyacinthus is most common (50% cover), with considerable Pavona and large patches of staghorn Acropora present as well.

--- SENTENCE 2696 ---
At least 25 species representing 13 genera are present on the reef off Nu'usetoga and in Asaga Strait.

--- SENTENCE 2697 ---
The coral assemblage lacks Acropora formosa, A. aspera, and others noted in Masefau

# ASAGA STRAIT

On the north side of Asaga Strait, limestone spurs on the upper reef face are scoured by waves and coral cover is only about 5%.

# NU'USETOGA ISLET AND ASAGA STRAIT

During low tide and calm seas, the southwestern to western side of Nu'usetoga Islet is accessible across a reef platform from Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2712 ---
Villagers from Masefau pole fish in Asaga Strait on the Masefau Bay side of the reef (ASCRI).

#### COAST BETWEEN ASAGA STRAIT AND VAINUU POINT

--- SENTENCE 2713 ---
The cliffed coastline between Lepua Point and Tapisi Point lacks beaches or fringing reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2714 ---
West of Tapisi Point is a small cove fronting the family land of Oa.

--- SENTENCE 2715 ---
The eastern margin of the cove is a high cliff.

--- SENTENCE 2716 ---
Toward the head of the cove is a boulder beach which merges with sand at the mouth of a stream.

--- SENTENCE 2717 ---
The beach along the southwest perimeter of the cove is interrupted in one place by an outcrop of lava rock.

--- SENTENCE 2718 ---
The west shore of the cove is a cliff fronted by a narrow basalt bench 6 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) across (ASCRI-12S1).

--- SENTENCE 2719 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF OA

A reef fringes the small cove fronting the family land of Oa.

--- SENTENCE 2720 ---
Rubble is conspicuous on the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 2721 ---
Small patch reefs rise to near the water surface from a depth of 30 feet (9 m) in the cove (ASCRI-12B1).

Distribution of the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) between Asaga Strait and Lepua Point was more or less limited to the coral bottoms off points of land in June 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 2724 ---
Coral kills attributable to this starfish are obvious along the coast between Lepua Point and Anape'ape'a Cove (Afono Bay), where 50 to 100% destruction of coral bottom is common.

--- SENTENCE 2725 ---
Only occasional Acanthaster are evident (35;74).

--- SENTENCE 2726 ---
In August and September 1979, only about 20% of corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off Lepua Point were alive and Acanthaster were relatively abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2727 ---
About 10% of corals on the upper reef front off 0a were living at that time, and some A. planci were present (75).

--- SENTENCE 2728 ---
Acanthaster are conspicuous on patch reef slopes (30 feet or 9 m deep) off 0a, where corals consist mainly of Porites and table Acropora (ASCRI-12B1).

--- SENTENCE 2729 ---
The headland projecting seaward between Oa Village and Anape ape a Cove lacks a reef.

--- SENTENCE 2730 ---
The bottom slopes abruptly to depths of 30 to 40 feet (9 to 12 m) a short distance offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2731 ---
All the coral in areas formerly having up to 90% coral cover at depths of 30 to 40 feet (9 to 12 m) is dead (ASCRI-12B2).

COAST BETWEEN VAINU'U POINT AND CRAGGY POINT (AFONO BAY)

PAGO STREAM

--- SENTENCE 2733 ---
The position of Pago Stream, which enters Afono Bay, was probably determined by the bulky and dense Pioa and Afono volcanic cones (54).

--- SENTENCE 2734 ---
EASTERN SHORE OF AFONO BAY (ANAPE'APE'A COVE)

--- SENTENCE 2735 ---
The eastern margin of Afono Bay is known as Anape'ape'a Cove.

--- SENTENCE 2736 ---
A pocket beach is present along the shore in the Cove, although elsewhere, the shoreline is generally rocky and caves are present at the head of the Cove.

--- SENTENCE 2737 ---
A neck of land about 50 feet (15 m) in elevation separates Oa Cove from Anape'ape'a Cove.

--- SENTENCE 2738 ---
The land is well vegetated but probably allows easy access between the two coves (ASCRI-12S2).

--- SENTENCE 2740 ---
A pocket beach of white sand occupies the head of a small cove at Gatia Point.

--- SENTENCE 2741 ---
The steep, rocky shore along the eastern side of inner Afono Bay merges with a narrow beach composed primarily of basalt and limestone rubble fronting Afono Village at the bay head (49;ASCRI-12S2).

--- SENTENCE 2742 ---
This beach is backed by a rubble berm.

--- SENTENCE 2743 ---
Northwest of the village, the shoreline fronting the school is protected by a steep rock revetment rising to elevations of 9 to 14 feet (3 to 4 m).

--- SENTENCE 2744 ---
West of the revetment is a narrow beach of basalt cobbles and calcareous sand.

CAVES

Two caves are located at Anape'ape'a Cove, about 2,500 feet (760 m) northeast of Afono Village.

--- SENTENCE 2750 ---
Access by land is difficult because of high cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 2751 ---
At extreme low tide, both cave entrances are accessible over the exposed reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2752 ---
At high tide, entrance is gained only by canoe or boat.

--- SENTENCE 2753 ---
The major cave is large and is almost hidden by dense vegetation.

--- SENTENCE 2754 ---
An entrance about 30 feet (9 m) wide by 50 feet (15 m) high opens into a room at least 250 feet (76 m) long.

--- SENTENCE 2755 ---
The cave gradually narrows in width and height and, through an opening 10 feet (3 m) wide by 3 feet (1 m) high, opens into another room about 30 feet (9 m) wide, 20 feet (6 m) high, and 50 to 60 feet (15 to 18 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 2756 ---
The floor of the cave is covered with deep guano deposits, and the back room is flooded with water.

--- SENTENCE 2757 ---
The smaller cave is located at the water's edge about 200 feet (60 m) north of the larger cave.

--- SENTENCE 2758 ---
The entrance is about 20 feet (6 m) wide and 10 feet (3 m) high, and a single large room is about 75 feet (23 m) long.

--- SENTENCE 2759 ---
The floor of this cave also is covered with guano (15).

--- SENTENCE 2760 ---
# FRINGING REEF (ANAPE'APE'A COVE)

--- SENTENCE 2761 ---
The reef front in Anape'ape'a Cove exhibits limestone buttresses separated by narrow sand channels, 6 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) wide and 5 to 10 feet (1.5 to 3 m) deep (ASCRI-12B3).

--- SENTENCE 2762 ---
# FRINGING REEF (AFONO BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2763 ---
The fringing reef at the head of Afono Bay extends 200 to 500 feet (60 to 150 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2764 ---
The reef flat is irregular off the central part of Afono Village, where small channels or borrow pits are evident (49).

--- SENTENCE 2765 ---
A long, narrow ava (channel) bissects the reef at the head of Afono Bay (62).

--- SENTENCE 2766 ---
The bottom consists of volcanic and limestone boulders embedded in muddy sand at depths of 20 to 30 inches (50 to 80 cm).

--- SENTENCE 2767 ---
The bottom east of the school, off a culvert, consists of smoothly rounded but somewhat flattened boulders at depths of 4 to 5 feet (1.2 to 1.5 m)(43).

--- SENTENCE 2768 ---
A large rubble fan is exposed at low tide on the inner reef fronting Afono Village and Pago Stream.

--- SENTENCE 2769 ---
Volcanic boulders are exposed at low tide on the inner reef flat flanking the western perimeter of the bay (ASCRI-12B5).

--- SENTENCE 2770 ---
Rock surfaces are thinly covered by a matrix of sand, forams, and algae.

--- SENTENCE 2771 ---
Bands of calcareous sand varying in width from 10 to 30 feet (3 to 9 m) lie between boulder areas about 50 feet (15 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2776 ---
Overall, the substratum is relatively even.

--- SENTENCE 2777 ---
The reef margin drops off an average of 6 feet (2 m) to the reef front, which is furrowed by surge channels whose floors are paved with smoothly rounded but somewhat flattened rocks averaging about 4 inches (10 cm) across.

--- SENTENCE 2778 ---
Some rocks are of volcanic origin -- others are limestone (48).

--- SENTENCE 2779 ---
The reef front is characterized by considerable coral rubble at a depth of 40 feet (12 m) off Gatia Point (ASCRI-1284).

--- SENTENCE 2780 ---
The two caves are the only known nesting sites on Tutuila the white-rumped swiftlet (pe'ape'a; Collocalia spodiopygia spodiopygia).

--- SENTENCE 2781 ---
Their breeding cycle is disrupted by human sions into the caves.

--- SENTENCE 2782 ---
Trash and the remains of several wood fires are scattered about the floor of the caves.

--- SENTENCE 2783 ---
Children reportedly play in the caves.

--- SENTENCE 2784 ---
Adults frequently enter to capture be used as toys for younger children.

--- SENTENCE 2785 ---
Smoldering fires are set to facilitate capture of the birds.

--- SENTENCE 2786 ---
Although the swiftlet is widely distributed in American Samoa, it nests and breeds deep in caves, a scarce habitat.

--- SENTENCE 2787 ---
Several hundred sacks of guano were collected in the two caves several years ago for sale to the Damage caused to the nesting swiftlet colony by the government.

--- SENTENCE 2788 ---
collection of guano is unknown, but the purchase alerted land -owners to the availability and value of the guano and publicized the existence of the caves.

--- SENTENCE 2789 ---
The major roost for the uncommon, sheath-tailed bat (pe'ape'avai; Emballonura semicaudata) in American Samoa is the larger of the two caves at Anape'ape'a Cove.

--- SENTENCE 2790 ---
Thousands of bats inhabit the back of the cave, with only a few found in the smaller cave.

--- SENTENCE 2791 ---
The length of the larger cave probably accounts for the difference, as most of the bats occupy a single room at the rear of the cave.

--- SENTENCE 2792 ---
The cave floor in this room is covered with a water and guano mixture and access to the room is difficult through the small entrance.

--- SENTENCE 2793 ---
Fires built in the front room may disturb these bats when entering and leaving the cave, but the narrow opening and the wet, guano-covered floor keeps most people out.

--- SENTENCE 2794 ---
Human disturbance may disrupt breeding cycles (15).

--- SENTENCE 2795 ---
# FRINGING REEF (ANAPE'APE'A COVE)

--- SENTENCE 2796 ---
All table <u>Acropora</u> on the reef front off Anape'ape'a Cove has been killed by an infestation of the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; <u>Acanthaster planci</u>).

--- SENTENCE 2797 ---
A heavy mat of brown algae covers the dead coral heads.

--- SENTENCE 2798 ---
<u>Porites</u> and some staghorn <u>Acropora</u> are the only corals remaining alive.

--- SENTENCE 2799 ---
<u>Acanthaster</u> is still present in this area (ASCRI-12B3).

# FRINGING REEF FRONT (AFONO BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2816 ---
Coral growth is lush (90% cover) on the upper reef front to a depth of 40 feet (12 m) off Gatia Point and elsewhere in Afono Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2817 ---
Table and staghorn Acropora are most abundant.

--- SENTENCE 2818 ---
Some large stands of Millepora and one large faviid (6 feet long by 3 feet wide or 2 by 1 m) are notable (ASCRI-12B4;48).

--- SENTENCE 2819 ---
Below 40 feet, dead corals and coral rubble predominate.

--- SENTENCE 2820 ---
Corals formerly covered about 75% of the bottom at this depth, but most heads are now dead, and the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) is abundant (ASCRI-12B4).

--- SENTENCE 2821 ---
About half of the coral on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) was alive in August and September 1979, and Acanthaster were common (75).

--- SENTENCE 2822 ---
The diversity of fishes is high along the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 2823 ---
The dominant species is Acanthurus lineatus.

--- SENTENCE 2824 ---
Other common fishes are the wrasses, Thalassoma hardwickei, T. quinquevittata, Halichoeres marginatus, H. margaritaceus, H. centriquadrus, and Gomphosus varius, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus glaucopareius, A. nigrofuscus, A. triostegus, and Ctenochaetus striatus (toward the base of the reef front), the damselfishes, Glyphidodontops leucopomus, G. uniocellatus (toward the base of the reef front), Stegastes albofasciatus, S. fasciolatus, and Plectroglyphidodon dickii, the file fish, Oxymonacanthus longirostris, and the butterflyfishes, Chaetodon citrinellus and Ç. reticulatus (48).

#### AFONO BAY

The steep, rocky eastern margin of Afono Bay is accessible by traversing the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2835 ---
A sand beach at the head of the bay provides easy access to the reef flat (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2836 ---
The reef fringing the western portion of Afono Bay is considered a "critical use reef area" which supports subsistence fishing by villagers Both the reef flat and deeper waters seaward of the reef are frequented by fishermen (20).

--- SENTENCE 2837 ---
An informant living in Afono Village reports that fishing occurs mostly on the reef front, with occasional gleaning for fe'e (octopus) on the reef flat, and night torching for lobsters near the outer part of the reef flat Pole and line fishing is the most active fishery.

--- SENTENCE 2838 ---
Throw-netting ranks second in popularity, and night-time handlining from canoes ranks third.

Diving with home-made spears (mata) follows Catches from these fisheries are generally similar popularity.

# COAST BETWEEN CRAGGY POINT AND VATIA BAY

#### COASTLINE

The many-colored fruit dove (manu ma; <u>Ptilinopus perousi</u> perousi), considered an endangered species of land bird in American Samoa by one source, frequents the coast from Afono Village to just west of Vatia Village (15).

#### OFFSHORE BETWEEN CRAGGY POINT AND AMALAU

The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was not evident on forereef slopes between Craggy Point and Amalau in June 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 2842 ---
A legendary stone called Tu'ulaumea lies on the path along the ridge between Amalau Cove and Vatia Village.

#### VATIA BAY

The Vatia coast represents a pumice cone built with simultaneous flows of dense lavas.

--- SENTENCE 2845 ---
Erosion has removed most of the pumice and all the basalt surrounding the north side of the cone.

--- SENTENCE 2846 ---
The cone extended the shoreline near Vatia and diverted an abnormally large area of drainage into Vatia Stream, causing this stream to cut faster and deeper than adjcent streams (54).

--- SENTENCE 2847 ---
The result was the deep, narrow embayment of Vatia Bay (49).

--- SENTENCE 2848 ---
# VATIA WETLANDS

Behind the village of Vatia is a low-lying area of marshy soil covering nearly 7 acres (3 ha) which was formerly a coastal marsh.

--- SENTENCE 2849 ---
Like most such marshes, little remains of the natural vegetation due to cultivation of taro.

--- SENTENCE 2850 ---
A small area of mangrove trees is found along a stream at the opposite end of Vatia Village (77).

--- SENTENCE 2851 ---
# SHORELINE (VATIA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2852 ---
A white sand beach fronts the major part of Vatia Village at the head of Vatia Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2853 ---
The 50-foot (15 m) wide foreshore slopes up to a vegetated backshore at an elevation of 7 or 8 feet.

--- SENTENCE 2854 ---
Three small streams enter the bay, each forming a sand delta.

--- SENTENCE 2855 ---
The northwestern section of the beach has undergone severe erosion, which has toppled coconut trees and undercut a bridge.

--- SENTENCE 2856 ---
The 40-foot (12 m) wide beach contains limestone rubble and terminates in a 2- to 3-foot scarp (to 1 m) eroded in the backshore.

--- SENTENCE 2857 ---
North of the beach, the shoreline is characterized by rudimentary shoreline protection structures, including concrete pilings, seawalls, randomly-dumped rock, and an eroding revetment of concrete-filled sandbags.

--- SENTENCE 2858 ---
The structures are in poor condition and probably prevent sand from reaching the beach.

--- SENTENCE 2859 ---
A steep rock revetment stabilizes a section of the shoreline along the western perimeter of the bay and fronting a public school.

--- SENTENCE 2860 ---
Northeast of the school there is a steep beach of limestone rubble with numerous basalt boulders at the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 2861 ---
The 50-foot (15 m) wide beach slopes up to a steep, densely-vegetated backshore at an elevation of 7 feet (49).

--- SENTENCE 2862 ---
A remnant of raised reef 8 feet (2.4 m) across projects 5 feet (1.5 m) above the fringing reef on the eastern side of Vatia Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2863 ---
This feature is considered evidence of a former higher stand of sea (54).

RINGING REEF FLAT (VATIA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2867 ---
The fringing reef bordering Vatia Bay is about 400 feet (120 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 2868 ---
The depth is typically 0.5 to 1.0 feet (0.15 to 0.3 m).

--- SENTENCE 2869 ---
The reef is bissected by a deep channel (ava) penetrating to within 100 feet (30 m) of shore off Vatia Village (49).

--- SENTENCE 2870 ---
In general, a broad reef platform has not developed at Vatia and numerous surge channels cut through the reef into the mid-reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2871 ---
The bottom slopes gradually to depths of over 60 feet (18 m) in the center of Vatia Bay (62).

--- SENTENCE 2872 ---
Smooth basalt boulders, exposed at low tide, cover three-quarters of the inner reef flat fronting the school along the western margin of Vatia Bay.

--- SENTENCE 2873 ---
Sand pockets occur between the In one area, a large patch of calcareous sand extends nearly to the seawall from about 35 feet (10 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2874 ---
60 feet (20 m) offshore, the number of exposed boulders is greatly reduced, and a low profile surface of sand and algae covered rocks is present from 80 to 165 feet (25 to 50 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2875 ---
Depth is about one foot (0.3 m) in this area.

--- SENTENCE 2876 ---
Surge channels extending from the front of the reef penetrate as much as 130 feet (40 m) into shore.

--- SENTENCE 2877 ---
Irregular sand channels about 1.5 feet (0.5 m) deep separate areas of elevated limestone (one foot or 0.3 m in depth) from which sand is mostly absent.

--- SENTENCE 2878 ---
The inshore portions of the surge channels represent a drop to a sand and limestone bottom of about 2.3 feet (0.7 m).

--- SENTENCE 2879 ---
Just short of the reef front, at between 245 and 330 feet (75 to 100 m) offshore, depth varies from one foot (0.3 m) on the tops of spurs to nearly 6 feet (2 m) in grooves (48).

--- SENTENCE 2880 ---

The reef margin and reef front exhibit a highly irregular surface more complex than a spur-and-groove system.

--- SENTENCE 2882 ---
Many large, isolated mounds of limestone project as high or nearly as high as the reef flat but are separated from the main reef by narrow channels about 6 feet (2 m) deeper than the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2883 ---
This region is characterized by a maze of ever-deepening channels reaching a depth of about 20 feet (6 m) some 330 feet (100 m) One patch reef at the outer edge of the reef measures offshore.

FRINGING REEF FRONT (EASTERN VATIA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2915 ---
Although fishes are not particularly abundant, the fauna is diverse on the reef front along the eastern margin of Vatia Bay.

FRINGING REEF FRONT (INNER VATIA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 2920 ---
In the outer portions of the surge channels and off the reef front, the dominant corals are Acropora hyacinthus and A. humilis.

--- SENTENCE 2921 ---
Some very large heads of Porites lutea are present.

--- SENTENCE 2922 ---
Live coral cover approximates 30% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 2923 ---
In one place, a large mass of Porites lutea and P. (Synaraea) undulata measures 24 feet (7 m) across at the base and rises to a height of 15 feet (5 m).

--- SENTENCE 2924 ---
A considerable amount of an alga (Halimeda sp.) grows on this coral block and a part of the surface is overgrown by an immense colony of alcyonarian (soft) coral (48).

--- SENTENCE 2925 ---
In the seaward portions of the surge channels and just over the reef front, the same fishes occur as are found in the surge channels behind the reef margin, but additional species are abundant as well, including the damselfishes, Stegastes fasciolatus, Pomacentrus vaiuli, and Chromis caerulea, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus glaucopareius, Zebrasoma scopas, and Ctenochaetus striatus, the wrasse, Stehojulis trilineata, and the filefishes, Amanses scopas and Oxymonacanthus longirostris.

--- SENTENCE 2926 ---
Adult squirrelfishes, Myripristis adustus and M. borbonicus, as well as snappers, Lutjanus fulvus, are common in a cave at the base of the patch reef.

--- SENTENCE 2927 ---
The small damselfishes, Chromis iomelas and C. acares, are the dominant plankton-feeding fishes above this patch reef (48).

--- SENTENCE 2928 ---
Several red algae (Amphiroa foliacea, Cheilosporum sp., and Hypnea sp.) and Halimeda sp. are common in crevices on limestone along the sides of surge channels.

--- SENTENCE 2929 ---
The lower portion of the reef face is cut by channels whose rubble bottoms are encrusted by pink coralline algae (48).

--- SENTENCE 2930 ---
Live coral covers 30 to 40% of the lower reef slope at depths from 20 to 52 feet (6 to 16 m).

--- SENTENCE 2931 ---
The upper portion of this region consists mainly of Acropora humilis, A. hyacinthus, Psammocora contigua, and some mounds of Porites sp.

--- SENTENCE 2932 ---

--- SENTENCE 2958 ---
# VATIA BAY

Considerable freshwater seeps into Vatia Bay along its western margin.

--- SENTENCE 2959 ---
Underwater visibility is about 50 feet (15 m) on the reef flat and 80 to 165 feet (25 to 50 m) offshore from the school (48).

--- SENTENCE 2960 ---
The reef fringing Vatia Bay is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 2961 ---
Both the reef flat and deeper waters beyond the reef are fished regularly (20), but effort is concentrated on the outer reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 2962 ---
Much of the fishing effort is devoted to spearing, with some torch fishing at night for lobster and fish (48).

--- SENTENCE 2963 ---
Handlining at night from canoes, which usually takes place in deep water beyond the reef (20;43), is a preferred fishing method here.

--- SENTENCE 2964 ---
Spearing (mata) ranks second and pole and line fishing ranks third in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 2965 ---
Throw-netting (kili) and rod and reel fishing are less common activities.

--- SENTENCE 2966 ---
Catches from nighttime handlining, spearing, pole and line fishing, and throw-netting are generally the same fish species taken at Afono, Masefau, and elsewhere along the northeastern coast of Tutuila (20).

/MAP12.TEX/ - /AUG-80/

--- SENTENCE 2968 ---
THE NORTHWEST COAST OF TUTUILA

Much of the northern coast of Tutuila consists of ridges and steep slopes extending down to a nearly reefless shore.

--- SENTENCE 2969 ---
Drainage occurs in deeply-incised stream valleys radiating from the summit of the old volcanic cone (15).

--- SENTENCE 2970 ---
The major paved road which extends along the southern coast of Tutuila ends at Poloa Village (MAP 21) at the northwestern end of the island (64).

--- SENTENCE 2971 ---
An unpaved road continues from the crest of Poloa road and winds through several valleys connecting the villages (MAP 20) of Fagali'i, Maloata (where only a single family lives), and Fagamalo (with a population of approximately 200) (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2972 ---
A short paved road extends from Fagasa Village (MAP 16) to Pago Pago (MAP 1) on the south shore of Tutuila (23).

--- SENTENCE 2973 ---
An unimproved road descending to Maloata Village and Bay is chained off for private use only (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 2974 ---
Other villages on the north shore are not accessible by road and can be reached only by boat or by hiking over trails across the mountains of Tutuila (23).

# COAST BETWEEN POLA ISLET AND VA'AOGEOGE COVE

#

--- SENTENCE 2977 ---
POLA ISLET AND POLAUTA RIDGE

Erosion has sculpted sheer cliffs in the rocks of a massive volcanic plug at the northernmost point on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2978 ---
Pola Islet and the headland of Polauta Ridge are remnants of a larger land mass which projected northward in the geologically recent past (72).

--- SENTENCE 2979 ---
The eastern side of Pola Islet is exposed to rough, wind driven seas.

--- SENTENCE 2980 ---
A sea arch is present.

--- SENTENCE 2981 ---
The bottom deepens rapidly immediately offshore.

--- SENTENCE 2982 ---
The western or lee side of the Island is a sheer cliff.

--- SENTENCE 2983 ---
Waters on the lee of the Island are somewhat protected.

--- SENTENCE 2984 ---
The shoreline at Matalia Point at the northern tip of Pola Islet is composed of low-lying volcanic rocks (ASCRI-13S2, B3).

--- SENTENCE 2985 ---
# VAIAVA STRAIT

Valava Strait is the narrow pass between Tutuila and Pola Islet.

--- SENTENCE 2986 ---
Volcanic rocks are awash at high tide along the Tutuila shore of the strait (ASCRI-13S1).

--- SENTENCE 2987 ---
The shallow reef in Valava Strait slopes rapidly to depths of 30 to 40 feet (9 to 12 m) along its western face (ASCRI-13B2).

--- SENTENCE 2988 ---
# POLA ISLET AND POLAUTA RIDGE

Pola Islet and the northwestern face of Polauta provide nesting sites for at least eight species of seabirds, including the white-tailed tropicbird (tava'e; Phaethon lepturus dorotheae), brown booby (fua'o; <u>Sula leucogaster plotus</u>), red footed booby (fua'o; <u>Sula sula rubipes</u>), grey-backed tern (<u>Sterna</u> cerulea), lunata), blue-grey noddy (laia; <u>Procelsterna</u> noddy (gogo; Anous stolidus pileatus), black noddy (gogo; Anous tenuirostris minutus), and white tern (manu sina; Gygis alba pacifica).

--- SENTENCE 2989 ---
Possible nesters include the great frigatebird (atafa; Fregata minor palmerstoni), lesser frigatebird (atafa; Fregata ariel ariel), wedge-tailed shearwater (ta'i'o; Puffinus pacificus pacificus), and white-throated storm petrel (Nesofregetta albigularis).

--- SENTENCE 2990 ---
Pola Islet is a potential roosting and nesting site the reef heron (matu'u; Egretta sacra sacra).

--- SENTENCE 2991 ---
Bird populations number in the thousands.

--- SENTENCE 2992 ---
Many of the Pola Islet birds, especially frigatebirds, boobies, and noddies, have been subjected to hunting pressure by residents of north shore villages.

--- SENTENCE 2993 ---
The Australian gray duck (toloa; Anas superciliosa pelewensis), a rare resident waterbird, has been sighted occasionally at Vatia Bay (MAP 13) east of Polauta Ridge.

--- SENTENCE 2994 ---
The west side of Polauta Ridge is one of only two localities in American Samoa where the many-colored fruit dove (manu ma; Ptilinopus perousi perousi) occurs (15).

--- SENTENCE 2995 ---
#### VAIAVA STRAIT - POLA ISLET

Vaiava Strait is passable in small boats only at high tide

--- SENTENCE 2999 ---
The Strait and Pola Island are natural features of both geologic and scenic interest.

--- SENTENCE 3000 ---
Waters in the lee of Pola Islet are relatively calm and have good potential for SCUBA diving.

--- SENTENCE 3001 ---
Vaiava Strait offers skin diving opportunities over a shallow reef, although water conditions are rough (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3002 ---
Pola Islet and Polauta Ridge are recommended as a wildlife sanctuary to be closed to hunting, because of the large numbers of seabirds that nest there and because of the presence of the many-colored fruit dove (manu ma; Ptilinopus perousi perousi) (15).

--- SENTENCE 3003 ---
Vaiava Strait is of considerable geologic and scenic interest and has been designated a National Natural Landmark.

--- SENTENCE 3004 ---
The landmark site includes Matalia Point, Cockscomb Point, Pola Islet, and Polauta Ridge (72).

--- SENTENCE 3011 ---
# SAMITU'UTU'U POINT (=POINT NELSON)

--- SENTENCE 3012 ---
Small streams near Samity'utu'u Point (Pt. Nelson) flow in hanging valleys because waves have cut back the coast faster than streams have cut downward.

--- SENTENCE 3013 ---
Marine erosion is rapid because the coast is without a reef and composed of thin-bedded, weak lavas and tuffs.

--- SENTENCE 3014 ---
The drainage area of each stream is small (54).

--- SENTENCE 3023 ---

--- SENTENCE 3024 ---

--- SENTENCE 3025 ---

# COAST BETWEEN SI'UFAGATELE POINT AND CAPE LARSEN (FAGASA BAY)

# FAGASA BAY AND HINTERLAND

Fagasa Bay is a deep indentation in the predominently cliffed northern coast of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3028 ---
The valley is much larger than its neighbors because its tributaries extended northeastward and southwestward along the weak junction of the pre-caldera and caldera-filling lavas and captured an abnormally large area of drainage (54).

--- SENTENCE 3029 ---
The villages of Fagatele, Fagasa, and Fagalea are situated on a narrow coastal plain at the head of the bay (49).

--- SENTENCE 3030 ---
# LE'ELE STREAM

Perennial Le'ele

--- SENTENCE 3031 ---
Stream discharges into Fagasa Bay near the village of Fagasa (71).

#### SHORELINE

The eastern perimeter of outer Fagasa Bay is a sea cliff eroded in volcanic rock.

--- SENTENCE 3032 ---
The foreshore fronting Fagalea Village is a beach composed of basalt cobble and boulders and silty-sand 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 3033 ---
A large proportion of the beach material is of volcanic origin.

--- SENTENCE 3034 ---
The beach merges offshore with sand and silt deposits on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3035 ---
Along much of this shore, a single row of large boulders has been placed at the waterline.

--- SENTENCE 3036 ---
The shore to the southwest is characterized by a narrow foreshore of basalt rubble backed by a scarp 5 or 6 feet (2 m) high cut in recent roadway fill.

--- SENTENCE 3037 ---
The shoreline near Lesina Stream mouth is protected by randomly-dumped boulders forming a steep slope from sea level up to the 10- or 12-foot (3 to 4 m)

--- SENTENCE 3051 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF FAGALEA VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 3052 ---
A 300-foot (90 m) wide reef fringes inner Fagasa Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3053 ---
The reef is indented by two deep channels (ava) positioned off Agasi'i and Le'ele Streams (49).

--- SENTENCE 3054 ---
The inner reef flat fronting Fagalea Village consists of silty-sand to 150 feet (45 m) offshore, with silt-covered rubble and small boulders out to a distance of 300 feet (90 m) from shore (ASCRI-16B1).

--- SENTENCE 3055 ---
The depth of the reef flat is one to two feet (0.3 to 0.6 m).

--- SENTENCE 3056 ---
The outer reef shoals to an algal ridge at the reef margin (ASCRI-16B2;B3).

--- SENTENCE 3057 ---
The reef front is steep and irregular, with an abrupt vertical drop to a silty-sand bottom at a depth of 20 to 25 feet (6 to 8 m).

--- SENTENCE 3058 ---
Although spurs and grooves are not well developed, considerable relief and undercuts occur along the reef front (ASCRI-16B4).

--- SENTENCE 3059 ---
# REEF FLAT (OFF FAGALEA VILLAGE)

Coral is nearly absent from the inner reef flat off Fagalea Village.

--- SENTENCE 3063 ---

--- SENTENCE 3064 ---
Coral cover varies between 10 and 30% on the outer reef flat beyond 360 feet (110 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3065 ---
Encrusting Leptastrea purpurea and Acropora humilis are most common, with some encrusting Montipora sp. present.

# FRINGING REEF FLAT (OFF FAGATELE VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 3095 ---
Volcanic boulders, 1 to 5 feet (0.3 to 1.5 m) across, are exposed at low tide off the seawall at Fagatele Village.

--- SENTENCE 3096 ---
The inner reef flat, which extends 50 to 60 feet (15 to 18 m) from shore, is partly silty-sand near shore, but predominantly consolidated limestone (ASCRI-16B6).

--- SENTENCE 3097 ---
The mid-reef flat extending out to about 150 feet (45 m) from shore is a consolidated limestone bottom about 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) deep (ASCRI-16B7).

--- SENTENCE 3098 ---
The outer reef is irregular, with channels and depressions scoring the limestone bottom.

FRINGING REEF FRONT - FAGASA BAY (OFF FAGATELE VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 3103 ---
The reef front drops abruptly to a silty-sand and rubble bottom of inner Fagasa Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3104 ---
Some large boulders are present on the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 3105 ---
Depth in the inner bay ranges from 20 feet (6 m off the reef front to 40 feet (12 m) off Sa'afelo Point (ASCRI-16B9).

--- SENTENCE 3106 ---
FRINGING REEF FLAT (OFF FAGATELE VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 3107 ---
Coral cover is only about 1% on the inner reef flat off Fagatele Village.

--- SENTENCE 3108 ---
Only occasional <u>Leptastrea purpurea</u> are conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 3109 ---
A limpet-like mollusc (<u>Siphonaria</u> sp.) and small barnacles inhabit silt-covered boulders near shore.

--- SENTENCE 3110 ---
The most common algae are <u>Halimeda discoidea</u>, <u>Actinotrichia</u> sp., and blue-greens (ASCRI-1686).

--- SENTENCE 3111 ---
Coral cover is 1 to 5% on the middle reef flat about 150 feet (46 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3112 ---
Most common are small encrusting or flattened colonies of several species.

--- SENTENCE 3113 ---
The stiff, red alga, Actinotrichia sp., is abundant.

--- SENTENCE 3114 ---
Encrusting coralline algae and Halimeda discoidea are common (ASCRI-16B7).

--- SENTENCE 3115 ---
Irregular spur and groove-like structures are nearly choked with short-branched Acropora and Millepora, colonies of Acropora intermedia, sheets of Acropora hyacinthus, A. cf.

--- SENTENCE 3116 ---
digitifera, and scattered Porites lutea, totalling up to 60% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 3117 ---
Encrusting coralline algae (Porolithon sp.) are abundant, and Actinotrichia sp. is common in depressions.

--- SENTENCE 3118 ---
Halimeda discoidea is common at the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 3119 ---
Scattered patches of a white sponge are conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 3120 ---
Burrows of the sea urchin, Echinostrephus, are common (ASCRI-1688).

--- SENTENCE 3121 ---
A November 1978 survey of the spur-and groove formations recorded considerable Acropora nana and Astreopora sp.

--- SENTENCE 3122 ---
setchelli, P. meandrina, and large heads of P. eydouxi occur in this area.

--- SENTENCE 3123 ---
Although considerable dead Acropora humilis was observed in deeper water near the surf break, the cause did not appear to be Acanthaster predation.

--- SENTENCE 3124 ---
Neither crown-of-thorns starfish nor feeding scars was evident (34).

--- SENTENCE 3125 ---
Fishes are abundant on the reef flat fronting Fagatele Village, but most individuals are juveniles.

--- SENTENCE 3126 ---
At least 26 species are recorded.

--- SENTENCE 3127 ---
Large schools of atherinids feed along the shore.

--- SENTENCE 3128 ---
A surgeonfish (Acanthurus nigrofuscus) is common, as are juvenile parrotfishes (Scarus spp.).

--- SENTENCE 3129 ---
Damselfishes (Dascyllus trimaculatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea, and G. leucopomus) are conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 3130 ---
The most common butterflyfish is Chaetodon critinellus (ASCRI-16F3).

# REEF FRONT (OFF FAGATELE VILLAGE)

Coral cover is around 30% of the bottom on the reef face off Fagatele Village.

--- SENTENCE 3134 ---
Major species include branching Acropora robusta, A. intermedia, tabular A. hyacinthus, and encrusting Montipora.

--- SENTENCE 3135 ---
At least 23 species of coral in 17 genera are present on the reef flat and front off Fagatele Village.

--- SENTENCE 3136 ---
Some areas of vertical reef front are covered by an anemone in colonies up to 20 feet (6 m) long.

--- SENTENCE 3137 ---
Another anemone (Rhodactis howesi) is present but not common.

--- SENTENCE 3138 ---
Non-coralline algae are not conspicuous (ASCRI-16B9).

--- SENTENCE 3139 ---
Fishes are more diverse and abundant on the reef front than on the reef flat opposite Fagatele Village.

--- SENTENCE 3140 ---
The fish assemblage numbers at least 34 species.

--- SENTENCE 3141 ---
Dominant species include the surgeonfishes, Ctenochaetus striatus, Naso lituratus, the butterflyfish, Chaetodon citrinellus, and the damselfish, Glyphidodontops cyanea and G. glaucus.

--- SENTENCE 3142 ---
Juvenile parrotfishes, Scarus spp., are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 3143 ---
Wrasses are generally conspicuous, especially Gomphosus varius.

--- SENTENCE 3144 ---
The surgeonfish, C. striatus, is most common along the upper reef slope, whereas N. lituratus is more common at the base of the reef (ASCRI-16F4).

--- SENTENCE 3145 ---
# OUTER FAGASA BAY

The reef slopes off Siufaga Point were first infested by Acanthaster in early 1978 (45).

--- SENTENCE 3146 ---
Coral cover in the surge zone off Siufaga Point reaches nearly 95% and is predominantly tabular Acropora hyacinthus.

--- SENTENCE 3147 ---
In Acanthaster-devastated areas below -20 feet (-6 m), encrusting coralline algae and filamentous algal turf cover the skeletons of dead tabular and branching Acropora and account for 90% bottom cover (3).

--- SENTENCE 3148 ---
Although Fagasa Bay was free of <u>Acanthaster</u> in February 1978, little live coral was found on deeper reef slopes ( 150 feet or 45 m or more) in a November 1978 survey.

--- SENTENCE 3149 ---
Coral cover was high on the shallow forereef slopes, but numerous starfish were observed moving into this area (74).

--- SENTENCE 3150 ---
In August/September 1979, about 40% of corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) were alive.

--- SENTENCE 3151 ---
Few <u>Acanthaster</u> were present (75).

--- SENTENCE 3152 ---
An abundant and relatively diverse fish assemblage inhabits the upper reef front off Siufaga Point.

--- SENTENCE 3153 ---
Most abundant of at least 54 species are Glyphidodontops leucopomus and Thalassoma quinquevittata.

--- SENTENCE 3154 ---
Although much less abundant, Spratelloides sp. and Stegastes fasciolatus are common.

--- SENTENCE 3155 ---
Fish life is somewhat more diverse but much less abundant at greater depths.

--- SENTENCE 3156 ---
At least 67 species are present, with none particularly abundant.

--- SENTENCE 3157 ---
Chromis amboinensis is most common (76).

--- SENTENCE 3158 ---
An inland spring near the village of Fagasa is said to represent the site where the daughter of the King of Fiji went for water but was left behind because she dallied.

--- SENTENCE 3161 ---
# ISLETS (FAGASA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3162 ---
Two islets off Fagasa Bay are named Le-ma'a-o-Sina and Le-ma'a-o-Li'ava'a in memory of a Fijian king and his daughter who, according to legend, were lost from their canoe (30).

#### FAGASA BAY

Tropical cyclone "Elenore" (January 1973) damaged a seawall and boat ramp and washed out about 800 feet (245 m) of roadway at Fagasa (61;66).

--- SENTENCE 3163 ---
The waters over the inner reef flat fringing Fagalea Village are turbid.

--- SENTENCE 3164 ---
Underwater visibility is about 20 feet (6 m), improving over the outer reef (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3165 ---
Nearshore waters off Fagatele Village are turbid.

--- SENTENCE 3166 ---
Underwater visibility is limited to about 20 feet (6 m) within 60 feet (18 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3167 ---
Visibility improves to about 60 feet (18 m) over the middle and outer reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3168 ---
Rubbish drifts down the ava from the shoreline and is conspicuous at a depth of 30 feet (9 m) along the channel margin northwest of Fagatele Village (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3169 ---
A freshwater surface lens after heavy rainfall interferes with visibility off the northwestern side of Fagatele Village near Sa'afelo Point (34).

--- SENTENCE 3170 ---
A road to link Fagasa Pass to the television transmitter on top of Mt. Alava was undertaken in early 1976 as a training exercise by the U.S. Army 84th Engineer Battalion.

--- SENTENCE 3171 ---
Complaints of pollution in Fagasa Bay resulted when soil washing down from the barren roadcuts on the steep hillsides turned the bay water Soon after completion, the gravel-surfaced road was washing away during torrential rains (15).

--- SENTENCE 3172 ---
During construction of the Mt. Alava Road, the normally clear waters of Fagasa Bay became turbid because of soil erosion (39).

--- SENTENCE 3173 ---
However, washouts do not prevent jeeps from getting almost to the television towers The reef fringing Fagasa Bay below the Mt. Alava Road shows extensive damage due to sedimentation of eroded soil from the barren road cuts above.

--- SENTENCE 3174 ---
Sediment has completely covered an extensive fringing reef area, causing damage so complete that the reef is nearly devoid of life (39).

--- SENTENCE 3175 ---
Freshwater is evident on the surface of the bay following rainstorms (34).

--- SENTENCE 3176 ---
# SHORELINE (FAGASA BAY)

The shoreline fronting the village of Fagatele is accessible down a concrete bag and block revetment.

--- SENTENCE 3177 ---
Access to the shore at Sa'afelo Point is restricted by a cliff.

--- SENTENCE 3178 ---
The reef flat can be traversed on foot when low surf permits (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3179 ---

--- SENTENCE 3182 ---
[](_page_265_Picture_9.jpeg)

is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3183 ---
The reef flat is a regularly used fishing ground, but fishermen also fish deeper waters off the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 3184 ---
Spearing with homd-made spears (mata) is the most popular activity, followed by pole fishing with rod and reel.

--- SENTENCE 3185 ---
Throw-netting (kili) is less popular.

--- SENTENCE 3186 ---
Some seine netting (upega) is also practiced.

--- SENTENCE 3187 ---
Spearing yields day and night catches of pone (chocolate surgeonfish), alogo (lined surgeonfish), and laea (large parrotfish).

--- SENTENCE 3188 ---
Day catches of malauli (large jack), fe'e (octopus), fuga (small parrotfish), and faisua (giant sea clam) are common.

--- SENTENCE 3189 ---
Night catches of crab, papata (slipper lobster), ula (spiny lobster), and eel are common.

--- SENTENCE 3190 ---
Throw-netting, practiced primarily by day, brings in catches of manini (convict tang), alogo, pone, anae (adult mullet), fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota (small jack), and, in season, atule (big-eye scad), lo (rabbitfish), and i'asina (juvenile goatfish) (20).

--- SENTENCE 3191 ---
Gill netting occurs on the outer reef flat at low tide between Si'ufaga Point and Fagalea Village.

--- SENTENCE 3192 ---
Fish are driven into the net from shore by splashing.

--- SENTENCE 3193 ---
Throw-netting and gill-netting are undertaken near shore off Fagasa Village.

--- SENTENCE 3194 ---
Fagasa Bay is one of the most popular and accessible areas for boaters along the north shore of Tutuila because of a boat launching ramp.

--- SENTENCE 3195 ---
The area is reached by a short drive from Pago Pago over a road whose crest offers scenic views (41).

--- SENTENCE 3196 ---
Fishing with throw-nets and bamboo poles takes place off the boat ramp.

--- SENTENCE 3197 ---
Reef gleaning is practiced on the reef flat northwest of the ramp.

--- SENTENCE 3198 ---
The outer reef and reef slope on the southwestern side of Fagasa Bay is one of the more popular areas used by sport divers.

--- SENTENCE 3199 ---
The narrow reef shelf off Sa'afelo Point descends steeply to depths of 40 to 60 feet (12 to 18 m).

--- SENTENCE 3200 ---
The calm, clear waters offer excellent SCUBA diving opportunities (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3201 ---
# COAST BETWEEN FATUELO POINT AND FALEOTEINE POINT

--- SENTENCE 3202 ---
The coastline westward from Fatuelo Point to the head of Sita Bay is predominantly a sea cliff.

--- SENTENCE 3203 ---
Sea caves are conspicuous features especially east of Faleoteine Point (ASCRI-16S3).

--- SENTENCE 3204 ---
The cave located near Faleoteine Point is said to be the largest on Tutuila (30).

--- SENTENCE 3205 ---
In places between Cape Larsen and Sita Bay, a sloping shelf of volcanic rock borders the base of the cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 3206 ---
This shelf is best developed near Agalua Rock, which is a series of seastacks.

--- SENTENCE 3207 ---
Pools form in depressions in the shelf at the head of a small cove west of Agalua Rock (ASCRI-16S3).

#### OFF FATUELO POINT

Only 15% of corals on the bottom at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off Fatuelo Point were living in August/September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 3208 ---
Only a single crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was recorded as present (43).

--- SENTENCE 3212 ---
VI.C.2 (21)

# OFF CAPE LARSEN

Fishes are abundant in relatively shallow waters off Cape Larsen.

--- SENTENCE 3213 ---
Abundance decreases markedly with depth to moderate depths, but the deep water fishes are relatively abundant.

--- SENTENCE 3214 ---
Diversity increases with depth.

--- SENTENCE 3215 ---
At least 58 species are represented at shallow depths, at least 99 species at moderate depths, and at least 134 species in deep waters.

--- SENTENCE 3216 ---
Most abundant in shallow waters are Glyphidodontops leucopomus and Thalassoma quinquevittata.

--- SENTENCE 3217 ---
Although much less abundant, Stegastes fasciolatus and Plectroglyphidodon leucozona are common.

--- SENTENCE 3218 ---
Pomacentrus vaiuli, P. melanopterus, and Chromis iomelas are most common at moderate depths.

--- SENTENCE 3219 ---
Pomacentrus melanopterus and Plectroglyphidodon dickii dominate in deep water.

--- SENTENCE 3220 ---
P. lacrymatus, Ctenochaetus striatus, and Chromis acares are common (76).

--- SENTENCE 3221 ---
# OFFSHORE BETWEEN CAPE LARSEN AND AGALUA ROCK

--- SENTENCE 3222 ---
Although no <u>Acanthaster planci</u> were observed on the bottom between Cape Larsen and Agalua Rock in January 1973, many dead corals provided evidence of the prior presence of starfish in the area (74).

#### OFF FALEOTEINE POINT

About 85% of corals on the bottom at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) off Faleoteine Point were living in August/September 1979.

--- SENTENCE 3223 ---
A few crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) were present (75).

--- SENTENCE 3224 ---
# FATUELO ROCK TO SITA BAY

Shoreline access from Fatuelo Rock west to Sita Bay is severely restricted by steep sea cliffs and the absence of roads and trails along the coast.

--- SENTENCE 3225 ---
This section of coast is accessible by small boat during calm seas.

--- SENTENCE 3226 ---
The erosional features near and including the seastacks known as Agalua Rock are of considerable geologic as well as scenic interest.

--- SENTENCE 3227 ---
The clear waters around Agalua Rock have good potential for SCUBA diving during calm seas.

--- SENTENCE 3228 ---
However, offshore waters can be rough along this wave exposed coast (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3232 ---
VI.C.1 (21)

# COAST BETWEEN FALEOTEINE POINT AND OGEGASA POINT (SITA BAY)

# SHORELINE

At the head of Sita Bay

--- SENTENCE 3233 ---
there is a gently-sloping beach of calcareous sand with some gravel and rubble.

--- SENTENCE 3234 ---
The beach merges with the reef flat, except along one section of the southeastern shore where basalt boulders are present and the sand beach lies behind the boulders (ASCRI-16S3).

--- SENTENCE 3235 ---
The western margin of the bay is a rocky shore extending around Ogegasa Point (ASCRI-17S1).

--- SENTENCE 3236 ---
# FRINGING REEF FRONT

--- SENTENCE 3237 ---
The reef slope off the eastern side of Sita Bay drops to depths of over 50 feet (15 m) and has two distinct profiles: in places the reef face exhibits spurs projecting within 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) of the surface from depths of 20 to 25 feet (6 to 8 m); elsewhere the reef face is characterized by a relatively steep dropoff with less prominent spur-and-groove development (ASCRI-16B10).

--- SENTENCE 3238 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

Fishes are moderately abundant on the reef flat fringing the western side of Sita Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3239 ---
Glyphidodontops leucopomus is the most abundant form of at least 50 species.

--- SENTENCE 3240 ---
Glyphidodontops glaucus, Acanthurus lineatus, and A. triostegus are common (76).

--- SENTENCE 3241 ---
# FRINGING REEF FRONT

Coral growth on the reef face along the eastern side of Sita Bay is among the lushest in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 3242 ---
Cover approaches 100%, with abundant Acropora, unusually large numbers of Astreopora sp., and considerable Pavona clavus and favids.

--- SENTENCE 3243 ---
The algae, Ralfsia sp., Sphacelaria sp., and Halimeda are evident in addition to encrusting corallines.

--- SENTENCE 3244 ---
The burrowing sea urchin, Echinostrephus sp., is common, especially along the sides of grooves on the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 3245 ---
Sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus) occur on the shallow outer reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 3246 ---
There is no evidence of Acanthaster (ASCRI-16B10).

--- SENTENCE 3247 ---
Fishes are moderately abundant on reef slopes along the eastern side of Sita Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3248 ---
At least 54 species are present.

--- SENTENCE 3249 ---
Wrasses are conspicuously absent along the reef front, although common on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3250 ---
Dominant species are the butterflyfish, Chaetodon reticulatus, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus lineatus and A. nigrofuscus, the damselfishes, Dascyllus reticulatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea and Pomacentrus coelestis, the wrasses, Gomphosus varius and Thalassoma hardwickei, and several species of adult parrotfishes, Scarus spp.

--- SENTENCE 3251 ---
The mullet, Mugil vaiglensis, is less common inshore over the reef flat (ASCRI-16F5).

--- SENTENCE 3252 ---
A highly diverse assemblage including at at least 97 species, occurs along the reef front in the western portion of Sita Bay.

SITA BAY

The waters of Sita Bay are clear (ASCRI).

#### SITA BAY

Although a sand beach at the head of Sita Bay provides easy access to the water, the absence of roads or trails along this coast restricts visitation.

--- SENTENCE 3257 ---
The relatively calm, clear waters along the reef front offer good opportunities for SCUBA diving for those who approach by boat (ASCRI).

#### COAST BETWEEN OGEGASA POINT AND FAGATIALE POINT

West of Ogegasa Point is a boulder and cobble beach.

--- SENTENCE 3258 ---
From there to Fagafue Bay, the coast is a sea cliff.

--- SENTENCE 3259 ---
Several seastacks lie off Ogegasa Point.

--- SENTENCE 3260 ---
A low outcrop projects seaward from the western side of the point, and several rock outcrops extend below sea level at Fagatiale Point.

--- SENTENCE 3261 ---
An open inlet indents the coastline southwest of Fagatiale Point (ASCRI-17S1).

--- SENTENCE 3262 ---
# OFFSHORE BOTTOM

Off Ogegasa Point a vertical face of basalt rock descends to a depth of 10 feet (3 m).

--- SENTENCE 3263 ---
Below 10 feet, a rocky surface with scattered coral heads extends 165 feet (50 m) offshore to a depth of 25 feet (7 m).

--- SENTENCE 3264 ---
Farther seaward there is a slope with "spurs and grooves" dropping to a depth of 50 feet (15 m), becoming a still steeper slope to a depth of 100 feet (30 m) and terminating in an extensive sand bottom (10).

--- SENTENCE 3265 ---
West of Ogegasa Point, the bottom consists of consolidated limestone at depths of 25 to 30 feet (8 to 9 m).

--- SENTENCE 3266 ---
Coral rubble predominates at depths of 50 to 60 feet (15 to 18 m) (ASCRI-17B1).

--- SENTENCE 3267 ---
Although Acanthaster planci was not observed on offshore slopes between Ogegasa Point and Fagatiale Point in January 1978, the many dead coral heads in the area provided evidence of feeding by this starfish (74).

--- SENTENCE 3268 ---
Coral cover and species diversity are high off Ogegasa Point (10).

--- SENTENCE 3269 ---
Just west of Ogegasa Point, live corals (mostly Acropora hyacinthus and A. intermedia) cover about 75% of the limestone bottom at depths of 25 to 30 feet (8 to 9 m).

--- SENTENCE 3270 ---
At depths of 50 to 60 feet (15 to 18 m), the bottom is mostly coral rubble (ASCRI-17B1).
