USE CONSIDERATIONS

# SHORELINE

Sea cliffs and the absence of roads and trails along the coast severely restrict access to the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 3273 ---
Ogegasa Point and offshore areas have been proposed as a coastal and reef reserve (9).

--- SENTENCE 3274 ---
# FAGAFUE BAY

#### SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 3275 ---
The eastern perimeter of Fagafue Bay is a cliff, penetrated at one point by a deep sea cave.

--- SENTENCE 3276 ---
A fan of volcanic boulders has accumulated at the mouth of Leaveave Stream at the head of the bay.

--- SENTENCE 3277 ---
West of the stream outlet is a small sand beach.

--- SENTENCE 3278 ---
A rocky shoreline extends along the western perimeter of Fagafue Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3279 ---
A bench is present near sea level at the point defining the northwest tip of the bay mouth (ASCRI-17S2).

--- SENTENCE 3280 ---
# FRINGING REEF

A reef fringes Fagafue Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3281 ---
Limestone patch reefs (one exposed above water) occur off the reef front at the head of the Bay (ASCRI-17B3).

--- SENTENCE 3282 ---
# FRINGING REEF

Live coral covers between 25 and 50% of the reef southwest of Fagatiale Point.

--- SENTENCE 3283 ---
Cover increases on a steep dropoff down the outer reef front (ASCRI-17B2).

--- SENTENCE 3284 ---
Coral, mostly Acropora, covers 75 to 80% of the reef front at a depth of 30 feet (9 m), off the northwestern tip of Fagafue Bay mouth.

--- SENTENCE 3285 ---
Fagafue Bay is one of the only areas along the north coast of Tutuila besides Sita Bay where corals appear virtually untouched by the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci).

--- SENTENCE 3286 ---
Acanthaster is not present on the reef front (ASCRI-17B4).

#### FAGAFUE BAY WATERS

Inshore waters of Fagafue Bay near the mouth of Leaveave Stream are turbid.

--- SENTENCE 3287 ---
Offshore waters are clear (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3288 ---
# ABANDONED VILLAGE

Fagafue Valley once harbored several houses which made up the village of Fagafue.

--- SENTENCE 3289 ---
This village has been abandoned (30).

--- SENTENCE 3290 ---
# FAGAFUE BAY

A sand beach at the head of Fagafue Bay provides easy access to the shoreline, but the absence of roads and trails along the coast greatly restricts visitation.

--- SENTENCE 3291 ---
The bay and beach are accessible by small boat, which can be landed at all but the lowest tides (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3292 ---
For fishing uses see: AASU / USE CONSIDER-

#### MASSACRE BAY

# SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 3295 ---
The roof of a sea cave along the western side of Massacre Bay is 50 feet (15 m) above sea level and is considered evidence of a stand of the sea about 25 feet (8 m) higher than present sea level (54).

--- SENTENCE 3296 ---
A beach of calcareous sand and rubble fronts the village of Aasu on Massacre Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3297 ---
Shoreline erosion is evident near the mouth of Aasu Stream, where coconut trees have been toppled.

--- SENTENCE 3298 ---
A short section of rubble beach occurs along the margin of Massacre Bay east of Aasu Village.

--- SENTENCE 3299 ---
Northwest of the village is a rocky shoreline (ASCRI-17S3).

--- SENTENCE 3300 ---
# FRINGING REEF (MASSACRE BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3301 ---
An outcrop of limestone is exposed at low tide on the shallow reef flat northeast of Aasu village.

--- SENTENCE 3302 ---
The inner reef fronting Aasu Village is predominantly limestone rubble, with volcanic boulders exposed at low tide near shore (ASCRI-17B5).

--- SENTENCE 3303 ---
The middle reef is a platform of consolidated limestone at a depth of 3 feet (1 m), with occasional depressions reaching to depths of 6 or 8 feet (2 or 2.5 m) (ASCRI-17B6).

--- SENTENCE 3304 ---
A relatively wide channel through the reef and approaches shore at the head of the Massacre Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3305 ---
The margins of the steep-sided channel support coral thickets above a bottom of large boulders at depths of 20 to 25 feet (6 to 8 m).

--- SENTENCE 3306 ---
Isolated limestone knolls and depressions in the reef provide bottom relief (ASCRI-1787).

--- SENTENCE 3307 ---
Low (Porites) wheels and consolidated limestone form the coral southwestern margin of the channel where the latter shoals to 2 to 3 feet (0.6 to 1.0 m) approaching shore.

--- SENTENCE 3308 ---
Some areas are silted (ASCRI-1788).

--- SENTENCE 3309 ---
The inner reef flat west of the ava consists of sand, with rubble and boulders increasing toward shore (ASCRI-17B10).

--- SENTENCE 3310 ---
The mid-reef is consolidated limestone (ASCRI-17B9).

--- SENTENCE 3311 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT (MASSACRE BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3312 ---
Coral is sparse on rubble flats of the inner reef off Aasu Village.

--- SENTENCE 3313 ---
Encrusting coralline algae, Lyngbya sp., and Ralfsia sp. are common.

--- SENTENCE 3314 ---
Conspicuous invertebrates include the burrowing sea urchin, Echinostrephus sp., the sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, a white sponge, and the mollusc, Turbo sp.

--- SENTENCE 3315 ---
Barnacles occur on large boulders exposed at low tide near shore (ASCRI-17B5).

--- SENTENCE 3316 ---
Coral cover is about 20% on the mid-reef southeast of the ava.

--- SENTENCE 3317 ---
Acropora aspera is most common (ASCRI-17B6).

--- SENTENCE 3318 ---
West of the ava, the middle reef has luxuriant coral cover (up to 90%),

--- SENTENCE 3321 ---
Coral is sparse on the rubble and boulder-covered inner reef along the southwestern side of Massacre Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3322 ---
Sparse algal cover on the seaward portion of this area includes Actinotrichia sp., a turf of undetermined brown species, an unidentified green spongy alga, and Halimeda discoidea.

--- SENTENCE 3323 ---
Cerithids, cowries, and other molluscs are common under rock slabs and boulders.

--- SENTENCE 3324 ---
Other invertebrates include a sea cucumber (Stichopus chloronotus), a xanthid crab (Actaea tomentosa), and occasional soft coral colonies (ASCRI-17B10).

--- SENTENCE 3325 ---
The fish fauna is moderately diverse and fishes are moderately abundant on the reef flat at Massacre Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3326 ---
Glyphidodontops leucopomus is most abundant of at least 56 species.

--- SENTENCE 3327 ---
Also abundant is Stegastes albofasciatus.

--- SENTENCE 3328 ---
Halichoeres marginatus, Acanthurus lineatus, and Ctenochaetus striatus are common (76).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT AND AVA MARGINS

Acropora formosa and A. exigua are common in thickets along the margin and sides of the ava to -20 feet (-6 m).

--- SENTENCE 3329 ---
At least 19 stony coral species in 7 genera are represented on the Aasu reef flat and ava margins.

--- SENTENCE 3330 ---
The black coral, Cirrhipathes sp., is found along the ava margin (ASCRI-17B7).

--- SENTENCE 3331 ---
The shallow southwestern margin of the ava harbors around 50% coral cover, with staghorn and tabular acroporans (A. humilis and A. hyacinthus) most common.

--- SENTENCE 3332 ---
Sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus) occur here (ASCRI-17B8).

--- SENTENCE 3333 ---
No crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) nor damage to corals attributable to this species was observed on forereef slopes between Aasu Village and Siliaga Point in January 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 3334 ---
As of September 1979, about 90% of the corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) in Massacre Bay are alive, and few crown-of-thorns starfish are present (75).

--- SENTENCE 3335 ---
High bottom relief on the reef front provides habitat for a diverse fish assemblage.

--- SENTENCE 3336 ---
Fishes are not, however, as abundant as on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3337 ---
At least 126 species are recorded from the reef slopes and the ava margins.

--- SENTENCE 3338 ---
Surgeonfishes, butterflyfishes, wrasses, and damselfishes are the best represented families.

--- SENTENCE 3339 ---
The predominate species are Chaetodon citrinellus, C. reticulatus, Acanthurus nigrofuscus, Chromis caerulea, Eupomacentrus metallicus, Ctenochaetus striatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea, G. leucopomus, Plectroglyphidodon leucozona, P. dickii, Pomacentrus coelestris, Thalassoma hardwickei, atherinids, and several species of adult parrotfish (Scarus spp.)

--- SENTENCE 3340 ---
#### MASSACRE BAY

Underwater visibility is relatively poor (20 to 30 feet or 6 to 9 m) on the inner and mid-reef fronting Aasu Stream mouth.

--- SENTENCE 3341 ---
Waters in and along the margins of the ava are likewise generally turbid and the shallow southwestern margin is silted near shore.

--- SENTENCE 3343 ---
# MASSACRE BAY HISTORIC MONUMENT

A monument at Aasu Village commemorates the 1787 massacre of members of a shore party from a vessel commanded by the French explorer, La Perouse (41).

#### FRINGING REEF

The reefs fringing Fagafue Bay and Massacre Bay are frequently-used fishing areas.

--- SENTENCE 3344 ---
Fishermen utilize deep water areas beyond the reefs as well as the shallow reef flats.

--- SENTENCE 3345 ---
activities along the face of these reefs are diving and handlining at night from canoes (20).

--- SENTENCE 3346 ---
The reef fringing Massacre Bay is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3347 ---
Spearing is the favored fishing .method, with pole and line fishing second most popular.

--- SENTENCE 3348 ---
Handlining at night from canoes and reef gleaning follow in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 3349 ---
Pone (chocolate surgeonfish), alogo (lined surgeonfish), and laea (large parrotfish) are caught by spearing day and night.

--- SENTENCE 3350 ---
usual day catch includes malauli (large jack), fe'e (octopus), (small parrotfish), and faisua (giant clam).

--- SENTENCE 3351 ---
Night catches of crab, papata, ula (spiny lobster), and eel are common.

--- SENTENCE 3352 ---
and line fishing yields day and night catches of gatala (honeycomb grouper), lupota (small jack), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper).

--- SENTENCE 3353 ---
Night catches usually include malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), and filoa (large emperor fish).

--- SENTENCE 3354 ---
Handlining at night from canoes provides malau, matapula, malai, mataeleele, savane, and filoa.

--- SENTENCE 3355 ---
Day gleaning picks up fe'e, eel, tuitui (sea urchin), pipi, sisi (sea snail), and matapisu (limpet).

--- SENTENCE 3356 ---
Alili and sisi (sea snails) are the usual catch from night gleaning (20).

--- SENTENCE 3357 ---
Boulders and rubble on the inner reef along the western side of Massacre Bay shelter a rich shell life.

--- SENTENCE 3358 ---
This area appears to have good potential for shell collecting (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3359 ---
# COAST BETWEEN SILIAGA POINT AND AOLOAU BAY

The coastline from Siliaga Point westward to Aoloau Bay is predominantly cliffed.

--- SENTENCE 3360 ---
West of Siliaga Point occurs a large seastack: Nu'utavana Rock.

## SHORELINE

Large boulders lie along the base of the seacliff south of Nu'utavana Rock.

--- SENTENCE 3361 ---
Southeast of the seastack, a sea cave and waterfall are conspicuous along the coast.

--- SENTENCE 3362 ---
Southwest of the seastack, twin caves are eroded in the cliff behind a wave-cut bench about 6 feet (2 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 3363 ---
The platform is well-developed at a point west of the twin caves, were it slopes from the base of the cliff for about 200 feet (61 m) to the seaward margin.

In places, narrow reefs deeply penetrated by surge channels fringe small coves along the coast between Siliaga Point and Aoloau Bay (ASCRI-18B1).

--- SENTENCE 3371 ---
# OFF NU'UTAVANA ROCK

--- SENTENCE 3372 ---
Although few Acanthaster planci were observed in January 1978 on the bottom around Nu'utavana Rock, considerable dead coral provided evidence of passage of starfish through the area (74).

--- SENTENCE 3373 ---
About 60% of corals at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) are living (as of September 1979) and no crown-of-thorns starfish are evident (75).

--- SENTENCE 3374 ---
# OFFSHORE BOTTOM

Bottom areas southwest of Nu'utavana Rock to Aoloau Bay had areas of mostly living coral interspersed with dead coral heads, the latter off more prominent points of land.

--- SENTENCE 3375 ---
Coral cover is about 50% southwest of Nu'utavana Rock, with areas of mostly live coral adjacent to areas where much of the coral is dead (ASCRI-18B1).

--- SENTENCE 3376 ---
Nearly all of the corals (which formerly covered 75% of the bottom at a depth of 50 feet or 15 m) are now dead off a prominent point of land east of Aoloau Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3377 ---
Reef slopes east of this point have only about 30% coral cover in areas where corals formerly covered about 90% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 3378 ---
The red alga, Ahnfeltia concinna, is conspicuous along shore (ASCRI-18B2).

--- SENTENCE 3382 ---
No crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; <u>Acanthaster planci</u>) or damage to coral heads attributable to this starfish was observed on forereef slopes at Aoloau Bay in January 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 3383 ---
In August/September 1979, about 80% of corals on the upper reef front at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) were still alive.

In October 1979, Acropora covered about 50% of the reef slope at a depth of 40 feet (12 m) in the northeastern part of Aoloau Bay (ASCRI-18B3).

--- SENTENCE 3387 ---
# ABANDONED VILLAGE

The coastal village of Aoloautuai (at the head of Aoloau Bay) was abandoned in 1951 to allow villagers closer contact with other villages.

--- SENTENCE 3388 ---
Previously, the villagers of Aoloautuai had to travel several miles by longboat through rough seas to the village of Fagasa (MAP 16) in order to get food, goods, and mail.

--- SENTENCE 3389 ---
The inland trail was over steep, densely-vegetated ridges.

--- SENTENCE 3390 ---
The entire village relocated to the plateau of Olotele and a new village called Aoloaufou (30).

--- SENTENCE 3391 ---
# FRINGING REEF (AOLOAU BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3392 ---
The reef fringing Aoloau Bay is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3393 ---
The reef flat is a frequently used fishing area, and fishermen also frequent deep water beyond the reef edge.

--- SENTENCE 3394 ---
Spearing with home-made spears (mata) is the preferred fishing activity.

--- SENTENCE 3395 ---
Pole and line fishing is the second most popular method.

--- SENTENCE 3396 ---
Spearing provides day and night catches of pone (chocolate surgeonfish), alogo (lined surgeonfish), and laea (large parrotfish).

--- SENTENCE 3397 ---
Day catches often include malauli (large jack), fe'e (octopus), fuga (small parrotfish), and faisua (giant clam).

--- SENTENCE 3398 ---
Crab, papata (slipper lobster), ula (spiny lobster), and eel are the usual night catches.

--- SENTENCE 3399 ---
Pole and line fishing brings in day and night catches of gatala (honeycomb grouper), lupota (small jack), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper).

--- SENTENCE 3400 ---
Malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), and filoa (large emperor fish) are among the usual night catches (20).

--- SENTENCE 3401 ---
# COAST BETWEEN MANUELO ROCK AND SQUARE HEAD

# MANUELO ROCK

Manuelo Rock, a seastack north of Aoloau Bay, supports a small nesting colony of brown boobies (fua'o; <u>Sula leucogaster</u> plotus), a seabird uncommon in American Samoa (15).

--- SENTENCE 3402 ---
# MATAUTUTELE (GREYHOUND) POINT

Volcanic talus lies along the base of the coastal cliff southwest of Mataututele (Greyhound) Point.

--- SENTENCE 3403 ---
A wave-cut bench 6 to 20 feet (2 to 6 m) above sea level is conspicuous fronting the rocky promontories (ASCRI-18S3).

--- SENTENCE 3404 ---

A cave and waterfall are conspicuous coastal features on the eastern side of Tolotolo'oleoti Point.

# OFFSHORE BOTTOM

A small number of <u>Acanthaster planci</u> were observed offshore between Mataututele Point and Tolotolo'oteoti Point in January 1978 but no coral damage was evident (74).

--- SENTENCE 3424 ---
By October 1979, all coral (which covered 50 to 75% of the bottom) was dead at depths of 30 to 40 feet (9 to 12 m) southwest of Matautulele Point (ASCRI-1884).

#### NU'UO'OTI

--- SENTENCE 3425 ---
COVE

In August/September 1979, about 30% of coral heads on the bottom at depths of 6 to 33 feet (2 to 10 m) in Nu'uo'oti Cove were living, although no crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was observed (75).

--- SENTENCE 3426 ---
However, all acroporan corals, which once covered 75 to 80% of the bottom slopes in Nu'uo'oti Cove are now dead.

--- SENTENCE 3427 ---
Species spared from attack by the starfish cover only about 5% of the bottom (ASCRI-1982).

--- SENTENCE 3428 ---
# LALONIU COVE

The narrow reef sloping from shallow waters to depths of 40 to 60 (12 to 18 m) in Laloniu Cove affords good SCUBA diving opportunities.

--- SENTENCE 3429 ---
The clear, relatively calm waters are accessible only by boat (ASCRI).

A small bay indents the coastline at Fagamalo Village.

# FRINGING REEF

The inner reef flat extends about 100 feet (30 m) from shore at depths of one to three feet (0.3 to 1.0 m)

--- SENTENCE 3446 ---

--- SENTENCE 3447 ---

# FRINGING REEF

Coral cover is about 5% to 10% on the inner reef flat fronting Fagamalo Village.

--- SENTENCE 3455 ---
Short-branched <u>Acropora</u> are most common, but large <u>Porites</u> colonies are conspicuous east of the ava (ASCRI-20B1).

--- SENTENCE 3456 ---

--- SENTENCE 3457 ---
Branched and tabular Acropora predominate.

--- SENTENCE 3458 ---

--- SENTENCE 3459 ---

--- SENTENCE 3460 ---

--- SENTENCE 3461 ---
Corals are diverse: at least 31 species in 17 genera are present on Fagamalo reef.

--- SENTENCE 3462 ---

--- SENTENCE 3463 ---

--- SENTENCE 3464 ---

--- SENTENCE 3465 ---
A few sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus) occur here (ASCRI-20B3).

--- SENTENCE 3466 ---
The steep-sided western margin of the ava harbors little coral in the zone between shore and a depth of 15 feet (5 m).

--- SENTENCE 3467 ---
Farther seaward, tabular Acropora spp.

--- SENTENCE 3470 ---

# COAST BETWEEN FAGA POINT AND LEOPARD POINT

#### SHORELINE

Fagali'i Village is situated on a narrow alluvial plain, across which three streams discharge into the sea.

--- SENTENCE 3505 ---
The beach fronting Fagali'i consists of basalt rubble and boulders, with a scattering of alluvial sand.

--- SENTENCE 3506 ---
Severe floods in November 1979 littered the foreshore with tree trunks and debris.

--- SENTENCE 3507 ---
The 30-foot (9 m) wide foreshore slopes up to a backshore berm of basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 3508 ---
The coast lacks a well-defined fringing reef, so that shore is subject to direct wave attack (49).

--- SENTENCE 3509 ---
The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) was common offshore between Faga Point and Faialulu Point in January 1978, bux coral damage was not evident (74).

Crown-of thorns starfish was not evident (75).

The reef in front of Fagali'i Village is regularly fished.

# POLOA BEACH

--- SENTENCE 3526 ---
The village of Poloa is fronted by a crescent-shaped sandy beach separated into two sections by a basalt outcrop.

--- SENTENCE 3527 ---
The northern section of beach has a narrow foreshore backed by a 14-foot (4 m) scarp where erosion has exposed tree roots and bare earth.

--- SENTENCE 3528 ---
The road closely parallels the scarp.

--- SENTENCE 3529 ---
The southern section is a calcareous sand foreshore, typically 40 feet (12 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 3530 ---
Basalt cobbles and limestone rubble covers about half of the sand (49;ASCRI-21S1).

--- SENTENCE 3531 ---
Basalt content in the sand increases from 20% at the south end to 50% near Vaitele Stream.

--- SENTENCE 3532 ---
Silt content also increases near the stream mouth (49).

--- SENTENCE 3533 ---
A school located south of the village is protected by a rock revetment (49;60).

--- SENTENCE 3534 ---
The revetment is flanked by two pocket beaches of calcareous sand and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 3535 ---
The foreshores are approximately 40 feet wide and slope gently up to the vegetated backshore at the 6- to 8-foot elevation (49).

--- SENTENCE 3536 ---
During the hurricane of January 1973, the beach fronting this revetment receded about 25 feet (8 m), and waves overtopped and flanked both ends of the revetment.

--- SENTENCE 3537 ---
Some lost sand returned over the following 12 months, reforming a low beach along the front of the revetment (60).

--- SENTENCE 3538 ---
The revetment has been extended to a length of 490 feet (149 m) (70).

--- SENTENCE 3539 ---
# FRINGING REEF

A fringing reef extends about 400 feet (120 m) offshore of Poloa Village.

--- SENTENCE 3540 ---
Typical depths over the reef flat are 0.5 to 1.5 feet (49).

--- SENTENCE 3541 ---
Low, flat boulders and rubble cover about half of the inner reef flat which extends to 50 feet (15 m) offshore in front of Poloa Village.

--- SENTENCE 3542 ---
Sand patches account for the remainder of the bottom cover (ASCRI-21B1).

--- SENTENCE 3543 ---
Off the rock outcrop which divides Poloa Beach into two sections, volcanic boulders surrounding pockets of silty-sand dominate the shallow depths (ASCRI-21B2).

--- SENTENCE 3544 ---
The mid-reef flat is predominantly consolidated limestone extending from 50 to 150 feet (15 to 45 m) offshore at a depth of 2 to 3 feet (0.5 to 1 m).

--- SENTENCE 3545 ---
Sand and rubble patches cover about 10% of the bottom (ASCRI-21B3).

--- SENTENCE 3546 ---
The outer reef flat shoals to a depth of 1 or 2 feet (0.3 or 0.6 m) as an elevated platform of limestone rubble cemented by encrusting coralline algae some 200 feet (60 m) from shore (ASCRI-21B4).

--- SENTENCE 3547 ---
A narrow channel indents the reef opposite the rock outcrop at the south end of Poloa Village.

--- SENTENCE 3548 ---
The steep-sided channel has a boulder bottom (ASCRI-21B5).

# POLOA BAY

A paved road runs along the backshore between Poloa Village and the beach (60).

--- SENTENCE 3589 ---
Three small villages northeast of Poloa (Fagamalo, Maloata, and Fagali'i) are linked to the paved coastal highway by a jeep trail.

--- SENTENCE 3590 ---
Severe floods and landslides caused the road to Fagali'i to be barely passable in November 1979, and road washouts prevented access to Maloata and Fagamalo (49).

--- SENTENCE 3591 ---
The reef flat fronting Poloa Village is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3592 ---
Both the reef flat and deeper water along the reef front are frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 3593 ---
Diving with home-made spears is the preferred fishing method.

--- SENTENCE 3594 ---
Pole and line fishing is second most popular, followed by reef gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 3595 ---
Rod and reel fishing, lay netting, and handlining from canoes follow in frequency of use.

--- SENTENCE 3596 ---

--- SENTENCE 3597 ---
Surfing is possible year-round off Poloa Village at high tide.

--- SENTENCE 3598 ---
However, conditions tend to be poor during periods of strong northwest winds (51).

ATLAS MAPS COVERING THE SOUTHWEST COAST OF TUTUILA, AMERICAN SAMOA

#

--- SENTENCE 3601 ---
THE SOUTHWEST COAST OF TUTUILA

STREAMS

Northwest of Leone Village (MAP 23), deeply-incised stream valleys radiate from the summit of the volcanic cone and drain into a series of small bays separated by headlands (64).

--- SENTENCE 3602 ---
Stream deltas consisting of basalt rocks and alluvium are common along this coast (49).

--- SENTENCE 3603 ---
At least five perennial streams discharge the ocean along the southwestern coast of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3604 ---
So'onapule Stream (MAP 22) flows through the coastal village of Se'etage before discharging into Nua-Se'etage Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3605 ---
The stream bed consists of boulders and gravel.

--- SENTENCE 3606 ---
Two tributaries Utanuatele) are diverted upstream to supply drinking water.

--- SENTENCE 3607 ---
Atauloma Stream (MAP 23) drains a relatively small watershed and flows through Afao Village before discharging into the ocean.

--- SENTENCE 3608 ---
Asili Stream (MAP 23) empties into the reef-protected northwestportion of Leone Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3609 ---
An upstream diversion and catchment supplies drinking water to Afao and Asili Villages.

--- SENTENCE 3610 ---
Leafu Stream (MAP 23), drains a relatively large watershed, and discharges small estuary inland from Leone Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3611 ---
Its flood plain is densely inhabited and small scale farming occurs there.

--- SENTENCE 3612 ---
Significant diversions located in the upper reaches of Leafu Stream provide drinking water to six nearby villages, including Leone.

--- SENTENCE 3613 ---
Fuafua (also known as Puapua) Stream (MAP 24) has a long channel flowing through the northwestern corner of the Leone Plain and discharging into Leone Bay over an elevated rock shelf.

--- SENTENCE 3614 ---
Homesites and agricultural activities occur along most of its lower course.

--- SENTENCE 3615 ---
Portions of the lower reach are altered, and surface waters are diverted upstream for domestic use (71).

--- SENTENCE 3616 ---
The upper reaches of So'onapule and Asili Streams are relatively unmodified and their natural value is considered high (71).

--- SENTENCE 3617 ---
Lower Asili Stream drains an area influenced by agriculture and frequently shows concentrations of fecal coliforms far in excess of water quality standards (40).

--- SENTENCE 3618 ---
COASTAL AREAS

Highway transportation along the southwestern coast of Tutuila centers on the two-lane paved highway which parallels the shore between Amanave (MAP 22) and Leone (MAP 23).

--- SENTENCE 3619 ---
The highway runs inland across the Tafuna plain east of Leone and Vailoatai (MAP 24); at Amanave, the road turns inland across Olotafatafa Ridge and terminates at Poloa Village (MAP 21) (64).

--- SENTENCE 3620 ---
The villages of Vailoatai (MAP 24) and Taputimu (MAP 25) are accessible by paved roads from the main highway across the Tafuna plain.

--- SENTENCE 3621 ---
Steps Point (MAP 25) is accessible by an unpaved road from the village of Futiga (39).

CAPE TAPUTAPU

MAP 21

USE CONSIDERATIONS

#### CAPE TAPUTAPU .

--- SENTENCE 3624 ---
Cape Taputapu is a ridge of dense lava remaining from the volcanic dome which formed the western end of Tutuila (54).

--- SENTENCE 3625 ---
The Cape demonstrates the work of waves eroding massive lavas typical of much of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3626 ---
Outliers of resistant volcanic rock are prominent offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3627 ---
A number of blowholes occur along the coast.

--- SENTENCE 3628 ---
Among the offshore seastacks there is one identified as a volcanic vent from which lavas issued during the major period of island building (72).

--- SENTENCE 3629 ---
# TAPUTAPU ISLET

Taputapu Islet is a remnant of the volcanic cone which formed the western end of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3630 ---
It has withstood marine planation because it is composed of exceptionally dense lava (54).

--- SENTENCE 3631 ---
# TAPUTAPU ISLET

Taputapu Islet is a potential roosting and nesting site for the reef heron (matu'u; <u>Egretta sacra sacra</u>), a resident seabird uncommon in American Samoa (15).

--- SENTENCE 3632 ---
# CAPE TAPUTAPU

The steep, winding road from Amanave Village across a ridge to Poloa Village affords scenic views back toward Amanave and Utusiva Rock.

--- SENTENCE 3633 ---
However, the lack of pullover areas along this road limits opportunities for scenic viewing or photography (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3634 ---
Cape Taputapu and the offshore seastacks are of significant geological and scenic interest and an area of 170 acres (68 ha) of land and water has been designated as a National Natural Landmark (72).

--- SENTENCE 3635 ---
# VAVA COVE AND LOA COVE

The reef fringing Vava and Loa Coves between Cape Taputapu and Fagao'o Point is regularly used for fishing.

--- SENTENCE 3636 ---
Fishermen frequent deep water seaward of the reef and the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3637 ---
Rod and reel is the favored fishing method, and pole and line fishing second in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 3638 ---
Gatala (honeycomb grouper), lupota (small jack), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper) are taken day and night by pole fishing.

--- SENTENCE 3639 ---
In addition, malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), and filoa (large emperor fish) are frequently caught at night (20).

# COAST BETWEEN MALAMA POINT AND ROCKY POINT

# SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 3642 ---
The coastline around Cape Taputapu to Malama Point is steep and rocky.

--- SENTENCE 3643 ---
A number of seastacks lie offshore (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3644 ---
A crescent sand beach bounded by two volcanic headlands fronts the village of Amanave.

--- SENTENCE 3645 ---
Utusiva Rock divides the beach into two sections.

--- SENTENCE 3646 ---
The western portion, composed of 80% calcareous sand and 20% volcanic sediment, is approximately 50 feet (15 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 3647 ---
Beachrock outcrops are exposed at intervals at the water's edge.

--- SENTENCE 3648 ---
backshore is defined by either a basalt bench or by large basalt boulders up to 8 feet (2.4 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 3649 ---
An earth scarp rising above the boulders to the 13- to 15-foot (4 to 4.6 m) elevation shows evidence of wave erosion.

--- SENTENCE 3650 ---
Backing the central part of Amanave Beach is an irregular 3- to 4-foot scarp.

--- SENTENCE 3651 ---
Between the mouths of Leafu and Maululu Streams there is a landfill protected by a revetment of randomly-dumped rocks.

--- SENTENCE 3652 ---
Backfill is eroding and the soil bank above the revetment is collapsing in places (48;49).

--- SENTENCE 3653 ---
A tombolo behind Utusiva Rock consists of limestone rubble, basalt cobbles, alluvium, and some calcareous sand.

--- SENTENCE 3654 ---
The origin of the alluvial material is Leafu Stream (49).

--- SENTENCE 3655 ---
Southeast of Utusiva Rock, the beach is only 25 feet (8 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 3656 ---
The upper beach consists of 85% calcareous and 15% volcanic sand.

--- SENTENCE 3657 ---
The foreshore is covered with limestone rubble and basalt cobbles (43;49).

#### FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 3658 ---
The fringing reef is between 400 and 500 feet (120 to 150 m) wide off Amanave (49).

--- SENTENCE 3659 ---
A low profile bottom immediately seaward of a narrow band of limestone cobbles at the composed of consolidated limestone scoured by sand.

--- SENTENCE 3660 ---
Depth is generally 1 to 1.5 feet (0.3 to 0.5 m).

--- SENTENCE 3661 ---
The bottom is veneered by sand held in an algal turf.

--- SENTENCE 3662 ---
Sand covers up to 30% of the bottom in some areas.

--- SENTENCE 3663 ---
Sand bottom increases about 80 feet (25 m) seaward of the landfill area between the mouths of Leafu and Maululu Streams, where depth is slightly greater (2 feet or 0.6 m) than elsewhere on the inner reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3664 ---
A few large, scoured boulders up to 2 feet (0.6 m) across are scattered over the inner reef, especially near Utusiva Rock, where some rather large rocks occur on the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 3665 ---
The middle reef area, from 165 to 245 feet (50 to 75 m) offshore, is 2 feet (0.6 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 3666 ---
Sand patches as such are absent, although sand is interspersed with rubble and is bound with an algal turf on rock surfaces.

--- SENTENCE 3667 ---
Sand is generally absent from the outer reef lying beyond 245 feet (75 m) Near the reef margin, 330 to 410 feet (100 to 125 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3668 ---
offshore, the limestone bottom is furrowed by small grooves.

--- SENTENCE 3669 ---
Surge channels penetrate into the reef flat from the reef front to about 340 feet (104 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3670 ---
The reef margin is only slightly awash (48).

--- SENTENCE 3671 ---

**AMANAVE** 

MAP 22

WATER CONDITIONS

# UTUSIVA ROCK

OTHERT CONT

Utusiva Rock is a prominent seastack surrounded by the fringing reef in Amanave Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3672 ---
A tombolo consisting of limestone rubble, basalt cobbles, alluvium, and some calcareous sand, connects the seastack to shore (48;49).

--- SENTENCE 3673 ---
# FRINGING REEF

The inner reef flat fronting Amanave Village is nearly devoid of live coral.

--- SENTENCE 3674 ---
Small patches of the coral, Leptastrea purpurea, occur on the upper surfaces of larger rocks between 80 and 165 feet (25 to 50 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3675 ---
Most rock surfaces are carpeted by a sand binding, algal turf.

--- SENTENCE 3676 ---
The green alga, Valoniopsis sp., is evident nearshore, as is Dictyosphaeria sp.

--- SENTENCE 3677 ---
Few fishes inhabit waters within 80 feet (25 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3678 ---
Most common in the outer part of this zone is Glyphidodontops glaucus.

--- SENTENCE 3679 ---
Other species present include G. leucopomus, juvenile Trachinotus sp., Therapon jarbua, Abudefduf sordidus, Acanthurus triostegus, Halichoeres margaritaceus, and H. trimaculatus.

--- SENTENCE 3680 ---
Near Utusiva Rock, common fishes include Stethojulis bandanensis, Halichoeres marginatus, Canthigaster solandri, and Abudefduf sordidus, but none is abundant.

--- SENTENCE 3681 ---
Scattered, small colonies of Porites andrewsi and P. lutea are the only corals present (48).

--- SENTENCE 3682 ---
Coral cover is around 2% on the middle reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3683 ---
Small heads of Pocillopora verrucosa, P. damicornis, Leptastrea purpurea, encrusting Montipora, and Acropora formosa are present.

--- SENTENCE 3684 ---
Closer to the outer reef flat, Montipora and P. verrucosa are most common, with a small number of branching Acropora and Favites present.

--- SENTENCE 3685 ---
Coral cover increases to about 5% on the outer reef near the margin.

--- SENTENCE 3686 ---
Acropora humilis is common together with low stands of other corals occurring more seaward.

--- SENTENCE 3687 ---
Pink, encrusting Porolithon alga, Dictyosphaeria sp., and Jania sp. increase in abundance seaward across the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3688 ---
The burrowing sea urchin, Echinostrephus sp., is evident near the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 3689 ---
On the outer half of the reef flat, Glyphidodontops leucopomus replaces G. glaucus as the dominant fish.

--- SENTENCE 3690 ---
Fishes common on the outer reef are Halichoeres margaritaceus, Stegastes albofasciatus, Acanthurus nigrofuscus, and juvenile A. lineatus (48).

--- SENTENCE 3691 ---
The reef margin exhibits an abundance of low-growing coral species totalling about 40% cover.

--- SENTENCE 3692 ---
Acropora humilis, Pocillopora damicornis, P. verrucosa, low-branching acroporans, and an encrusting form are most conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 3693 ---
The limestone bottom has a pink cast due to encrusting Porolithon sp.

--- SENTENCE 3694 ---
Scattered, green Dictyosphaeria sp., Halimeda sp., and the branching coralline, Actinotrichia rigida, occur there (48).

--- SENTENCE 3695 ---
# FRINGING REEF (AMANAVE BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3696 ---
A strong longshore current flows northwest to an ava which drains the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3697 ---
This current is particularly hazardous in the shallow channel between Amanave Beach and Utusiva Rock (ASCRI).

USE CONSIDERATIONS

Considerable freshwater runoff enters Amanave Bay from Leafu and Maululu Streams following heavy rains.

--- SENTENCE 3699 ---
At such times a broad band of turbid water spreads west and northwest from the mouth of Leafu Stream.

--- SENTENCE 3700 ---
Plumes of discolored water extend offshore toward the ava which serves as the principal point of discharge for reef flat waters.

--- SENTENCE 3701 ---
Some discolored water also hugs the northwestern shore of Utusiva Rock and surrounds the landfill between the two stream mouths.

--- SENTENCE 3702 ---
At 30 feet (25 m) offshore of the landfill, underwater visibility is only 6 feet (2 m).

--- SENTENCE 3703 ---
Visibility is zero within 80 feet (25 m) of the mouth of Maululu Stream and is little improved (around 1.5 feet) near the reef margin about 330 feet (100 m) west of the stream mouth.

--- SENTENCE 3704 ---
Northwest of the streams, visibility is much improved (about 46 feet or 14 m) on the outer reef flat (48).

--- SENTENCE 3705 ---
# MAMANAVE LEGENDARY SITES

Amanave Village is named after a tupua, or spirit stone, known as Ma'a-o-Nave.

--- SENTENCE 3706 ---
The tupua is said to cause misfortune if a passing traveler does not make an offering of green leaves or flowers.

--- SENTENCE 3707 ---
Portions of the ridge between the villages of Amanave and Fa'ilolo are believed to represent bodies of two Samoan warriors who turned to stone and now guard the passage between the two villages (30).

--- SENTENCE 3708 ---
BEACH

Amanave Beach is easily accessible from the nearby coastal road (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3709 ---
The waters off the beach are used for swimming, with access granted courtesy of Amanave Village.

--- SENTENCE 3710 ---
Year-round surfing is possible off Amanave, but high tide is necessary because of the shallow reef (41).

--- SENTENCE 3711 ---
The reef fringing Amanave Bay is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3712 ---
The reef flat is the most frequently fished area.

--- SENTENCE 3713 ---
Diving with home-made spears (mata) is most often practiced, followed in popularity by pole and line fishing.

--- SENTENCE 3714 ---
Reef gleaning and throw-netting (kili) are less common activities.

--- SENTENCE 3715 ---
Alogo (lined surgeonfish), laea (large parrotfish), and eel are taken day and night by spearing.

--- SENTENCE 3716 ---
Usual day catches include malauli (large jack), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), fuga (small parrotfish), (octopus), and ume (unicornfish).

--- SENTENCE 3717 ---
Usual night catches include anae (adult mullet), ula (spiny lobster), and crab.

--- SENTENCE 3718 ---
Gatala (honeycomb grouper), lupota (small jack), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and savane (blue-lined snapper) are taken day and night by pole fishing.

--- SENTENCE 3719 ---
Additional nighttime catches usually include malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), and filoa (large emperor fish).

--- SENTENCE 3720 ---
gleaning collects fe'e, eel, tuitui (sea urchin), pipi, sisi (sea snail), and matapisu (limpet).

--- SENTENCE 3721 ---
Alili and sisi (sea snails) are the principal catches from night gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 3722 ---
Throw-netting is a daytime activity bringing in fuafua (juvenile mullet), anae,

--- SENTENCE 3723 ---
# COAST BETWEEN ROCKY POINT AND FAGAONE POINT

# SHORELINE

A steep, 70-foot (21 m) wide beach fronts the village of Fa'ilolo.

--- SENTENCE 3724 ---
The sand is predominantly calcareous.

--- SENTENCE 3725 ---
Floods cover the foreshore with rocks and debris (49).

--- SENTENCE 3726 ---
East of Fa'ilolo, boulders line the base of a road embankment extending around Fa'alagiumu Point (ASCRI-22S1).

--- SENTENCE 3727 ---
A small pocket beach of volcanic cobbles and boulders and scattered patches of calcareous sand fronts Agugulu Village.

--- SENTENCE 3728 ---
Floods in November 1979 completely buried the beach with debris and eroded a 10-foot (3 m) high scarp in the backshore (49).

--- SENTENCE 3729 ---
East of Agugulu, around Lepisi and Fagaone Points, the shoreline is a cliff with boulder talus along the base (ASCRI-22S2).

--- SENTENCE 3730 ---
The fringing reef off Fa'ilolo is 500 feet (150 m) wide and depths are typically 1 to 1.5 feet.

--- SENTENCE 3731 ---
A very narrow channel crosses the reef flat to within 200 feet (60 m) of shore off the mouth of Leaute Stream (49).

--- SENTENCE 3732 ---
Much of the reef flat is exposed at low tide (ASCRI-22B1).

--- SENTENCE 3733 ---
The fringing reef off Agugulu is only 100 feet (30 m) wide (49).

--- SENTENCE 3734 ---
The reef flat is strewn with boulders (ASCRI-22B2).

--- SENTENCE 3735 ---
# FRINGING REEF OFF FA'ILOLO

Rip currents flow seaward in a narrow channel through the reef flat off Fa'ilolo.

--- SENTENCE 3736 ---
Nearshore, silty waters move seaward through the channel (49).

--- SENTENCE 3737 ---
# LEPISI POINT

Shoreline access is limited at Lepisi Point by lack of parking space off the coastal road (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3738 ---
Lepisi Point and offshore waters have potential as a coastal and reef reserve (9).

--- SENTENCE 3739 ---
The reef fringing the coast between Rocky Point and Lepisi Point (in front of the villages of Fa'ilolo and Agugulu) is frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 3740 ---
The reef flat is the focal point of this activity (20).

--- SENTENCE 3741 ---
The portion of reef flat between Rocky Point and Fa'alagiumu Point is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3742 ---
Fishing by outsiders, however is not permitted (203).

--- SENTENCE 3743 ---
Diving with home-made spears is the most common method of fishing, followed in popularity by pole and line fishing.

--- SENTENCE 3744 ---
Throw-netting and seine netting (upega) are less often practiced.

--- SENTENCE 3745 ---
Catches from each method are generally the

# COAST BETWEEN FAGAONE POINT AND SE'ETAGA VILLAGE (NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY)

Nua-Se'etaga Bay is one of the largest bays along the southwestern coast of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 3748 ---
Three villages occupy the backshore area: Utumea, Se'etaga, and Nua.

--- SENTENCE 3749 ---
The fringing reef varies in width from 250 to 400 feet (75 to 120 m) along the flanks of the bay but in narrower at the head of the bay.

--- SENTENCE 3750 ---
Maugatele Rock is a seastack about 1.5 feet in elevation located 100 feet offshore (49).

#### SHORELINE

A 25- to 50-foot (8 to 15 m) wide beach fronts the villagd of Utumea.

--- SENTENCE 3751 ---
The foreshore consists largely of calcareous sand, with some volcanic sediment, as well as scattered limestone and basalt rubble.

--- SENTENCE 3752 ---
Beachrock is exposed at the water's edge in some places.

--- SENTENCE 3753 ---
The narrow beach slopes up to a 1- to 4-foot high backshore scarp (48;49).

--- SENTENCE 3754 ---
Maugatele Rock acts as a natural groin, blocking sand transport to the northeast.

--- SENTENCE 3755 ---
For this reason, the foreshore northeast of the seastack consists of basalt gravel, cobbles, and small boulders, intermixed with mud supplied by Vaialae Stream.

--- SENTENCE 3756 ---
This reach was a calcareous sand beach 10 to 12 years ago.

--- SENTENCE 3757 ---
The original shoreline was reported to extend 50 feet seaward of the present shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 3758 ---
Erosion may be linked to removal of material from the reef flat for use as road fill.

--- SENTENCE 3759 ---
The 40-foot (12 m) wide foreshore terminates at a 6-foot (2 m) scarp, the base of which is protected by randomly placed boulders.

--- SENTENCE 3760 ---
Fronting the village of Se'etaga there is a 30- to 40-foot (9 to 12 m) wide foreshore consisting largely of calcareous sand, but with about 20% volcanic grain content.

--- SENTENCE 3761 ---
Large basalt boulders litter the foreshore and reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3762 ---
The backshore scarp decreases in height near the mouth of So'onapule Stream (49).

--- SENTENCE 3763 ---
So'onapule Stream enters Nua-Se'etaga Bay through a culvert at Se'etaga Village (ASCRI-22S3).

--- SENTENCE 3764 ---
A delta at the stream mouth consists of basalt cobbles, boulders, and alluvium.

--- SENTENCE 3765 ---
A major flood in November 1979 washed debris onto the delta (49).

--- SENTENCE 3766 ---
A foreshore between 30 and 50 feet (9 to 15 m) wide east of So'onapule Stream has outcroppings of basalt which extend onto the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3767 ---
The upper  $\hat{o}$  inches of beach material is alluvium.

--- SENTENCE 3768 ---
Calcareous sand underlies the basalt material, the latter accounting for about 30% of the beach sediment.

--- SENTENCE 3769 ---
The proportion of alluvium decreases away from the stream mouth.

--- SENTENCE 3770 ---
The beach fronting Alataua Lua School is severely eroding.

--- SENTENCE 3771 ---
The 40-foot (12 m) wide foreshore consists of calcareous sand littered with basalt boulders and terminates at a 6- to 8-foot (2 to 3 m) eroding scarp of bare earth (49).

# FRINGING REEF (WESTERN NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3774 ---
The fringing reef is 200 to 300 feet (60 to 90 m) wide off the village of Utumea.

--- SENTENCE 3775 ---
Typical depth is 1.0 foot.

--- SENTENCE 3776 ---
A 2-foot (0.6 m) deep channel extends 100 feet (30 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3777 ---
The reef flat surrounding Maugatele Rock is about 350 feet (105 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 3778 ---
At the head of Nua-Se'etaga Bay, the fringing reef narrows to less than 100 feet (30 m) in width (49).

--- SENTENCE 3779 ---
A zone of sand and scattered boulders extends about 10 feet (3 m) seaward from the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 3780 ---
Beyond this to about 80 feet (25 m) offshore there is a bottom of rock (mainly basalt) and sand in pockets.

--- SENTENCE 3781 ---
Most rocks are covered by algal turf.

--- SENTENCE 3782 ---
Out to about 165 feet (50 m) from shore, the reef lies about 5 inches (13 cm) deep.

--- SENTENCE 3783 ---
The bottom is even, with a few irregularities created by low, isolated limestone mounds or shallow depressions.

--- SENTENCE 3784 ---
From 165 to 330 feet (50 to 100 m) offshore, the depth reaches 2.5 feet (0.8 m) over a more uneven bottom.

--- SENTENCE 3785 ---
Close to the major channel (ava) which crosses Nua-Se'etaga reef, inshore areas are much more uneven and are strewn with boulders of various sizes, many partially exposed at low tide (48).

#### FRINGING REEF

Fronting Se'etaga Village, the inner reef is covered by patches of two species of sponges (a dark grey encrusting form and a light bluish upright form several centimeters high).

--- SENTENCE 3786 ---
Sponges account for about 50% bottom cover, with algal turf carpeting the remainder of the inner reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 3787 ---
Some small colonies of Pavona decussata, Leptastrea purpurea, Favites abdita, and Porites lutea are present.

--- SENTENCE 3788 ---
The only fishes on the inner reef flat are a few damselfishes of the species Glyphidodontops glaucus and G. leucopomus (43).

--- SENTENCE 3789 ---
Coral diversity and abundance increases offshore (although bottom cover is only about 5%) with mostly Acropora formosa and A. humilis present.

--- SENTENCE 3790 ---
Colonies of the soft coral, Palythoa sp., cover the margins of depressions in the outer part of the zone from 164 to 328 feet (50 to 100 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3791 ---
The only additional fishes in this zone are Halichoeres margaritaceus and a blenny.

--- SENTENCE 3792 ---
Fishes are more abundant toward the margins of the ava at the head of Nua-Se'etaga Bay where coral cover is low (48).

--- SENTENCE 3793 ---
# NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY

Underwater visibility is only about 6 feet (2 m) on the inner reef flat fronting Se'etaga Village and the mouth of So'onapule Stream (48).

--- SENTENCE 3794 ---
#### BEACHES

The segment of coast near Utumea is posted with "no parking" and "private beach" signs.

--- SENTENCE 3795 ---
Se'etaga beach is posted with a sign setting a 5 p.m. curfew on beach use every day of the week

COAST BETWEEN SE'ETAGA VILLAGE AND MU POINT (NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY)

# SHORELINE

A steep calcareous sand beach (30% volcanic content) 40 to 50 feet (12 to 15 m) wide fronts Nua.

--- SENTENCE 3799 ---
The beach terminates at a narrow basalt outcrop known as Suesave Point.

--- SENTENCE 3800 ---
Southeast of Suesave Point there is a calcareous sand beach about 25 feet (8 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 3801 ---
The foreshore is composed of sand with limestone and basalt rubble.

--- SENTENCE 3802 ---
Beachrock forms a continuous strip at the water's edge.

--- SENTENCE 3803 ---
A backshore scarp varies in height between 3 and 20 feet (1 to 6 m) (49;ASCRI-23S1).

--- SENTENCE 3804 ---
# FRINGING REEF (EASTERN NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3805 ---
The reef off Nua Village extends approximately 445 feet (135 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3806 ---
Nearest to shore is a narrow zone of shifting sand and scattered boulders.

--- SENTENCE 3807 ---
Seaward of this zone there is a nearly flat bottom of consolidated limestone strewn with shingle.

--- SENTENCE 3808 ---
Some of these rocks are partially cemented to the substratum by coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 3809 ---
The depth at 80 feet (25 m) from shore is about 1 foot (0.3 m).

--- SENTENCE 3810 ---
Beyond 80 feet, the bottom exhibits irregular relief and boulders exposed at low tide (48).

--- SENTENCE 3811 ---
Southeast of Suesave Point, the fringing reef is 650 feet (200 m) wide (49).

--- SENTENCE 3812 ---
# FRINGING REEF (EASTERN NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY)

Small numbers of <u>Therapon</u> <u>jarbua</u> and several juvenile Mulloidichthys flavolineatus inhabit the inshore zone of shifting sand and boulders just off the beach.

--- SENTENCE 3813 ---
Pinkish coralline and blue green algae are the most conspicuous forms on the flat limestone bottom within 80 feet (25 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3814 ---
A dark grey sponge is evident in the outer part of this zone, forming about 10% bottom cover at 80 feet (25 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3815 ---
Three fishes are moderately Glyphidodontops glaucus, Acanthurus triostegus, and Halichoeres margaritaceus.

--- SENTENCE 3816 ---
Flora and fauna are more diverse (25 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 3817 ---
Small encrustations of the beyond 80 feet green alga, Dictyosphaeria sp., considerable coralline red algae, sponges, matted turf-forming algae, and sea cucumbers (Stichopus chloronotus) are conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 3818 ---
Low-growing colonies of the corals Favites, and Porites total about 5% bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 3819 ---
Scattered low heads of dead Acropora are apparent in the zone 165 to 245 feet (50 to 75 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3820 ---
Occasional small colonies of  $\underline{A}$ .

--- SENTENCE 3821 ---
formosa inhabit depressions here.

--- SENTENCE 3822 ---
From 245 to 330 feet (75 to 100 m) offshore, coral cover is 15%.

--- SENTENCE 3823 ---

## BEACHES

Nua Beach is easily accessible from the coastal road which lies only a few meters inland from the high tide mark (43).

--- SENTENCE 3829 ---
Some swimming occurs off the beach, with access provided by courtesy of Nua Village (41).

--- SENTENCE 3830 ---
FRINGING REEF (NUA-SE'ETAGA BAY)

--- SENTENCE 3831 ---
The reef fronting the villages of Utumea, Se'etaga, and Nua is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3832 ---
The reef flat is most frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 3833 ---
Throw-netting is the most popular activity, followed by spearing (mata).

--- SENTENCE 3834 ---
Rod and reel fishing ranks third in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 3835 ---
Catches from spearing and throw-netting are similar to those taken at Amanave.

--- SENTENCE 3836 ---
Rod and reel fishing occurs principally in the daytime and yields catches of malauli (large jack), lupota (small jack), and gatala (honeycomb grouper)(20).

--- SENTENCE 3837 ---
# COAST BETWEEN MU POINT AND ASILE POINT

#### SHORELINE

East of the cliff at Mu Point there is a pocket beach fronting Afao Village.

--- SENTENCE 3838 ---
The steep, 25- to 40-foot (3 to 12 m) wide foreshore is composed of 70% calcareous sand and 30% volcanic sediment (49; ASCRI-23S3).

--- SENTENCE 3839 ---
Beachrock is exposed along shore in the western section of the beach.

--- SENTENCE 3840 ---
A basalt bench and boulders crop out from the base of a backshore scarp ranging from 4 to 7 feet (1 to 2 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 3841 ---
Atalauma Stream has built a small delta of alluvial material at its mouth (49).

--- SENTENCE 3842 ---
# NU'UTAI ROCK

Nu'utai Rock is a seastack rising about 10 feet (3 m) above the reef flat off Mu Point.

--- SENTENCE 3843 ---
The volcanic islet is divided by a low saddle rising about 2 feet (0.6 m) above the reef flat and containing a few small tide pools and a sea cave (ASCRI-23S2).

--- SENTENCE 3844 ---
The surface of the inner reef flat off Mu Point is a platform of consolidated <u>Pavona</u>, grading offshore into linear tracts of limestone rubble that run perpendicular to shore.

--- SENTENCE 3845 ---
Sections of consolidated limestone at mid-reef are separated by tracks of rubble.

--- SENTENCE 3846 ---
Large basalt boulders are exposed at low tide

--- SENTENCE 3879 ---
CAVES

A shallow cave known as Le-ana-o-Sina (Cave of Sina) is located on the promontory between Afao and Asili villages, along the western side of the outcrop called Fao (30).

--- SENTENCE 3880 ---
The western side of Asili Bay (near Asili Point) is mostly volcanic boulders (ASCRI-23S4).

--- SENTENCE 3881 ---
A pocket beach occupies the head of the bay.

--- SENTENCE 3882 ---
Two streams (Malagateine and Asili) discharge into the bay and have formed an alluvial delta at the western end of the beach.

--- SENTENCE 3883 ---
The foreshore is 30 feet (9 m) wide and consists of alluvium with scattered basalt and limestone rubble (49).

--- SENTENCE 3884 ---
The beach narrows to about 16 feet (5 m) along the eastern perimeter of the bay, where the steep slope is more boulder than sand (48).

#### FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 3885 ---
The fringing reef is generally 800 feet (240 m) wide off Asili.

--- SENTENCE 3886 ---
A large channel indents the center of the reef and approaches to within 300 feet of shore (49).

--- SENTENCE 3887 ---
Much of the reef flat off Asili Point is covered by limestone rubble exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 3888 ---
An underlying platform of consolidated limestone is exposed in some areas (ASCRI-23B4).

--- SENTENCE 3889 ---
A sand flat is exposed at low tide fronting Asili Village (ASCRI-23B5).

--- SENTENCE 3890 ---
Inshore areas of northeastern Asili Bay consist mostly of silty-sand and low, isolated masses of dead coral.

--- SENTENCE 3894 ---
Near the central channel (ava) which serves as the main drainagd for reef flat waters in Asili Bay, the reef flat has a high proportion of sand bottom.

--- SENTENCE 3895 ---
At the inshore end of the ava, silty-sand deposits at a depth of about one foot (0.3 m) merge with the head of the channel, which deepens to sand and rubble bottom at a depth of 6 feet (2 m).

--- SENTENCE 3896 ---
The margins of the outer part of the ava are consolidated limestone at a depth of one foot (0.3 m) (48).

--- SENTENCE 3897 ---
The inner reef flat fringing the eastern perimeter of Asili Bay is shallow at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 3898 ---

--- SENTENCE 3899 ---

# COAST BETWEEN SINAMANO'O POINT AND APOLIMA POINT

# SHORELINE

A pocket beach between basalt headlands occupies the head of a small bay fronting the village of Amaluia.

--- SENTENCE 3938 ---
The foreshore is approximately 30 feet (9 m) wide and is composed of alluvial material with a trace of calcareous sand.

--- SENTENCE 3939 ---
Vaipuna Stream divides the beach into two sectors.

--- SENTENCE 3940 ---
West of the stream mouth, the backshore is defined by a 12-foot (4 m) scarp, the base of which is protected by a basalt outcropping.

--- SENTENCE 3941 ---
East of the stream, the backshore scarp is generally less pronounced.

--- SENTENCE 3942 ---
Basalt outcroppings along the shoreline are common throughout the area (49;ASCRI-23S5).

--- SENTENCE 3943 ---
The reef between Nua-Se'etaga Bay and Apolima Point, fronting the villages of Afao, Asili, and Amaluia, is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 3944 ---
The reef flat between Nua-Se'etaga Bay and Sinamano'o Point, opposite the villages of Afao and Asili, is the most frequently fished area.

--- SENTENCE 3945 ---
Spearing (mata) is the most active fishery, with reef gleaning second most common.

--- SENTENCE 3946 ---
Pole and line fishing and throw-netting follow in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 3947 ---
Spearing and throw-netting result in catches of fish of the same general types taken off Amanave (See: AMANAVE / USE CONSIDERATIONS).

--- SENTENCE 3948 ---

The village of Leone is located at the western end of the Tafuna-Leone Plain.

--- SENTENCE 3954 ---
The shoreline near Apolima Point consists of a 10- to 15-foot (3 to 5 m) wide bench in tuff at the 3- to 5-foot (1 to 1.5 m) elevation, backed by a 5-foot (1.5 m) scarp rising to the road.

--- SENTENCE 3955 ---
Near the bridge over Pala Lagoon, a vertical wall of basalt boulders rises from the water's edge to the 6-foot (2 m) elevation.

--- SENTENCE 3956 ---
An alluvial flat lies seaward of the wall (49).

--- SENTENCE 3957 ---
Many of the homes bordering Pala Lagoon have protective seawalls to retard shoreline erosion.

--- SENTENCE 3958 ---
Refuse and solid wastes litter the banks and bottom of the lagoon fronting homesites (5).

--- SENTENCE 3959 ---
Southeast of Pala Lagoon, fronting Leone Village, there is an alluvial beach about 20 feet (6 m) wide (49; ASCRI-23S7).

--- SENTENCE 3960 ---
Low tide exposes a 20- to 50-foot (6 to 15 m) wide flat of dark sand off Leone.

--- SENTENCE 3961 ---
The beach and subtidal sand is predominantly volcanic material (ASCRI-23S7).

--- SENTENCE 3962 ---
The southeastern portion of Leone Beach narrows to 12 feet (4 m).

--- SENTENCE 3963 ---
Volcanic and limestone rubble is scattered along an alluvial foreshore.

--- SENTENCE 3964 ---
The beach is backed by a 4- to 5-foot (to 1.5 m) seawall constructed of loosely-placed basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 3965 ---
The shore fronting Fagatele Junior High School consists of boulders and a bench at the 5-foot elevation (49).

--- SENTENCE 3966 ---
The estuary of Leafu Stream forms a wide area of mudflat inland from the coast.

--- SENTENCE 3967 ---
Leafu Stream divides into two channels which enter upper Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 3968 ---
At low tide, water is confined to a channel one foot (0.3 m) deep on the exposed mudflat (ASCRI-23B6).

--- SENTENCE 3969 ---
Leafu estuary flows into outer Pala Lagoon beneath the highway bridge connecting Auma and Leone villages.

--- SENTENCE 3970 ---
At low tide, the channel is 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) deep between relatively wide, silty-sand banks out to a low barrier of tuff rock at the lagoon mouth.

--- SENTENCE 3971 ---
The sand is composed primarily of dark (volcanic) grains.

--- SENTENCE 3972 ---
The tidal flat slopes gently to the outer lagoon, where the sand bottom is submerged at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 3973 ---
and scattered areas of hard bottom are present.

--- SENTENCE 3974 ---
A few boulders are exposed on the tidal flat at low tide (ASCRI-23B7).

--- SENTENCE 3975 ---
# PALA LAGOON - LEONE MANGROVE SWAMP

The mudflat at Leone is covered by a mangrove forest with an area of approximately 9 acres (3.6 ha).

--- SENTENCE 3976 ---
This forest differs from others at Pala Lagoon (MAP 29) and Masefau (MAP 11) in that a considerable amount of red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) is mixed with oriental mangrove (Bruguiera gymnorhiza).

--- SENTENCE 3977 ---
The forest is dense and mostly under 16 feet (5 m) in height, due to fire-

--- SENTENCE 3978 ---
Behind the mangrove swamp, the soil is wet but not saline.

--- SENTENCE 3979 ---
This is probably the location of the very rare shrub, Erythrina fusca, collected only once in American Samoa -- at Leone in 1929 (77).

--- SENTENCE 3980 ---
Large numbers of fiddler crabs (Uca sp.) burrow in exposed mud banks of Leafu Stream estuary, especially along the northern margin of inner Pala Lagoon (ASCRI-23B6).

--- SENTENCE 3981 ---
A shallow channel at the mouth of Pala Lagoon northwest of Papaloa Rock contains considerable quantities of the brown alga, <u>Padina</u> sp., as well as some <u>Actinotrichia</u> sp. (ASCRI-23B7).

--- SENTENCE 3982 ---
# PÁPALOA ROCK AND NIUAVEVE ROCK

Papaloa Rock, a low barrier across much of the mouth of Pala Lagoon, consists of three shelves of volcanic tuff, between 200 and 300 feet (60 and 90 m) long and separated from the main shoreline by narrow channels of shallow water (30).

--- SENTENCE 3983 ---
The tuff rock rises 1 to 3 feet (0.3 to 1.0 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 3984 ---
The surface slopes seaward in a manner similar to beachrock.

--- SENTENCE 3985 ---
Its relatively smooth surface has some small depressions containing limestone rubble and hermit crabs in cerithiid shells (ASCRI-23S6).

--- SENTENCE 3986 ---
Niuaveve Rock is a small seastack a short distance seaward of Papaloa Rock (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 3987 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

The fringing reef in the northwestern corner of Leone Bay is over 700 feet (215 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 3988 ---
The reef flat widens to 1,200 feet (365 m) outside Pala Lagoon (49).

--- SENTENCE 3989 ---
Silty-sand covers the inner reef flat to 150 feet (45 m) offshore of Leone Village.

--- SENTENCE 3990 ---
Scattered occurrences of rubble and large silted mounds of Pavona shoaling to near sea level occur on the silty-sand bottom, which reaches depths of 3 to 4 feet (1.0 to 1.2 m) (ASCRI-23B8).

--- SENTENCE 3991 ---
The nearshore channel of silty-sand continues south to the cliff off the southeastern end of Leone Village.

--- SENTENCE 3992 ---
The channel contains considerable silted algae and debris (especially fallen coconut trees) (ASCRI-23B13).

--- SENTENCE 3993 ---
The inner and middle reef flat extending seaward from Papaloa Rock is covered mostly by loose limestone rubble and sand grading to an outer reef of unconsolidated rubble (ASCRI-23S6).

--- SENTENCE 3994 ---
The middle reef consists mainly of consolidated limestone and dead coral heads at depths from 1 to 4 feet (0.3 to 1.2 m) (ASCRI-23B9).

--- SENTENCE 3995 ---
Toward the outer reef is a 200-foot (-120 m), horseshoe-shaped rampart of coral rubble rising about 6 feet (2 m) above the reef surface.

--- SENTENCE 3996 ---
The rampart base is composed of heavy, worn coral plates or shingle (tabular Acropora), with fragments of staghorn acroporans piled on top.

--- SENTENCE 3997 ---
Within the shoreward-facing concavity of the rampart, the bottom is mostly dead coral rubble and shingle at a depth of 4 feet (1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 3998 ---
The top of the rampart has several young coconut trees.

--- SENTENCE 3999 ---
East of the rampart there is a channel with depths to 5 feet (1.5 m).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

Spur-and-groove systems are irregularly developed on the reef front and the steep slope is characterized by surge channels to depths of 20 feet (6 m).

--- SENTENCE 4006 ---
Irregular limestone buttresses up to 40 feet (12 m) in length with shelves of coral and calcareous algae growing toward each other are separated by deep undercuts forming tunnels and caves (ASCRI-23B12).

--- SENTENCE 4007 ---
Off Logologo Point, the shallow reef flat extends offshore to a poorly developed spur-and groove system.

--- SENTENCE 4008 ---
A large sand body occurs at a depth of 50 feet (15 m).

--- SENTENCE 4009 ---

# FRINGING REEF FLAT

A

Corals are limited to scattered occurrences of hard bottom on an inner reef flat of mostly silty-sand off Leone Village.

--- SENTENCE 4011 ---
Coral cover totals about 5%, with Leptastrea purpurea most common.

--- SENTENCE 4012 ---
Small heads of Porites lutea are also present, as are some large silt-covered mounds of Pavona near shord.

--- SENTENCE 4013 ---
Algae are not abundant, although some Padina sp. and Ralfsia sp. grow on scattered areas of rubble bottom.

--- SENTENCE 4014 ---
Two types of sponges cover large areas.

--- SENTENCE 4015 ---
A low-spreading blue-grey species is more common.

--- SENTENCE 4016 ---
The other is an orange, upright and somewhat rigid species (ASCRI-23B8).

--- SENTENCE 4017 ---
Soft coral (Zoanthid) colonies are uncommon in the sand channel off the south end of Leone Village.

--- SENTENCE 4018 ---
Small grapsid crabs inhabit crevices in the rocks near the waterline (ASCRI-23B13).

--- SENTENCE 4019 ---
Pavona frondifera dominates the middle reef, with coral cover at nearly 50%.

--- SENTENCE 4020 ---
Heads of Porites lutea occupy areas where the depth reaches 4 feet (1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 4021 ---
The red alga, Actinotrichia sp., is common.

--- SENTENCE 4022 ---
Other algae include Halimeda discoidea (patchy at the base of limestone outcrops), Dictyosphaeria versluysii, Ralfsia sp., an algal turf of several species, and encrusting Porolithon sp. on coral rubble.

--- SENTENCE 4023 ---
A spikey, branching coralline alga (Amphiroa sp.) is present.

--- SENTENCE 4024 ---
Cowries (Cypraea annulus) also occur (ASCRI-23B9).

--- SENTENCE 4025 ---
Virtually all of the bottom enclosed by the elevated shingle rampart consists of dead but still standing Pavona coral rubble covered by encrusting coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 4026 ---
Live coral cover is only 2%.

--- SENTENCE 4027 ---
Porites lutea is present as microatolls in a channel east of the rampart.

--- SENTENCE 4028 ---
Vermitids are conspicuous on some of the microatolls (ASCRI-23B10).

Corals cover up to 75% of the steep reef front at depths to 20 feet (6 m).

#### FASTERN LEONE BAY

Considerable refuse (discarded junk and beer cans) occurs on the beach and in shallows fronting Leone Village.

--- SENTENCE 4061 ---
At least two storm drains empty into the Bay from the village.

--- SENTENCE 4062 ---
Silt mixed with sand on the inner reef flat is easily disturbed, causing nearshore waters to be quite turbid.

--- SENTENCE 4063 ---
Inshore waters are also noticeably warm.

--- SENTENCE 4064 ---
Underwater visibility is limited to about 15 feet (4.6 m) over the silty-sand bottom nearshore, improving to 30 feet (9 m) over the mid-reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 4065 ---
East of a rampart on the reef flat, visibility reaches 50 feet (15 m) in a channel through which a current flows seaward on a falling tide.

--- SENTENCE 4066 ---
Visibility is excellent (100 feet or 30 m) over the reef margin and reef front.

--- SENTENCE 4067 ---
Inshore waters off the low cliff at the southern end of Leone Village appear to have poor circulation and are turbid (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4068 ---
The reef margin off Leone Village is exposed to strong wave action (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4069 ---
# LEONE CAVES AND PETROGLYPHS

A cave at Leone, regarded as the home of the aitu called Tuiatua, king of the gods, is located above Leone Junior High School.

--- SENTENCE 4070 ---
It is a narrow shelter of overhanging rocks with a low depression or crater in the ground.

--- SENTENCE 4071 ---
This area is avoided by Leone villagers.

--- SENTENCE 4072 ---
A second, small cave in Leone Valley called Aitu-cave is said to be the home of a ghost or demon who journeys from the valley to the seashore, where he gathers shellfish for his supper.

--- SENTENCE 4073 ---
Shells are said to be strewn over the entrance to this cave, located on the steep slope above the area called Ologa to'i (30).

--- SENTENCE 4074 ---
A large concentration of grinding stones, or whetstones, are found on the western promontory bounding Leone Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4075 ---
They occur on a low-lying rock shelf which is submerged at high tide.

--- SENTENCE 4076 ---
Another cluster of whetstones is found on a wave-washed shelf of basalt on the eastern side of Leone (30).

--- SENTENCE 4077 ---
# PAPALOA AND NIUAVEVE ROCKS

--- SENTENCE 4078 ---
Two large rock shelves in Leone Bay, called Papaloa and Niuaveve, are considered "tupua", or spirit stones.

--- SENTENCE 4079 ---
According to legend, two cannibals competed in a rock throwing contest.

--- SENTENCE 4080 ---
One pitched his rock and it landed on the western side of Leone Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4081 ---
This rock is named Papaloa.

--- SENTENCE 4082 ---
The other hurled his rock beyond.

--- SENTENCE 4083 ---
This rock is called Neve.

--- SENTENCE 4084 ---
On the central shelf of Papaloa there is a concentration of pre-European petroglyphs (30).

LEONE

Leone has historical significance as the first landing place of western missionaries (41).

--- SENTENCE 4089 ---
A structure built between 1855 and 1885 to house the former Fagalele Boy's School is considered to be the oldest foreign-built structure on Tutuila (41).

#### SHORELINE

Leone Beach is easily accessible from the coastal road.

--- SENTENCE 4090 ---
Access is by village approval (41).

--- SENTENCE 4091 ---
The basalt boulder revetment behind the beach can be crossed through breaks.

--- SENTENCE 4092 ---
Broken glass and trash on and fronting Leone Beach may discourage swimming and other uses (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4093 ---
Swimming is popular off the rocky, but accessible shoreline below the old mission grounds.

--- SENTENCE 4094 ---
Access across the grounds is by consent of the church (41).

--- SENTENCE 4095 ---
A rugged cliff south of the mission grounds limits shoreline access.

--- SENTENCE 4096 ---
This section of coast is relatively inaccessible except in a few places where erosion or slumping has created a gentler slope.

--- SENTENCE 4097 ---
Waves pound against this coast (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4098 ---
FRINGING REEF (EASTERN LEONE BAY)

Development of a harbor to serve barges and interisland vessels is presently under consideration for Leone Bay (68).

--- SENTENCE 4099 ---
The reef fringing Apolima Point and Pala Lagoon is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 4100 ---
The reef flat is frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 4101 ---
Pole and line fishing is the most common activity, followed in popularity by throw-netting.

--- SENTENCE 4102 ---
Rod and reel fishing and spearing (mata) are less active fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 4103 ---
Pole and line fishing results in day and night catches of gatala (honeycomb grouper), mataeleele (small emperor fish), and filoa (large emperor fish).

--- SENTENCE 4104 ---
Lupo (juvenile jack) and lupota (small jack) are among the usual day catches.

--- SENTENCE 4105 ---
and malau (squirrelfish), malai (paddletail snapper), matapula (bigeye snapper), and savane (blue-lined snapper) are among the usual night catches.

--- SENTENCE 4106 ---
Throw-netting yields day catches of fuafua (juvenile mullet), anae (adult mullet), manini (convict tang), alogo (lined surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), mutu, laea (large parrotfish), and, seasonally, i'asina (juvenile goatfish), and lo (rabbitfish).

--- SENTENCE 4107 ---
Rod and reel fishing is practiced in the daytime and brings in malauli (large jack), lupota, and gatala (20).

--- SENTENCE 4108 ---
A good swimming and bodysurfing area is located below the old mission grounds northeast of Logologo Point (49).

--- SENTENCE 4109 ---
COAST BETWEEN LOGOLOGO POINT AND PUPUALOA POINT

LEONE PLAIN

The Tafuna-Leone Plain was formed by relatively recent lava flows.

--- SENTENCE 4110 ---
Late eruptions along a north-south fissure three miles (5

km) long formed tuff cones where lava erupted undersea and cinder cones where eruptions occurred on land.

--- SENTENCE 4111 ---
Voluminous lava covered a submerged reef and added about 8 square miles (21 sq km) of land to the island.

--- SENTENCE 4112 ---
The lava exposed along the coast south from Leone Village came chiefly from Futiga cone and is overlain with 5 to 20 feet (1.5 to 6 m) of tuff.

--- SENTENCE 4113 ---
Where hot rising lavas hurling contacted sea water, they exploded violently, high into the air.

--- SENTENCE 4114 ---
Winds blowing at the time carried the cinder and ash northwestward across the island.

--- SENTENCE 4115 ---
Deposits of this material later hardened into tuff.

--- SENTENCE 4116 ---
Tuff deposits 2 to 3 feet (0.6 to 1.0 m) thick along the shores of bays as far northwest as Amanave (6 miles or 10 km northwest of the vents) (MAP 22) indicate that strong trade winds blew during the eruptions (54).

#### SHORELINE

A sea cliff rising from 4 to 30 feet (1 to 9 m) above the ocean characterizes much of the shoreline south of Leone Village.

--- SENTENCE 4117 ---
In a few places, the cliffs have eroded or slumped, creating a more gentle slope to the water.

--- SENTENCE 4118 ---
This rugged coast continues around the southernmost tip of Tutuila (ASCRI-23S8).

--- SENTENCE 4119 ---
The Le'ala coastline is a rugged and spectacular exposure of interbedded basalt flows and tuff deposits.

--- SENTENCE 4120 ---
A bench along the shore is fractured and pitted with pools, one of which is 100 feet (39 m) long and over 12 feet (4 m) deep (72).

--- SENTENCE 4121 ---
The fringing reef narrows south of Leone Bay, and the coast south of Faleapoi Point lacks a reef (49).

--- SENTENCE 4122 ---
A shallow reef flat off Logologo Point has an irregular spur-and-groove system on the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 4123 ---
A sand bottom is present at -50 feet (-15 m).

--- SENTENCE 4124 ---
Isolated reef knolls rise from -80 feet (-25 m).

--- SENTENCE 4125 ---
Coral cover approaches 100% on the reef front off Logologo Point (10).

--- SENTENCE 4126 ---
# LE'ALA

Post-European petroglyphs are located on the coastline of Le'ala near the village of Vailoatai.

--- SENTENCE 4127 ---
More recent carvings of the names of students from the Marist Brothers School and other features are carved in thinly-stratifed tuff deposits.

--- SENTENCE 4128 ---
These are being rapidly eroded by wind, rain, and salt spray (30).

--- SENTENCE 4129 ---
The impressive grave of High Chief Salate Moasegi is situated on a low, rocky point where Vailoatai South Road meets the coast (41).

#### OFFSHORE BETWEEN LEONE AND FALEAPOI POINT

--- SENTENCE 4130 ---
Offshore waters between Leone Village and Faleapoi Point are frequently visited by fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 4131 ---
Pole and line fishing is the preferred method and catches are generally of the sand species as taken off Afao and Leone.

--- SENTENCE 4132 ---
Spearing (mata) is less common (20).

# COAST BETWEEN PUPUALOA POINT AND FA'ASOUGA POINT

# VAILOATAI

--- SENTENCE 4134 ---
CRATER

Vailoatai Crater is the eroded remnant of one of three volcanic tuff cones which resulted from explosive submarine eruptions in recent geologic time.

--- SENTENCE 4135 ---
The 75-foot (23 m) high crater, with a depression in its summit, lies just inland from the shore and was probably formed by the rising lava exploding on contact with sea water (54).

--- SENTENCE 4136 ---
The shore fronting the village of Vailoatai consists of a 50- to 100-foot (15 to 30 m) wide bench about 5 feet (1.5 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 4137 ---
The coast lacks an offshore reef and is directly exposed to trade wind waves which deposit calcareous sand and limestone rubble inland of the bench as small storm beaches.

--- SENTENCE 4138 ---
The bench is backed by a plateau at the 15- to 20-foot (5 to 6 m) elevation (49).

--- SENTENCE 4139 ---
Cove is a shallow recess in a well-formed shoreline bench of volcanic tuff which lies near sea level along the coast southeast from Vailoatai Crater.

--- SENTENCE 4140 ---
Behind the platform is a 10 to 20 foot (3 to 6 m) high cliff.

--- SENTENCE 4141 ---
The bench is dry at low tide, but inside the cove there is a relatively narrow, 2-foot (0.6 m) deep pool connected to the ocean across a shelf which reduces surge.

--- SENTENCE 4142 ---
The pool bottom is scoured smooth, with rubble and boulders (both limestone and volcanic) scattered in depressions.

--- SENTENCE 4143 ---
Inland of the pool there is a storm beach composed of calcareous sand.

--- SENTENCE 4144 ---
A major component of the sand is a star-shaped, light yellow foraminiferan (Bacculogypsina) (ASCRI-24S1).

--- SENTENCE 4145 ---
# SHORELINE EAST OF PAPAFA'ASE'E COVE

Toward Avaloa Point, the tuff platform varies in width from 150 to 250 feet (45 to 75 m) and is backed by a cliff about 30 feet (9 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 4146 ---
The tuff platform is irregular in width and elevation and shows exposures of dark pahoehoe lava.

--- SENTENCE 4147 ---
In one area there is a grotto and freshwater stream with a canopy of vegetation overhanging the walls (ASCRI-24S1).

--- SENTENCE 4148 ---
A number of surge pools occur in the tuff shore between Papafa'ase'e Cove and Avaloa Point.

--- SENTENCE 4149 ---
Waves washing through depressions between the tuff ridges feed the pools.

--- SENTENCE 4150 ---
A blowhole has formed between two ridges of tuff.

--- SENTENCE 4151 ---
The cliff rises to approximately 70 feet (21 m) southeast of the pools, but the inland portion of the tuff has slumped and broken to form a gorge and expose limestone fragments embedded in the tuff.

--- SENTENCE 4152 ---
Near Avaloa Point there is an isolated platform in tuff about 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 4153 ---
