--- SENTENCE 4156 ---
COVE

Much of the bottom of a surge pool recessed in the tuff bench at Papafa'ase'e

--- SENTENCE 4157 ---
Cove is covered by an algal turf.

--- SENTENCE 4158 ---
The green alga, <u>Halimeda discoidea</u>, and small colonies of <u>Sphacelaria</u> spare present.

--- SENTENCE 4159 ---
Cone shells are conspicuous, particularly <u>Conusebraeus</u>.

--- SENTENCE 4160 ---
Corals are uncommon, with only scattered heads of <u>Porites</u> aff.

--- SENTENCE 4161 ---
<u>lutea</u> and <u>Leptastrea purpurea</u> present.

--- SENTENCE 4162 ---
Fishes typical of surge-swept areas (surgeonfish, wrasses, damselfishes, and surf perch) are present (ASCRI-24SI).

--- SENTENCE 4163 ---
Corals are absent from pools fronting the cliff between Papafa'ase'e Cove and Avaloa Point.

--- SENTENCE 4164 ---
Larger pools contain considerable algae.

--- SENTENCE 4165 ---
Encrusting nullipores cover about 60% of the pool bottom and edges.

--- SENTENCE 4166 ---
Valonia sp. is most common of the fleshy algae.

--- SENTENCE 4167 ---
Ahnfeltia sp., Dictyosphaeria sp., Caulerpa sp., Sargassum sp. (in shallower sections), and Turbinaria sp. are present.

--- SENTENCE 4168 ---
Barnacles cover some shallow pool margins.

--- SENTENCE 4169 ---
Juvenile lobster (Panulirus sp.), crabs (Thalamita sp.), and a mollusc (Turbo sp.), inhabit the pools.

--- SENTENCE 4170 ---
Ahnfeltia sp. and various brown algae are common on the bench.

--- SENTENCE 4171 ---
Fishes typical of shallow waters are present (e.g., Acanthurus guttatus, A. triostegus, gobies, blennies, damselfishes, Kuhlia mugil, Mugil sp.)(ASCRI-24S2).

--- SENTENCE 4172 ---
The shoreline around the Village of Vailoatai lacks beaches and safe swimming areas, but is scenic.

--- SENTENCE 4173 ---
Access is by courtesy of the Village (41).

--- SENTENCE 4174 ---
The coastline from Papafa'ase'e Cove southeast to Avaloa Point is one of the most scenic along the "Ironbound" coast of southern Tutuila (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4175 ---
Le'ala shoreline, from northwest of Avaloa Point to Fa'asouga Point, is a National Natural Landmark (72).

--- SENTENCE 4176 ---
This wave-pounded coastline is of both geologic and scenic interest.

--- SENTENCE 4177 ---
Opportunities for nature photogra; hy are numerous (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4178 ---
Beaches are absent along the coast and swimming takes place in surge pools along the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 4179 ---
The pools between Papafa'ase'e Cove and Avaloa Point can be dangerous for swimming because waves washing over the bench can cause considerable surge in the Reportedly, several persons have drowned after being washed seaward from the pools.

--- SENTENCE 4180 ---
The shallow pool recessed in the tuff platform at Papafa'ase'e

--- SENTENCE 4181 ---
Cove is a popular swimming spot, although exposed to moderately strong wave surge.

--- SENTENCE 4182 ---
offers shoreline access, but can become hazardous during periods of high surf when covered unexpectedly by uprushing waves.

--- SENTENCE 4183 ---
These waves cause a strong backwash when reflected back to sea from the elevated tuff cliff behind the bench (ASCRI; 41).

--- SENTENCE 4184 ---
rocks on the tuff bench southeast of the cove are known as "sliding rocks" because of the local sport of running and sliding barefoot on the slippery surface.

--- SENTENCE 4185 ---
Visitors unaware of this condition could easily fall if not cautious (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4186 ---
"Beach-combing" is a popular activity along this shore (72).

#### OFFSHORE

The waters extending southeast from Pupualoa Point to near Le'ala

--- SENTENCE 4188 ---
School are considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fashing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 4189 ---
Both the "reef" flat and waters seaward of the "reef" are frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 4190 ---
Pole and line fishing is the most active fishery, followed in popularity by spearing.

--- SENTENCE 4191 ---
Rod and reel fishing is less common.

--- SENTENCE 4192 ---
The usual catch from pole fishing consists of generally the same fish species taken off Leone and Afao.

--- SENTENCE 4193 ---
Spearing is generally limited to daytime because the area is too far from villages for regular night diving.

--- SENTENCE 4194 ---
The usual catch includes laea (large parrotfish), malauli (large jack), anae (adult mullet), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), alogo (lined surgeonfish), ume (unicornfish), and fe'e (octopus).

--- SENTENCE 4195 ---
Rod and reel fishing is also primarily a daytime activity resulting in catches of malauli and lupota (small jack)

--- SENTENCE 4196 ---
COAST BETWEEN FA'ASOUGA POINT AND STEPS POINT (FAGATELE BAY)

#### FAGATELE BAY

A volcanic tuff cone erupted in relatively recent geologic time to form Fagatele Crater.

--- SENTENCE 4197 ---
The seaward side of the cone was breached by the ocean, and the flooded crater became Fagatele Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4198 ---
Fagatele Crater may be older than the large-scale eruptions along a 3 mile (5 km) long fissure which formed the western end of Tutuila (54).

#### SHORELINE

Fagatele Point, at the western side of Fagatele Bay, is relatively inaccessible.

--- SENTENCE 4199 ---
A cliff rises abruptly 200 feet (60~m) above the ocean.

--- SENTENCE 4200 ---
Seumalo Ridgd, northeast of the seacliff, is steep and rocky (15).

--- SENTENCE 4201 ---
The perimeter of Fagatele Bay is a cliff in volcanic tuff.

--- SENTENCE 4202 ---
A small pocket beach occurs along the eastern margin.

--- SENTENCE 4203 ---
The beach, composed largely of calcareous sand with a small admixture of volcanic sediment, slopes gently and is only about 20 feet (6 m) wide at high tide.

--- SENTENCE 4204 ---
The beach is backed by a steep vegetated embankment of volcanic rock.

--- SENTENCE 4205 ---
On either side of the beach, a tuff cliff extends below the water surface, terminating in a sand deposit in shallow (1 to 4 feet or 0.3 to 1.2 m) water (ASCRI-25S1).

#### FRINGING REEF

A sand deposit extends offshore from the pocket beach and adjacent cliffs in Fagatele Bay for distances of 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m), merging with a reef platform of mainly consolidated limestone and encrusting coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 4206 ---
Depth reaches 2 feet

--- SENTENCE 4208 ---
The width of the platform is 200 feet (60 m) or less (ASCRI-25B1).

--- SENTENCE 4209 ---
The reef front drops nearly vertically 5 to 10 feet (1.5 to 3.0 m) then the bottom slopes gently seaward.

--- SENTENCE 4210 ---
Broken portions of the reef front occur as widely separated pinnacles which rise from depths of 15 to 20 feet (5 to 6 m) to within 4 or 5 feet (1.2 or 1.5 m) of the surface and occur as far offshore as 300 feet (90 m)(ASCRI-25B2).

--- SENTENCE 4211 ---
Spur-and-groove formations extend to a depth of about 20 feet (6 m).

--- SENTENCE 4212 ---
Depths increase rapidly to 120 feet (36 m) in mid-bay, where the bottom is predominantly rubble (34).

--- SENTENCE 4213 ---
# SEA CLIFF

The sea cliff from Fa'asouga Point to Fagatele Point and along the northwestern side of Fagatele Bay is a nesting area for at least five species of seabirds.

--- SENTENCE 4214 ---
Major colonies of the brown booby (fua'o; Sula leucogaster plotus), grey-backed tern (Sterna lunata), blue-grey noddy (laia; Procelsterna cerulea), brown noddy (gogo; Anous stolidus pileatus), and white tern (manu sina; Gygis alba pacifica), are found here.

--- SENTENCE 4215 ---
White-tailed tropicbirds (tava'e; Phaethon lepturus dorotheae), brown noddies, and white terns also nest in the coastal forest covering steep, rocky Suemalo Ridge.

--- SENTENCE 4216 ---
Fagatele Point is the main roost on Tutuila for flying foxes or fruit bats (pe'a; Pteropus samoensis).

--- SENTENCE 4217 ---
Thougands of bats roost in the coastal forest at the southern tip of Seumalo Ridge (15).

--- SENTENCE 4218 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

The reef flat along the eastern margin of Fagatele Bay supports 10% coral cover.

--- SENTENCE 4219 ---
Dead coral heads are conspicuous (about 5% bottom cover).

--- SENTENCE 4220 ---
Species present include Pocillopora verrucosa, Favia sp., Montipora sp., Galaxea sp., and Goniastrea sp., as well as some Acropora humilis and Porites lutea (ASCRI-25B1).

--- SENTENCE 4221 ---
A December 1978 survey of the reef at a depth of 10 feet (3 m) recorded coral cover at less than 25% (34).

--- SENTENCE 4222 ---
The crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) is relatively common on the reef and was reportedly more abundant in shallow water during the summer of 1979.

--- SENTENCE 4223 ---
Some patches of soft coral (Palythoa sp.) are present.

--- SENTENCE 4224 ---
Encrusting coralline algae are common and Cheilosporum sp. and Bryopsis sp. are present (ASCRI-25B1).

--- SENTENCE 4225 ---
The fish fauna of Fagatele Bay is diverse and fishes are moderately to highly abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4226 ---
At least 86 species are recorded from two surveys in the area from the reef flat to the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 4227 ---
Consistently abundant species (in both surveys) include Stegastes albofasciatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea, G. leucopomus, Acanthurus nigrofuscus, and Thalassoma hardwickei (76; ASCRI-25F1).

--- SENTENCE 4228 ---
Although absent in one survey (ASCRI-25F1), Ctenochaetus striatus was common in another (76).

--- SENTENCE 4229 ---
Dominant species include the butterflyfish, Chaetodon reticulatus, the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus lineatus, A. nigrofuscus, and A. triostegus, the damselfishes, Stegastes albofasciatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea, G.

# FRINGING REEF FRONT

Fagatele Bay was free of the crown-of-thorns starfish Acanthaster planci) in February 1978.

--- SENTENCE 4233 ---
However, by November 1978/there was very little coral alive to depths of 150 feet (45 m) or more as a result of heavy infestation by Acanthaster.

--- SENTENCE 4234 ---
At that time, the upper parts of the forereef slopes still had considerable amounts of live coral.

--- SENTENCE 4235 ---
but numerous starfish were moving into the live coral zone (74).

--- SENTENCE 4236 ---
Most of the front shows evidence of once extensive living coral, which covered nearly 100% of the bottom at a depth of 30 feet (9 m)(ASCRI-25B2;34).

--- SENTENCE 4237 ---
Coral cover at this depth is presently around 5%, with dead coral heads accounting for 95% bottom cover (35).

--- SENTENCE 4238 ---
Numerous Acanthaster are still present; some feeding on staghorn and tabular corals (mostly Acropora) (ASCRI-25B2).

--- SENTENCE 4239 ---
At least 30 coral species representing 16 genera were recorded in late 1978, but only about 11 species in 9 genera remain.

--- SENTENCE 4240 ---
A few patches of corals (Acropora humilis, A. intermedia, A. aff.

--- SENTENCE 4241 ---
staghorn pinquis) are alive.

--- SENTENCE 4242 ---
Some Millepora and considerable Galaxea fasicularis have also escaped predation.

--- SENTENCE 4243 ---
Encrusting coralline algae cover wide depressions in the gently-sloping reef front.

--- SENTENCE 4244 ---
In some areas, especially northwest of the pocket beach, a thick, low-growing cover of fleshy algae (browns and reds) occurs, especially on dead coral heads.

--- SENTENCE 4245 ---
Patches of a whitish sponge are extensive in depressions at depths between 15 and 30 feet (5 and 9 m).

--- SENTENCE 4246 ---
No new colonies of coral are evident in this depth range (ASCRI-25B2).

--- SENTENCE 4247 ---
Waters off the southeastern tip of Fagatele Bay harbor a highly diverse fish fauna of moderate abundance.

--- SENTENCE 4248 ---
Plectroglyphidodon dickii and Chromis acares are most abundant of at least 114 species (76).

--- SENTENCE 4249 ---
The endangered green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) is reported in small numbers from Fagatele Bay (15).

#### FAGATELE BAY

Underwater visibility in eastern Fagatele Bay is 50 feet (15 m) or better (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4250 ---
# ABANDONED VILLAGES

Old maps of Tutuila mark Fagalua and Fagatele, two small villages formerly located along the margins of Fagatele Bay but since abandoned.

--- SENTENCE 4251 ---
Remains of old grave sites occur along the coast (30;203).

--- SENTENCE 4254 ---
# FAGATELE BAY

Fagatele Bay is reached overland by turning off the paved highway at Futiga and traversing an unimproved road for approximately 0.8 miles (1.3 km).

--- SENTENCE 4255 ---
At this point a chain blocks the road.

--- SENTENCE 4256 ---
The eastern perimeter of the bay is reached by walking the road and turning west onto a small, poorly-marked foot trail before reaching the American Can Company sewage settling pond to the east.

--- SENTENCE 4257 ---
The narrow path is steep in places but the distance from the chain to the shoreline is traversed in about 20 minutes.

--- SENTENCE 4258 ---
Access to the water is afforded by a small pocket beach.

--- SENTENCE 4259 ---
Fagatele Bay is more easily reached by small boat and attracts sport divers and fishermen (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4260 ---
Fagatele Bay has been recommended as a marine preserve because of its relatively pristine reef, diverse fish fauna, and extensive coral resources (15;39;41).

--- SENTENCE 4261 ---
Waters along the eastern side of Fagatele Bay are frequently used for fishing.

--- SENTENCE 4262 ---
Diving with home-made spears (mata) is the most common activity, followed in popularity by rod and reel fishing.

--- SENTENCE 4263 ---
Both methods result in catches consisting of generally the same species taken off Vailoatai (20).

--- SENTENCE 4264 ---
# STEPS POINT

# CLIFF AREAS

Seabird colonies are found along the sea cliff near Steps Point.

--- SENTENCE 4265 ---
The brown booby (fua'o; Sula leucogaster plotus), an uncommon resident seabird, nests on the sea cliff northeast of Matautuloa Point.

--- SENTENCE 4266 ---
The blue-grey noddy (laia; Procelsterna cerulea), the grey-backed tern (Sterna lunata), and the common white tern (manu sina; Gygis alba pacifica) nest at Steps Point (15).

# OFF STEPS POINT

Offshore slopes off Steps Point were free of the crown-of thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) in early 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 4267 ---
Fishes are abundant and the fauna diverse west of Steps Point.

--- SENTENCE 4268 ---
C. acares, Plectroglyphidodon dickii and Ctenochaetus striatus are most abundant of at least 113 species.

--- SENTENCE 4269 ---
Stegastes fasciolatus is common (76).

--- SENTENCE 4270 ---
# INLAND OF STEPS POINT

A disposal site for sludge from the Van Camp tuna cannery in Pago Pago Harbor is located on the eastern side of the peninsula which leads to Steps Point.

--- SENTENCE 4271 ---
Several pits dug out of the hillside above Larsen Bay are reported to be completely filled with sludge.

--- SENTENCE 4272 ---
Overflow from the pits during heavy rains may eventually reach the Bay (15).

STEPS POINT

Steps Point is the southernmost point on Tutuila and the southernmost point of U.S. territory.

--- SENTENCE 4274 ---
A controlled-access road lead to the point where there is a lighthouse (41).

ATLAS MAPS COVERING THE THE SOUTH/CENTRAL COAST OF TUTUILA, AMERICAN SAMOA

# THE SOUTH/CENTRAL COAST OF TUTUILA

A two-lane highway linking the western district of Tutuila to Pago Pago Harbor parallels the shoreline from Pago Pago to Nu'uuli (MAP 29/30).

--- SENTENCE 4277 ---
West of Nu'uuli, the highway runs inland across the Tafuna-Leone plain to the village of Leone (MAP 23).

--- SENTENCE 4278 ---
This road is the only vehicular link between villages on the southwestern coast of Tutuila (63).

--- SENTENCE 4279 ---
Nu'uuli is the second largest village on Tutuila (23).

--- SENTENCE 4280 ---
A paved road extends from the main highway to Pago Pago International Airport along the western perimeter of Pala Lagoon (MAP 29) (39).

--- SENTENCE 4281 ---
Another paved road connects the inland village of Futiga to Vaitogi (MAP 26) on the coast.

--- SENTENCE 4282 ---
A small network of unimproved roads extends over the Tafuna Plain, connecting a number of the villages along the shore.

--- SENTENCE 4283 ---
In general, these roads are eroded and bumpy, and generally impassable during wet conditions except by four-wheel drive vehicles (23).

--- SENTENCE 4284 ---
The broad plain between Leone (MAP 23) and Nu'uuli (MAP 29) formed as a result of lavas and tuffs deposited in recent geologic time by a series of eruptions along a long, north-south fissure.

--- SENTENCE 4285 ---
Voluminous lava flowed eastward into the ocean, covering a reef which is now about 200 feet (61 m) below sea level, building the island at some points nearly to the edge of the reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 4286 ---
The late lava flows extended the southwestern shoreline of Tutuila as far as the present site of Tafuna (12;54).

--- SENTENCE 4287 ---
The youthful Tafuna coast is cliffed and incised by numerous surge channels and blowholes.

--- SENTENCE 4288 ---
No continuous fringing reef has developed (12).

# COAST BETWEEN STEPS POINT AND SAIL ROCK POINT (LARSEN BAY)

#

--- SENTENCE 4291 ---
FOGAMA'A CRATER AND LARSEN BAY

Fogama's consists of a crater nested within a crater, the seaward rim breached by the ocean to form Larsen Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4292 ---
Fogama's was one of three tuff cones formed by explosive submarine eruptions in recent geologic time along a north-south fissure which extended the western end of Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 4293 ---
Fifty feet (15 m) of pahoehoe lava overlain by 10 feet (3 m) of tuff forms the outer crater rim along the western margin of Larsen Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4294 ---
Overlapping tuff deposits occur at Steps Point (54).

--- SENTENCE 4295 ---
Fragments of reef limestone are embedded in the tuff (12).

--- SENTENCE 4296 ---
#### SHORELINE

The perimeter of Larsen Bay is a series of cliffs in volcanic tuff, notched in some areas 6 feet (2 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 4297 ---
In addition, the base of the cliffs (especially the short promontory separating Fagalua Cove from Fogama'a Cove) are deeply pitted by borings of the sea urchin, Echinometra mathaei.

--- SENTENCE 4298 ---
Sea caves are eroded into the promontory between Fagalua Cove and Fogama'a Cove and around Leti Point.

--- SENTENCE 4299 ---
Narrow beaches of white sand are situated at the heads of Fagalua and Fogama'a Coves (ASCRI-26S1).

--- SENTENCE 4300 ---
Bordering the southwestern side of Fagalua Cove there is a low, irregular exposure of beachrock mostly covered by sand.

--- SENTENCE 4301 ---
A steep-sloping beach of coarse white sand (and some gravel) borders the northeastern cove margin.

--- SENTENCE 4302 ---
At high tide, the 20 foot (6 m) wide beach is swept by surge.

--- SENTENCE 4303 ---
At low tide, a 30 to 40 foot (9 to 12 m) wide expanse of sand is uncovered (ASCRI-26S1).

--- SENTENCE 4304 ---
# OFFSHORE BOTTOM (LARSEN BAY)

--- SENTENCE 4305 ---
A reef extending about 100 feet (30 m) from the shore fringes Fagalua Cove.

--- SENTENCE 4306 ---
The inner reef flat, out to 60 feet (18 m) from shore, is a sand-scoured limestone bottom at a depth of 3 to 4 feet (1.0 to 1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 4307 ---
From 50 to 75 feet (15 to 25 m) offshore, the bottom is consolidated limestone shoaling to a depth of about 2 feet (0.6 m) (ASCRI-26B1).

--- SENTENCE 4308 ---
The reef front is composed of irregular limestone mounds and buttresses separated by narrow surge channels having depths of 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m).

--- SENTENCE 4309 ---
The mounds afford high relief.

--- SENTENCE 4310 ---
Fragments of staghorn coral rubble accumulate in the surge channels and areas between limestone mounds.

--- SENTENCE 4311 ---
Limestone banks and rubble/sand-bottomed channels extend to depths of over 60 feet (18 m) (ASCRI-26B2).

--- SENTENCE 4312 ---
At the base of the cliff, limestone mounds rise to within 6 feet (2 m) of the surface between parallel sand-bottom channels about 16 feet (4.8 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 4313 ---
The cliff wall is pitted with deep

#### LARSEN BAY COASTLINE

The blue-gray noddy (laia; <u>Procelsterna cerulea</u>) a resident seabird uncommon in American Samoa, roosts and nests along the perimeter of Larsen Bay, as well as at Sail Rock Point, Toa Point, and Laumeimamalie Point northeast of the Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4316 ---
The common brown noddy (gogo; <u>Anous stolidus pileatus</u>) nests along sea cliffs from Fagatele Point (MAP-25) east to Toa Point (15).

--- SENTENCE 4317 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT

A filamentous green alga (cf.

--- SENTENCE 4318 ---
<u>Cladophora</u> sp.) occupies shallow pools on tuff outcrops along the shore of Fagalua Cove (ASCRI-26S1).

--- SENTENCE 4319 ---
Coral cover is 1 to 3% on the sand-scoured reef flat within 60 feet (18 m) from the shore in Fagalua Cove.

--- SENTENCE 4320 ---
Porites (Synaraea) sp. is most common.

--- SENTENCE 4321 ---
Coral cover is highly varied on the middle reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 4322 ---
Areas of up to 20% cover occur near the reef margin, where Acropora humilis and Pocillopora verrucosa are most common.

--- SENTENCE 4323 ---
Conspicuous algae include Dictyosphaeria versluysii and encrusting corallines on consolidated limestone (ASCRI-26B1).

--- SENTENCE 4324 ---
The reef flat is inhabited by at least 22 species of fishes present in moderate to high numbers.

--- SENTENCE 4325 ---
Most individuals are juveniles.

--- SENTENCE 4326 ---
Surgeonfishes, wrasses, and damselfishes predominate.

--- SENTENCE 4327 ---
At least 7 species of surgeonfishes are present, with Acanthurus nigrofuscus and A. triostegus most abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4328 ---
Thalassoma hardwickei is the most common of at least five different wrasses.

--- SENTENCE 4329 ---
Although damselfishes are conspicuous, abundance is moderate to low.

--- SENTENCE 4330 ---
Glyphidodontops cyanea and G. glaucus are most common.

--- SENTENCE 4331 ---
Adult Lisa vaigiensis occur in small schools (ASCRI-26F1).

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

Coral cover is highly varied on the reef front, with no coral in some areas and up to 50% cover in other areas.

--- SENTENCE 4332 ---
Overall, corals cover less than 30% of the bottom and include considerable tabular Acropora hyacinthus, encrusting Acropora, Pocillopora verrucosa, large patches of A. rotumana, and some A. robusta.

--- SENTENCE 4333 ---
The coral in deep water is mostly dead as a result of predation by the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci).

--- SENTENCE 4334 ---
Standing branches of dead staghorn Acropora cover large areas.

--- SENTENCE 4335 ---
The coral rubble bottom at a depth of 30 feet (9 m) over 600 feet (185 m) offshore is devoid of living coral.

--- SENTENCE 4336 ---
On or between coral branches are encrusting coralline algae, Ralfsia sp., and a filamentous algal turf.

--- SENTENCE 4337 ---
Limestone mounds extend to depths of 60 feet (18 m) with some large colonies of soft coral 10 to 25 feet (3 to 8 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 4338 ---
A wide patch of sea anemones is also evident (ASCRI-26B2).

--- SENTENCE 4339 ---
Fronting the cliff between Fagalua Cove and Fogama'a Cove, shoaling limestone mounds have patches of Galaxea, low Pocillo-

--- SENTENCE 4341 ---
The sea urchin, Echinometra mathaei, occupies burrows in the pitted cliff face.

--- SENTENCE 4342 ---
Large colonies of soft coral occur in deep water offshore (ASCRI-26B3).

--- SENTENCE 4343 ---
Despite reports of crown-of-thorns starfish in deep portions of Larsen Bay in early 1978 (45), none was observed on forereef slopes of Fagalua Cove in January and February 1978 (74).

--- SENTENCE 4344 ---
Fagalua Cove and other parts of Larsen Bay were infested by Acanthaster later in 1978.

--- SENTENCE 4345 ---
Acanthaster is still present on the reef front (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4346 ---
Prior to starfish predation, corals in Larsen Bay were spectacularly lush -- cover reached 100% in places (201).

--- SENTENCE 4347 ---
The reef front harbors large numbers of fishes (mostly adults).

--- SENTENCE 4348 ---
Surgeonfishes, butterflyfishes, wrasses, and damselfishes dominate an assemblage of at least 132 species (ASCRI-26F2;76).

--- SENTENCE 4349 ---
Large parrotfish are present in low abundance.

--- SENTENCE 4350 ---
Chaetodon reticulatus is the most common butterflyfish.

--- SENTENCE 4351 ---
Acanthurus lineatus and Ctenochaetus striatus are dominant surgeonfishes.

--- SENTENCE 4352 ---
Glyphidodontops leucopomus and Plectroglyphidodon lacrymatus are the most common damselfishes.

--- SENTENCE 4353 ---
Wrasses are conspicuous but not dominant in the overall fish population.

--- SENTENCE 4354 ---
Thalassoma hardwickei, T. lutescens, and T. fuscum are common.

--- SENTENCE 4355 ---
Small (less than 3 feet or 1 m long) blacktip sharks, Carcharhinus melanopterus, occur here (ASCRI-26F2).

--- SENTENCE 4356 ---
Chromis acares was most abundant in one survey.

--- SENTENCE 4357 ---
Pomacentrus melanopterus, Plectroglyphidodon dickii, and Chromis iomelas are common (76).

--- SENTENCE 4358 ---
The endangered green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) is reported in small numbers from Larsen Bay (15).

--- SENTENCE 4359 ---
# FAGALUA COVE

Strong rip currents through two channels (avas) and an uneven limestone bottom cause difficulties and hazards for water activities.

--- SENTENCE 4360 ---
Sport divers exploring the reef front may encounter difficulty in returning to shore against the currents flowing seaward through the avas.

--- SENTENCE 4361 ---
Inshore conditions are safest at low tide and with low wave surge.

--- SENTENCE 4362 ---
Moderate wave surge keeps sand covering the inner reef stirred up and causes turbid water near shore in Fagalua Cove (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4363 ---
#### ABANDONED VILLAGES

Three villages (Fagatele, Fagalua, and Fogama'a) were once located near Fagatele (MAP 25) and Larsen Bays.

--- SENTENCE 4364 ---
These villages have been abandoned.

--- SENTENCE 4365 ---
Old samoan grave sites remain in the area (30;204).

--- SENTENCE 4366 ---
#### FAGALUA COVE

Fagalua Cove is reached by leaving the main highway at Futiga Village and following an unimproved road southward along Matautuloa Ridge separating Fagatele Bay from Larsen Bay.

# LARSEN BAY AND FOGAMA'A CRATER

Fogama'a Crater, inland from Larsen Bay, has been designated as a National Natural Landmark because it illustrates the latest phase of volcanic activity in American Samoa (72).

--- SENTENCE 4375 ---
A picturesque and isolated beach at the head of Fogama'a Cove is not directly accessible (41).

--- SENTENCE 4376 ---
Larsen Bay is being considered as a site for a marine preserve in part because of its pristine reefs (39;71).

--- SENTENCE 4377 ---
However, nearby Fagatele Bay (MAP 25), also a candidate site for a marine preserve, is more sheltered and accessible by boat than is Larsen Bay.

--- SENTENCE 4378 ---
The northwestern portion of Larsen Bay is frequently used for fishing.

--- SENTENCE 4379 ---
Spearing (mata) is the preferred method, but rod and reel fishing also occurs.

--- SENTENCE 4380 ---
Spearing is primarily a daytime activity because the Bay is too far from villages for regular night fishing trips.

--- SENTENCE 4381 ---
Good catches of laea (large parrotfish), malauli (large jack), anae (adult mullet), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), alogo (lined surgeonfish), ume (unicornfish), and fe'e (octopus) are possible.

--- SENTENCE 4382 ---
Rod and reel fishing is also primarily a daytime activity resulting in catches of malauli and lupota (small jack)

#### COAST BETWEEN SAIL ROCK POINT AND FATUASINA POINT

#### SHORELINE

The Vaitogi coast lacks a fringing reef.

--- SENTENCE 4384 ---
The consists of a 250- to 300-foot (75 to 90 m) wide bench of volcanic rock at the 5-foot (2 m) elevation (49).

--- SENTENCE 4385 ---
A storm beach, composed largely of calcareous sand (with about 30% volcanic content) has been thrown up behind the bench -- above the limits of normal wave action (49:ASCRI-26S2).

--- SENTENCE 4386 ---
Shallow splash pools form at the back of the broad platform of smooth, black lava or adjacent to surge channels incising the platform.

--- SENTENCE 4387 ---
Pool bottoms are covered by a thin layer of sand.

--- SENTENCE 4388 ---
A pocket beach occupies the head a small, uunamed cove near Vaitogi Village.

--- SENTENCE 4389 ---
The small beach, composed largely of calcareous sand and gravel, extends inland as a long storm beach.

--- SENTENCE 4390 ---
The pocket beach is bounded by two points of lava rock.

--- SENTENCE 4391 ---
A naturally-eroded tunnel and blowhole are along the southwestern perimeter of the cove.

--- SENTENCE 4392 ---
An amphitheater is carved in the opposite side of the headland just southwest of the Southwest of the pocket beach, the coastline increases in height, becoming a jagged cliff of lava rock (ASCRI-26S2).

# OFFSHORE OF SAIL ROCK POINT

--- SENTENCE 4397 ---
The fish fauna is highly diverse off Sail Rock Point, but populations are only moderately abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4398 ---
At least 102 species occur, most abundant of which are <u>Chromis vanderbilti</u> and <u>Pomacentrus richardsoni</u> (76).

--- SENTENCE 4399 ---
# OFF VAITOGI VILLAGE

The shoreline platform of lava rock fronting Vaitogi is carpeted by dense algal cover, predominantly <u>Sargassum echinocarpum</u> in depressions, with <u>Ahnfeltia</u> sp. present on sloping edges and exposed surfaces.

--- SENTENCE 4400 ---
Also present are <u>Caulacanthus</u> sp., <u>Valonia</u> aff.

--- SENTENCE 4401 ---
<u>aegagropila</u>, and <u>Cladophoropsis</u> sp.

--- SENTENCE 4402 ---
Lower sides of natural arches, tunnels, and amphitheater areas are painted with pink <u>Porolithon</u>.

--- SENTENCE 4403 ---
<u>Sargassum</u> is common in shallow tidepools behind the shoreline bench and adjacent surge channels.

--- SENTENCE 4404 ---
Considerable algae occur on the seaward portion of the bench (ASCRI-26S2).

--- SENTENCE 4405 ---
The endangered green sea turtle (<u>Chelonia mydas</u>) is reported in small numbers off the coast near Vaitogi Village (15).

#### VAITOGI CLIFFS

The scenic Vaitogi cliffs figure in the popular "Turtle and Shark" legend sung by school children.

--- SENTENCE 4406 ---
Chanting to the sea from the cliffs near Vaitogi is said to cause the appearance of turtle and sharks.

--- SENTENCE 4407 ---
The legend has been reinacted for tourists visiting the cliffs in tour buses (ASCRI; 41).

--- SENTENCE 4408 ---
Access to the site is through Vaitogi Village on an unimproved road lacking parking and turnouts (41).

--- SENTENCE 4409 ---
# SHORELINE

A pocket beach at the head of a small cove provides the only good access to the water along the rocky Vaitogi coast.

--- SENTENCE 4410 ---
Access is by courtesy of Vaitogi Village (41).

--- SENTENCE 4411 ---
Although swimmers use the inner cove, strong surge and large swells can make this area dangerous.

--- SENTENCE 4412 ---
Traversing the low platform of lava rock northeast of the cove requires care because of surf and surge (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4413 ---
# OFF VAITOGI

The waters off Vaitogi Village are a frequently used fishing ground.

--- SENTENCE 4414 ---
Handlining and rod and reel fishing are the principal methods employed here.

--- SENTENCE 4415 ---
Daytime catches include malauli (large jack) and lupota (small jack)

--- SENTENCE 4416 ---

# COAST BETWEEN FATUASINA POINT AND MATAUTUOTAFUNA POINT

#### SHORELINE

--- SENTENCE 4424 ---
Fronting Fogagogo there is a 75-foot (25 m) wide bench of lava rock, backed by a storm beach of calcareous sand.

--- SENTENCE 4425 ---
The sand beach is approximately 75 feet wide and 500 feet (150 m) long (49).

--- SENTENCE 4426 ---
#### VAI COVE

The coast lacks a fringing reef and lava cliffs, 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) high, are exposed to the full force of waves.

--- SENTENCE 4427 ---
Several blowholes are conspicuous along this coast (49;ASCRI-27S1).

--- SENTENCE 4428 ---
During periods of strong onshore trade winds, spray from the blowholes is a hazard to incoming airplanes.

--- SENTENCE 4429 ---
Attempts to cap the blowholes have been only partially successful (49).

--- SENTENCE 4430 ---
Seastacks lie a short distance offshore northeast of Vai Cove (ASCRI-27S1).

#### OFF FATUASINA

--- SENTENCE 4431 ---
The fish fauna is highly diverse, but populations are only moderately abundant off Fatuasina Point.

--- SENTENCE 4432 ---
Ctenochaetus striatus dominates an assemblage of at least 114 species.

--- SENTENCE 4433 ---
Although far less abundant, Chromis acares and Plectroglyphidodon dickii are relatively common (76).

--- SENTENCE 4434 ---
# VAI COVE

The encrusting coralline alga, <u>Porolithon</u> sp., coats the base of the sea cliff near Vai Cove.

--- SENTENCE 4435 ---
The common shoreline crab, <u>Grapsus tenuicrustatus</u>, and gobies are conspicuous shoreline fauna (ASCRI-27S1).

--- SENTENCE 4436 ---
#### VAI COVE

Wastewater from the Tafuna collection system enters the Tafuna treatment plant west of Pago Pago International Airport (5).

--- SENTENCE 4437 ---
An outfall discharges about 0.03 mgd of primary treated sewage from the Tafuna plant.

--- SENTENCE 4438 ---
The outfall is located at a depth of about 70 feet (21 m) in Vai Cove.

--- SENTENCE 4439 ---
An increase in the volume of effluent has been proposed.

--- SENTENCE 4440 ---
The present discharge causes no detectable degradation in water quality because of good mixing and circulation in offshore waters (40).

VAI COVE

Fogagogo is accessible by unimproved road.

--- SENTENCE 4443 ---
The storm beach located backing the shoreline bench is known as "Freddie's Beach".

Access to the ocean is difficult even during calm conditions (49).

# COAST BETWEEN MATAUTUOTAFUNA POINT AND AVATELE POINT (INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT)

# PAGO PAGO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT

The reef on which the runway for Pago Pago International Airport stands was formerly the widest reef on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 4452 ---
The airport was constructed in the 1940's with a runway extending from the village of Tafuna eastward across the reef fronting Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4453 ---
In 1959, a new runway was constructed south of the original one, extending the airport farther onto the reef (16).

#### SHORELINE - AIRPORT PONDS

--- SENTENCE 4454 ---
The reef runway is bordered by a man-made shoreline revetment of basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 4455 ---
The seaward embankment slopes steeply to the bottom of a borrow pit (ASCRI-28S1).

--- SENTENCE 4456 ---
A 1,600-foot (500 m) revetment is under construction to replace original, inadequate shore protection along the central part of the airport embankment.

--- SENTENCE 4457 ---
The crest of the improved revetment is 7 to 7.5 feet (2.1 to 2.3 m) above sea level (49).

--- SENTENCE 4458 ---
Bordering the base of the rock wall at its east end are two piles of limestone boulders and rubble.

--- SENTENCE 4459 ---
One is a bank exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 4460 ---
The second projects 10 feet (3 m) above the water surface (ASCRI-28S1).

Between the reef runway and the taxiways are enclosed areas of borrow pits and limestone outcrop remnants left by dredging.

--- SENTENCE 4461 ---
The turbid water of these "lagoons" or ponds drains under the reef runway to a borrow pit which lies behind a protective revetment seaward (south) of the reef runway.

--- SENTENCE 4462 ---
The most conspicuous animal in the enclosed ponds is a sea cucumber (synaptid) (ASCRI).

# AIRPORT LAGOON AND REEF

--- SENTENCE 4477 ---
Coral cover is about 5% on the submerged rock revetment which borders the northeastern section of the reef runway.

--- SENTENCE 4478 ---
Pocillopora damicornis is most common.

--- SENTENCE 4479 ---
Other corals present include patches of blue Montipora, large clumps of Acropora humilis, several other acroporans and other species (ASCRI-28B1).

--- SENTENCE 4480 ---
Thickets of staghorn Acropora 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 m) across and up to 6 feet (2 m) high populate limestone outcrops above the predominantly sand bottom of the borrow pit.

--- SENTENCE 4481 ---
Coral cover totals about 10%, almost entirely Acropora formosa, with some A. hyacinthus.

--- SENTENCE 4482 ---
Coral coverage has increased noticeably in the borrow pit since 1971.

--- SENTENCE 4483 ---
Common algae are <u>Gelidiopsis</u> intricata and <u>Amphiroa</u> sp. growing at the base of staghorn <u>Acropora</u>.

--- SENTENCE 4484 ---
The sea cucumber, <u>Stichopus chloronotus</u>, is abundant on the steep slope of the seaward margin of the borrow pit.

--- SENTENCE 4485 ---
The snail, <u>Terebra maculata</u>, is evident on the sand bottom (ASCRI-28B2).

--- SENTENCE 4486 ---
The shallow, seaward portion of the borrow pit is a rich coral bottom, with cover approaching 90%.

--- SENTENCE 4487 ---
In the northeast corner of the borrow pit are extensive banks of staghorn Acropora.

--- SENTENCE 4488 ---
To the southwest there are stands of Psammocora and a large area of Porites andrewsi up to 100 feet (30 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 4489 ---
Farther southwest along the inner reef margin are stands of Pavona frondifera, Acropora humilis, A. aspera, and occasional Pocillopora damicornis and Pavona decussata heads.

--- SENTENCE 4490 ---
Off the center of the borrow pit there occurs a solid bank of Acropora formosa rising to within one-half foot of the surface.

--- SENTENCE 4491 ---
Deeper reef pools contain Porites lutea.

--- SENTENCE 4492 ---
Algae (Halimeda) are conspicuous between branches of P. andrewsi.

--- SENTENCE 4493 ---
Sea urchins (Echinometra mathaei), live between

--- SENTENCE 4495 ---
Live coral cover is about 50% along the inner margin of the reef platform bordering the northeast corner of the dredged borrow pit.

--- SENTENCE 4496 ---
Large thickets of staghorn Acropora (mostly A. formosa with some A. aspera) up to 15 to 20 feet (5 to 6 m) across rise to within about one foot (0.3 m) of the surface.

--- SENTENCE 4497 ---
Dead coral rubble accumulates beside the large thickets of living Acropora.

--- SENTENCE 4498 ---
Small, free nodules of Porites lutea cover about 5% of the rubble.

--- SENTENCE 4499 ---
Algae cover much of the remainder and include Porolithon gardineri, encrusting Ralfsia sp., Peyssonnelia sp., patchy Lyngbya sp., Cladophora sp., and Bryopsis sp.

--- SENTENCE 4500 ---
The sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, is conspicuous toward the northeast corner of the borrow pit, although not as abundant as at the seaward edge of the center section (ASCRI-28B4).

--- SENTENCE 4501 ---
The outer reef flat and margin off Pago Pago International Airport was reportedly infested by crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) in early 1978 (45).

--- SENTENCE 4502 ---
By January 1979, numerous Acanthaster occurred in scattered concentrations at depths of 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 m) off the eastern end of the runway.

--- SENTENCE 4503 ---
Many dead corals were observed, but some areas of live coral were interspersed with starfish concentrations.

--- SENTENCE 4504 ---
Numerous starfish were also evident off the Vortoc Station (radio facility), but not as abundant as to the east (74).

--- SENTENCE 4505 ---
Very few Acanthaster were observed on the reef flat in October 1979 (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4506 ---
The protected water of the dredged lagoon south of the reef runway shelters an extremely diverse and abundant fish assemblage.

--- SENTENCE 4507 ---
Similar densities of fishes occur on the Pavona and Porites reef flat seaward of the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4508 ---
Although the lagoon and reef flat are primarily a nursery area for juveniles, adults of many species are present.

--- SENTENCE 4509 ---
Juvenile scarids are most abundant of at least 82 species of fish and feed throughout the area in large Surgeonfishes, wrasses, and damselfishes are also abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4510 ---
In some areas, several thousand fishes of many species concentrated within a radius of 150 feet (45 m).

--- SENTENCE 4511 ---
Most abundant species of butterflyfishes are schools of Chaetodon citrinellus, C. reticulatus, and C. trifasciatus.

--- SENTENCE 4512 ---
Although not as common, C. unimaculatus and C. bennetti are conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 4513 ---
Six species of surgeonfishes are common, of which Acanthurus nigrofuscus and Ctenochaetus striatus are most abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4514 ---
Thalassoma hard-wickei is the most abundant of the wrasses.

--- SENTENCE 4515 ---
Dascyllus aruanus, Stegastes albofasciatus, Glyphidodontops cyanea, G. glaucus, and G. leucopomus are most common of the damselfishes.

--- SENTENCE 4516 ---
Mullids of several species are seen primarily in the dredged lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4517 ---
High coral cover and high bottom relief provide shelter for the large fish assemblage.

--- SENTENCE 4518 ---
Larval fishes, probably atherinids, are conspicuous in surface waters.

--- SENTENCE 4519 ---
Small black-tipped sharks (Carcharinus melanopteru ) may be seen in shallow parts of the lagoon and over the nearby reef flats (ASCRI-28F1).

# FRINGING REEF AND BORROW PIT

The borrow pit bordering the seaward revetment of the reef runway is well protected from waves.

--- SENTENCE 4521 ---
However, the outer reef flat off the eastern tip of the reef runway (near Avatele Point) is exposed to heavy surf and strong currents (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4522 ---
Underwater visibility is fairly good in the outer portion of the borrow pit and along the inner consolidated margin of the reef flat off the reef runway.

--- SENTENCE 4523 ---
However, water becomes increasingly turbid approaching the runway revetment.

--- SENTENCE 4524 ---
An inner pond, enclosed on all sides by the airport runway and taxiways, drains into the seaward lagoon, causing water near the shoreline revetment to become very turbid and smelly in certain areas.

--- SENTENCE 4525 ---
The ponds are highly turbid (ASCRI).

PALA LAGOON

PHYSIOGRAPHY

Pala Lagoon is the only large, well-protected lagoon on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 4529 ---
It is roughly circular, approximately one mile (1.6 km) across, and has a surface area of about one square mile (3 sq km).

--- SENTENCE 4530 ---
Approximately two-thirds of the inner lagoon is very shallow, with depths varying from 1 to 5 feet (0.3 to 1.5 m) depending on the tide.

--- SENTENCE 4531 ---
A large area (about one-sixth of the lagoon) adjacent to the airport has been subject to extensive dredging to obtain fill material.

--- SENTENCE 4532 ---
The dredged portion has a very irregular depth shoreward of the sill which restricts the entrance channel.

--- SENTENCE 4533 ---
Average depth of the dredged basin is roughly 10 feet (3 m) (24).

--- SENTENCE 4534 ---
Pala Lagoon was formed as a result of shoaling of a submerged reef by late lava flows, which formed the Tafuna/Leone plain.

--- SENTENCE 4535 ---
Subsequent development of a sand hook or spit, formed in response to current patterns resulting from the lava flow, left an entrance to the lagoon behind the fringing reef to the south (6;54).

--- SENTENCE 4536 ---
# TRIBUTARY STREAMS

Fresh water enters the lagoon from seven streams several fresh water springs.

--- SENTENCE 4537 ---
Papa Stream flows through about 350 feet (100 meters) of mangrove forest before discharging into the Vaitele Stream flows through the northeastern corner Tafuna Plain, draining a large watershed before discharging into the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4538 ---
This channel appears to be realigned in places along the lower reach where it is bordered by residences.

--- SENTENCE 4539 ---
The Stream's lower reach above a bridge near the mouth is choked with a grass (Brachiaria sp.).

--- SENTENCE 4540 ---
Papa Stream, among the more perennial streams on Tutuila, is considered to have exceptional natural value by virtue of its relatively condition (71).

--- SENTENCE 4541 ---
The concentration of watershed drainage into the lagoon is due to the original form of Matafao peak (54).

--- SENTENCE 4542 ---
The lagoon is bounded on the south by a taxiway (the old runway) embankment at the Pago Pago International Airport.

--- SENTENCE 4543 ---
The western margin is occupied by a residential area and vegetated land.

--- SENTENCE 4544 ---
The northern side is bordered by mangrove swamps and rocky outcrops.

--- SENTENCE 4545 ---
A vegetated sand peninsula (Coconut Point) forms the eastern margin of Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4546 ---
The opening to the sea is aligned east to west across a fringing reef in the southeastern corner of the lagoon where there occurs a shallow, narrow pass (24).

--- SENTENCE 4547 ---
The shoreline at Tafuna Beach Park is basalt boulders, rubble, and gravel extending inland to park grounds one to three feet (0.3 to 1 m) above sea level (ASCRI-29S1).

The bottom of inner Pala Lagoon grades from mud nearshore to silty-sand.

--- SENTENCE 4550 ---
The water is usually turbid (24).

--- SENTENCE 4551 ---
Offshore of Tafuna Beach Park there is a shallow bottom of silty-sand deepening from around 6 inches (15 cm) nearshore to 12 to 24 inches (30 to 60 cm) about 100 feet (30 m) from shore (ASCRI- 29B1).

--- SENTENCE 4552 ---
The outer lagoon near the entrance channel and the International Airport is a shallow sand flat.

--- SENTENCE 4553 ---
Deeper areas adjacent to the south shore represent dredging activities carried out between 1959 and 1961 when a new airport runway was constructed on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 4554 ---
Depths in this region vary from 3 to 23 feet (1 to 7 m)(24).

## AVATELE PASSAGE

Avatele Passage (the entrance to Pala Lagoon) has considerably altered by airport construction and dredging for landfill material for the airport and various other public works projects.

--- SENTENCE 4555 ---
The channel is approximately 1300 feet (400 m) across between Coconut Point and the runway embankment (33).

--- SENTENCE 4556 ---
of the passage nearest to Coconut Point is a shallow sand flat, partially exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 4557 ---
Deeper areas adjacent to the airport embankment are excavations from dredging activities carried out between 1959 and 1961 (24).

--- SENTENCE 4558 ---
The outer portion of Avatele Passage includes a narrow, meandering channel along the southern This channel is approximately 985 feet (300 m) long.

--- SENTENCE 4559 ---
Tidal currents are strong within the channel.

--- SENTENCE 4560 ---
Depths range from 3 to 26 feet (1 to 8 m) and the bathymetry is highly irregular.

--- SENTENCE 4561 ---
The seaward portion of this channel has a rubble bottom.

--- SENTENCE 4562 ---
The reef flat across Avatele Passage is exposed at nearly every low tide, restricting tidal flow between the ocean and Pala Lagoon to the narrow channel bordering the airport embankment (24).

--- SENTENCE 4563 ---
The sand flat across Avatele Passage contains only scattered occurrences of limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 4564 ---
Shallow scour channels reveal reef limestone approximately 4 inches (10 cm) beneath the sand deposits on the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 4565 ---
Sand eroded from the shoreline of Coconut Point has fanned out across the Passage with significant deposition in the nearby borrow pits.

--- SENTENCE 4566 ---
On a rising tide, strong currents around Mulinu'u Point deposit sand just inside the lagoon (16).

--- SENTENCE 4567 ---
The reef flat off Coconut Point has shoaled considerably since 1969.

--- SENTENCE 4568 ---
The middle and outer reef are now fully exposed at low tide (36).

--- SENTENCE 4569 ---
Bottom surveys at standard locations in 1972, 1974, and 1978 indicate increasing proportions of rubble and sediment in Avatele Passage (24;33;36).

--- SENTENCE 4570 ---
# MANGROVE SWAMP

The northern and eastern shores of Pala Lagoon are bordered by 85 acres (34 ha) of well-developed mangrove forest which is by far the largest such forest in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 4571 ---
Predominant vegetation is a well-developed stand of large oriental mangrove, Bruguiera gymnorhiza (some trees up to 66 feet or 20 m in height).

Along the western side of Coconut Point there is a strip of red mangrove.

# INNER PALA LAGOON

--- SENTENCE 4580 ---
The biota of inner Pala Lagoon lacks diversity, but the lagoon is considered an important nursery and spawning ground for fishes and invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 4581 ---
Larval fish and egg concentrations indicate that Pala Lagoon serves as a nursery ground for certain species of fish.

--- SENTENCE 4582 ---
Larvae are present of those fish resident in the inner lagoon, such as gobies, and those which range in and out of the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4583 ---
Small fishes of several species, most notably mullet, frequent shallow areas of the lagoon (24).

--- SENTENCE 4584 ---
Corals are absent from inner Pala Lagoon, the major portion of which is sand and mud flats covered by a dense growth of Acanthophora spicifera.

--- SENTENCE 4585 ---
Cover by A. spicifera and Halimeda discoidea, averages about 75% in the western half of the inner lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4586 ---
<u>Halimeda tuna</u> occurs at one location near center of the inner layoun.

--- SENTENCE 4587 ---
In addition, dense mats of the green alga, Enteromorpha sp., along with A. spicifera, appear on rocks along the western shore of the lagoon in the vicinity of fresh water springs.

--- SENTENCE 4588 ---
The inner lagoon harbors a few echinoderms: Polyand Holothuria sp.

--- SENTENCE 4589 ---
Both are confined to the sandy SD.

--- SENTENCE 4590 ---
flats near the lagoon entrance (24).

--- SENTENCE 4591 ---
Other organisms of consequence in the inner lagoon are bivalve molluscs.

--- SENTENCE 4592 ---
One species of clam, Gafrarium tumidum, is abundant on the muddy bottom the north shore, where it is harvested by women and children (19;24).

--- SENTENCE 4593 ---
Colonies of small oysters are common on rocks along the western shore.

--- SENTENCE 4594 ---
Clam shells of several species are abundant among shoreline debris (24).

--- SENTENCE 4595 ---
Mangrove crabs (pa'alemago; Scylla serrata) are said to be common at various places in the lagoon (24; ASCRI), particularly in the mangrove swamp along the north shore.

--- SENTENCE 4596 ---
Shoreline invertebrates at Tafuna Beach Park include neritids (Nerita plicata) on basalt boulders and clusters of bivalves (Isognomon sp.) in crevices of intertidal rocks (ASCRI-29S1).

--- SENTENCE 4597 ---
At the northern end of Tafuna Beach Park, dense windrows of green, filamentous algae (Enteromorpha sp.) occur on the silty-sand bottom near shore, as well as on basalt boulders at the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 4598 ---
The red alga, Acanthophora spicifera, forms dense mats on the shallow, silty-sand bottom 75 to 100 feet (25 to 30 m) off the park.

--- SENTENCE 4599 ---
The seagrass, Syringodium isoetifolium, reported only once before from American Samoa, is uncommon.

--- SENTENCE 4600 ---
Cone-shaped mounds and holes made by burrowing animals are conspicuous on the bottom (ASCRI-29B1).

# SOUTHERN PALA LAGOON

Except for colonies of <u>Porites lutea</u>, corals are nearly absent from the reef flat in Avatele Passage.

--- SENTENCE 4609 ---
In deeper, excavated pits, <u>Pocillopora damicornis</u>, <u>Goniopora sp.</u>, and <u>Leptastrea purpurea</u> are present.

--- SENTENCE 4610 ---
Corals are mostly confined to walls or ledges of dredged areas where sediment is not accumulating.

--- SENTENCE 4611 ---
Algae and sand dominate the bottom of the outer lagoon near Avatele Passage.

--- SENTENCE 4612 ---
Algal cover is about 28%, primarily by <u>Halimeda</u>.

--- SENTENCE 4613 ---
The sea cucumbers, <u>Stichopus chloronotus</u>, <u>Polyplectana sp.</u>, and <u>Actinopyga</u> sp., are common on shallow sand flats adjacent to Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4614 ---
The sea urchins, <u>Echinothrix</u> sp. and <u>Echinometra mathaei</u>, are rare.

--- SENTENCE 4615 ---
The goatfish, <u>Mulloidichthys</u> <u>flavolineatus</u>, is abundant along the southern margin of the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4616 ---
At least 20 other fish species are present in this area, where the silty-sand bottoms of dredged borrow pits reach a depth of about 25 feet (8 m).

--- SENTENCE 4617 ---
Relatively common species in some areas include moray eels, <u>Gymnothorax richardsoni</u>, herring, <u>Herklotsichthys</u> sp., the snake eel, <u>Leiruanus semicinctus</u>, and the worm eel, <u>Moringua</u> sp.

--- SENTENCE 4618 ---
Scorpionfishes are abundant in this area (24).

--- SENTENCE 4619 ---
# AVATELE PASSAGE

The subtidal portion of the broad sand flat extending south of Mulinu'u Point across Avatele Passage harbors a population of the conch snail (Strombus maculatus), tubeworms, and patches of a sea grass (Halophila ovalis).

--- SENTENCE 4620 ---
Another sea grass (Syringodium isoetifolium), previously unreported from American Samoa, occurs here (16).

--- SENTENCE 4621 ---
Inside Avatele Passage, live coral patches are replaced by coral rubble and boulder fields which seem to be dead masses of Porites, some forming huge blocks several meters across (24).

--- SENTENCE 4622 ---
Some areas of inner Avatele Passage harbor large concentrations of sea cucumbers.

--- SENTENCE 4623 ---
Stichopus is abundant on reef flats adjacent to Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4624 ---
Holothuria pervicax occurs under rocks and is randomly distributed.

--- SENTENCE 4625 ---
Sea urchins are common in this area, but this is apparent only at night when they are active.

--- SENTENCE 4626 ---
Generally, sea cucumbers are more common on reef flats in the inner passage, whereas sea urchins are more common in the outer passage.

--- SENTENCE 4627 ---
Echinometra mathaei is by far the most abundant of the echinoids.

--- SENTENCE 4628 ---
A substantial colony of large mantis shrimp (Lysio-

--- SENTENCE 4630 ---

At least 30 species are recorded from the shallow reef flat extending south from Mulinu'u Point.

#### STREAMS

Near the mouth of Papa Stream, surface flow disappears during dry weather periods occuring only as ground moisture fed by gravity seepage until a minor surface flow reforms approximately 100 feet (30 m) from the shore of Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4633 ---
This ground moisture is rich in nutrients derived from seepage through cesspools and is capable of supporting large concentrations of bacteria.

--- SENTENCE 4634 ---
Such inputs explain the high nutrient and coliform concentrations in the northwestern portion of Pala Lagoon when the major stream, Vaitele, is dry (24).

--- SENTENCE 4635 ---
The physical configuration of Pala Lagoon is largely responsible for the restrictive circulation pattern in the shallow basin.

--- SENTENCE 4636 ---
Tidal exchange is inhibited and circulation patterns limit dilution of contaminants entering the northern and western portions.

--- SENTENCE 4637 ---
Prevailing easterly winds reinforce this pattern by driving surface water and pollutants into the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4638 ---
Wind mixing keeps the waters turbid in much of the lagoon and reduces visibility underwater to a few inches.

--- SENTENCE 4639 ---
Because over half of Pala Lagoon is less than 3 feet (1 m) in depth and is fed by six small streams subject to largd fluctuations in flow, the lagoon is a highly variable environment (24).

--- SENTENCE 4640 ---
During tidal exchanges, currents are strong within the narrow channel along the southern margin of Avatele Passage (24;34).

--- SENTENCE 4641 ---
Strong currents flow around Mulinu'u Point into Pala Lagoon on a rising tide (16).

--- SENTENCE 4642 ---
On the basis of high microbial density, the western and northwestern regions of Pala Lagoon show evidence of fecal contamination, with high coliform levels maintained through subsurface seepage from the numerous cesspools along the western edge of the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4643 ---
Pala Lagoon is subject to large and rapid fluctuations in freshwater input, resulting in similar fluctuations of bacterial concentrations.

--- SENTENCE 4644 ---
Bacteriological pollution makes the extreme western portion of the lagoon an unacceptable area for the propagation of shellfish although shellfish are most intensively harvested from the mud flat bordering the northwestern shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 4645 ---
Consumption of sea foods from these areas represents a potential health hazard (24).

--- SENTENCE 4651 ---
Nutrient levels are generally high outside the entrance channel, decreasing through the channel and northward but increasing in the western corner (24;32).

--- SENTENCE 4652 ---

--- SENTENCE 4658 ---
# SHORELINE AND MANGROVE AREAS

--- SENTENCE 4659 ---
The mangrove forest along the north shore of Pala Lagoon is an example of a unique plant assemblage that is rapidly being eliminated from American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 4660 ---
Of particular significance is the puzzle-nut or "le'ile'i" tree (Xylocarpus moluccensis), which has been identified as a potentially threatened species and is restricted to a few specimens located just north of Tafuna Beach Park and on Aunu'u Island.

--- SENTENCE 4661 ---
The only large stand of the red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) in American Samoa occurs here in a band along the western edgd of Coconut Point peninsula.

--- SENTENCE 4662 ---
The Pala Lagoon mangrove forest is one of seven areas in American Samoa proposed as natural areas closed to hunting and other public disturbance in order to preserve plant and animal life (15).

#### TAFUNA BEACH PARK

Tafuna Beach Park, along the western perimeter of Pala Lagoon, is easily accessible by vehicle.

--- SENTENCE 4663 ---
Swimmers use the sandy, nearshore area.

--- SENTENCE 4664 ---
Park facilities attract other users.

--- SENTENCE 4665 ---
The shoreline is littered with broken glass and some trash (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4666 ---
# PALA LAGOON

Pala Lagoon is considered a unique body of water and is a nursery area for marine life, particularly the mangrove crab (pa'alemago; <u>Scyla serrata</u>) (39).

--- SENTENCE 4667 ---
The southern, western, and northern margins and all shallow areas of Pala Lagoon are frequently used for subsistence fishing.

--- SENTENCE 4668 ---
Rod and reel fishing is the preferred activity along the airport (south) shore and also along the western perimeter of Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4669 ---
However, shoreline access across the airport property is restricted to authorized personnel and requires a pass (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 4670 ---
Throw-netting is popular along the western shore, as well as in the shallow areas of the north lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4671 ---
Fuafua (juvenile mullet), anae (adult mullet), and lupota (small jack) are the usual catch.

--- SENTENCE 4672 ---
Seining (upega) takes place in the shallows in both the western

--- SENTENCE 4674 ---
Trapping crabs and clam digging are practiced along the northern perimeter of Pala Lagoon (20).

--- SENTENCE 4675 ---
Crab fishermen employ small traps in the northeastern portion of the lagoon and along Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4676 ---
A few reportedly use gill nets to catch crabs in the deeper pockets along the western side of the lagoon (24).

Perhaps the most important fishery is that for clams, which are intensively harvested on intertidal mudflats in the northern and northwestern portions of the lagoon (19).

# COAST BETWEEN AVATELE POINT AND NU'UO'OSEGI COVE (COCONUT POINT)

--- SENTENCE 4683 ---
Coconut Point is a natural sand spit nearly one mile (1.6 km) long and varying in width from 200 to over 1,000 feet (60 to 300 m).

--- SENTENCE 4684 ---
Elevation is between 6 and 10 feet (2 to 3 m).

--- SENTENCE 4685 ---
The spit built southward from the shore at the base of Matafao Peak across a reef flat along the eastern side of Pala Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 4686 ---
The village of Nu'uuli, second largest in American Samoa, occupies the northern portion of the Point (49;66).

--- SENTENCE 4687 ---
The western shore of Coconut Point is a mangrove forest.

--- SENTENCE 4688 ---
The eastern shore was once a wide beach, but in recent years the shoreline has eroded along the entire length of Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4689 ---
Some sand loss is attributable to high waves accompanying tropical storms and hurricanes, but most is due to longshore currents which displace sand toward Mulinu'u Point (66).

--- SENTENCE 4690 ---
The southern portion of the eastern shore is a narrow undergoing active erosion.

--- SENTENCE 4691 ---
The foreshore is 25 feet (8 m) wide at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 4692 ---
Coconut tree roots are exposed, and several trees are ready to topple (49).

--- SENTENCE 4693 ---
An eroded sand bank varies in height from 1.5 to 6 feet (0.5 to 2 m) and has formed as a consequence of progressive erosion of the sand material comprising Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4694 ---
Structures (concrete bunkers) now located offshore provide additional evidence of extensive shoreline erosion.

--- SENTENCE 4695 ---
shoreline along the southern one-third to one-half of Coconut Point has eroded back an average of 3 to 5 feet (1 to 1.5 m) per year over the 35-year period between 1942 and 1977 (66).

--- SENTENCE 4696 ---
According to one resident, the shoreline has retreated about 40 feet (12 m) since the airport was constructed.

--- SENTENCE 4697 ---
Evidence for this is a concrete pillbox which now is partly submerged on the flat off Mulinu'u Point (24).

--- SENTENCE 4698 ---
Situated on the beach in 1969 and built at the vegetation line during World War II, the now about 115 feet (35 m) offshore (36).

--- SENTENCE 4699 ---
A remnant of the original sand beach is located portion of the shore.

--- SENTENCE 4700 ---
The northern portion of Coconut Point is characterized by a nearly continuous series of rudimentary rubble seawalls and other shore protection structures.

--- SENTENCE 4701 ---
structures offer marginal protection, even under normal wave conditions, and are in various stages of failure.

--- SENTENCE 4702 ---
Two walls at the north end of the Point are more substantial than the rest.

--- SENTENCE 4703 ---
Unprotected areas in the center of the eastern shore are eroding, limestone and with basalt rubble on the foreshore damage occurs along the 900 feet (270 m) of protected shoreline during storm conditions.

--- SENTENCE 4704 ---
Little sand remains in of the walls, the foundations of which extend to sea level (49:66) -- thus, beaches are absent or restricted to narrow sections exposed only at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 4705 ---
The sand is coarse with a higher proportion of basalt material than along the southern the reach.

PHYSIOGRAPHY

Nu'uuli borrow pits, the shoreline is an eroded embankment over 1.5 feet (0.5 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 4707 ---
A flat of fine, dark sediment and basalt stones fronts the mouth of Amaile Stream (16;66).

--- SENTENCE 4708 ---
The shoreline along the northern one-half to two-thirds of the point has eroded an average of 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) per year since World War II (66).

--- SENTENCE 4709 ---
Longshore currents, strongest during periods of high surf, consistently move sand toward Avatele Passage.

--- SENTENCE 4710 ---
On a falling tide, water flows over the reef fringing Coconut Point and flows through a channel paralleling and just off the beach.

--- SENTENCE 4711 ---
This flow moves toward Mulinu'u Point at the southern tip of the peninsula, where it joins the outflow from Pala Lagoon (33).

--- SENTENCE 4712 ---
Erosion occurs in the area of Mulinu'u Point when this current, flowing along shore, cuts sharply around the point into Pala Lagoon (16).

## FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 4713 ---
The reef off Coconut Point is perhaps the widest fringing reef in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 4714 ---
Prior to the construction of the reef runway at Pago Pago International Airport, this reef extended south from Pala Lagoon (16;24).

--- SENTENCE 4715 ---
The reef varies in width from about 1,900 feet (580 m) off Nu'uuli to 1,200 feet (360 m) off Mulinu'u Point.

--- SENTENCE 4716 ---
At its widest point, the reef flat extends 2,400 feet (730 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 4717 ---
The inshore area is dominated by sand.

--- SENTENCE 4718 ---
Dead coral rubble is a major constituent of the middle reef (24).

--- SENTENCE 4719 ---
From about 330 feet (100 m) offshore, the bottom is largely consolidated limestone pavement.

--- SENTENCE 4720 ---
The outermost part, 1150 to 1300 feet (350 to 400 m) offshore, is strewn with rubble up to a consolidated algal ridge at the reef margin (34).

--- SENTENCE 4721 ---
Depth of the reef flat varies from one to 3 feet (49).

--- SENTENCE 4722 ---
Much of the reef platform is exposed at lowest tides.

--- SENTENCE 4723 ---
The reef platform is generally shallower in the middle and southern regions than in the northern region (16).

--- SENTENCE 4724 ---
A "boat channel" paralleling nearly the entire length of Coconut Point is a conspicuous nearshore feature and constitutes the deepest part of the reef flat with the exception of the borrow pits at the north end.

--- SENTENCE 4725 ---
Channel width and depth vary from place to place.

--- SENTENCE 4726 ---
Average depth is about 3 feet (1 m).

--- SENTENCE 4727 ---
The channel disappears as a distinct feature around Mulinu'u Point.

--- SENTENCE 4728 ---
ately south of the borrow pits, the seaward boundary of the channel is difficult to establish.

--- SENTENCE 4729 ---
Irregular shaped masses of reef rock and coral litter the bottom at a depth similar to that of the channel.

--- SENTENCE 4730 ---
Borrow pit excavations have impinged on the channel near Amaile Stream, but sediment outwash from the stream probably inhibit development of a nearshore channel.

--- SENTENCE 4731 ---
Sand is the dominant bottom type in the channel, with coral rubble and small boulders scattered over the bottom in some areas.

--- SENTENCE 4732 ---
The seaward margin of the channel has more small boulders and rubble than the landward margin, which is essentially a subtidal extension of the Along the southern part of Coconut Point, the innel bottom shallows gently seaward, with a low but sand beach.

--- SENTENCE 4737 ---
Off the central part of the peninsula, the channel expands into a large triangular-shaped pool with a flat, sandy bottom.

--- SENTENCE 4738 ---
Along the seaward margin of this pool, massive coral blocks rise from the sand bottom to the level of the reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 4739 ---
The blocks, varying from one to several feet across and over three feet (1 m) high, coalesce seaward with the reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 4740 ---
Similar blocks of reef conglomerate form parts of the seaward margin of the channel fronting the northern part of Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4741 ---
They alternate with sections where the channel margin shallows toward the reef platform as a rounded bank of loose sand and coral rubble.

--- SENTENCE 4742 ---

--- SENTENCE 4747 ---
# COCONUT POINT

The uncommon shrub, <u>Sophora</u> tomentosa, grows mixed with other species in the sandy soil at the tip of Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4748 ---
This plant is restricted in its distribution in American Samoa and is known from only one other location (15).

--- SENTENCE 4749 ---
# SHORELINE

A snail, <u>Planaxis sulcatus</u>, is abundant on intertidal rocks at the northern end of Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4750 ---
Hermit crabs and cerithid gastropods are abundant on rubble and small boulders at and just below the base of the beach (16).

--- SENTENCE 4751 ---
# FRINGING REEF FLAT (AT AVATELE PASSAGE)

--- SENTENCE 4752 ---
Living coral has declined on the reef flat and reef front across Avatele Passage since about 1973.

--- SENTENCE 4753 ---
A massive coral kill occurred on the reef flat east and southeast of the tip of Coconut Point sometime between November 1972 and July 1973.

--- SENTENCE 4754 ---
The area of affected reef was about 20 acres (8 ha), of which about 15 acres (6 ha) had previously supported luxurient coral growth.

--- SENTENCE 4755 ---
All corals of the genera Acropora, Montipora, and Pocillopora were killed within a sharply delimited area.

--- SENTENCE 4756 ---
Corals of the genera Pavona, Porites, Leptastrea, Galaxea, and Psammocora appeared unaffected.

--- SENTENCE 4757 ---

A 1972 survey measured much higher coral cover on the reef flat off Avatele Passage than is now present.

--- SENTENCE 4797 ---
In 1972 coral cover averaged about 20% over the first 80 feet (25 m) from shore to greater than 50% of the bottom out to 165 feet (50 m) from shore (24).

--- SENTENCE 4798 ---
Today, coral cover is only 10% in the first 330 feet (100 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 4799 ---
From 330 to 660 feet (100 to 200 m) off shore, cover is less than 4%.

--- SENTENCE 4800 ---
From 660 to 990 feet (200 to 300 m) off shore, cover is about 7%.

--- SENTENCE 4801 ---
Porites (Synaraea) undulata is common on the outer reef flat, 990 to 1300 feet (300 to 400 m) off shore, where coral cover is less than 2% (34;36).

--- SENTENCE 4802 ---
About 1300 feet (400 m) from shore is an algal ridge, where small Acropora humilis occur (34).

--- SENTENCE 4803 ---
At least 43 fish species are recorded in outer Avatele Passage along the margin of the dredged channel which borders the airport.

--- SENTENCE 4804 ---

--- SENTENCE 4806 ---
Older residents remember an episode of infestation by the crown-of-thorns starfish on the reef off Nu'uuli about 50 years ago (34).

# FRINGING REEF FLAT (OFF COCONUT POINT)

--- SENTENCE 4809 ---
Coral cover is low in the nearshore channel off Coconut Point.

--- SENTENCE 4810 ---
Small colonies of Porites lutea, Pocillopora damicornis, and Cyphastrea microphthalma are present.

--- SENTENCE 4811 ---
Nearshore, the sand-bottom channel harbors several large sponges (more prominent on the central and northern reef segments), a sea cucumber (Synapta maculata), and several species of sand-dwelling gastropods, of which a conch (Strombus maculatus) is most conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 4812 ---
Tubeworms (Chaetopteridae) are locally abundant, particularly in the central and southern sectors.

--- SENTENCE 4813 ---
In the northern sector, alpheid shrimp, sharing burrows with a goby fish, are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4814 ---
Colonies of soft coral (Palythoa sp.) occur in the central sector.

--- SENTENCE 4815 ---
The seaweed, Halimeda macroloba, and the seagrass, Halophila oyalis, are common.

--- SENTENCE 4816 ---
Algae are the dominant forms on rubble and small boulders along the seaward margin of the channel and on the reef platform (16).

--- SENTENCE 4817 ---
Algal turfs cover most of the solid surfaces in the channel with fleshy crusts also common on limestone fragments.

--- SENTENCE 4818 ---
Cover by turf-forming species decreases toward the seaward margin of the reef flat to be replaced by encrusting coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 4819 ---
Halimeda opuntia is common in interstices of rubble on the reef flat (8).

--- SENTENCE 4820 ---
The abundance of benthic algae increases in the direction of Mulinu'u Point, where total cover reaches 50 percent or more in some areas (16;34).

--- SENTENCE 4821 ---
Dictyota sp. is dominant and Halimeda opuntia is conspicuous (16).

--- SENTENCE 4822 ---
Well-developed heads of Porites andrewsi, Porites sp., soft coral, Sinularia conferta, occur widely scattered over the seaward margin of the "boat channel".

--- SENTENCE 4823 ---
Coral cover is generally less than 10% along this margin and on the inner reef flat beyond.

--- SENTENCE 4824 ---
Regions of higher cover (15 to 25%) occur where Pavona frondifera predominates (16).

--- SENTENCE 4825 ---
Coral covers up to 50% of the bottom in at least one area north of Mulinu'u Point, where Pavona is the chief contributor to a low irregular bank along the outer margin of the nearshore channel (33;34).

--- SENTENCE 4826 ---
\*Psammocora Pocillopora damicornis was very abundant near this ridge".

In 1978, it had disappeared from this area.

--- SENTENCE 4828 ---
No trace of corals of the genera Acropora, Pocillopora, or Montipora were observed within 660 feet (200 m) from Mulinu'u Point in 1978.

--- SENTENCE 4829 ---
Substantial numbers of these species were present in 1974, prior to a major kill of corals on this part of the reef (36).

--- SENTENCE 4830 ---
The coral assemblage on the inner reef flat off the southern part of Coconut Point is dominated by <u>Pavona frondifera</u> and an assemblage of <u>Porites andrewsi</u> and the soft coral, <u>Sinularia conferta</u>.

--- SENTENCE 4831 ---
<u>Psammocora contigua</u> is the dominant species off Mulinu'u Point.

--- SENTENCE 4832 ---
A belt of rubble largely barren of live coral or fleshy algae occurs over 330 feet (100 m) offshore (16).

--- SENTENCE 4833 ---
Diversity of live corals is greater along the central portion of the inner reef platform fronting Nu'uuli than elsewhere, but most colonies are small and cover is less than 10%.

#### FRINGING REEF FRONT

--- SENTENCE 4850 ---
The fish fauna associated with the reef front is much more diverse than that of the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 4851 ---
At least 107 species are present, but none are particularly abundant.

--- SENTENCE 4852 ---
Pomacentrus melanopterus, Plectroglyphidodon dickii, and Ctenochaetus striatus are most common (76).

--- SENTENCE 4853 ---
The shoreline of Coconut Point is vulnerable to damage from storm waves.

--- SENTENCE 4854 ---
During the January 1966 hurricane, high waves damaged seawalls and caused extensive flooding in Nu'uuli.

--- SENTENCE 4855 ---
Many houses had to be rebuilt as a result of the hurricane and some of these have been built directly on the beach berm.

--- SENTENCE 4856 ---
Since the hurricane, a number of seawalls have been built seaward of the existing berm and fill placed behind them (66).

--- SENTENCE 4857 ---
At times, a strong current flows through Avatele Passage, especially in the dredged channel contiguous to the airport extension at Avatele Point (34).

--- SENTENCE 4858 ---
Strong currents flow around Mulinu'u Point into Pala Lagoon on a rising tide (16;36).

--- SENTENCE 4859 ---
Longshore currents flowing through the channel bordering the entire length of Coconut Point are also strong under high surf conditions (16).

#### FRINGING REEF

The broad reef fringing Coconut Point and Nu'uuli Village northeastward toward Utulaina Point is frequently used for fishing.

--- SENTENCE 4866 ---
The reef flat is the focal point for most activity (20), and the portion directly offshore of Nu'uuli Village is considered a "critical use reef area" because of subsistence fishing villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 4867 ---
Reef gleaning is the most popular activity, followed by fishing with rod and reel and/or bamboo poles.

--- SENTENCE 4868 ---
Throw netting (kili) is practiced to a lesser extent.

--- SENTENCE 4869 ---
Day gleaning yields fe'e (octopus), tuitui and sava'e (sea urchins), and eel.

--- SENTENCE 4870 ---
Night gleaning is primarily for alili (sea snails).

--- SENTENCE 4871 ---
Day fishing with rod and reel results in catches of malauli (large jack), lupota (small jack), and gatala (honeycomb grouper).

--- SENTENCE 4872 ---
mataeleele (small emperor fish) are caught day and night with bamboo poles.

--- SENTENCE 4873 ---
Day catches include lupo (juvenile jack), lupota, (small parrotfish), and other coral reef species.

--- SENTENCE 4874 ---
Niglt catches include malau (squirrelfish), malai (paddletail snapper), savane (blue-lined snapper), matapula (bigeye snapper), and sumu (triggerfish) (20).

--- SENTENCE 4875 ---
The channel along Coconut Point and Avatele Passage are sometimes used for net fishing and trapping (using wire-mesh fish traps).

--- SENTENCE 4876 ---
Most pole and line fishing is accomplished from the reef margin when the surf is down.

--- SENTENCE 4877 ---
Octopus is taken from the reef flat, but the Nu'uuli reef is not as productive as many other areas.

--- SENTENCE 4878 ---
The nearshore sand bottom is a popular swimming area for Nu'uuli villagers.

--- SENTENCE 4879 ---
Prior to loss of sand due to erosion, the Coconut Point beach was a popular recreation area (16).

--- SENTENCE 4880 ---
# COAST BETWEEN NU'UO'OSEGI COVE AND UTULAINA POINT

#### SHORELINE

Villages between Nu'uuli and Pago Pago Harbor are situated at the mouths of short, narrow valleys.

--- SENTENCE 4881 ---
A coastal highway follows the shore.

--- SENTENCE 4882 ---
The highway appears to have been constructed partly on the beach berm, partly on revetted fill, and partly cut into steep rock slopes that extend to the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 4883 ---
Consequently, most of this highway is subject to shoreline erosion, particularly during storm wave attack.

--- SENTENCE 4884 ---
Much of the shoreline is protected by a concrete-grouted, boulder revetment, showing evidence of random dumping of rock and concrete rubble (63).

--- SENTENCE 4885 ---
Some sections of the revetment have collapsed or are failing due to erosion of material from beneath the toe.

# NU'UO'OSEGI COVE

A man-made causeway 3 to 5 feet (1 to 1.5 m) high projects from shore near the mouth of Amaile Stream.

--- SENTENCE 4891 ---
The 45-foot wide peninsula, extending 150 feet from shore into Nu'uo'osegi Cove, was used in the excavation of borrow pits on the northern portion of Nu'uli reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 4892 ---
Most of the causeway has been removed (49; ASCRI-30S1).

--- SENTENCE 4893 ---
Nearshore is a depression containing silty-sand, rubble, and basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 4894 ---
Depth at low tide is 3 to 4 feet (1.0 to 1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 4895 ---
Nearshore areas on both sides of the causeway were dredged for fill.

--- SENTENCE 4896 ---
The foreshore is the delta of Amaile Stream, consisting of basalt cobbles and limestone rubble (49).

--- SENTENCE 4897 ---
Northeast of the old causeway, the backshore bank is a steep scarp rising from the rubble foreshore to the 16-foot (5 m) elevation.

--- SENTENCE 4898 ---
The scarp is partially vegetated (49).

--- SENTENCE 4899 ---
The nearshore depression is not evident in the northeastern portion of Nu'uo'o-segi Cove, where nearshore areas are covered by volcanic boulders, gravel, and sand (ASCRI-30B1).

--- SENTENCE 4900 ---
The middle reef, from 200 feet (60 m) to about 550 feet m) offshore, shoals to a depth of 6 inches (15 cm), with depressions to 4 feet (1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 4901 ---
Sand and rubble cover is considerbetween areas of consolidated limestone (ASCRI-30B2).

--- SENTENCE 4902 ---
Irregular limestone formations separated by a rubble bottom to feet (0.6 m) deep grade to a more regular and uniform platform of consolidated limestone shoaling to 3 inches (8 cm).

--- SENTENCE 4903 ---
The outer reef, from 500 to 900 feet (155 to 275 m) offshore, is generally less than one foot (0.3 m) in depth at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 4904 ---
Areas of rubble and dead coral are considerable, covering about half the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 4905 ---
Some areas near the reef margin are exposed at low Boulders are exposed at low tide on the outer reef south Nu'uo'osegi Cove.

--- SENTENCE 4907 ---

#### FRINGING REEF

Coral cover ranges from 5% to 25% in a nearshore depression northeast of the old causeway in Nu'uo'osegi Cove.

--- SENTENCE 4909 ---
Porites lutea, P. andrewsi, and Pavona frondifera are the principal coral species.

--- SENTENCE 4910 ---
The brown alga, <u>Dictyota</u> sp., is abundant and <u>Halimeda opuntia</u>, <u>Actinotrichia</u> sp., <u>Valonia</u> sp., and <u>Galaxaura marginata are present.

Numbers of the crown-of-thorns starfish (alamea; Acanthaster planci) were first reported on reef flats between Nu'uuli and Pago Pago Harbor in late 1977 (74).

--- SENTENCE 4940 ---

--- SENTENCE 4943 ---
