--- SENTENCE 5882 ---
The outer reef platform is a well-cemented limestone pavement with little relief (ASCRI-04B3).

#### VAOTO MARSH

In recent years cultivation has been neglected and the vegetation in Vaoto Marsh is reverting back to natural conditions.

--- SENTENCE 5883 ---
Dominant plants are Rhynchospora, Eleocharis, and Ludwigia (77).

--- SENTENCE 5884 ---
The rare Australian gray duck (toloa; Anas superciliosa pelewensis) has been sighted in this area (15).

--- SENTENCE 5885 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF PAPALOLOA POINT)

--- SENTENCE 5886 ---
The inner reef flat, 900 feet (275 m) northwest of Papalo-Point, is relatively barren with low coral cover (ASCRI-04B1).

--- SENTENCE 5887 ---
A nearshore depression extending about 600 to 900 feet (180 to 275 m) northwest from Papaloloa Point has the appearance of a lagoon, which contains rich and diverse corals.

--- SENTENCE 5888 ---
corals are Porites lutea, Millepora (especially M. tortuosa), and Heliopora, which form large microatolls.

--- SENTENCE 5889 ---
Thick-branched staghorn Acropora intermedia grows in thickets in deeper, more seaward parts of the depression.

--- SENTENCE 5890 ---
Large patches of Montipora sp. also.

--- SENTENCE 5891 ---
Other corals present include two kinds of Platygyra, Acropora aff.

--- SENTENCE 5892 ---
variabilis, Hydnophora exesa, and Favia helianthila.

--- SENTENCE 5893 ---
The area of microatolls may have resulted from regrowth of corals dredged to obtain fill material for Ofu airport.

--- SENTENCE 5894 ---
The sea cucumber, Holothuria hilla, is abundant, found with H. atra, H. argus, nobilis, and Stichopus chloronotus in sandy depressions.

--- SENTENCE 5895 ---
The green alga, Halimeda discoidea, is abundant and fragments of Halimeda are a noticeable component of sand deposits (ASCRI-04B2).

--- SENTENCE 5896 ---
The reef fronting the eastern end of the Ofu runway has a highly diverse fish assemblage, numbering at least 72 species.

--- SENTENCE 5897 ---
The damselfish, Glyphidodontops glaucus, and the surgeonfish, Acanthurus triostegus, dominate rubble areas near shore.

--- SENTENCE 5898 ---
The damselfishes, Stegates albofasciatus and S. nigricans, dominate beds of live coral and Acropora thickets in shallow areas.

--- SENTENCE 5899 ---
Fish diversity is highest in depressions between coral formations.

--- SENTENCE 5900 ---
The large number of species confuses the question of dominance, but the most common genera are Scarus, Acanthurus, and Chaetodon (ASCRI-04F1).

# FRINGING REEF (OFF PAPALOLOA POINT)

--- SENTENCE 5904 ---
Underwater visibility is excellent in the nearshore depression extending northwest from Papaloloa Point.

--- SENTENCE 5905 ---
Approaching the point, water clarity is reduced.

--- SENTENCE 5906 ---
Longshore currents flow to the northwest.

--- SENTENCE 5907 ---
The ouxer reef flat can be inaccessible due to heavy surf (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 5908 ---
The lagoon-like features of a nearshore depression extending northwest from Papaloloa Point offer excellent and safe sport diving.

--- SENTENCE 5909 ---
Rich coral beds provide opportunities for underwater photography.

--- SENTENCE 5910 ---
The lagoon is easily accessible from Ofu airport and Ofu Village, and has potential for marine eduation as well as casual underwater exploration by tourists.

--- SENTENCE 5911 ---
Diverse and abundant fishes make this area good for fishing, especially collecting of aquarium fishes.

--- SENTENCE 5912 ---
The fringing reef lacks an ava, so there is no ready access to the reef front except by crossing the shallow reef flat, where high surf would usually prove hazardous (ASCRI).

# COAST BETWEEN FATUANA POINT AND FATUAGA POINT

# SHORELINE

Northeast of Fatuana Point is a short, narrow strip of sand beach terminating at a point of basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 5914 ---
A densely-vegetated backshore slopes up to the road at the 10 to 12-foot (3 to 4 m) elevation.

--- SENTENCE 5915 ---
A white sand beach curves gently along the shore fronting Toaga and Fa'ala'aga for nearly 1.5 miles (2 km) and is considered one of the most beautiful beaches in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 5916 ---
The foreshore is typically about 60 feet (18 m) wide and rises to the vegetation line at the 10-foot (3 m) elevation.

--- SENTENCE 5917 ---
The road is set 80 to 100 feet (25 to 30 m) inland of the beach.

--- SENTENCE 5918 ---
Beachrock outcroppings are extensively exposed along the shore (49).

#### FRINGING REEF

The southern coast of Ofu is exposed to trade wind waves, particularly in the vicinity of Toaga.

--- SENTENCE 5919 ---
A fringing reef decreases in width from 700 feet (215 m) fronting Toaga to 300 feet (90 m) off Fa'ala'aga.

--- SENTENCE 5920 ---
Depths vary from 6 to 12 inches (15 to 30 cm) with little bottom relief.

--- SENTENCE 5921 ---
Scattered sand patches on the inner reef flat extend about 100 feet (30 m) offshore to a consolidated limestone bottom (49).

--- SENTENCE 5922 ---
A disturbed littoral forest along the southern coast of Ofu includes a large amount of the uncommon shrub, Sophora tomentosa

#### FO'ISI'A ROCK

--- SENTENCE 5928 ---
According to legend, a large rock known as Fo'isi'a off the coast of Ofu is a warrior turned to stone.

--- SENTENCE 5929 ---
When a high chief saw his army in defeat during the war between Ofu and Olesega Islands, he jumped into the sea and swam to a tiny island where he turned into a stone (30).

# FA'ALA'AGA BEACH

Swimming takes place off Fa'ala'aga Beach.

--- SENTENCE 5931 ---
This white sand beach is the longest and considered the most photogenic in American Samoa (41).

--- SENTENCE 5932 ---
The scenic road along the southern coast of Ofu is of potential interest to tourists expected to visit a resort development about 200 feet (60 m) inland from Asagatai Point (74).

--- SENTENCE 5934 ---
THE ISLAND OF OLOSEGA, MANU'A GROUP, AMERICAN SAMOA

## OLOSEGA ISLAND . .

--- SENTENCE 5935 ---
The sister islands of Olosega and Ofu are the remnants of a single, extensively eroded, volcanic mass.

--- SENTENCE 5936 ---
They are separated by 500-foot (150 m) wide Asaga Strait.

--- SENTENCE 5937 ---
Both islands rise abruptly from the ocean and have little flat land other than the narrow coastal plain.

--- SENTENCE 5938 ---
Olosega, similar to Ofu in shape, covers an area of approximately 2 square miles (5.2 sq km).

--- SENTENCE 5939 ---
One shield of the volcanic mass is centered off the northwest coast of Olosega near Sili Village (MAP OL1) (55).

--- SENTENCE 5940 ---
The latest episode of volcanic activity in American Samoa was a submarine eruption reported between the islands of Oloseya and Ta'u about 1866, building a cone to within 150 feet (46 m) of the ocean surface (54;55).

--- SENTENCE 5941 ---
#### STREAMS

Streams occur only on the eastern slopes of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 5942 ---
Because Olosega is lower in elevation and smaller in area than nearby Ta'u Island, Olosega receives considerably less rainfall and runoff.

--- SENTENCE 5943 ---
Streams are neither as large nor as numerous as on Ta'u and most have cut only shallow valleys.

--- SENTENCE 5944 ---
Only at Va'aui and Sinapoto have streams cut deep valleys.

--- SENTENCE 5945 ---
All streams are intermittent, flowing only after heavy rains (55).

--- SENTENCE 5946 ---
# SEA CLIFFS

An extensive period of inactivity between eruptions permitted the erosion of deep valleys and the formation of sea cliffs around Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 5947 ---
The cliffs originated as volcanic faults but have been much modified by wave erosion.

--- SENTENCE 5948 ---
A cliff reaches a height of 2,000 feet (610 m) along the northwest coast between Tamatupu Point and Faiava (MAP OL1).

--- SENTENCE 5949 ---
Behind Olosega Village (MAP OL2), a cliff rises over 2,000 feet (610 m) to the summit of the island.

--- SENTENCE 5950 ---
The cliff is 200 feet (61 m) high at Leala Point and 120 feet (37 m) high at Maga Point (MAP OL2), a buried tuff cone.

--- SENTENCE 5951 ---
Apparently, the curved bay bordered by the high southwestern cliff of Olosega and the high southeastern cliff of Ofu originated as a caldera collapse (enlarged by marine erosion)(55).

--- SENTENCE 5952 ---
Boulders break off from the cliff and fall onto the reef flat below.

--- SENTENCE 5953 ---
Talus and landslide materials accumulate at the base of the cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 5954 ---
Large landslide deposits occur inland of Olosega Village.

--- SENTENCE 5955 ---
At Sili, large boulders on the reef flat, scars on the cliffs, and Samoan tales testify to active erosion (55).

--- SENTENCE 5956 ---
COASTAL TERRACE

A terrace of calcareous sand is well developed along the southern coast of Olosega, where it rises to 20 feet  $(6\ m)$  in places.

--- SENTENCE 5957 ---
Probably formed by hurricane and storm waves, the terrace attains a maximum width of over 1,000 feet  $(305\ m)$  at

OLOSEGA IS.

--- SENTENCE 5958 ---

Olosega Village and averages 300 feet (90 m) wide elsewhere.

--- SENTENCE 5960 ---
Sili Village is also built on this terrace.

--- SENTENCE 5961 ---
Typically, the terrace rises steeply to an elevation of about 18 feet (5.5 m) either as a beach foreslope or as an erosional escarpment.

--- SENTENCE 5962 ---
From its high point near the upper beach berm, the terrace generally descends toward inland cliffs with a gentle backslope.

--- SENTENCE 5963 ---
A marsh is present in the lowland between Olosega Village and the talus slopes at the base of the cliff.

--- SENTENCE 5964 ---
The plain is narrow and poorly-developed at Tafalau and in the Sili area, where it has been highly modified by landslide debris.

--- SENTENCE 5965 ---
At Pouono Point (MAP OL2), the terrace has been nearly covered by a large landslide.

--- SENTENCE 5966 ---
Hurricane waves overtop the berm on wave-exposed coasts but probably not on protected coasts (55).

#### SHORELINE

Much of the shoreline of Olosega consists of 40 to 50-foot (12 to 15 m) wide beaches of calcareous sand and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 5967 ---
On a few beaches, volcanic fragments are present as minor components of the sand (49).

--- SENTENCE 5968 ---
Beaches experience little seasonal variation, probably because of the fringing reef offshore.

--- SENTENCE 5969 ---
The northern section of the beach at Oge, on the eastern coast, is composed of limestone boulders about 6 inches (15 cm) in diameter.

--- SENTENCE 5970 ---
These form a steep foreslope and a high berm (55).

--- SENTENCE 5971 ---
Beachrock outcroppings are common at sea level on most beaches (49;55).

--- SENTENCE 5972 ---
Considerable beach erosion has occurred at the head of the channel off Olosega Village, where beachrock sections over 6 feet (2 m) thick are exposed.

--- SENTENCE 5973 ---
Large basalt boulders have been cemented into beachrock along the eastern coast of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 5974 ---
Beachrock is also deposited over benched surfaces of lava rock at Leaumasili Point, Imoa Point, and Leala Point.

--- SENTENCE 5975 ---
A few beaches along the northeastern coast of Olosega contain beachrock with embedded basalt cobbles and occasional boulders (55).

--- SENTENCE 5976 ---
Poorly-preserved remnants of benches eroded about 12 to 15 feet (4 to 5 m) above sea level occur at Leaumasili Point, at Leala Point -- where a bench over 100 feet (30 m) wide occurs -- and at Imoa Point -- where the bench is relatively narrow (55).

#### FRINGING REEF

The reef is continuous around Olosega except off the eastern coast exposed to trade wind seas.

--- SENTENCE 5977 ---
The reef is not continuous around Leaumasili Point, Leala Point, or Maga Point.

--- SENTENCE 5978 ---
The reef flats are relatively uniform, littered in places with large basalt boulders which have fallen from the cliff with sufficient momentum to cross the coastal plain (49;55).

--- SENTENCE 5979 ---
A large, dredged channel cuts through the reef off Olosega Village.

--- SENTENCE 5980 ---
Reletively deep, extensive sand deposits lie offshore of this channel.

--- SENTENCE 5981 ---
Smaller channels cross the reef at Sili and Oge.

--- SENTENCE 5982 ---
Strong currents flow seaward through these channels during ebbing tide (55).

# COAST BETWEEN LEAUMASILI POINT AND TUMATOLU POINT

The northwest coast of Olosega consists of a narrow coastal plain backed by a steep ridge rising to an elevation of 1,600 feet (490 m).

--- SENTENCE 5986 ---
This coast is in the lee of the trade winds, but is exposed to ocean swell from the north and northwest (49).

--- SENTENCE 5987 ---
# SHORELINE

Southwest of Leaumasili Point there is a steep foreshore consisting of basalt boulders and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 5988 ---
Extensive beachrock is exposed along shore (49).

--- SENTENCE 5989 ---
A steep, narrow beach of calcareous sand and some volcanic material fronts the villages of Faiava and Sili.

--- SENTENCE 5990 ---
In places, the foreshore is extensively covered with limestone rubble and basalt cobbles and boulders.

--- SENTENCE 5991 ---
Beachrock is prominent at the waterline.

--- SENTENCE 5992 ---
Numerous basalt cobbles and limestone fragments occur behind the vegetation line at the 90-foot (27 m) elevation, indicative of occasional storm waves.

--- SENTENCE 5993 ---
Mollusc fragments including those of Cypraea depressa and some Turbo sp. are found in the beach rubble at Sili (49;ASCRI-OLIS2).

--- SENTENCE 5994 ---
A short section of boulders occurs along the shore southwest of Sili Village.

--- SENTENCE 5995 ---
Farther on there is another beach, 40 to 60 feet (12 to 18 m) wide, of sand with an extensive cover of limestone rubble and basalt cobbles.

--- SENTENCE 5996 ---
A large fraction of the sand (30 to 40%) is of volcanic origin.

--- SENTENCE 5997 ---
Beachrock is extensive along the shore.

--- SENTENCE 5998 ---
The coastal road parallels the shoreline and, in places, is close to the beach crest at the 10-foot (3 m) elevation.

--- SENTENCE 5999 ---
The road and backshore areas may be overtopped during severe storms.

--- SENTENCE 6000 ---
Houses immediately inland of the road against the cliff face have 4-foot (1.2 m) high protective walls.

--- SENTENCE 6001 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF FAIAVA)

--- SENTENCE 6002 ---
The coast is protected by a shallow, fringing reef varying from 150 to 450 feet (45 to 135 m) in width.

--- SENTENCE 6003 ---
Much of the fringing reef offshore is about 160 feet (50 m) wide and approximately 6 inches (15 cm) deep at Mean Low Water (49).

--- SENTENCE 6004 ---
The inner reef flat is one to two feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 6005 ---
Nearshore, there occurs a narrow band of sand and rubble strewn with microatolls and basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 6006 ---
A microatoll off Faiava (Porites sp.) measures 40 feet (12 m) across and 1.5 feet (0.4 m) feet high, representing hundreds of years of coral growth (ASCRI-OL1B1).

--- SENTENCE 6007 ---
Much of the middle reef flat is consolidated limestone cut by sinuous channels, 12 to 15 feet (4 to 5 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 6008 ---
The bottom of these channels consists of sandy-rubble at a depth of about 4 feet (1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 6009 ---
The outer reef is a scoured limestone platform without a well-developed algal ridge (ASCRI-OL1B2).

# FRINGING REEF (OFF SILI)

--- SENTENCE 6012 ---
A man-made channel was cut through the reef near Sili Village in the 1960's.

--- SENTENCE 6013 ---
At its head, the channel is 2 to 6 feet (0.6 to 2 m) wide and 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) deeper than the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 6014 ---
Active upward and lateral growth of the reef has apparently reduced the channel width.

--- SENTENCE 6015 ---
Accretion is also apparent in the middle and at the reef margin where the channel shoals (ASCRI-OL1B3).

--- SENTENCE 6016 ---
The outer reef flat is a consolidated pavement of smooth limestone, with a slightly elevated sill at the reef margin which drops steeply to the reef front (ASCRI-OL1B4).

--- SENTENCE 6017 ---
The reef margin and upper reef front are grooved by shallow, surge channels about 4 feet (1.2 m) in width.

--- SENTENCE 6018 ---
Some of the channels are closed over by active reef growth.

--- SENTENCE 6019 ---
The reef front is broken in places by narrow sand channels at the base of a steep slope.

--- SENTENCE 6020 ---
Seaward of the channels, limestone banks rise to within 10 feet (3 m) of the surface.

--- SENTENCE 6021 ---
The reef front slopes gradually into deep water (ASCRI-OL1B5).

--- SENTENCE 6022 ---
The fruitbat or flying fox (pe'a; <u>Pteropus samoensis</u>) roosts on the rocky cliff above the village of Sili along the northwest coast of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6023 ---
Small numbers of sheath-tailed bats (pe'ape'avai; <u>Emballonura semicaudata</u>) roost in a cave located on the cliff above Sili Village.

--- SENTENCE 6024 ---
The common brown noddy (<u>Anous stolidus pileatus</u>) nests in trees along the coast (15).

# FRINGING REEF (OFF FAIAVA VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 6025 ---
Some living coral tissue occurs around the margins of large Porites lutea microatolls near shore on the inner reef fronting Faiava Village.

--- SENTENCE 6026 ---
The alga, Laurencia cf.

--- SENTENCE 6027 ---
succisa, is relatively abundant, covering about 10% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 6028 ---
Other conspicuous organisms present include the star-shaped foram, Bacculogypsina sp., abundant in sand and the cowries, Cypraea moneta and C. annulus (ASCRI-OL1B1).

--- SENTENCE 6029 ---
The sides of the sinuous passages through consolidated limestone of the middle reef are lined with live coral, covering up to 20% of the surface.

--- SENTENCE 6030 ---
Corals are remarkably diverse, with at least 48 species in 24 genera represented.

--- SENTENCE 6031 ---
Unusual components of the coral assemblage include numerous clumps of Stylophora cf.

--- SENTENCE 6032 ---
mordax and considerable Turbinaria cf.

--- SENTENCE 6033 ---
frondens, a rare species in Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 6034 ---
The corals, Plesiastrea versipora and three species of Goniopora, are present.

--- SENTENCE 6035 ---
The outer reef appears wave scoured.

--- SENTENCE 6036 ---
The alga, Laurencia succisa, remains conspicuous on the middle to outer reef but abundance is reduced compared to inshore areas.

--- SENTENCE 6037 ---
The algae, Halimeda discoidea and Porolithon gardineri, occur in channels and depressions.

--- SENTENCE 6038 ---
About 20% of the hard bottom is encrusted by coralline algae (ASCRI-OL1B2).

--- SENTENCE 6039 ---

Most of these fishes probably move onto the reef flat during high tide (ASCRI-OLIF1).

--- SENTENCE 6045 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF SILI VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 6046 ---
The inner reef platform adjoining a narrow channel off Sili Village appears relatively barren and scoured, with less than 5% coral cover (ASCRI-OLIB3).

--- SENTENCE 6047 ---
Corals occur along the edges of the channel at mid-reef, but are not abundant.

--- SENTENCE 6048 ---
Most of the bottom cover is encrusting coralline algae.

--- SENTENCE 6049 ---
A sparse cover of fleshy algae includes Dictyosphaeria versluysii, Laurencia succisa, and Actinotrichia sp.

--- SENTENCE 6050 ---
Live corals cover 50% to 70% of the steep reef front, with encrusting coralline algae accounting for the remaining bottom cover.

--- SENTENCE 6051 ---
dominate the coral assemblage.

--- SENTENCE 6052 ---
Corals adapted to high wave energy (e.g. Acropora humilis and Pocillopora sp.) inhabit the upper slopes near the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 6053 ---
Some soft coral colonies up to 20 feet (6 m) across are present.

--- SENTENCE 6054 ---
A few sea urchins, Echinostrephus sp., occur in holes.

--- SENTENCE 6055 ---
Upright yellow sponges, the mollusc, Trochus sp., and the brown alga, Ralfsia sp, are occasional (ASCRI-OLIB5).

--- SENTENCE 6056 ---
Fish diversity is greater on the reef front than on the reef flat off Sili Village (as elsewhere around Olosega Island).

--- SENTENCE 6057 ---
The fish assemblage along the reef front numbers at least 83 species and the question of species dominance is confused by the high diversity.

--- SENTENCE 6058 ---
However, dominant species appear to be the surgeonfishes, Acanthurus glaucopareius and Ctenochaetus striatus; the damselfish, Plectroglyphidodon dickii; and the wrasse, Thalassoma hardwickei.

--- SENTENCE 6059 ---
In shallow areas along the reef slope between surge channels, the surgeonfish, Acanthurus lineatus, and the damselfish, Stegastes fasciolatus, are dominant (ASCRI-OL1F2).

#### FRINGING REEF

Waters over the reef in front of Faiava Village are clear (ASCRI).

# FRINGING REEF

--- SENTENCE 6064 ---
A twin-hulled fishing boat on Sili Beach was donated to the village by the Government of American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 6065 ---
A man-made channel dredged through the reef in the 1960's is now too narrow to easily accommodate paopao (canoes).

--- SENTENCE 6066 ---
Active reef accretion may be responsible for reducing the width of the channel (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6067 ---
The reef flat fringing the northwest shore of Olosega Island from north of Faiava Village to west of Lalomoana Village is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 6068 ---
The entire reef flat, as well as deeper waters beyond the reef edge, extending from north of Faiava Village to Asaga Strait is frequently used for fishing.

--- SENTENCE 6069 ---
Pole and line fishing and reef gleaning are the most active Spearing and throw-netting (kili) fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 6070 ---
follow Less common are handlining from canoes and rod and popularity.

--- SENTENCE 6071 ---
Pole and line fishermen bring in day and night catches of gatala (honeycomb grouper), filoa (large emperor fish), mataeleele (small emperor fish), sumu (triggerfish), jack), savane (blue-lined snapper), and mataele lupota (small (scarlet sea bass).

--- SENTENCE 6072 ---
In addition, lupo (juvenile jack) is caught by day, and malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), and mutu are taken by Spearing results in day and night catches of alogo (line) surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), malauli (larye jack), lupota, and anae (adult mullet).

--- SENTENCE 6073 ---
In addition, sugale (wrasse), fugausi and laea (parrotfishes), fe'e (octopus), eel, and faisua (giant sea clam) are speared during the day, and manini (convict tang), ula (spiny lobster), crab, and papata (slipper lobster) are speared at night.

--- SENTENCE 6074 ---
Throw-netting (kili) yields day catches of manini, fuafua (juvenile mullet) and anae, lupota, i'a usi (threadfin), sugale, fuga, pone, and alogo.

--- SENTENCE 6075 ---
Handlining from canoes results in day and night catches of matapula, mataeleele, malai, filoa, savane, and mataele.

--- SENTENCE 6076 ---
Malau are taken at night by this method.

--- SENTENCE 6077 ---
Lau (drive-netting) occurs seasonally off Sili and results in catches of atule (big-eye scad), i'asina (juvenile goatfish), and lo (rabbitfish) (20).

--- SENTENCE 6078 ---
#### TAMATUPU POINT AND ASAGA STRAIT

#### SHORELINE

Tamatupu Point is the westernmost point of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6079 ---
A narrow beach of basalt boulders with scattered sand patches extends around the point, a distance of nearly three-quarters of a mile (1.2 km).

--- SENTENCE 6080 ---
A narrow road parallels the shoreline at the 10 to 15-foot (3 to 4 m) elevation, connecting Olosega Village to Sili Village (49).

--- SENTENCE 6081 ---
At Tamatupu Point, bordering Asaga Strait, the shoreline is largely basalt boulders, with a small proportion of sand (ASCRI-OLIS3).

#### FRINGING REEF AND PASSAGE

A shallow (less than one foot deep) reef fringes the shoreline south of Tamatupu Point.

--- SENTENCE 6084 ---
An inner reef flat of volcanic rubble with a small proportion of sand and a few larger boulders extends 200 to 300 feet (60 to 90 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 6085 ---
Limestone rubble and small boulders occur between 150 and 200 feet (46 and 60 m) offshore (ASCRI-OL1B7).

--- SENTENCE 6086 ---
A mid-reef of consolidated limestone and limestone rubble at depths of one to two feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) begins about 300 feet offshore.

--- SENTENCE 6087 ---
Asaga Strait is a shallow reef flat separating the islands of Olosega and Ofu.

--- SENTENCE 6088 ---
The width of the strait at its narrowest point is approximately 500 feet (140 m).

--- SENTENCE 6089 ---
The strait exhibits irregular bathymetry -- the depth reaches 10 feet (3 m).

--- SENTENCE 6090 ---
Generally, the portion nearest Olosega is characterized as having a limestone rubble or sand bottom and depths ranging from 2 to 6 feet (0.6 to 2.0 m).

--- SENTENCE 6091 ---
Scoured channels reach depths of 8 feet (2.4 m) toward the center of the strait.

--- SENTENCE 6092 ---
The Ofu portion of the strait is generally shallower (1 to 5 feet or 0.3 to 1.5 m) and is characterized by consolidated limestone and coral heads .(74).

--- SENTENCE 6093 ---
North of the Asaga Strait causeway, inshore areas are covered by limestone rubble, which merges with a shallow sand flat toward the center of the strait.

--- SENTENCE 6094 ---
The portion nearest Ofu is a shallow, consolidated limestone flat (74;ASCRI-OL1B6).

--- SENTENCE 6095 ---
The shallow reef south of the causeway is covered by limestone rubble and a small proportion of consolidated limestone (ASCRI-OL39).

--- SENTENCE 6096 ---
# ASAGA STRAIT

Some portions of Asaga Strait support flourishing coral communities.

--- SENTENCE 6097 ---
Coral abundance and diversity is generally higher on the Ofu side of the strait than on the Olosega side.

--- SENTENCE 6098 ---
In general, species of Porites and Acropora are much more common than other corals although coral diversity is high, with at least 26 species representing 16 genera present.

--- SENTENCE 6099 ---
Porites andrewsi and Millepora spp. are very common.

--- SENTENCE 6100 ---
Less common species included P. lutea, Montipora hoffmeisteri and other Montipora spp., Goniastrea retiformis, Acropora humilis, A. formosa, and Pavona varians.

--- SENTENCE 6101 ---
Porolithon and other coralline algae are prominent on elevated surfaces of the reef flat, whereas fleshy and turf-formang algae are common in crevices and near shore (74).

--- SENTENCE 6102 ---
A causeway and bridge have recently been constructed here and the present status of the coral community is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 6103 ---
Coral cover is generally low on the reef flat off Olosega north of the causeway spanning Asaga Strait.

--- SENTENCE 6104 ---
<u>Porites andrewsi</u> is most common inshore.

--- SENTENCE 6105 ---
Small areas of consolidated limestone provide a substratum for at least 16 species of coral (ASCRI-OL1B6).

--- SENTENCE 6106 ---
Coral cover reaches 15% in shallow parts of the reef flat south of the strait.

--- SENTENCE 6107 ---
Porites is especially common.

--- SENTENCE 6108 ---
Heliopora and Stylophora are present.

--- SENTENCE 6109 ---
Banks of Porites are conspicuous

Most of the fishes in this zone are juveniles or sub-adults.

--- SENTENCE 6121 ---
Toward the center of the strait, in areas of rich coral growth, the dominant species are the surgeonfish, Ctenochaetus striatus, the damselfish, Stegastes nigricans, and the parrotfishes, Scarus oviceps and Scarus spp.

--- SENTENCE 6122 ---

# FRINGING REEF (SOUTH OF ASAGA STRAIT.)

--- SENTENCE 6125 ---
The inner reef flat southeast of Tamatupu Point is nearly devoid of coral, with only occasional <u>Porites lutea</u> heads.

--- SENTENCE 6126 ---
Turf forming algae cover about 75% of the rubble bottom.

--- SENTENCE 6127 ---
Encrusting coralline algae are common, with some <u>Halimeda discoidea</u> and <u>Jania</u> sp. present (ASCRI-OL1B7).

--- SENTENCE 6128 ---
Coral cover reaches 10% on the middle reef, about 300 feet (90 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 6129 ---
A bank of staghorn Acropora is conspicuous.

--- SENTENCE 6130 ---
The upper parts of the coral branches (a few inches from the surface at low tide) appear dead.

--- SENTENCE 6131 ---
At the interface of the Acropora and rubble bottoms, the sea cucumber, Holothuria argus, is common.

--- SENTENCE 6132 ---
The sea urchins, Diadema sp. and Echinometra mathaei, are evident (ASCRI-OL1B8).

--- SENTENCE 6133 ---
# ASAGA STRAIT

Prior to construction of a bridge and causeway across Asaga Strait, underwater visibility was over 40 feet (12 m).

--- SENTENCE 6134 ---
Strong currents are reported in the deepest parts of a sand channel through the center of the strait but currents are much less elsewhere (74).

--- SENTENCE 6135 ---
During construction of the viaduct, the strait was temporarily closed by a boulder causeway (200;202).

# COAST BETWEEN TAMATUPU POINT AND MAGA POINT

--- SENTENCE 6140 ---
The southwestern coast of Olosega Island consists of a high cliff, at the base of which is a narrow coastal plain.

--- SENTENCE 6141 ---
The village of Olosega, one of two on the Island, is situated on the higher part of this plain near the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 6142 ---
Between the Village and the cliff is a long, narrow depression which at one time was a coastal marsh (77).

#### SHORELINE

Between Tamatupu Point and Vaisaili Point, the shoreline consists of crescent-shaped beaches of either calcareous sand or basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 6143 ---

Tamatupu Point, the foreshore terminates in a vertical scarp up to 8 feet (2.4 m) high.

--- SENTENCE 6145 ---
The road is within 25 feet (7.6 m) of The scarp is most pronounced in the vicinity of a channel which has been cut across the reef in the central part of the reach.

--- SENTENCE 6146 ---
An increase in limestone cobble here is indicative of high surf washing the shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 6147 ---

--- SENTENCE 6148 ---

# FRINGING REEF (OFF OLOSEGA VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 6164 ---
A shallow fringing reef between 300 and 900 feet (90 to 270 m) wide occurs off Olosega Village.

--- SENTENCE 6165 ---
Live coral and scattered sand patches cover the reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 6166 ---
A small channel has been cut across the reef (49).

--- SENTENCE 6167 ---
# FRINGING REEF FRONT (OFF OLOSEGA VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 6168 ---
The reef front is irregular with small channels indenting the margin (49).

--- SENTENCE 6169 ---
The bottom is rocky and large limestone blocks form valleys and ridges at depths of 65 to 85 feet (20 to 25 m) about 650 feet (200 m) offshore of Olosega Village.

--- SENTENCE 6170 ---
Coral cover is extensive, mostly large colonies of tabular Acropora and Porites cf. lobata.

--- SENTENCE 6171 ---
Alcyonarians are abundant (10).

--- SENTENCE 6172 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF POUONO POINT)

--- SENTENCE 6173 ---
Just off the beach north of Pouono Point there is a narrow depression 2 to 3 feet (0.6 to 1.0 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 6174 ---
This rubble and sand-bottom "boat channel" is 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 m) wide and bordered seaward by a consolidated reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 6175 ---
The incised, inner margin of the reef flat extends 6 inches (15 cm) above the level of the boat channel (ASCRI-OL2BI).

--- SENTENCE 6176 ---
Beyond the boat channel there is a platform of consolidated limestone and rubble becoming more irregular and deeper (up to 4 feet or 1.2 m) at mid-reef.

--- SENTENCE 6177 ---
Extending out from 150 feet (45 m) from shore occur extensive thickets of staghorn Acropora interspersed with areas of sand and rubble (ASCRI-OL2B2).

--- SENTENCE 6178 ---
From 360 to 800 feet (110 to 240 m) offshore, the outer reef shoals gradually to a bottom of rubble and small, flat limestone boulders at a depth of two feet (0.6 m) (ASCRI-OL2B3).

--- SENTENCE 6179 ---
#### COASTLINE

The fruitbat or flying fox (pe'a; <u>Pteropus samoensis</u>) roosts along the rocky cliff above the village of Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6180 ---
The common brown noddy (<u>Anous stolidus pileatus</u>), nests in trees along the sea cliff (15).

--- SENTENCE 6181 ---
#### OLOSEGA MARSH

A narrow marsh behind Olosega Village is backed by a nearly vertical cliff rising to over 2,000 feet (600 m) elevation (74).

--- SENTENCE 6182 ---
Nearly the whole marsh area (approximately 6 acres or 2.4 ha) between the village of Olosega and the cliff is covered with taro (15).

--- SENTENCE 6183 ---
Coastal marsh plants (<u>Ludwigia</u>, <u>Rhynchospora</u>, and <u>Eleocharis</u>) displaced from their normal dominance survive along with weedy species commonly associated with taro (77).

--- SENTENCE 6184 ---
The Australian gray duck (toloa; <u>Anas superciliosa pelewensis</u>), a rare resident waterbird, has been reported from this area (15).

## COAST BETWEEN MAGA POINT AND LEALA POINT

#### MAGA POINT

--- SENTENCE 6222 ---
Maga Point is the major breeding area for seabirds on Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6223 ---
Brown boobies (fua'o; Sula leucogaster plotus) nest on the sheer cliffs east of Maga Point, and white terns (Gygis alba pacifica), nest inland on trees.

--- SENTENCE 6224 ---
Four additional seabird species potentially breed here.

--- SENTENCE 6225 ---
The blue-gray noddy (Procelsterna cerulea) nests on the east and west sides of the point, as well as along cliffs just northwest of the base of the point.

--- SENTENCE 6226 ---
The common brown noddy (Anous stolidus pileatus) also nests on the cliffs.

--- SENTENCE 6227 ---
The great frigatebird (atafa; Fregata minor palmerstoni) and lesser frigatebird (atafa; Fregata ariel ariel), uncommon resident seabirds, are believed to roost on the rocky top of Maga Point.

--- SENTENCE 6228 ---
The reef heron (matu'u; Egretta sacra sacra), another uncommon shorebird, probably nests in isolated coastal areas around Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6229 ---
Maga Point supports littoral scrub vegetation unlike other areas of Olosega and Ofu (74).

--- SENTENCE 6230 ---

--- SENTENCE 6231 ---
The reef flat and deeper waters beyond the reef edge from north of Maga Point to near Leala Point are frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 6232 ---
Fishing methods and catches are similar to those off Faiava and Sili (20).

# COAST BETWEEN LEALA POINT AND LEAUMASILI POINT

OFFSHORE (LEPUA TO NU'UTUTAI ROCK)

--- SENTENCE 6235 ---
The reef flat, as well as deep waters seaward of the reef (from north of Lepua to Nu'ututai Rock), are frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 6236 ---
Fishing methods and catches are similar to those off Faiava and Sili (20).

THE ISLAND OF TA'U, MANU'A GROUP, AMERICAN SAMOA

# TA'U ISLAND

Ta'u Island, largest of the Manu'a Group, is about 6.5 miles (10 km) southeast of the sister islands of Ofu and Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6240 ---
The island is the northern half of the Mt. Lata shield volcano.

--- SENTENCE 6241 ---
The southern half and the original caldera have been entirely eroded away by waves and possibly by faulting.

--- SENTENCE 6242 ---
Ta'u covers an area of about 17 square miles (44 sq. km).

--- SENTENCE 6243 ---
The roughly rectangular-shaped island measures 6 miles (10 km) wide and 8 miles (13 km) long.

--- SENTENCE 6244 ---
Mt. Lata is over 3000 feet (900 m) high (55).

--- SENTENCE 6245 ---
The summit of the original volcanic shield collapsed to form a caldera, and subsequent explosive eruptions from cinder cones within the caldera and on the northern flanks of the volcano continued to build up the island.

--- SENTENCE 6246 ---
The lavas forming Ta'u are believed to be relatively recent in age and are exposed in a spectacular 1,400-foot (425 m) high escarpment along the southern side of the island.

--- SENTENCE 6247 ---
This cliff was formed by the collapse of the caldera.

--- SENTENCE 6248 ---
Two, almost inaccessible, sloping plateaus are associated with this cliffed coast (55).

#### SEA CLIFFS

Marine erosion during a long period of volcanic quiescence sea cliff about 200 feet (60 m) in height around Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 6249 ---
Along the north shore, the sea cliff reaches a maximum height of 2,400 feet (730 m).

--- SENTENCE 6250 ---
Along the north central coast, where pre-caldera lavas are exposed, the sea cliff cannot be distinguished because stream erosion has been more active than marine erosion.

--- SENTENCE 6251 ---
Along the south central coast, the cliff is locally as high as 1.200 feet (360 m).

--- SENTENCE 6252 ---
Post-erosional lava flows occasionally spilled over this cliff from cones on the flanks above it.

--- SENTENCE 6253 ---
In two places, extensive late eruptions built large areas of land in front of the sea cliff.

--- SENTENCE 6254 ---
Late lavas from at least two vents built a platform seaward of the old sea cliff on the northeastern Fitiuta corner of Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 6255 ---
Village is now situated where these flows extended the northeastern corner of the island.

--- SENTENCE 6256 ---
The sea is eroding a 150-foot (46 m) high cone named Maluatia revealing its internal structure.

--- SENTENCE 6257 ---
The sea cliff is buried under tuff at the northwestern corner of Ta'u, including Faleasao Village and extending east beyond Si'ulagi Point to Tulatula.

--- SENTENCE 6258 ---
A complex of tuff cones occur here, with one centered at Faleasao, another at To'a Cove, and possibly a third, smaller one at Fa'asamene Cove.

--- SENTENCE 6259 ---
At Tulatula, the tuff appears to have buried an Offshore bathymetry suggests that the base of older sea stack.

--- SENTENCE 6260 ---
the tuff complex is about 600 feet (180 m) below sea level.

--- SENTENCE 6261 ---
Coral fragments incorporated in the tuff indicate that the eruptions came from vents cutting through a fringing reef (55).

#### **STREAMS**

The radial drainage pattern of the original Lata volcanic shield is still present, although somewhat modified by faulting

--- SENTENCE 6264 ---
Along the north coast, Avatele, Matautu'ao, and Au'auli Streams have cut deep valleys into pre-caldera lava flows where later volcanism is not apparent.

--- SENTENCE 6265 ---
The lowermost 1,000 feet (300 m) of Laufuti Stream on the southern coast of Ta'u is the only perennial stream on the island (55).

--- SENTENCE 6266 ---
Laufuti Falls cascades 1,000 feet (300 m) into the ocean (41).

--- SENTENCE 6267 ---
Few other streams exist, except for several along the northern coast.

--- SENTENCE 6268 ---
These are poorly developed and drain shallow valleys.

--- SENTENCE 6269 ---
None of the streams are sufficiently mature to have flood plains and alluvial material is present only in the narrow stream beds, many of which contain boulders up to 10 feet (3 m) across (55).

--- SENTENCE 6270 ---
COASTAL TERRACE

A relatively wide coastal terrace borders parts of western and northern coasts of Ta'u Island.

--- SENTENCE 6271 ---
This terrace rises to 15 feet (5 m) above sea level in several areas.

--- SENTENCE 6272 ---
Ta'u Village built on the widest portion of the terrace, 10 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) above sea level, between the shoreline and the base of the sea cliff.

--- SENTENCE 6273 ---
Terraces at this elevation are also found at Faleasao, Faga, Saua, Tufu, Amouli, and Si'ufa'alele.

--- SENTENCE 6274 ---
Along the southern coast, the coastal terrace is composed of sand and coral but elsewhere it is entirely sand (dunes of sand blown inland by wind or storm beaches of material washed inland by high surf).

--- SENTENCE 6275 ---
Hurricane waves top the terraces and may, in part, be responsible for their development.

--- SENTENCE 6276 ---
During the hurricane of 1959, waves destroyed a trail on the terrace more than 200 feet (60 m) inland at the base of the sea cliff near Saua.

--- SENTENCE 6277 ---
The remainder of the coastline is generally characterized by steep cliffs and narrow coastal plains (55).

--- SENTENCE 6278 ---
The southern coast of Ta'u is accessible only by foot-trail and consists primarily of a sea cliff rising as high as 1,000 feet (300 m) above sea level (49).

--- SENTENCE 6279 ---
# SHORELINE

Much of the coastline of Ta'u is bordered by long, narrow beaches, typically 40 to 60 feet (12 to 18 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 6280 ---
Some beaches are nearly submerged at high tide, when waves wash up the foreslope to the berm crest.

--- SENTENCE 6281 ---
Layers of limestone rubble are exposed in escarpments on the backshore.

--- SENTENCE 6282 ---
Vegetation covers the backshore, usually extending to within a few feet of the berm crest.

--- SENTENCE 6283 ---
Beachrock is exposed both above and below present sea level along many of the beaches.

--- SENTENCE 6284 ---
Beach material varies in size from medium sand to gravel and is predominantly calcaerous grains, except along the north shore of Ta'u, where streams carry down volcanic debris.

--- SENTENCE 6285 ---
A bench is eroded 5 feet (1.5 m) above present sea level in tuff cliffs on the northwestern coast of Ta'u (55).

--- SENTENCE 6286 ---
North of Saua, the narrow beach of calcareous rubble has beachrock platforms at and above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 6287 ---
Large boulders are conspicuous along the north shore of Ta'u near Faga.

--- SENTENCE 6288 ---
Boulder beaches accumulate at the mouths of streams entering Avatele Cove and Au'auli Cove farther westward along the north shore (ASCRI).

#### FRINGING REEF

A nearly continuous reef fringes the Island of Ta'u (55).

--- SENTENCE 6295 ---
The reef averages 400 to 500 feet (120 to 150 m) in width off the southern portion of the Ta'u village complex but decreases to a width of 100 feet (30 m) or less off the northern end of the village complex (Luma).

--- SENTENCE 6296 ---
From Fa'asouga Point north, the effects of trade wind waves decreases steadily (49).

--- SENTENCE 6297 ---
The state of the state of the state of

reef flat contains patches of sand, coral, The coralline algae, whereas the reef front is composed of colonies of fast growing coral and algae.

--- SENTENCE 6298 ---
Surge channels varying from 15 to 25 feet (5 to 8 m) wide and 9 to 15 feet (3 to 5 m) deep interrupt the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 6299 ---
The small channels cut perpendicularly across the forereef, terminating seaward at a depth of about 30 feet (9 m).

--- SENTENCE 6300 ---
The grooves rarely exceed 200 feet (60 m) in length and usually occur about 75 feet (25 m) apart.

--- SENTENCE 6301 ---
The heads of these channels terminate in the surf zone in depressions, some of which (5 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 6302 ---
The bottom of the surge channels are feet usually covered by a veneer of sand or may be paved with limestone boulders.

--- SENTENCE 6303 ---
Channel sides overhang due to growth of coral the reef surface.

--- SENTENCE 6304 ---
In some channels, overhanging corals on opposite sides have grown together to form natural arches.

--- SENTENCE 6305 ---
Large channels (ava) cross the reef and approach shore off the mouths streams.

--- SENTENCE 6306 ---
The floors of these large channels are covered with coarse sand and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6307 ---
Extensive areas of coarse sand often marked by large ripples lie at -30 to -50 feet (-9 to -15m) off the mouths of these channels (55).

## LEGENDARY STONES

A number of legendary stones occur on the island of Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 6308 ---
The eastern coast of Ta'u has two large stones, one at the waterline and the other on the beach near Tufu Point.

--- SENTENCE 6309 ---
According to legend, the stones, called Ui and Luama'a, are the parents of the god Tagaloa-lagi, who were petrified after swimming the long distance from Atafu Island in the Tokelau group.

--- SENTENCE 6310 ---
A large boulder in Fitiuta is said to be the petrified body of a man who came to Fitiuta from Atafu in a large canoe and was killed by Fitiuta villagers.

--- SENTENCE 6311 ---
Along the coast behind Fitiuta is a stone called Nu'u o-Sina.

--- SENTENCE 6312 ---
Offshore of Tavalagi Ridge, east of Faleasao, is a large boulder in the rough water called Moega-o-Uila after a mythical woman.

--- SENTENCE 6313 ---
An islet off the northern end of Luma Village is named Ma'a-Fe'e.

--- SENTENCE 6314 ---
This seastack is said to be the body of a squid (30).

--- SENTENCE 6315 ---
# TA'U BEACHES

The endangered green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) reportedly bred in recent times on the isolated sand beaches of Ta'u, especially along east, south, and west shores, but has only been sighted offshore in recent years (15).

--- SENTENCE 6320 ---
TA'U ISLAND

Three settlements on the island of Ta'u include the Ta'u village complex extending from Luma to Fusi along the western coast, the village of Faleasao on the northwestern tip of the island, and Fitiuta on the northeastern tip (49).

--- SENTENCE 6321 ---
The principal means of transportation to and from Ta'u is by inter-island vessel.

--- SENTENCE 6322 ---
A harbor to serve light-draft vessels is under construction near Matavai Point, close to the village of Fusi on the western coast of Ta'u (39;59).

--- SENTENCE 6323 ---
A boat launching ramp is part of the new harbor (41).

--- SENTENCE 6324 ---
A landing strip to accomodate light aircraft was constructed by private interests at an elevation of 185 feet (47 m) inland and north of the village of Luma in 1973 Road development is minimal on Ta'u, with a few miles of unpaved road connecting villages along the northwestern coast with Fitiuta at the northeastern corner of the island (59).

--- SENTENCE 6325 ---
An war and unimproved one-lane road provides vehicular transportation from Vaitele Point northward to Faleasao Village along the western coast of Ta'u.

--- SENTENCE 6326 ---
Access south of Vaitele Point is by foot only.

--- SENTENCE 6327 ---
Another road runs along the northern coast of the island from Ta'u and Si'ufaga Villages to Fitiuta and Saua on the eastern coast.

--- SENTENCE 6328 ---
The road ends at Saua, but coastal areas to the south are accessible by a trail across coral rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6329 ---
Improvement of the road on the eastern side of Ta'u is expected to extend it to a point on the southern coast.

--- SENTENCE 6330 ---
Here, the road bed consists of crushed coral deposited by a tsunami in 1946 (39).

--- SENTENCE 6331 ---
Sections of this road are subject to landslides and washouts (23).

# COAST BETWEEN SI'ULAGI POINT AND UTUMANU'A POINT

(4) 2 1 4 1 1 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1

# TO'A COVE

A sand beach occupies the head of To'a Cove.

--- SENTENCE 6333 ---
Basalt outcrops bound the beach which is up to 40-foot (12 m) wide.

--- SENTENCE 6334 ---
The central portion of the beach is covered by large basalt boulders.

--- SENTENCE 6335 ---
Limestone rubble and small boulders predominate on the upper beach (49;ASCRI-T1S1).

--- SENTENCE 6336 ---
A 300-foot (90 m) wide reef fringes the cove (70).

--- SENTENCE 6337 ---
The sandy, lower beach merges with an inner reef flat of consolidated limestone.

--- SENTENCE 6338 ---
The reef platform lacks an ava (channel) (ASCRI-T1S1).

--- SENTENCE 6339 ---
# FA'ASAMENE COVE

At the head of Fa'asamene Cove there is a small pocket beach of calcareous sand and limestone and basalt rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6340 ---
The beach is steep and has a width of about 40 feet (12 m) (49;ASCRI-T1S2).

--- SENTENCE 6341 ---
Basalt boulders up to 8 feet (2.4 m) across are scattered on the foreshore and reef flat, which extends offshore about 150 feet (46 m) and is nearly exposed at low tide (49).

--- SENTENCE 6342 ---
Fa'asamene Cove is named after a freshwater spring issuing from the side of the cliff.

--- SENTENCE 6343 ---
On the trail above the cove there is a small platform of rocks which formerly served as a table where villagers placed coconut bowls to collect dripping water.

--- SENTENCE 6344 ---
The spring has not been used since the introduction of piped water into Faleasao Village (30).

#### FALEASAO CAVE

A large cave inland from Faleasao Village is called Mata-ana and was used as a refuge during the 1915 hurricane which devastated the islands (30).

--- SENTENCE 6345 ---
# SHORELINE (FALEASAO)

The eastern end of Faleasao Beach is a 30-foot (9 m) wide strip of calcareous sand and rubble sloping up to a backshore of fine calcareous sand (49;ASCRI-TIS3).

--- SENTENCE 6346 ---
Homes behind the backshore are protected by walls, which are reported to be hit by storm waves every few years (65).

--- SENTENCE 6347 ---
Some beachrock is exposed along the center of the beach (ASCRI-TIS4).

--- SENTENCE 6348 ---
This section of the beach is eroding.

--- SENTENCE 6349 ---
A wave-cut scarp varying in height from one to 8 feet (0.3 to 2.4 m) backs a 35-foot (11 m) wide foreshore of sand and limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6350 ---
In places, the sand is entirely eroded and the foreshore consists of limestone rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6351 ---
Erosion first became apparent after a longboat channel (60 feet or 18 m wide by 3 feet or 1 m deep) was dredged across the reef flat 15 years ago (49).

--- SENTENCE 6352 ---
Seaward-sloping exposures of beachrock at the western end of Faleasao Beach are backed by a 60 to 100-foot (18 to 30 m) wide strip of calcareous sand and rubble (49;ASCRI-TIS5).

--- SENTENCE 6353 ---
Basalt boulders adjoin the western end of Faleasao Beach.

--- SENTENCE 6354 ---

--- SENTENCE 6359 ---
Waves wash over the point (ASCRI-T1S6).

--- SENTENCE 6360 ---
The reef fringing Faleasao Bay is about 350 to 400 feet (110 to 120 m) in width.

--- SENTENCE 6361 ---
Inshore areas of the eastern bay contain large basalt boulders -- larger ones with a distinct nip at the base.

--- SENTENCE 6362 ---
The boulders overlie a bottom of consolidated limestone.

--- SENTENCE 6363 ---
The inner reef extends about 75 feet (23 m) offshore with depths to about two feet (0.6 m) (ASCRI-T1B1).

--- SENTENCE 6364 ---
The outer reef platform of consolidated limestone shoals to about one foot (0.3 m) (ASCRI-T1B2).

--- SENTENCE 6365 ---
Inshore areas just below the beach are characterized by limestone rubble and rounded boulders at depths of 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) (ASCRI-T1B3).

--- SENTENCE 6366 ---
A narrow channel believed to have been blasted by the U.S. Navy after World War II penetrates the outer reef in eastern Faleasao Bay (59).

--- SENTENCE 6367 ---
West of this channel there is an extensive tract (225 feet or 70 m wide) of exposed boulders overlying the reef flat in the center of Faleasao Bay (ASCRI-T1B4).

--- SENTENCE 6368 ---
The inner reef fringing the western side of Faleasao Bay was dredged about 20 years ago and has the appearance of a lagoon extending about 250 feet (65 m) offshore with many areas of dead coral consolidated in an irregular pattern and about one foot (0.3 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 6369 ---
Large thickets of living and dead (but still standing) staghorn Acropora occur over the bottom, with areas of sand and limestone rubble in between at depths of 2 to 4 feet (0.6 to 1.2 m).

--- SENTENCE 6370 ---
Some of the coral banks rise to within 6 inches (15 cm) of the surface.

--- SENTENCE 6371 ---
Coral thickets provide relief of 3 to 4 feet (1.0 to 1.2 m) (ASCRI-TIB5).

--- SENTENCE 6372 ---
Inshore areas bordering Si'ua'i

--- SENTENCE 6373 ---

--- SENTENCE 6374 ---
The outer reef flat is a platform of consolidated limestone rising abruptly from the outer edge of the dredged, nearshore lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 6375 ---
Depth at high tide is about one foot (0.3 m) (ASCRI-T1B7).

# FALEASAO CAYE

A cave located in the rock cliff near Faleasao Village on the northwest tip of Ta'u Island is used by the white-rumped swiftlet (pe'ape'a; Collocalia spodiopygia spodiopygia) and by sheath-tailed bats (pe'ape'avai; Emballonura semicaudata) as a roosting and nesting site (15).

#### TIDEPOOL

The sea cucumber, <u>Holothuria cinerascens</u>, is conspicuous on the silty-rubble bottom of a small, shallow tidepool between boulders along the western margin of Faleasao Bay.

# OFF OLOSEGA ISLAND

Green sea turtles (<u>Chelonia mydas</u>) are reported to have previously nested in small numbers on sand beaches around Olosega Island, but none have been observed in recent years (15).

--- SENTENCE 6383 ---
# VILLAGES ON OLOSEGA

--- SENTENCE 6384 ---
Although road development is minimal on Olosega, the island is now linked to Ofu by a one-lane highway bridge across Asaga Strait (41).

--- SENTENCE 6385 ---
An unimproved road provides vehicular transportation from the village of Sili around Tamatupu Point to Olosega Village (39;ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6386 ---
The prinicipal means of transportation between Olosega and islands other than Ofu is by inter-island boats which cannot go in to shore at Olosega.

--- SENTENCE 6387 ---
They remain outside the reef, where passengers and cargo are transferred to and from shore by shallow-draft boats.

--- SENTENCE 6388 ---
Olosega can be reached also by small plane from Tutuila to Ofu Island, then driving or hiking along the south coast of Ofu for almost three miles (4.8 km) and crossing a causeway spanning the Asaga Strait to Olosega Island.

--- SENTENCE 6389 ---
No commercial hotels are available for visitors who wish to stay overnight (64).

# FRINGING REEF

Inshore areas flanking the eastern margin of Faleasao Bay have only about 5% coral cover.

--- SENTENCE 6394 ---
Porites lutea is most common.

--- SENTENCE 6395 ---
Encrusting coralline algae and Sphacelaria sp. are the most common algae.

--- SENTENCE 6396 ---
Conspicuous invertebrates include the sea cucumbers, Holothuria cinerascens, H. difficilis, and H. atra (ASCRI-T1B1).

--- SENTENCE 6397 ---
The outer reef platform is scoured by strong surge.

--- SENTENCE 6398 ---
Coral cover is generally about 20%, consisting mostly of <u>Porites lutea</u>, and some <u>Pavona</u>, <u>Acropora aspera</u>, and <u>A. humilis</u>.

--- SENTENCE 6399 ---
Coral cover reaches 30% in one area of staghorn acroporans.

--- SENTENCE 6400 ---
An equivalent proportion of this area is covered by large patches of dead <u>Acropora</u> branches encrusted by algae.

--- SENTENCE 6401 ---
At least 10 coral species representing 8 genera are present in western Faleasao Bay.

--- SENTENCE 6402 ---
The algae, <u>Sphacelaria</u> sp. and <u>Dictyosphaeria</u> sp. are common.

--- SENTENCE 6403 ---
<u>Caulerpa serrulata</u> is present.

--- SENTENCE 6404 ---
Conspicuous invertebrates include numerous sea cucumbers (<u>Stichopus chloronotus</u> and <u>Holothuria difficilis</u>) (ASCRI-T1B2).

--- SENTENCE 6405 ---
The sea cucumbers,  $\underline{\text{Holothuria}}$  atra and  $\underline{\text{H}}$ .

--- SENTENCE 6406 ---
$\underline{\text{difficilis}}$  are common under boulders in inshore areas bordering the eastern end of Faleasao Beach (ASCRI-T1B3).

--- SENTENCE 6407 ---
Fish diversity is low in eastern Faleasao Bay.

--- SENTENCE 6408 ---
At least 17 species are represented.

--- SENTENCE 6409 ---
Dominant species in the nearshore area of scattered depressions and large volcanic boulders are damselfishes (Abudefduf septemfasciatus and Glyphidodontops glaucus), surgeonfish (Acanthurus triostegus), and wrasses (Halichoeres trimaculatus and H. margarataceus).

--- SENTENCE 6410 ---
In shallower areas seaward of the boulders, dominant species are damselfishes (Glyphidodontops leucopomus and G. glaucus), juvenile surgeonfish (Acanthurus triostegus), and a wrasse (Halichoeres margarataceous).

--- SENTENCE 6411 ---
In areas of higher bottom relief, a damselfish (Abudefduf septemfasciatus) is most abundant (ASCRI-TIFI).

--- SENTENCE 6412 ---
Large thickets of live, as well as recently killed, staghorn coral occupy a lagoon dredged about 20 years ago in the inner reef at the western end of Faleasao Bay.

--- SENTENCE 6413 ---
Live coral covers about 30% of the bottom, with an equal proportion of dead coral heads present.

--- SENTENCE 6414 ---
At least 22 genera and 46 species of corals are recorded making this one of the more diverse coral assemblages in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 6415 ---
Acropora nana and A. cf.

--- SENTENCE 6416 ---
formosa are the most abundant species.

--- SENTENCE 6417 ---
Encrusting corals are abundant along the seaward margin of the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 6418 ---
Sandy areas between consolidated banks of staghorn corals are carpeted by the green alga, Caulerpa serrulata.

--- SENTENCE 6419 ---
The encrusting alga, Porolithon gardineri, is very common.

--- SENTENCE 6420 ---
Stands of dead staghorn corals support a turf of brown, filamentous algae.

--- SENTENCE 6421 ---
The sea cucumber, Holothuria atra, is abundant and Stichopus chloronotus is common on sand bottom areas (ASCRI-T1B5).

USE CONSIDERATIONS

294

The reef fringing the southwestern portion of Faleasao Bay over 6 feet (2 m) deep, with considerable bottom relief and coral cover present.

--- SENTENCE 6425 ---
For these reasons, fish life is more diverse than in the northeastern portion of Faleasao Bay.

--- SENTENCE 6426 ---
Diversity is greatest at the southwestern end of the bay near Si'ua'i Point, where at least 56 species find shelter.

--- SENTENCE 6427 ---
Dominant species are the damselfishes, Stegastes nigricans, S. albofasciatus, Dascyllus aruanus, Glyphidodontops cyanea (in deep areas), and G. leucopomus (on the shallow flat on the seaward side), the wrasse, Thalassoma hardwickei, and juvenile parrotfishes, Scarus sordidus and Scarus spp.

--- SENTENCE 6428 ---
Areas of sand bordering Si'ua'i

--- SENTENCE 6429 ---
Point harbor numerous sea cucumbers (Holothuria atra).

--- SENTENCE 6430 ---
Seaward, there are large patches of the coral Porites (Synaraea) spp.

--- SENTENCE 6431 ---
The green alga, Caulerpa serrulata, forms an extensive cover on the sand bottom.

--- SENTENCE 6432 ---
A bubble shell is quite common on the Caulerpa (ASCRI-T1B6).

--- SENTENCE 6433 ---
Coral cover is only about 5% on the outer reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 6434 ---
Pavona sp. increases in abundance toward the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 6435 ---
The green alga, <u>Dictyosphaeria</u> versluysii, is conspicuous (ASCRI-T1B7).

--- SENTENCE 6436 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF FALEASAO)

--- SENTENCE 6437 ---
The waters of a shallow area dredged in the reef fringing the western side of Faleasao Bay are relatively calm.

--- SENTENCE 6438 ---
However, a noticeable longshore current flows over the shallow inner reef on the eastern side of the bay, and surge increases seaward toward the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 6439 ---
The reef fringing the coast off Faleasao Village is characterized by clear water (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6440 ---
# TO'A COVE

To'a Cove is considered to be an area of pristine marine life relatively undisturbed by man (59).

--- SENTENCE 6441 ---
The only access from the land to To'a Cove is by trail from the northeastern side of Faleasao Bay.

--- SENTENCE 6442 ---
Although scenic, the trail is narrow and moderately steep and slippery in places (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6443 ---
Swimming can take place in To'a Cove.

--- SENTENCE 6444 ---
Access is by courtesy of Faleasao Village (41).

--- SENTENCE 6445 ---
The reef fringing To'a Cove is regularly fished by villagers from Faleasao (46).

--- SENTENCE 6446 ---
Villagers fish in To'a Cove using bamboo poles and nets.

--- SENTENCE 6447 ---
Ula (spiny lobster) are said to be common on the outer reef.

--- SENTENCE 6448 ---
Some atule (bigeye scad) are caught in season (March to June), but this fishery was more active in the past than it is today.

--- SENTENCE 6449 ---
High surf breaking over the reef margin restricts use of the cove (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6450 ---
#### FA'ASAMENE COVE

Access to Fa'asamene Cove is by footpath from Faleasao (49).

--- SENTENCE 6451 ---
The trail connecting To'a Cove and Faleasao Bay dips down to provide easy access to the beach at the head of Fa'asamene Cove.

--- SENTENCE 6452 ---

--- SENTENCE 6454 ---

--- SENTENCE 6455 ---
AT FALEASAO

Swimming occurs at Faleasao Beach.

--- SENTENCE 6456 ---
Access is by courtesy of Faleasao Village (41).

--- SENTENCE 6457 ---
The top of the cliff at Si'ua'i Point is easily climbed and offers scenic views of both Faleasao Bay and Utusegisegi Cove (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6458 ---
The reef flat bordering the coast between Tufu Point and Si'ua'i Point is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 6459 ---
Both the reef flat and deeper waters seaward of the reef edge between To'a Cove and Si'ua'i Point are frequently fished.

--- SENTENCE 6460 ---
Pole and line fishing and " spearing (mata) are the most common activities.

--- SENTENCE 6461 ---
Handlining and night from canoes and throw-netting follow in popularity.

--- SENTENCE 6462 ---
Rod and reel fishing and seine netting are less active fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 6463 ---
Gatala (honeycomb sea bass), filoa (large emperor emperor fish), mataeleele (small sumu (triggerfish), (small jack), savane (blue-lined snapper), and mataele (scarlet sea bass) are taken day and night by pole fishing.

--- SENTENCE 6464 ---
In addition, lupo (juvenile jack) are taken by day and malau (squirrelfish), matapula (bigeye snapper), malai (paddletail snapper), and mutu are taken at night.

--- SENTENCE 6465 ---
Spearing results in day and night catches of alogo (zebra surgeonfish), pone (chocolate surgeonfish), malauli (large jack), and anae (adult mullet).

--- SENTENCE 6466 ---
Additional day catches frequently include lupota, sugale (wrasse), fugausi and laea (parrotfishes), fe'e (octopus), eel, and faisua (giant clam).

--- SENTENCE 6467 ---
Additional night catches often include manini (convict tang), ula (spiny lobster), crab, and papata (slipper lobster).

--- SENTENCE 6468 ---
Handlining from canoes yields day and night catches of matapula, mataeleele, malai, filoa (long-nosed emperor fish), savane (blue-lined snapper), and mataele (scarlet sea bass).

--- SENTENCE 6469 ---
Malau is often caught at night by handlining.

--- SENTENCE 6470 ---
Throw-netting is primarily a daytime activity resulting in catches of manini, anae and fuafua (juvenile mullet), lupota, i'a usi (threadfin), sugale (wrasse), fuga (parrotfish), pone, and alogo (20).

--- SENTENCE 6471 ---
Canoes on the upper beach at Faleasao attest to the popularity of paopao fishing (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6472 ---
Surfing is possible off Faleasao during periods of north swell and incoming tide.

--- SENTENCE 6473 ---
Most wind conditions permit surfing except calm periods or winds from the north or west.

--- SENTENCE 6474 ---
Waves over 6 feet (2 m) high are not surfable here (41).

--- SENTENCE 6475 ---
COAST BETWEEN UTUMANU'A POINT AND FA'ASOUGA POINT

Ma'afe'e Islet is a 30-foot (9 m) high seastack off Luma Village (ASCRI).

**PHYSIOGRAPHY** 

WEST COAST MAP T1

SHORELINE

A narrow beach of calcareous sand and scattered limestone rubble fronts Ta'u Village.

--- SENTENCE 6478 ---
The sand is progressively coarser (with an increase in size and quantity of limestone rubble) toward Luma Village.

--- SENTENCE 6479 ---
In some areas, the foreshore consists entirely of limestone rubble (49).

--- SENTENCE 6480 ---
Beach width varies from 50 to 60 feet (15 to 18 m).

--- SENTENCE 6481 ---
The foreshore slopes up to a vegetated backshore at the 10-foot (3 m) elevation (49;ASCRI-T1S7).

--- SENTENCE 6482 ---
A narrow strip of beachrock is exposed along a 150 to 180-foot (45 to 55 m) length of shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 6483 ---
A submerged and more eroded outcrop of beachrock is located near shore (ASCRI-T1S7).

--- SENTENCE 6484 ---
# SHORELINE (OFF SI'UFAGA)

--- SENTENCE 6485 ---
The predominant feature of the backshore at Si'ufaga is a lava rock seawall reaching 6 feet (2 m) in height at its southern end.

--- SENTENCE 6486 ---
The steep, 30 to 50-foot (9 to 15 m) wide foreshore grades from limestone boulders to rubble and then to calcareous sand on the upper beach (ASCRI-T1S8;49).

--- SENTENCE 6487 ---
The boundary between the foreshore and backshore is delineated by a 1 to 2-foot (0.3 to 0.6 m) wave-cut scarp (49).

--- SENTENCE 6488 ---
At low tide a band of limestone rubble and algal-stained beachrock is exposed at the base of the beach (49;ASCRI-T1S8).

--- SENTENCE 6489 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF LUMA)

--- SENTENCE 6490 ---
The reef fronting the northern end of Luma Village is poorly developed and deep enough to permit large waves to reach the shore (49;ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6491 ---
At depths of 60 to 80 feet (18 to 25 m) about 1000 feet (300 m) offshore of Luma Village, the bottom consists of a rocky flat with large boulders (10).

--- SENTENCE 6492 ---
The reef fronting the Ta'u village complex gradually widens from 150 feet (45 m) off Luma to 400 feet (120 m) off Si'ufaga (49).

--- SENTENCE 6493 ---
The reef is indented by two major avas, one off the northern end (off Luma) and another off the southern end of the village complex (off Si'ufaga).

--- SENTENCE 6494 ---
Strong currents flow seaward through the channels (55).

--- SENTENCE 6495 ---
A narrow channel of rubble and sand parallels the shore in front of Ta'u Village.

--- SENTENCE 6496 ---
The inshore channel reaches a depth of about one foot (0.3 m) and extends about 25 feet (7.6 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 6497 ---
The channel merges with an inner reef flat of consolidated limestone with a few rubble-filled depressions having depths of up to 2 feet (0.6 m) (ASCRI-T1B8).

--- SENTENCE 6498 ---
The middle reef flat extends from 100 to 200 feet (30 to 60 m) offshore.

--- SENTENCE 6499 ---
The consolidated limestone bottom is broken by depressions up to 2 feet (0.6 m) deep.

--- SENTENCE 6500 ---
The outer reef flat, 200 to 300 feet (60 to 90 m) offshore, is mainly a consolidated limestone pavement at depths under one foot (0.3 m).

--- SENTENCE 6501 ---
Boulders are exposed at low tide (ASCRI-T189).

--- SENTENCE 6502 ---

FLORA AND FAUNA

( RARE WATERBIRD

MAP T1

The reef margin is about 30 feet (9 m) wide, having both an algal ridge and spur-and-groove development.

--- SENTENCE 6509 ---
A channel may be one of several said to have been blasted through the reef by the U.S. Navy in World War II to enable boats to be brought into shore.

--- SENTENCE 6510 ---
At present, the channel is accessible by boat only at high tide.

--- SENTENCE 6511 ---
Similar channels occur off Luma and Si'ufaga (ASCRI-TIB10).

--- SENTENCE 6512 ---
FRINGING REEF (OFF SI'UFAGA)

WEST COAST

An alongshore depression or "boat channel" parallels the shoreline between Ta'u and Si'ufaga.

--- SENTENCE 6513 ---
The sand- and rubble-bottom depression broadens somewhat toward Si'ufaga, where roily water (Schlieren effect) indicates freshwater seepage along shore.

--- SENTENCE 6514 ---
The channel extends to 75 feet (23 m) offshore and has depths to 3 feet (1 m) (ASCRI-TIBII).

--- SENTENCE 6515 ---
A freshwater spring below the high water mark off Si'ufaga is known as Vai-o-tuli and is associated with a legend about turtles coming ashore to lay eggs (30).

--- SENTENCE 6516 ---
The middle reef flat, from 75 to 175 feet (23 to 55 m) offshore, is characterized by limestone outcrops, boulders, sand and rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6517 ---
Depth is about one foot (0.3 m) deep with numerous deeper depressions present.

--- SENTENCE 6518 ---
A boulder tract over 200 feet (60 m) in length is exposed parallel to shore on the middle reef flat

--- SENTENCE 6519 ---
The outer reef flat shoals to a depth of 6 inches (15 cm).

--- SENTENCE 6520 ---
The shallow platform of consolidated limestone extends from 175 to 275 feet (55 to 85 m) offshore (ASCRI-T1B13).

--- SENTENCE 6521 ---
The reef margin exhibits little vertical relief.

--- SENTENCE 6522 ---
A few depressions with depths of one foot (0.3 m) contain rubble and small boulders (ASCRI-T1B14).

--- SENTENCE 6523 ---
A shallow channel cut across the reef is believed to have been blasted by the U.S. Navy during World War II to provide access to deep water.

--- SENTENCE 6524 ---
The reef is indented near the channel.

--- SENTENCE 6525 ---
Channel margins have irregular depressions containing boulders 1 to 3 feet (0.3 to 1.0 m) across.

--- SENTENCE 6526 ---
The channel is 2 feet (0.6 m) deep at its shoreward head, where a layer of sand covers unconsolidated rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6527 ---
A layer of fine sand covers a bottom of consolidated limestone toward the seaward end of the channel (ASCRI-T1B15;49).

--- SENTENCE 6528 ---
# MARSHLAND '

A large area of disturbed coastal marsh occupies a low-lying depression behind the village of Luma and extends to the foot of the high cliff that surrounds it on three sides.

--- SENTENCE 6529 ---
This marsh, covering an area of approximately 18 acres (7.5 ha), is extensively cultivated and little of the natural vegetation remains.

--- SENTENCE 6530 ---
The typical marsh plants such as Rhynchospora sp., Ludwigia sp., and Eleocharis sp. occur here (77).

--- SENTENCE 6531 ---
The rare Australian gray duck (toloa; Anas superciliosa pelewensis) has been sighted occasionally in this area (15).

# FRINGING REEF (OFF LUMA)

Fishes are neither abundant nor is the fauna diverse on the reef fronting Luma Village perhaps because of the lack of bottom relief.

--- SENTENCE 6534 ---
The assemblage includes at least 26 species.

--- SENTENCE 6535 ---
Dominant species are damselfishes (Glyphidodontops glaucus and G. leucopomus), wrasses (Halichoeres margarataceus and Thalassoma quinquevittata), and a surgeonfish (Acanthurus triostegus).

--- SENTENCE 6536 ---
With the exception of the damselfishes, most fishes present are juveniles or subadults (ASCRI-T1F3).

--- SENTENCE 6537 ---
Few corals are present at depths of 60 to 80 feet (18 to 25 m) some 1000 feet (300 m) offshore --mostly small heads of Porites and Pocillopora (10).

--- SENTENCE 6538 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF TA'U VILLAGE)

--- SENTENCE 6539 ---
Corals cover about 5% of the inner reef flat and nearshore channel fronting the main part of Ta'u Village.

--- SENTENCE 6540 ---
Porites lutea is most common.

--- SENTENCE 6541 ---
The green alga, <u>Dictyosphaeria versluysii</u>, and a brown algal turf are abundant.

--- SENTENCE 6542 ---
<u>Amphiroa</u> sp. is abundant along the sides and tops of limestone surfaces where the water depth reaches 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m).

--- SENTENCE 6543 ---
The sea cucumber, <u>Stichopus chloronotus</u>, is very common in depressions under loose rubble.

--- SENTENCE 6544 ---
<u>Holothuria difficilis</u> is common in the boat channel (ASCRI-TIB8).

--- SENTENCE 6545 ---
The middle reef flat, 100 to 200 feet (30 to 60 m) offshore, has coral cover up to 10%, mainly of low-growing Acropora aspera.

--- SENTENCE 6546 ---
Coral cover increases to 20% some 200 to 300 feet (60 to 90 m) from shore.

--- SENTENCE 6547 ---
Encrusting corals, such as Acropora humilis, are most common.

--- SENTENCE 6548 ---
At least 23 coral species representing 11 genera are present on Ta'u reef.

--- SENTENCE 6549 ---
Encrusting and branching coralline algae cover most of the outer reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 6550 ---
Low growing, filamentous green algae occur on boulders exposed at low tide.

--- SENTENCE 6551 ---
The brittle star, Ophiocoma dentata, is common under boulders.

--- SENTENCE 6552 ---
The sea cucumber, Stichopus chloronotus, is abundant on rubble surfaces (ASCRI-T1B9).

--- SENTENCE 6553 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF SI'UFAGA)

--- SENTENCE 6554 ---
Coral cover of 5% on the inner reef flat includes Pocillopora damicornis and Porites lutea.

--- SENTENCE 6555 ---
Algae cover about 20 to 30% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 6556 ---
Algal species represented include Caulerpa cf.

--- SENTENCE 6557 ---
serrulata, Dictyosphaeria versluysii, Sphacelaria sp., Actinotrichia sp., and Neomeris sp.

--- SENTENCE 6558 ---
Sea cucumbers (Holothuria difficilis and H. hilla) abound under boulders.

--- SENTENCE 6559 ---
Stichopus chloronotus is common on the reef flat (ASCRI-TIBII).

--- SENTENCE 6560 ---
Coral cover is low on the middle reef flat.

--- SENTENCE 6561 ---
Acropora aspera is most common (ASCRI-TIBI2).

--- SENTENCE 6562 ---
Of the 10% coral cover on the outer reef flat, most is accounted for by <u>Acropora humilis</u>.

--- SENTENCE 6563 ---
High algal cover consists largely of encrusting coralline species.

--- SENTENCE 6564 ---
Some fleshy <u>Dictyosphaeria versluysii</u> is present.

--- SENTENCE 6565 ---
The sea cucumber, <u>Stichopus chloronotus</u>, is common (ASCRI-T1B13).

--- SENTENCE 6566 ---
Turf-forming algae cover up to 80% of the bottom at the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 6567 ---

WEST CUAST MAP T1

<u>sluysii</u> and <u>Amphiroa</u> sp. are very common together with encrusting coralline algae (ASCRI-T1B14).

--- SENTENCE 6571 ---
The reef flat adjacent to a dredged channel off Si'ufaga has considerable algal cover of encrusting coralline species as well as an algal turf (ASCRI-T1B15).

--- SENTENCE 6572 ---
# FRINGING REEF (OFF SI'UFAGA)

--- SENTENCE 6573 ---
A relatively diverse fish fauna inhabits depressions on the inner reef flat fringing Si'ufaga Village.

--- SENTENCE 6574 ---
Dominating an assemblage of at least 38 species are the damselfishes, Glyphidodontops leucopomus, G. glaucus, and G. cyanea, the wrasse, Halichoeres margarataceus, the surgeonfish, Acanthurus triostegus, and the butterflyfish, Chaetodon citrinellus (ASCRI-T2F1).

--- SENTENCE 6575 ---
# **NEARSHORE WATERS**

The seaward margin of the fringing reef off Ta'u Village is swept by strong surge.

--- SENTENCE 6576 ---
Clear, warm water flows seaward during outgoing tides (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6577 ---
The reef flat is characterized by clear waters.

--- SENTENCE 6578 ---
Some refuse (especially bottles and cans) accumulates in the channel dredged through the reef flat off Si'ufaga.

--- SENTENCE 6579 ---
Strong currents flow seaward through this channel (ASCRI).

#### TA'U VILLAGE

A series of holes thought to be baitcups occur in a rock outcropping along the beach fronting Ta'u Village.

--- SENTENCE 6580 ---
The same type of hole drilled in stone in the Hawaiian Islands was used to crush bait or store bait while fishing (30).

--- SENTENCE 6581 ---
The tomb of the last Tui'manu'a is located along the coast below Papatea in north Luma on the western coast of Ta'u (41) (See FITIUTA / HISTORICAL/ARCHAEOLOGICAL).

--- SENTENCE 6582 ---
#### TA'U BEACH

The central channel offshore of tourist fales (houses) is a popular place for swimming along Ta'u Beach.

--- SENTENCE 6583 ---
Access is by courtesy of Ta'u Village (41).

#### FRINGING REEF

The reef flat fronting the Ta'u village complex of Luma, Si'ufaga and Fusi is considered a "critical use reef area" supporting subsistence fishing by villagers (39).

--- SENTENCE 6584 ---
Both the reef flat and deeper waters beyond the reef edge are frequently fished as far south as Faga Cove.

--- SENTENCE 6585 ---
The fishing methods and catches are similar to those off Faleasao (20).

--- SENTENCE 6586 ---
Although much of the reef flat is exposed at low tide, gleaners seek crabs, octopus, and fishes (particularly large wrasses or sugale) in pools which remain submerged.

--- SENTENCE 6587 ---
Fishes commonly caught on the reef front for home consumption include jacks, surgeonfishes, parrotfishes, and squirrelfishes (59).

--- SENTENCE 6593 ---
Fishing boats frequent nearshore waters off Ta'u Villages.

--- SENTENCE 6594 ---
The number of canoes on the backshore attest to the popularity of paopao fishing.

--- SENTENCE 6595 ---
The reef margan is considered a good area to collect ula (spiny lobster) at night during high tide (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6596 ---
Children fish with bamboo poles from rocky shoreline outcrops near Fa'asouga Point.

--- SENTENCE 6597 ---
Limestone rubble is collected in this area for use as fill for house foundations (ASCRI).

--- SENTENCE 6598 ---
Workmen involved in the construction of Ta'u Harbor have surfed the waves breaking offshore.

--- SENTENCE 6599 ---
# COAST BETWEEN FA'ASOUGA POINT AND VAITELE POINT

#### COASTAL PLAIN - MARSHLANDS

The coastal plain in the Fusi area extends inland approximately 400 feet (120 m) to the base of an old sea cliff.

--- SENTENCE 6600 ---
Part of the plain is a coastal marsh about 2 to 4 feet (0.6 to 1.2 m) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 6601 ---
Beachrock and limestone breccia underlie two to five feet (0.3 to 1.5 m) of alluvium and dune sand in the marsh.

--- SENTENCE 6602 ---
The coastal cliff rises steeply to a height of 200 feet  $(60 \, \text{fm})$  above the marsh.

--- SENTENCE 6603 ---
Talus and landslide deposits occur at the foot of the cliff.

--- SENTENCE 6604 ---
Much of the talus is heavily vegetated (59).

--- SENTENCE 6605 ---
A small marsh covering an area of about 2 acres (0.8 ha) occurs at Fusi, south of the Luma marsh.

--- SENTENCE 6606 ---
It occupies a narrow depression on a strip of land between the high coastal cliff and the shoreline (77).

--- SENTENCE 6607 ---
A beach 6 to 20 feet (2 to 6 m) wide and composed of limestone rubble occupies a shoreline indentation northwest of Fa'asouga Point between outcrops of basalt 3 to 6 feet (1 to 2 m) high (ASCRI-T2S1).

--- SENTENCE 6608 ---
A bench is eroded in the basalt outcrop 5 feet (1.5 m) above sea level at Fa'asouga Point.

--- SENTENCE 6609 ---
Width of the bench varies from 20 to 50 feet (6 to 15 m).

--- SENTENCE 6610 ---
A storm beach of calcareous sand and limestone rubble lies inland of the bench (49).

#### SHORELINE

A 60-foot (18 m) wide sand beach is bounded by Fa'asouga Point and the Ta'u small boat harbor.

--- SENTENCE 6611 ---
A scarp is eroded along a short length of the backshore adjacent to the harbor (49).

--- SENTENCE 6612 ---
Beach sand is predominantly calcareous, with a minor component of volcanic fragments.

--- SENTENCE 6613 ---
The layer of beach sand is thin.

--- SENTENCE 6614 ---
Sand is progressively coarser toward the northwest end of the beach.

--- SENTENCE 6615 ---
Beach sand grades into a dune sand ridge or storm beach inland (59).
